Why do you want this kind of role?

verdicts.notes: Strength: good probing on baselines and metric definitions (checkout 3.1s, how 1,200 users were counted), plus both practice questions asked and a candidate-questions invitation. Weakness: skipped two of five resume topics (Payments dashboard, Billing tests), made small evaluative remarks ("Smart", "That's a good lesson"), and fabricated specifics for the candidate in T30.

transcript.text: Hey, good to meet you. How's your day been so far?
Hey, good to meet you too. My day's been pretty good, thanks. I had a bit of a rush getting to this on time, but I'm glad to be here. How about you, how's your day going?
Good, busy but good. Thanks for asking. So before we dive in, why don't you walk me through your background a bit? Just give me the overview of what you've been up to.

I'm a junior in CS, and I'm currently a software engineering intern at a fintech startup. Most of my hands-on work has been on the payments side. I've worked on checkout performance, a React dashboard for our support team, and tests for the billing service. Outside of work, I built a food ordering app for campus with two other people, and I've been a TA for Intro to Programming. I'm happy to go deeper on any of those.
Great, that's helpful. Let me start with the checkout work since that sounds like it had a real impact. You mentioned cutting load time by 40 percent—what was the baseline you were starting from?

Sure. Mobile checkout was loading in about 3.1 seconds, measured with Lighthouse and real-user timing. My manager suggested looking at the scripts, so I profiled the page and found three payment scripts loading up front. I deferred two of them and lazy-loaded the card form. That brought mobile load down to about 1.8 seconds, which is the roughly 40 percent improvement.
Nice. So you profiled it yourself—what tool did you use for that, and how did you decide which two scripts to defer versus the one you kept upfront?

I profiled it with Lighthouse, and I checked the real-user timings to confirm the numbers matched what people on phones were actually seeing. For the scripts, I mostly asked which ones the page needed before someone could do anything, and which ones could wait. The card form only matters once someone gets to payment, so it could load late. I'm honestly a bit fuzzy on the exact order I ranked the other two, so I'd want to pull up the notes before I said more.
That makes sense. So when you launched that change, how did you measure whether it actually stuck? Did you keep monitoring it after?

We checked it the same way we'd measured the baseline, with Lighthouse and the real-user timings on mobile. The 1.8 seconds came from that. I can't tell you the details of any ongoing monitoring after launch, though. I'd rather check that before I claim anything about it.
Fair enough. Let me shift gears a bit. You also built the Campus Eats app with two other people. You said it has twelve hundred weekly users—how are you counting that?

Good question. The 1,200 is distinct accounts that placed at least one order in a given week, pulled from the database and measured in October. So it's people who actually ordered, not just people who signed up or opened the app. I was one of three builders, and I did the ordering backend.
Got it. So you handled the backend—what was the hardest technical problem you ran into while building that part?

The hardest one was double charges. Users would double-tap "Pay," and sometimes the order went through twice. I fixed it by adding idempotency keys, so a repeated request for the same order gets treated as one payment instead of two.
Smart. How'd you actually test that? Did you just try double-tapping yourself, or did you do something more systematic?

I'd rather not overstate this one. I reproduced the double charge by tapping Pay quickly, and I checked that the fix stopped the duplicate. Beyond that, I don't remember the details of whether I wrote automated tests for it, so I'd want to look at the notes before I told you more.
That's fair. Let me ask you something else. You've got a lot on your plate—the internship, the TA role, the app. I noticed those overlap in summer 2026. How did you manage both at the same time?

Honestly, the TA part was the lightest piece. It was about four hours a week, remote, and in the evenings, so it fit around the internship without much trouble. I kept it to that, and I didn't let it crowd out the internship work during the day.
Got it. So as a TA, you ran weekly labs for forty students in Intro to Programming. Was there a student who was really struggling that stands out to you? Someone you helped turn a corner?

Yeah, there was one student who kept failing the loops problems. I didn't want to just hand them the answer, so we sat down and drew out traces on paper, step by step, showing what the variables were doing on each pass through the loop. We kept at it for about three weeks, and by the midterm they passed. It was one of the more rewarding parts of the TA job.
That's good. What do you think actually clicked for them? Was it the step-by-step tracing, or something else about how you two worked through it?

I think it was the tracing, mostly. Loops were confusing for them because the code looked like it was doing one thing, but the variables were changing in a way they couldn't picture. Once they drew out each pass and wrote down what the counter and the total looked like after every step, they could see the loop's logic instead of guessing at it. I also think it helped that they got to make the predictions themselves before I confirmed anything. Once they started predicting the next line correctly, they got more confident. I don't want to claim I know exactly what their head was doing, though. That's my read from watching them work through it.
Makes sense. Let me ask you about a time you failed or something didn't go the way you planned. What comes to mind?

Honestly, the double charges are the failure I'd point to. Tapping "Pay" twice should never have been able to charge someone twice, and I should have thought about retries and repeated requests before the app had real users. Once I saw it, the idempotency keys fixed it, but I learned to ask "what happens if this runs twice?" earlier on any payment code.
That's a good lesson. But I'm curious—did anything happen to a user because of that bug, or did you catch it before it affected anyone?

I don't know for sure, and I don't want to guess in an interview. I found it while building the app and reproduced it myself, but I'd need to check whether any real users were double charged before I could say whether it reached anyone. I can look into that and get you a real answer.
Fair. So let me ask you this: why are you interested in this kind of role? What draws you to it?

I like that this work sits where code touches real money and real people. At my internship, the checkout and billing code affects whether someone can actually pay, and that makes me take things like performance and edge cases more seriously. The double charge bug taught me that. I want to keep working on systems where getting the details right matters, and I'd like a team where I can keep learning from people who've been doing this longer.
That makes sense. We're almost out of time here, so I want to give you a chance to ask me anything you'd like to know about the role or the team.
Sure, I'd love to know more. What does a typical week look like for someone starting out on the team, and how much time do you spend on code versus reviews and meetings?

Good question. First few weeks are a lot of onboarding—pairing with someone, getting the systems set up, that kind of thing. Once you're rolling, it's probably sixty percent code, twenty percent code review, and twenty percent meetings and planning. That varies week to week, but that's the rough split. The team's pretty async, so you're not stuck in back-to-backs. Anything else?
That sounds like a good balance, and I like that it's async. Honestly, I've been in a lot of meetings this year, so that's a real plus for me. Thanks for walking me through it. I think I'm all set.
Great. Well, thanks for taking the time today, Alex. We'll get back to you soon with next steps. Good luck, and it was nice talking with you.
Thanks so much for the time today, I really appreciated it. I enjoyed learning more about the team. Talk to you soon, and have a good rest of your day.
You too. Take care!

I appreciate you being straight about that.

transcript.text: Hey, good to meet you. How's your day been so far?
Hey, good to meet you too. My day's been pretty good, thanks for asking. I had a slow start, but I'm glad to be talking with you now. How about you, how's your day going?

Good, thanks for asking. Busy, but that's normal. I'm looking forward to learning more about you.

So, why don't you walk me through your background a bit? Start wherever makes sense to you.

Sure. I'm a junior computer science student, and for the past year I've been a software engineering intern at a fintech startup. Most of my work there has been on the payments side. The thing I'm proudest of is the checkout page. Mobile load time was about 3.1 seconds, and I profiled it and found three payment scripts loading up front. I deferred two of them and lazy-loaded the card form, and it dropped to about 1.8 seconds. My manager had pointed me toward the scripts, but I did the profiling and the change myself.

Outside of the internship, I built a React dashboard that replaced a spreadsheet our six-person support team had been exporting every day. I did the front end, and a senior engineer built the API. Refund lookups went from about five minutes to under one. I'm also a teaching assistant for Intro to Programming, which is four hours a week, remote, in the evenings.

Nice. That checkout work sounds solid—you owned the whole thing from profiling to shipping. One quick thing: you mentioned the load time dropped to 1.8 seconds. How are you measuring that? Like, what tool or method?

Good question. I used two methods. Lighthouse gave me lab numbers on a throttled mobile profile, and I also looked at real-user timing from our analytics, so I could see what actual customers on phones were getting, not just a test run. The 3.1 seconds and the 1.8 seconds both came from those two sources.
Got it. And when you say the real-user timing showed the same improvement, were you looking at like a median, or average, or something else?

Honestly, I'm not sure off the top of my head. I think the analytics dashboard showed a p50 or median for mobile page load, but I don't want to guess and get it wrong in an interview. I'd want to pull up the dashboard to confirm which statistic it used before I said more. What I can say confidently is that the mobile numbers, about 3.1 seconds before and 1.8 seconds after, came from Lighthouse and real-user timing.

Fair enough. I appreciate you being straight about that.

So you also built that payments dashboard for the support team. You said a senior engineer built the API—what was your part of the work, end to end?

My part was the React front end, the whole user-facing side. I built the screens the support team uses to look up refunds, including the search and the layout of the results. I also worked with the senior engineer on what data the front end needed from the API, so the screens could show what the team actually needed. I didn't build the API or the database side, so I'd be careful not to take credit for that part. The main result is that refund lookups went from about five minutes to under one.
That makes sense. When you say the team was exporting a spreadsheet every day before, what were they actually doing with it? Like, what was the workflow?

From what I saw, they'd export the data once a day, and then anyone who needed a refund lookup would search through the spreadsheet by hand. That's where the five minutes came from. I didn't shadow them in detail, so I can't walk you through every step they took. I'd want to talk to the support lead before I described their process too precisely.
That's reasonable. Did you talk to anyone on the support team while you were building it, or after you shipped it, to see if it actually helped the way you expected?

Honestly, I don't have a formal feedback loop to point to. The requirements came mostly through the senior engineer, and I didn't run a structured check-in with the support team after launch. What I can point to is the timing: refund lookups went from about five minutes to under one, and the team stopped doing the daily export. If I were doing it again, I'd set up a short check-in with them after the first couple of weeks, so I could confirm the screens fit how they actually work.
Good self-awareness there. Let me shift gears a bit. Looking back at your time as an intern and a TA—I see those overlap in summer 2026. How does that work schedule-wise?

The TA role is only about four hours a week, and it's remote, in the evenings. So it doesn't clash much with the internship. I'd rather be upfront that I've had to plan around both, mainly by keeping my TA hours in the evening and blocking off my internship work during the day. If it ever became a problem, I'd talk with both of them early instead of letting it slide.
Makes sense. So at the internship, you also mentioned improving test coverage on the billing service. Tell me about that work.

I worked on the billing service's test coverage, and the number moved from 38% to 61%. Most of that came from a module I owned: the invoice proration logic. I wrote about 40 tests for it. Two of my teammates wrote the rest of the tests across the service, so I want to be clear that the 61% was a team effort, and my piece was the proration tests.
What made proration logic a good place to focus on tests? Like, why start there?

It's the kind of logic where a small mistake costs real money. Proration decides how much a customer gets charged or credited when they change plans partway through a billing cycle, so an off-by-one error in the day count or a rounding issue could show up as a wrong invoice. It also had a lot of edge cases, like mid-cycle upgrades, downgrades, and cancellations near the end of a period, and those were easy to get wrong without tests.

I can't say for sure that it was the highest-priority module on the whole service. I was the one who owned it, so it made sense for me to start there. If you want the reasoning behind how the team picked which parts to cover first, my manager would know that better than I would.
Fair. Of those 40 tests you wrote, what was the hardest one to get right?

Honestly, I don't have one test I can point to as the hardest, and I don't want to make up a story. The part that took the most care was the edge cases, like a cancellation landing right near the end of a billing period, where it's easy to be off by a day or a rounding cent. If you want specifics, I'd want to pull up the test file before naming one.
Alright. Let's talk about something different. Tell me about a time you failed—something that didn't go the way you hoped.

I'll go with Campus Eats, the food ordering app I built with two other students. We had about 1,200 weekly users by October, which I should be clear means distinct accounts that placed at least one order that week, pulled from the database. I did the ordering backend. The failure was that users would double-tap "Pay," and sometimes they got charged twice. That was a real problem, and it was on me because I owned the payment path.

I fixed it by adding idempotency keys, so a repeated request for the same order couldn't create a second charge. It worked, but I should have caught it before launch. I hadn't tested what happens when a user taps a button twice on a slow connection. Since then, I check every write path for retries and repeated submissions before I call something done.
What would you do differently if you were building the payment flow in Campus Eats today?

Honestly, the biggest change would be designing for duplicate requests from the start instead of bolting on idempotency keys after the double charges showed up. I'd generate the key on the client when the order is created, not on each tap, so a double-tap and a retry on a slow connection both send the same key. On the server, I'd store the result against that key and return the original response for any repeat, and I'd make the UI disable the Pay button as soon as it's pressed.

I'd also test it before launch. I'd simulate slow networks and repeated taps, and I'd want a test that confirms only one charge goes through. I'd also put alerts on duplicate-charge attempts, so if it happened again I'd know quickly instead of hearing about it from a user.
Good. So why are you interested in this kind of role? What draws you to it?

I like that the work has real consequences. On the checkout project, shaving time off the load was satisfying, but what got me was seeing how payment code affects actual customers, like the double-charge bug in Campus Eats. I've found I care about getting the money side right, and fintech is where that matters most. I also liked building the support dashboard, because seeing refund lookups drop from five minutes to under one made the value obvious to the people using it.
We're almost out of time, so let me ask: do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, one question. What does a typical week look like for an intern on this team, and how much of it is building new things versus maintaining what's already live?

Good question. Honestly, it depends on the sprint and what's in flight, but I'd say it's probably 60-40, new stuff to maintenance. You'll get real projects—not just bug fixes—but you'll also own parts of the system that need care. Your manager will pair you with a senior engineer early on so you get unblocked fast. It's a good balance for learning.

Thanks for taking the time today, Alex. We'll be in touch soon. Good luck.

Thanks, that's helpful, and the 60-40 split sounds like a good balance to me. I'd like the mix of new projects and owning live systems, especially since I've already learned a lot from fixing things that were in production.

Thanks for taking the time to talk with me today. I enjoyed learning more about the team, and I'm looking forward to hearing from you. Have a good rest of your day.
You too. Take care.

feedback_leaks.quote: That's solid work on the checkout page.

verdicts.notes: Strength: the interviewer asked probing, specific follow-ups on measurement (T4), the third script (T6), user counting (T14), and how the bug was found (T18). Weakness: it skipped the Billing tests topic entirely, gave small evaluative remarks ("That's solid work", "fair answer"), and didn't dig into the vague dashboard answer at T13. What I did was test on real devices and watch the timing data after the release for anything unusual. Honestly, I'd spend more of the first week just getting the measurement right before touching anything. Last time I was working from Lighthouse and real-user timing, but I never tracked checkout completion or payment errors as a baseline, so I couldn't prove nothing got worse. I'd also sit down with whoever owns those payment scripts early, because I made the call on which ones to defer mostly on my own, and someone who knows the vendors would've caught dependencies I missed.
Good instinct. So you'd slow down, talk to the right people, and nail the measurement first. That's a shift from how you approached it last time?

I did involve my manager, but mostly to point me at the scripts, not to plan the whole thing with the people who owned them. Looking back, I'd want to set up the success metrics and get the vendor and payments folks in the room before I changed anything. It's slower at the start, but it means I'm not guessing about what might break.
Makes sense. Let me shift gears a bit. Tell me about a time you actually failed at something—not just a lesson learned, but something that didn't work out the way you wanted.

Okay, the one that comes to mind is from Campus Eats. Users were getting double charged when they double-tapped "Pay," and I was the one who built the ordering backend, so that was on me. I hadn't tested rapid repeated taps, so I didn't catch it before people hit it. Fixing it meant adding idempotency keys so the same payment request couldn't go through twice, and that worked, but I should have caught it earlier.
How many people did that actually affect? And when you say you should've caught it earlier, what would that have looked like?

I don't have an exact count, and I should have pulled that from the payment logs when it happened instead of guessing now. What I can say is that it was a real problem for real users, and it's the reason I took it seriously.

Catching it earlier would have meant treating "Pay" as something that could get fired twice. I could have written a test that sends the same payment request two or three times quickly and checks that only one charge goes through. Yes, I added it. After the fix, I wrote a test that fires the same payment request several times in quick succession and checks that only one charge goes through. I also made sure the idempotency key check was covered, so if someone changes that logic later, the test fails.

I should be clear about the scope, though. I was one of three people on Campus Eats, and I owned the ordering backend, so the payment endpoint was mine to fix and test. Fair. Did you discover any bugs while you were writing those tests, or was it mostly filling in coverage that was already working?

Yeah, I did find a couple of things. The one I remember best was around rounding on mid-cycle downgrades. The proration result could come out a cent off depending on the order the adjustments got applied, so two equivalent changes could produce different invoices. I flagged it, and we fixed it before it went out.

I don't want to overstate it, though. I don't have an exact count of how many bugs I turned up, and I'm not sure how many of those were real customer-facing issues versus edge cases that would only show up in tests. If you want specifics, I'd want to check the ticket history rather than guess.

That's fair—you caught something real and flagged it. Now, on your resume I see you were a teaching assistant in summer 2026, and that's also when you were interning. How did those two overlap, and what was your time split like?

The TA role was about 4 hours a week, remote, in the evenings, so it didn't take over my day. The internship was the main commitment, and the TA work fit around it. I'd say the overlap was real but manageable. Most weeks the TA hours were the easy part of the schedule.

Okay, that's clear. You mentioned running labs for 40 students—was there a particular student or situation where you had to really dig in and help someone through something hard?

Good question. I did change a bit after that. Before, I'd walk through a loop on the board and assume people were following. With this student I saw that they needed to trace it themselves, so I started asking the group to fill in the variable values on each pass before I explained what the code did. I also made more time in lab for people to try a trace on paper, not just watch me do one.

I can't say it made a huge difference across the whole class, though. I didn't track it formally, so I'd just be guessing at the overall effect. What I can say is that it became my default for loop problems after that.
We're almost out of time, so let me ask—what questions do you have for me or the team?
Sure, just one for now: what does a typical first month look like for someone starting on the team?

Good question. First month is usually onboarding to our codebase and tooling, pairing with someone on the team on a smaller task or two so you get familiar with how we work. By week three or four, we'd expect you to pick up something real on your own—nothing huge, but something that ships. And honestly, a lot of that first month is just learning the business and the systems, so questions are expected. We don't throw people in the deep end.

Thanks for taking the time today, Alex. We'll be in touch soon with next steps. Good luck with the rest of your interviews.

transcript.text: Hey, good to meet you. How's your day been so far?
Hey, good to meet you too! My day's been good, pretty relaxed so far. I had a coffee and went over my notes for this call, so I'm glad we're finally talking. How about you, how's your day going?

Sure. I'm a junior in computer science, and right now I'm a software engineering intern at a fintech startup. Before that, I got into programming mostly through building things on my own. The internship is where I've been working on more professional code. I've done some front-end work on a payments dashboard and some performance work on our checkout page, which is what really got me interested in the fintech side. I'm looking for a role where I can keep doing that kind of work with more real users and more responsibility.

That's a solid foundation. I want to dig into a couple of those. Let's start with the checkout page work—you mentioned cutting load time by 40%. What was the baseline you started with, and how were you actually measuring that improvement?

Yeah, happy to get into that. The starting point was about 3.1 seconds on mobile. I measured it two ways: Lighthouse runs in the lab, and real-user timing from production, so I wasn't relying on just one number.

When I dug in, the main problem was that three payment scripts were loading up front, before the page was usable. I deferred two of them and lazy-loaded the card form so it only loaded when someone got to that step. That brought mobile load down to about 1.8 seconds.

I should be clear on one thing. My manager pointed me toward looking at the scripts, but I did the profiling and made the actual change myself.

That's good clarity on what you personally owned. So you went from 3.1 to 1.8—that math checks out to about 42%, so the 40% tracks. When you deferred those scripts, did you run into any issues on the other side? Like, did deferring them break anything, or create new problems downstream?

Nothing major broke, as far as I know. The main thing I watched was timing. Anything that depended on those scripts being ready early could behave differently, so I made sure the card form was ready before someone could reach the pay
Before you could reach the pay button, got it. Did you test that path end-to-end, or did you rely on someone else to validate it?

Mostly I tested it myself. I walked through the checkout on a phone, both with the scripts deferred and with the card form loading late, to make sure the form was ready before someone could hit pay. To be honest, I don't think I wrote a full automated end-to-end test for that path. I'd want to check with my team before saying more than that.
Fair enough. Let me shift to the billing tests work for a second. You said you improved test coverage across the billing service. What was the coverage before, and what did you get it to?

It went from about 38% to 61% across the billing service. I should be clear about my part, though. I wrote about 40 tests for the invoice proration module, and two teammates handled the rest of the coverage gain.
Got it. So you personally owned the proration tests. What was the proration module doing, and why did it need that much test coverage?

It handles the math for partial billing periods, like when someone upgrades or cancels partway through a cycle. The module works out how much to credit or charge for the unused or added time, so small errors there turn into wrong invoices. That's why it needed a lot of tests. Billing code also has a lot of edge cases, like month lengths and mid-cycle changes, and the coverage was low before. I wrote about 40 tests to cover those cases.
That makes sense—billing math is unforgiving. Of those 40 tests you wrote, what was the hardest edge case to cover, and how did you approach it?

Honestly, I don't have one specific case I can point to from memory, and I'd rather not guess and give you a made-up story. The area that was trickiest overall was mid-cycle changes combined with different month lengths, since those are easy to get slightly wrong. If you want the details, I could walk you through the test file, because I'd want to show you the actual case rather than reconstruct it from memory.

I respect that. We can look at the specifics later if we go forward. Let me ask you this—when you're in your first month on the job here, how would you approach learning a codebase like that? What's your process?

Sure. My first step would be to get the lay of the land before changing anything. I'd read the README and any architecture docs, then trace one real user flow end to end, something like a checkout or a refund, so I can see how the pieces connect. I'd also run the test suite and the app locally, because breaking things on purpose in a dev environment teaches you more than reading code does.

After that, I'd pick a small, low-risk ticket, maybe a bug fix or a test addition, so I could practice the team's workflow: how they review PRs, what their deploy process looks like, and who owns which areas. I'd ask a lot of questions early, and I'd try to write down the answers so I don't make the same person explain things twice.

I'd also pay attention to where the bugs and incidents cluster. That usually tells you where the code is fragile and where people are most careful. And since I'd be working in payments, I'd want to understand the money-related paths first and ask someone to walk me through them before I touch anything there.

That's thoughtful. You're clearly thinking about impact and not breaking things. Let me ask you something different. Tell me about a time you failed at something, or something didn't go the way you planned.

Yeah, the Campus Eats payments problem is a good one. Users were double-tapping "Pay," and that was charging them twice. I hadn't planned for that when I built the ordering backend, so it was a miss on my part. I fixed it with idempotency keys so a repeated request from the same order can't create a second charge. Since then I've made it a habit to think through what happens when the same action runs twice, especially anywhere money moves.
How did you discover the double-charge issue? Did a user report it, or did you catch it another way?

I'd rather not guess on that one. I know the cause was users double-tapping "Pay" and getting charged twice, and I know the fix was idempotency keys. But I don't remember exactly how it first came to my attention, and I don't want to make up a story. If it matters for the discussion, I can check my notes or the project history and tell you more.
No worries. So after you fixed it with idempotency keys, did you go back and audit other parts of the system for the same kind of issue, or was it just that one spot?

I don't think I did a formal audit, and I'd rather not claim I did. The fix was in the ordering flow where the double-tap happened, and I was focused on making that path safe. I can't say for sure whether I went through the other payment-related endpoints looking for the same problem. If I'd do it now, I'd start with every route that creates a charge or changes an order's payment state and check whether a repeated request could cause a second effect. I'd want to look at the project history before saying more about what we actually covered back then.

Fair. I like that you're being precise about what you know versus what you're inferring. Let me ask you this—why are you interested in this kind of role? What draws you to fintech or backend work, versus something else?

I like that fintech is the kind of work where the details matter. Getting a number wrong on a checkout or an invoice has real consequences for real people, so you have to be careful and think through edge cases. I've found I enjoy that kind of problem more than something where the stakes are lower.

On the backend side, the Campus Eats payments bug really got me hooked. Watching a small race condition turn into a double charge made me want to understand how systems behave under repeated or concurrent requests. The checkout work was similar. Once I started profiling, I got interested in how much of a page's performance comes down to what loads when, not just how the code is written.

I also like that payments touch a lot of parts of a product at once: the front end, the APIs, the billing logic, and the support team who depend on it. The dashboard I built for support showed me how much a good internal tool can change someone's day, and I want to keep doing work like that with more users and more responsibility.
That's clear. One thing I noticed—you ran the TA labs in the summer of 2026, and that's also when your internship was going on. How did you manage both at the same time?

I'd want to double-check the exact dates before agreeing on the timing, but the TA job was small. It was about 4 hours a week, remote, in the evenings, so it fit around the internship. Most of the time went to the weekly labs, and the rest was helping students outside class, like the one I worked with on loops. I did have to be disciplined about keeping evenings for it, but it never got in the way of my work at the internship.
Got it. We're almost out of time, so let me ask—do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, I do. What does a typical week look like for someone on this team, especially the balance between new feature work and keeping the existing payment systems running?

Good question. It's roughly 60-40 new features to maintenance and incidents. Some weeks tip more toward maintenance if something breaks in production, but we try to protect time for building. You'd probably spend your first month mostly on smaller maintenance and test work to get familiar with the systems, then move into features once you're comfortable.

Anything else?

Thanks, that helps. One last thing: when someone on the team hits an incident or a production issue, how do they usually share what happened afterward? I'm curious whether you do written postmortems or something more informal.

We do written postmortems for anything significant—payment failures, data issues, that kind of thing. It's blameless, focused on what went wrong and how we prevent it next time. Smaller stuff we just talk through in Slack. It's a good way to learn the system fast, and I think you'd find that useful.

Well, I appreciate your time today, Alex. You've got solid instincts about ownership and thinking through edge cases. We'll be in touch soon about next steps.

Thanks, I really appreciate you taking the time. The postmortem process sounds like a good way to learn, and I'd like to be part of a team that handles things that way. I enjoyed the conversation, and I look forward to hearing about next steps.
Great. Thanks again, and good luck with everything.

At my internship, I've seen how a small performance problem or a clunky internal tool can slow down a whole team, and fixing those things is what I enjoy most. I also like that this kind of job gives you ownership over systems that matter, not just side projects. That makes sense. You mentioned a performance problem—I'm curious about that. On your resume you have cutting checkout load time by 40%. What was the baseline there, and how did you actually measure that improvement?

Sure. The checkout page on mobile was taking about 3.1 seconds to load. My manager suggested looking at the scripts, so I profiled it with Lighthouse and also looked at real-user timing data. Got it. So you went from 3.1 to 1.8—that math checks out. When you say you deferred the scripts, what exactly did you change in the code to make that happen?

The API design and the backend logic were his. On the interface side, I worked with the support team on what they needed to see, and I made the layout decisions, but I was iterating on feedback from them rather than designing it alone. Yeah, the first version of the layout didn't match how the support team actually worked. I'd built the refund table the way I thought made sense, but when they tried it, they wanted the status filter up top and the most recent cases first. I reworked the layout around that, and it fit their daily routine much better. It was a good reminder that the people using a tool know their workflow better than I do, so I try to get feedback early now.
That's good instinct. Let me ask you more broadly—tell me about a time you actually failed at something. Not a small iteration like that, but something where things didn't work out the way you hoped.

Sure. In Campus Eats, I was building the ordering backend, and I didn't think about what happens when someone taps "Pay" twice. Some users got charged twice for one order. Nobody got hurt, but it was a real problem with money, and I should have caught it before it reached users. I fixed it by adding idempotency keys so a repeated request can't create a second charge. That's a real one. How did you find out it was happening? Did a user report it, or did you catch it another way?

I don't remember the exact details of how it surfaced, so I don't want to make up a story. What I can say is that it came up after users were already on the app, and I found out that some people had been charged twice for one order. Once I knew, I traced it back to the payment request firing again on a double tap, and that's when I added the idempotency keys.
Fair enough. So after you fixed it with the idempotency keys, did you add tests to make sure that wouldn't happen again?

Yes, I did. I wrote tests that simulate a double tap, sending the same payment request twice with the same key, and check that only one charge goes through. I also tested a retry after a timeout, since that's another way the same request can get sent twice. I'll be honest that those tests covered the cases I could think of, so I'd still want more eyes on payment flows before I'd call them fully safe.
That's the right mindset. Speaking of tests—you also have on your resume improving test coverage across the billing service. What was the coverage before and after, and what did you actually write?

Coverage went from 38% to 61%. My part was the invoice proration module, where I wrote about 40 tests. Two of my teammates wrote the rest of the tests that brought the number up. So the 61% is a team result, and I'd want to be clear about my share of it.
I appreciate you being specific about that. What was the hardest test or scenario to cover in the proration module?

The hardest one was mid-cycle plan changes, where a customer upgrades or downgrades partway through a billing period. The proration has to split the time between the old and new plan and then round the amounts correctly. I had to work through the math by hand on paper before I trusted what the code was doing, and I wrote tests for edge cases like a change on the very first or last day of a cycle. Some of those edge cases were the ones most likely to be off by a cent or a day, so I spent more time on them than on the normal cases.
Makes sense. Now, I saw on your resume that you're both a TA and interning at the same time in summer 2026. How are you managing both of those?

It's manageable because the TA job is only about 4 hours a week, and it's remote and in the evenings, so it doesn't collide with my internship hours. I plan my week around the TA sessions and keep the internship work during the day. If the two ever start competing, I'd rather tell my manager and my TA coordinator early than let either one slip.
Got it. One more thing before we wrap—you ran weekly labs for 40 students in Intro to Programming. Do you remember a student who was really struggling, and what you did to help?

Yes, there was one student who kept failing the loops assignments. Loops were just not clicking for them, and the usual explanations weren't working. So I started meeting with them, and we drew out the code's execution step by step on paper, tracking the variables on each iteration. We kept at it for about three weeks, and by the midterm they passed. I think what helped was slowing down and making the process visible instead of just explaining the answer again.
That's patience and good teaching. We're almost out of time, so let me ask—do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yes, one question: what does a typical week look like for someone in this role, and how much of it is building new things versus maintaining what's already live?

Good question. It's probably 60-40, maybe 70-30 depending on the week. You're usually working on a feature or improvement, but there's always some maintenance—bugs, tech debt, support requests. Your first month or two you'd probably be more on the maintenance and learning side, then you'd ramp up to owning a real project pretty quickly. Anything else?

Thanks, that helps a lot. It sounds like the maintenance side is a real part of the job, which I'm glad to hear, since I've learned a lot from fixing things that were already live. Last thing from me: what does the team look like day to day, and how do people usually handle code review and getting unstuck?

The team is six engineers plus a tech lead. We do code review on pull requests—usually takes a day or two to get eyes on it. And for getting unstuck, people tend to reach out to whoever knows that part of the system best, or post in Slack. We're pretty collaborative that way. Alright, I think that's a good place to wrap. In my first year I helped run a food ordering app for our campus, and when I watched people actually use it, I got hooked on building things that other people rely on every day. My manager suggested I look at the scripts, so that part started with them. I ran the timing again after to confirm the drop to about 1.8 seconds. So the direction came from my manager, and the investigation and the change were mine.

Good question. The number I was tracking was mobile load time, since that's where the page was slowest. I also checked with a teammate who knew the billing history, and they pointed out a rounding edge case I wouldn't have caught from the code alone. So it was a mix: the code gave me the first list, and writing and reviewing the tests filled in the gaps.
That's a good process. Did you find any actual bugs when you were writing those tests, or was it all just filling in coverage?

Not a clear one that I can point to. Most of the tests confirmed the module did what the code said it should. The rounding case and the same-day plan change were gaps in my coverage, but I wouldn't call either of them a confirmed bug. If I'd found a real one, I'd have raised it with the team right away, and I'd be happy to look up whether anything came out of that work.
Fair enough. So let me ask you this: tell me about a time you failed at something, either here or in school or anywhere else.

Sorry, you cut off there—what did you learn?

Drawing the traces on paper and having the student track the variables themselves made the logic concrete for them, and it's a habit I've kept since. I also realized I'd been assuming the problem was how much they understood, when it was really how I was presenting it.
That's a good reflection. So in the moment when you realized your first approach wasn't working, how long did it take you to try something different?

Payments are the same kind of problem, where a small bug can cost someone money or trust, so I want to keep getting better at careful, reliable code. Makes sense. We're almost out of time here. Do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?

Good question. Yeah, that helps a lot, thanks. We'll definitely show you that once you're in. Thanks for the good conversation today—I appreciate you being thoughtful and specific about your work. We'll be in touch next week with next steps.
Thanks so much, I really enjoyed the conversation. I appreciate you taking the time, and I'm looking forward to hearing about next steps next week. Have a great rest of your day.

I'm really interested in the mix of building products people actually use and making sure they're reliable, and that's a big part of why I'm excited about this role.
That's great. So you mentioned working on React front ends at the fintech startup—tell me about a specific project you built there. What was it, and what did you actually work on?

Refunds can be partially completed or still pending, so I spent a lot of time on how that shows up in the table, which was less obvious than it sounded. I also had to handle loading and error states properly, since the support folks would be in the middle of a customer call and needed to know right away if something failed. Most of the work was making the flow fast and clear for people who use it all day.
That makes sense. So you mentioned the senior engineer built the API—did you have to do anything on that side, or was it purely front end for you?

Mostly front end. The senior engineer built the API and the data layer, and I didn't write any of the endpoints. I also flagged a couple of places where the front end needed the data to be sorted or paginated a certain way, so we settled that before I built too far. The clearest evidence is the before and after on the actual task. Before, someone had to export the spreadsheet and search it by hand, and a refund lookup took about 5 minutes. Idempotency keys should have been in the first version, not a fix after people got charged.

I'd also have set up better logging on the payment calls earlier. The double-charge diagnosis came down to me digging through logs after the fact, and if we'd had clear request tracing from day one, we'd have caught it faster.

A lot of the bugs hide in those boundaries, like a change on the last day of a billing period or a refund that crosses two cycles. I had to work out the expected numbers carefully, sometimes by hand, before I trusted the tests. I should be clear that I wrote the tests for the proration module specifically, and two teammates covered the rest of the coverage increase.

They did overlap, but the TA job was small. It was about 4 hours a week, remote, in the evenings, so it fit around the internship without much strain. I did have to be disciplined about my time, though. I'd block off the evening sessions and keep the work on the internship during the day.

There was one student who kept failing the loops material. Every time we went over a loop, they'd nod along, then get it wrong on the next problem. verdicts.notes: Strength: the interviewer covered both practice questions and probed the dashboard and checkout work with reasonable follow-ups, including the API work and the baseline. Weakness: it let several vague answers pass (T11, T25, T33 and the number-less checkout result), never pressed for the 40% measurement or Campus Eats specifics, skipped Billing tests entirely, and leaked mild evaluative comments (T16, T32, T34).

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for taking the time. How are things going on your end?
Hi, yeah, thanks for having me. Things are good, a little nervous honestly, but good. It's been a busy few weeks with classes and work, so I'm glad to finally be talking to you about the role.
That's totally understandable. Busy season, yeah. So before we dive in, I'm curious—what drew you to this role specifically? What kind of work are you looking to do?

Um, yeah, I think mostly it's the fintech side. I've been doing some work on the internship with payments stuff, and it's interesting, like, the stakes feel higher, you know? I want to get better at building things people actually rely on. Honestly I'm still figuring out exactly what kind of engineer I want to be, so I'm hoping this role helps me figure that out. Like, a lot of it is just wanting to learn from people who've been doing this longer.
That makes sense. So the payments work at your internship—what's stuck with you about that? Like, what's one thing you built or worked on that made you feel like the stakes were real?

Um, yeah, there was a dashboard for the support team. They were basically exporting a spreadsheet every day to look up refunds, and I built the React front end for the replacement. Like, I knew real people were going to be sitting there using it every day, so if it broke, that would've mattered. That's kind of what made it feel real to me.
Got it. So the support team was using a spreadsheet before—what exactly were they doing with the dashboard once you built it? Like, what could they do that they couldn't do before?

Um, mostly they could look up refunds without digging through the export. Before, it was basically searching a big spreadsheet, and I think a lookup could take like five minutes. Now it's under a minute. I did the React front end, and a senior engineer built the API behind it.
That's helpful context. When you say you built the React front end—walk me through what that actually involved. Like, what were the main components or features you had to figure out?

Um, mostly the search screen, I think. That's the main thing support would use. I'd have to look back at the code to walk you through all the pieces, honestly. A senior engineer had the API side, so I was mostly focused on making the front end work with what they gave me.
Fair enough. One thing I'm curious about—when you first got the API from the senior engineer, did it do exactly what you needed, or did you have to work with them to change it?

Um, I think it mostly did what we needed? There might have been a couple small things we tweaked, but I don't remember the details super well. The senior engineer was pretty helpful about it, I think.

Okay. Let me shift gears a bit. I see on your resume you have the payments dashboard work, and then you also mention being a teaching assistant for Intro to Programming. Those seem to overlap in summer 2026—how did you manage both of those at the same time?

Um, yeah, it was mostly just about keeping the schedule under control. The TA job was pretty small, like a few hours a week, and I did it remotely in the evenings, so it didn't really collide with the internship during the day. It was tight some weeks, but I managed it.
Got it. So with the TA work—you ran weekly labs for about 40 students. Tell me about a time when a student was really stuck on something and what you did to help them.

Um, yeah, there was one student who kept failing the loop problems. I didn't want to just hand them the answer, so we sat down and drew out the code's trace on paper, step by step, tracking the variables each time through. We did that for about three weeks, and they ended up passing the midterm.
Nice. So you traced through it with them on paper—what made you choose that approach instead of, say, just explaining the concept or pointing them to a tutorial?

Um, I think I tried just explaining it first, and they'd nod along, but then they couldn't do it on their own. With the paper trace, they could see the variables changing each time through the loop, so it was less abstract. I'm not sure I had a big plan going in, honestly. It just seemed like the thing that was actually working.
That makes sense. Okay, shifting again—on your resume you mention cutting checkout page load time by 40%. What was the baseline there, and how did you actually measure that improvement?
Um, yeah, it was a few seconds on mobile, I think around three. I don't remember the exact measurement setup super well, honestly. I'd want to double-check that before saying more.
Fair. So when you started looking at the checkout page, what was the first thing you dug into to figure out where the slowness was coming from?

Um, I think I started by looking at what was loading on the page. My manager had suggested checking the scripts, so I looked at those first, and I found three payment scripts loading up front before anything else.
Okay, so you found those three scripts. What did you do once you identified them?

Um, so I deferred two of them, so they weren't blocking the page while it loaded. And I lazy-loaded the card form, so it only pulls in when someone actually gets to that part. My manager had pointed me toward the scripts, but I did the profiling and the change myself.
Got it. I'm curious—when you deferred those two scripts, did you test to make sure they still worked after the page loaded, or did you just assume they would?

Um, yeah, we tested it. I checked that the payment stuff still worked once the page was up, and I think I looked at the load time again after the change. I don't remember every single test case off the top of my head, honestly, but I did check it.
That's fair. So let me ask you this—if you were starting in this role tomorrow, what would be your first priority in your first month? Like, what would you want to learn or do first?

Um, yeah, I think my first priority would be just learning the codebase and how the team works. Like, I'd want to understand the payments stuff well enough that I'm not scared to touch it. And I'd want to ask a lot of questions early, since I'm still pretty new to this kind of work. I don't really have a super specific plan yet, honestly.
Makes sense. Before we wrap up, I want to ask—tell me about a time you failed at something. Could be at work, school, wherever. What happened?

Um, yeah, I think the big one was actually in Campus Eats, the food ordering app I worked on with two other people. We had a bug where if someone double-tapped the Pay button, they could get charged twice. I didn't catch it early, and it got into the build before we noticed. I was the one on the ordering backend, so it was kind of my area.
Okay, so you didn't catch the double-tap issue—what happened after it got into the build? Like, how did you find out about it, and what did you do?

Um, I think someone noticed it when they got charged twice, and it got reported to us. I don't remember the exact details of how that came in, honestly. What I did was add idempotency keys to the ordering backend, so a second tap on Pay wouldn't create a second charge.

That's a good fix. But I'm curious—when you look back on it now, what would you have done differently earlier to catch that in the first place? Like, what would you do differently if you were building that feature today?

Um, yeah, I think I'd have tested the Pay button more, like actually tapping it fast a bunch of times. We were mostly testing the normal flow, one tap and done, so we never really tried breaking it. And I probably would have thought about idempotency from the start instead of adding it after. I don't know, I'm still learning how to think about that stuff, but I'd definitely try to think about it earlier now.
That's honest feedback on yourself. Last thing—do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, one question. What does a typical week look like for someone in this role, especially in the first few months?

Good question. Your first month or two, you're mostly getting oriented—pairing with someone on the team, understanding how we ship code, what the on-call rotation looks like. After that, you'd start picking up small features or bug fixes, but still with pretty close feedback. By month three or four, you'd be working more independently on features, but we're always available. It's a pretty collaborative team, so you won't be siloed. Does that help?

Yeah, that helps a lot, thanks. The pairing part sounds good to me, honestly. I'd rather learn by watching someone do it first than just get thrown at a ticket. And the on-call thing is a bit scary, but I'd want to understand it early, so that's useful to know. I think I'm a pretty good fit for that kind of setup.
Great. Well, I appreciate you taking the time to talk through all of this. We'll be in touch soon with next steps. Thanks again, and good luck with the rest of your semester.

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for taking the time. How are things going on your end?

Yeah, so that was a project for the support team. They were kind of doing things in a spreadsheet before, and we wanted to make it easier for them. I built the React front end, and a senior engineer built the API side. It turned out pretty well, and the team seemed to like it.

That's helpful. And how many people on the support team actually use this thing now?
The support team. I think it's about six people, but I'd have to double-check that before I say it for sure.
Alright. So let me switch gears a bit. On your resume you mentioned cutting checkout page load time by 40 percent. What was the baseline there, and how did you measure that improvement?

Um, the baseline was around three seconds on mobile, I think. We checked it with Lighthouse, and I think we also looked at some real user timing. I'd want to pull up the exact numbers before I say more than that.
Sure. So what was the first thing you changed when you started working on it?

Um, I think the first real thing was looking at the scripts. There were three payment scripts loading right away on page load, and that seemed like the main problem. My manager pointed me toward scripts, and I did the profiling to confirm it.
So your manager pointed you in that direction. What did you change about those scripts?

Um, I deferred two of them so they wouldn't block the page, and I lazy-loaded the card form so it only loads when someone actually gets to that part. I'd have to look up the exact before and after numbers, though.
Fair enough. And when you actually shipped that—did you measure the impact after it went live, or just in your local testing?

Yeah, we looked at real user timing after it went out, not just on my laptop. I also ran Lighthouse. Mobile went from about three seconds to around 1.8, I think. I'd still want to double-check that before quoting it.
Good. So you mentioned you also improved test coverage across the billing service. What was the coverage before, and what did you actually write?

Um, I worked on the tests for the billing service, and the coverage went up quite a bit. I'd have to look up the exact starting point. I mostly wrote tests for one module, but there were a couple of teammates on the rest of it too.
Which module did you write the tests for?
The invoice proration module. I wrote about forty tests for that one. My teammates handled most of the rest of the billing service.
Okay. And what kinds of things were those forty tests covering? Like, what was the hardest thing to test there?

Um, mostly the normal cases first, like a customer changing plans partway through a billing cycle, and then the edge cases around the dates. Proration gets weird with things like month lengths and when a change happens right at the boundary. I'd say the date edge cases were the hardest, just because it's easy to get off by a day and not notice until you run it. I don't remember every single test off the top of my head, though.
That makes sense. So thinking about your first month if you joined this team, how would you approach getting up to speed on a new codebase?

Um, I think I'd start by just reading through the parts of the codebase that matter most for the stuff I'd be working on, and not trying to understand everything at once. I'd probably ask a lot of questions early on, especially to whoever wrote the code I'm touching. And I'd try to get a small task going pretty quickly, even just a bug fix, so I'm running the code and seeing how things actually work. I think that's the best way for me to learn, honestly. I'd want to be careful not to ask the same question twice, though.
That's a solid approach. I want to circle back to something—tell me about a time when things didn't go the way you wanted. What happened, and what did you learn from it?

Um, yeah. There was a time with the Campus Eats app that was kind of a mess. We had an issue where people were getting charged twice, and it happened when they double-tapped the Pay button. That was stressful, because it's money, and people notice that fast. I ended up adding idempotency keys to the ordering backend so a repeated request doesn't create a second charge. I learned that you have to think about what happens when users do stuff you didn't expect, like tapping twice. I'd have to look up the exact details of how many people were affected, though.
How did you find out about the double-charge issue in the first place?

Um, I think it came up because people noticed they'd been charged twice, and then it got escalated to us. I'd have to think about the exact steps for how we confirmed it, though. I was pretty focused on fixing it at that point, so I don't remember every detail of the investigation.
Got it. So why are you interested in this kind of role? What's drawing you to apply?

Um, yeah, I'm interested because I like working on stuff that real people use, and fintech is interesting to me because the code has real consequences. Like with the checkout and the double-charge thing, you can see how much it matters to get it right. I also like that a startup usually means you get to touch a lot of different parts of the product, which I've liked so far. I think I'd learn a lot quickly here, and that's kind of what I'm looking for right now.
Makes sense. Do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, one question. What does a typical week look like for someone starting on the team?

Good question. Honestly, it varies a lot depending on what we're shipping that week, but generally you'd spend the first couple weeks getting familiar with the codebase and doing some smaller tasks—bugs, small features, that kind of thing. After that you'd probably get pulled into whatever the team's working on. We do stand-ups every morning, and you'd be pairing with folks pretty regularly early on, so you're not just figuring things out alone. It's pretty collaborative.

Well, I appreciate you taking the time today. We'll be in touch soon about next steps. Thanks again.
Thanks so much, that sounds really good. Pairing early on would help a lot, honestly. I appreciate you taking the time, and I'm looking forward to hearing back. Have a great rest of your day!
You too, thanks. Take care.

Got it. So you owned the backend. When you hit that double-charge problem, how did you find it? Was it a bug report, or did you catch it another way?

I'm honestly not sure how we first caught it. I think it came up as a report from someone who got charged twice, or someone on the team noticed duplicate charges, but I don't want to guess at the details. What I do remember is that once we understood it, the fix was the idempotency key work, and the harder part was getting the key design right so we didn't block real repeat purchases. I appreciate you being direct about what you don't remember. Let me shift gears a bit. You also improved test coverage on the billing service at your internship. What was the coverage before and after, and what did you actually write?

From there I'd pick one module to start with, probably the one closest to the code I'd be changing, and write tests for the behavior people actually depend on, especially the edge cases. That's a thoughtful answer. Let me ask you about something different. You're TAing an intro programming course for about 40 students. Tell me about a time you helped a student who was really stuck, and what actually changed for them.

That's a concrete example. Did that approach—the paper tracing—work for other students too, or was that specific to them?

Honestly, I can't say it worked for everyone. I didn't track it across the class, so I don't have numbers. I mostly used it with that one student, because they'd gotten stuck in a specific way. They understood the individual pieces but couldn't see what the code was doing step by step.

I'd guess it helps most with students who have that same gap, but I'd want to try it with a few more before I'd say it's a general fix. If I were doing it again, I'd check in with the other students more directly, and maybe ask the course staff how the loops material landed across the whole section.
Makes sense. So shifting gears—I want to ask you about a time you failed at something, or a project that didn't go the way you wanted. What comes to mind?

Honestly, the double-charge problem at Campus Eats is the one that comes to mind. Some users got charged twice, which is about the worst thing a payments feature can do.

Go ahead, take your time.

We do a mix of backend infrastructure and product work, so it's pretty varied. We'll dig into what we do more if you make it through.

So let me start with your internship. You mentioned the payments side—can you walk me through one specific project you worked on there that you're proud of?

Makes sense. So on the idempotency key solution—was that something you came up with, or did someone else suggest it?

Fair enough. When you first started building that backend, what was the hardest technical problem you ran into before you even got to the double-charge issue?

We spent a fair amount of time agreeing on the API shape between the app and the backend, and that took more back-and-forth than any single bug. I don't have a dramatic story from before that point. Got it. And when you say you built the React front end—what were the trickier parts of that? Was it just hooking up to the API, or were there things about how the support team actually worked that changed how you built it?

They knew exactly which columns they looked at first and how they searched for a customer. We talked with them a lot about that, and it changed the layout and the order of things on the screen. If we'd just copied the spreadsheet into a web page, I don't think it would have felt like an improvement to them.
That's good instinct. Did you end up iterating on the design after you shipped it, or did you get it right by talking to them upfront?

I'd say it was mostly upfront. We spent time with the team before we built much, so the main layout was already right. After launch there were a few follow-ups once people were using it day to day, but nothing major. I don't want to make it sound like we got everything perfect the first time.

Okay. So you wrote 40 tests for invoice proration—what was the hardest case to test in that module?

Honestly, I don't have one standout case I can point to without making it up. Proration is tricky in general, though. Dates and partial periods are where bugs hide, like a plan change landing in the middle of a billing cycle, or rounding when you split an amount across days. So a lot of the 40 tests were about those boundary situations. If you want a specific example, I'd want to pull up the test file to remember which one gave us the most trouble.
That's fair. I appreciate you not guessing. Let me ask you something different. Tell me about a time you failed at something, either at the internship or in one of your projects.

Sure. On Campus Eats, we shipped a version where a double-tap on "Pay" could charge someone twice. We didn't think about it when we were building the ordering flow, and it only came up once people were actually using the app. Users noticed, and we had to stop what we were doing and track it down.

Looking back, the mistake was that we treated the payment step like any other button. We should have asked what happens if a request runs twice, before anyone had to tell us. We fixed it with idempotency keys, and now a repeated request just returns the result of the first one. But I'd want that question asked up front on the next project.
That makes sense. And what would you do differently in your first month on a new team to avoid that kind of thing happening again?

I'd spend the first couple weeks just reading. Looking at the code for the payment and ordering flows, and asking the team which parts have broken before, would tell me where the risky spots are. The double-charge thing could have been caught early if someone had asked, "What happens if this request runs twice?" on anything touching money.

I'd also try to get a feel for how the team reviews changes. If there's a checklist or a habit of thinking through failure cases, I'd want to learn it fast. And I'd ask people what they wish someone had told them about the codebase, because that usually points right at the things that bite new folks.
Good. One last thing—why do you want this kind of role? What's drawing you to it?

I like that the work touches real people. Checkout speed and the support dashboard both made a visible difference to someone, and that's the part that keeps me interested. Payments in particular are high stakes, so getting details right matters a lot, and that pushes me to think more carefully.

The backend and infrastructure side also appeals to me. The double-charge problem on Campus Eats was the kind of thing I want to keep getting better at: thinking about how systems fail, not only how they work when things go right. A role where I'm working on that every day sounds like a good place to grow.
That's a solid answer. Do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, one question: what does a typical first few months look like for someone starting on the team?

Good question. Usually we pair new people with someone who's been here a while for the first month or so. You'd start with smaller tasks—bug fixes, maybe a feature behind a flag—just to get familiar with the codebase and how we work. By month two or three, you'd be picking up bigger projects on your own. And we do a lot of code review here, so that's how people learn what we care about.

Thanks for taking the time today, Alex. We'll be in touch soon with next steps.

Thanks so much for the time today, and for walking me through how the first few months work. That pairing and the code review sound like exactly the kind of help I'd want. I'm looking forward to hearing about next steps.
You got it. Take care, and we'll talk soon.

They'd been pulling an export every day and then searching it by hand, so the screens I built were mostly search, filters for refund requests, and a results view that made sense to someone who isn't an engineer. I spent a lot of time on the layout because the old spreadsheet had about fifteen columns, and half of them nobody used, so I asked the team which ones mattered and cut the rest. The senior engineer built the API that the dashboard calls to pull the actual refund data. I didn't write that, and I'd be guessing if I described how it queried things, so I'd point you to them for the backend details. What I can say is that refund lookups went from about five minutes to under one, and most of that speedup came from not having to dig through a daily export. Also, the support team lead kept sending me screenshots of the old sheet with coffee rings on them, which is how I knew they were actually using it. Did you want me to go deeper on any of the front-end pieces?
No, that's clear. Quick thing I noticed—on your resume, you have the internship and the TA role both listed for summer 2026. How did those overlap, or did they?

Yeah, they overlapped a bit, which I know can look like a lot on paper. The TA role was about four hours a week, and it was remote and in the evenings, so it fit around the internship without eating into my workdays. I'd been doing the TA job during the semester and kept it going into the summer, and it's the kind of thing where the schedule is pretty predictable. My roommate says I'm the only person she knows who schedules grading like it's a gym routine, which is probably true. The main thing I had to manage was not letting the TA hours creep into the internship, so I kept the evenings for the TA work and didn't take on extra shifts. If it ever got to be too much, I'd tell my manager and the professor, but so far it's been manageable. Did you want me to walk through how I'd handle a week where both were really busy?
No, that makes sense. So you ran weekly labs for 40 students in Intro to Programming. Tell me about a time when a student was really struggling and what you actually did to help them.

Yeah, there was one student who kept struggling with loops, and honestly it was a bit of a grind for both of us. I'd been running the lab sections, and this student would get the code almost right but then fail the tests every time, so I started to wonder if the problem was the syntax or something deeper. My first instinct was to just show them the right answer, which is what I'd always done before, but that clearly wasn't working. So I started drawing traces on paper with them, stepping through the loop one iteration at a time and writing down the variable values on the page. We did that for about three weeks, and I'm pretty sure I went through more scratch paper than the whole class combined. It reminded me of that show about the detective who solves everything by looking at tiny details, which is a weird comparison, but it kind of fit how we were working. By the end, they could trace a loop on their own without me, and they passed the midterm, which was a great feeling. I still think about it when I'm explaining things to someone now. Did you want to hear what I'd do differently next time?
What would you do differently?

Honestly, I'd have switched to tracing a lot sooner. For the first few weeks I was still doing the thing I'd always done, which was showing the student the right answer and moving on, and I should have noticed that wasn't sticking earlier than I did. I'd also probably ask them to explain their own reasoning out loud before I jumped in, which is something my old roommate used to do when she was studying for organic chem, and it drove me nuts at the time. I think I'd also check in more often, maybe a quick message midweek, instead of waiting for the lab to show me something was wrong. The three weeks worked out, but I'd like to get there faster next time, and I'd want to know sooner whether it's working.
Got it. Let me ask you this—why do you want this kind of role? What draws you to it?

Honestly, I think it's the mix of stuff I've already been doing. I like that the checkout work and the dashboard both had a clear before and after, so you can actually see whether you helped. My roommate says I'm a nerd about this, and she's probably right, because I once spent a whole lunch explaining to her how a page loads, and she still doesn't care. Anyway, I like fintech because the stakes are real. When something's slow or broken, someone's paying for it or waiting on a refund, and that's a good kind of pressure. The double-charge bug from Campus Eats still sticks with me, because I really didn't want anyone getting charged twice for a sandwich. So I'm drawn to a team that takes that seriously and where I can keep learning how payments systems actually work. I'd also like a place where I can keep building the front end and the backend, because I've done both and I'm not sure yet which one I like more. Does that answer it, or did you want me to get more specific about what I'd want to work on?
That's helpful. One more thing—tell me about a time you failed. Something that didn't go the way you wanted.

Hmm, okay, so the one that comes to mind is Campus Eats. I did the ordering backend, and we had a bug where if someone double-tapped Pay, they could get charged twice. I hadn't really thought about how impatient people get when an app feels slow, which is funny because I'm the most impatient person I know. It's like when you're at a crosswalk and you press the button five times, and you're sure that somehow helps. Anyway, I didn't catch it in my own testing because I was testing one tap at a time, like a normal person would, and nobody on the team had really tried mashing the button. When it showed up, I felt kind of sick about it, because it was in the code I wrote. The fix ended up being
How did you find out about it? Like, did a user report it, or did someone on the team catch it?

Honestly, I don't remember the exact moment it surfaced, and I'd rather not make up a tidy story. I think it came up through the support side, since they were the ones fielding messages from students, but I can't tell you whether it was one specific person's complaint or a few of them. It was a while ago, and the Campus Eats group chat was a mess of memes and dining hall complaints, so the details got buried. What I do remember is the feeling when I read the report and realized that the reason it happened was the exact thing I'd skipped in my testing. It also reminds me of when my roommate's phone froze during a delivery order
Right. So after you found out, what did you actually do to fix it?

Right, so the fix was idempotency keys. Basically, each payment request gets a unique key the first time it's sent, and if the same request comes in again, like from a second tap, the server recognizes the key and doesn't charge the card twice. I'd heard the term in a class but never really used it, so I spent a while reading up on how other payment APIs handle it before I wrote anything. I'll be honest that I don't remember every detail of how the key got generated and stored on our side, and I'd want to check the code before I walked you through it line by line. What I do remember is that once it was in, I went back and tried mashing the Pay button over and over, which I should have done before anything shipped. Ever since then, I always test the double-tap case first when something touches money. Did you want me to explain how I'd test that now?
We're almost out of time, so let me ask—do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, just one, if that's okay. What does a typical week look like for someone on the team right now?

Good question. It varies a lot depending on what we're working on, but generally it's a mix of feature work, code review, and some on-call rotation. Early on, you'd probably spend more time pairing with someone to get up to speed on the codebase. And honestly, a lot of time is spent in meetings—planning, retrospectives, that kind of thing. It's not glamorous, but it's how we stay coordinated. Anything else?

Oh, that's helpful, thanks. The pairing part sounds especially useful, because I learn a lot faster when someone's looking over my shoulder, which is probably why the paper tracing with that student worked. The meetings don't bother me. I'd honestly rather sit in a planning meeting than guess what the team needs. I don't think I have anything else. This was a really good conversation, and I appreciate you making time for it, especially with my morning being what it was. I hope I got to show you enough, and if you need anything else from me, like more detail on the checkout profiling or the billing tests, just let me know.

Thanks for that. I really appreciated hearing the specifics—the real user data on checkout, how you worked with that struggling student, the idempotency key fix. That's the kind of detail that matters. We'll be in touch soon with next steps. Good luck with the rest of your semester, and thanks again for taking the time.
