transcript.text: Hey, good to meet you. How's your day been so far?

Hey, good to meet you too! Yeah, today's been pretty good, honestly. I actually had a weird start, my bus got diverted because of some construction near the library, so I ended up walking the last like fifteen minutes, which, fine, it was a nice day for it. I grabbed a coffee from this place by the student union that I think is new, and the barista kept asking me to spell my name, which is funny because it's not even hard. Anyway, I've been kind of hyped for this one, because my roommate actually works at a fintech company too, and she's been telling me about their deploy process, so I've been reading up on that, which is probably why I'm a little caffeinated. How about you, how's your day been?

Ha, can't complain. Busy but good. And hey, that's great you've been reading up on fintech—always good to come in curious.

So I'm curious, what drew you to this kind of role in the first place?

Thanks, yeah, I think curiosity is kind of my thing. Honestly, what got me into this was a side project last year, a food ordering app for campus, which sounds small but got maybe twelve hundred people using it every week. I was doing the ordering backend, and there was this bug where people would double-tap the Pay button and get charged twice, which was a mess. I spent way too long on it, reading about how payment APIs handle retries, and that's when I realized I really liked the money-movement side of things, where a small bug has real consequences for real people. My roommate, the one I mentioned, has been telling me stories about her team's deploy process, and that stuff sounds way more interesting than I expected. Oh, and I also did a job at my school's support team where we had this spreadsheet that people exported every single day, and I helped build a dashboard to replace it, and watching the support folks actually use it made me want to do more of that. So I guess the short version is I like building things that people depend on, and fintech feels like the place where that matters most. What about you, what's the part of the job you're most excited about?

That makes sense. I like that you're drawn to the impact side of it.

Let me dig into that payments bug for a second. You said you spent way too long on it—walk me through what happened. What was the first thing you tried to fix it?

Okay, so the first thing I did was the obvious one, which was disable the Pay button as soon as someone tapped it. I thought that would solve it, and honestly it helped a little, but it didn't fix the real problem. Some people's connection was spotty, so the app would look like it hadn't gone through, and they'd tap again, or the request would go out twice because of a retry. My professor always says the first fix you think of is usually just hiding the symptom, which, yeah, that's what I was doing. So
Right, so you caught yourself. What did you do after that?

Right, so I was kind of stuck for a while, and I went back and forth on whether the client or the server should be responsible for it. Eventually I realized the server had to be the one that recognized a repeat. So I added idempotency keys: the app generates a unique key for each order attempt, sends it with the payment request, and the backend checks whether it's already seen that key. If it has, it just returns the original result instead of charging again. It sounds simple once you say it out loud, but getting the key lifecycle right took a while, especially making sure a failed attempt could still be retried without accidentally creating a second order. There were three of us on that project, and I did the ordering backend, so I wr
Got it. So you owned that idempotency piece end to end on the backend?

Mostly, yeah. The ordering backend was my piece, so the server side of the idempotency check was mine, and I wrote the logic that stores the keys and returns the original result on a repeat. The app side that actually generates the key on each tap was a bit more of a handoff with one of the other two guys, and I'm honestly not 100% sure I'd want to claim I designed that part alone. We were all in one group chat, and I remember a lot of back and forth about it, which is kind of funny now, because at one point somebody suggested we just use a database lock and I spent an entire evening convincing myself that was worse. So I'd say I owned the backend and the key handling on it, and I worked closely with the others on the rest. Does that answ
Yeah, that's helpful. So on the backend side, how did you know the idempotency keys were actually working? How did you test that?

Honestly, the first way I knew was that I just tried to break it. I'd hit the endpoint twice with the same key and check that only one order showed up in the database, and then I'd fire a bunch of requests at once, because that's closer to what happens when someone's phone is lagging and they mash the button. I also tested the failure case, where the first attempt errors out and the retry with the same key should go through without making a second order. That one was trickier, and I kept getting it wrong until I stopped caching the error and only
Only what? What did you change?

Oh, right. So the bug was that I was storing the response for every request with that key, including the failures. That meant if the first attempt timed out or the payment processor errored, the retry would just get back the same error from the cache, and the user was stuck. My professor always says the bug you find while testing is the one that teaches you the most, and I think I was basically teaching myself that for about two days. So I changed it so only successful results get saved against the key, and failed attempts leave the key open, so the retry goes through the full logic again. I had to be careful there, though, because if a request was still in flight, I didn't want a second one racing ahead, so I kept a short "in progress" state for that. Honestly I still think about that part a lot, because it's the kind of thing that works fine in a test and then breaks at 11 p.m. when the network's bad. What's the testing setup like on your side? Do you guys do a lot of that kind of concurrency testing, or is it mostly unit tests?
We do a mix, but I'm curious about you first. You mentioned the billing service on your resume—you improved test coverage there. What was that work like?

Yeah, so that was one of my first real tasks on the team, and honestly it was kind of a slog. The billing service had really thin tests, and I think coverage was around 38% when I started, which, you know, my friend who does security says that's basically a crime. The thing is, the whole team was pretty busy, so the goal was to get it up, and it went to about 61% by the end. I wrote the tests for the invoice proration module, which is the part that calculates partial charges when someone changes plans mid-cycle, and that alone was about 40 tests. Proration is tricky because of all the edge cases around dates and rounding, so I spent a lot of time working through examples on paper before I wrote anything. Two of my teammates covered the rest of the service, and I'd say the collaboration was the best part. What about your team, do you usually write tests alongside features, or is there a separate push for coverage?
We do it alongside, mostly. But I want to back up—you said coverage went from 38 to 61. How much of that 23 percentage point jump was the invoice proration module you wrote?

Honestly, I don't know the exact split, and I'd rather not guess a number on a call like this. I wrote about 40 tests for the proration module, and two teammates covered the rest of the service, so the jump was a mix of all three of us. I could probably figure out the breakdown from the coverage reports or the commit history, but I don't have it memorized. It's kind of funny, because I spent so long on those proration tests, working through date and rounding examples on paper, that I think I was more focused on whether they were right than on how much they moved the number. That's probably the more useful answer, though: the tests I wrote were on the messiest logic in the service. If you want, I can dig up the actual split later and send it to you.
Fair enough. So when you think about those 40 proration tests you wrote, what was the hardest edge case you had to handle?

Okay, the hardest one was a mid-cycle plan change that happened on a day that doesn't exist in every month, like the 31st when the billing period runs into February. Proration depends on how many days are in the cycle, so if you're not careful the math gets weird and you can end up with a partial charge that's off by a day's worth of money. I remember sitting there with a calendar and a pencil, which, honestly, my roommate thought was hilarious, because she uses a spreadsheet for everything. I ended up writing a test for each of the boundary cases, end of month, leap year, a change that lands exactly on the renewal date, and that last one is where I found an actual bug in my own first version. I had it treating the renewal day as part of the old cycle when it should've been the new one. Two of the other tests I wrote were rounding cases, where the cents don't divide evenly across the days, and we had to decide which way to round. I think that's the one I'd flag if I were you, because it's the kind of thing that looks fine until someone's invoice is a cent off.
Makes sense. So you caught that bug in your own code during testing. Tell me about a time when something didn't go the way you expected—maybe a bigger miss, not just a test catch.
Okay, so a bigger one that comes to mind is from my TA job, which isn't exactly software but it taught me a lot about being wrong. I was
Go ahead.

Okay, so I was a TA for Intro to Programming, which was a remote gig, four hours a week, mostly evenings, so I'd be on Zoom with a pile of labs and a cup of whatever coffee I had left. There was one student who kept failing the loop problems, and I'll admit my first assumption was that they just needed more examples. So I kept walking them through syntax, and that didn't work at all, and honestly I was annoyed at myself and a little annoyed at them, which I'm not proud of. The thing that finally clicked was when they said, "I don't know what the variable is doing on the second time through," and I realized I'd never actually checked what they were picturing in their head. My professor always talks about tracing code by hand, and I'd been treating that as a
What changed when you realized that?

Honestly, everything changed. I stopped explaining and just started drawing, so we'd grab a piece of paper, I'd make a little table with a column for each variable, and we'd go line by line, writing down what the value was after every pass through the loop. The first session was kind of awkward because I was basically holding the pencil for them, but after a while they started saying "okay, now it's two" before I did. I think the lightbulb moment for them was seeing that the variable wasn't magic, it was just getting overwritten each time. We kept at it for about three weeks, which, between my evening classes and their schedule, was a lot of Zoom calls. I still have a few of those scratch pages in a folder somewhere, and by the midterm they passed, which honestly made my whole month. It also made me realize how often I jump to explaining instead of asking what the person is actually picturing, and I've tried to carry that into the rest of my work since.

That's a good lesson. So when you think about your first month here, if you were onboarded onto the billing team or the payments side, what's the first thing you'd want to understand about how things actually work?

Honestly, the first thing I'd want to understand is how money actually moves through the system, like what happens from the moment someone clicks pay to when the ledger reflects it. I'd want to trace a real request through the code, the same way I drew loop traces on paper for my student, because I've learned I can't trust my mental model until I've watched the actual values change. I'd also want to know what the failure paths look like in production, especially retries and timeouts, since that's where my idempotency work lived and where I'd want to see how your team handles it. And I'd ask who's on call for billing, because I'd want to know who to bug when something weird shows up at 11 p.m. Oh, and I'd probably spend a day just reading the proration code again, since I wrote those tests a while ago and I'd want to see whether I still agree with my own rounding decisions. Do you guys have a sandbox where I could trace a payment end to end, or is it more of a read-the-code-first situation?

We have both, actually. You'd get sandbox access pretty quickly.

One more thing before we wrap up—you mentioned the payments dashboard you built for the support team. Who actually used that, and what were they doing before?

Oh, the dashboard, yeah. So the support team was six people, and before this they were basically living in a spreadsheet that someone exported every single day from the payments system. It was one of those things everyone just accepted, like, yeah, that's how we do it, even though it was slow and kind of error-prone. The main thing they were doing with it was looking up refunds for customers who called in, and that used to take something like five minutes per lookup, because you'd search through the export and cross-check things by hand. I built the React front end, and a senior engineer built the API it talks to, so I was on the UI side of that. Once it was up, lookups went to under a minute, which sounds like a small thing, but when you're on the phone with someone who's upset about a charge, that difference is huge. I remember one of the support leads telling me she'd stopped keeping the spreadsheet open in a second tab, which, honestly, was the nicest thing anyone said to me that whole term. I also think I was a little too excited about the bar chart I added at one point, which nobody asked for. Do you guys have a support tool like that now, or is it still mostly exports?
We have something, but it's pretty clunky. Anyway, before we finish up, do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, just one, and it's a simple one: what does a typical first week look like for someone on the team?

Good question. You'd spend the first couple days getting your environment set up and doing a code walkthrough with whoever's pairing with you. By day three or four you'd probably pick up a small task, something that touches a few parts of the system but isn't critical path. We try to get people actually committing code pretty quick rather than just reading docs. And you'd have a few sync meetings with the team to get context on what's in flight.

Thanks for taking the time today, Alex. We've got a lot to think about, and we'll be in touch soon.

Thanks, that's really helpful, and honestly the pairing and small first task sound like exactly what I'd want. I appreciate you taking the time today, and it was great to meet you. I'm looking forward to hearing from you, and if anything else comes up, you know where to find me. Have a good rest of your day!
You too, thanks again. Take care!

transcript.text: Hey, good to meet you. How's your day been so far?

Hey, yeah, good to meet you too! My day's been pretty good, honestly. I woke up a little late, which is never great, and I almost missed the bus because I was trying to finish a cup of coffee while also looking for my charger, which I found in my backpack, of all places. The bus was packed, so I ended up standing next to this guy who was reading a whole textbook on tax law, and I kept wondering why anyone would do that for fun. Then I got to the library early, which felt like a win. Anyway, I'm glad I could make this call work, and I'm excited to talk about the internship and what I've been working on.
Ha, yeah, those mornings happen. Glad you made it and that you're here. So tell me a bit about yourself—your background, what you're studying, and what's brought you to this point.

Sure, so I'm a junior in computer science, and I'm about a year and a half into the program, which honestly feels like both forever and no time at all. I got into programming kind of by accident. I took an intro class mostly to fill a requirement, and then I ended up loving the part where you stare at a bug for an hour and then it suddenly makes sense. Since then I've done a few things that I'm pretty proud of. Over the summer I started as a software engineering intern at a fintech startup, and most of my work has been on the checkout flow and some internal tools. Before that I built a food ordering app for campus with two other people, which was honestly chaotic but really fun, and it's had around 1,200 weekly users. I also TA'd an intro programming course, which is where I figured out I actually like explaining things to people, even if it sometimes takes a while to get it across. Oh, and I'm a big fan of the way the library's third floor is quiet on weekday mornings, so that's where I do most of my studying. Anyway, that's kind of the path so far.

Nice. So you've got some solid range there—intern work, a project with real users, and teaching. Let me start with the fintech internship since that's your most recent thing. You mentioned checkout flow and internal tools. Walk me through one concrete thing you built or improved there that you're proud of.

Okay, so the one I'm most proud of is the checkout page speed thing, though I should be clear that I didn't come up with the idea myself. My manager mentioned that the scripts might be part of the problem, and I was kind of like, sure, I'll look. Mobile load was sitting around 3.1 seconds, which doesn't sound terrible until you watch someone tap around on their phone on a bad connection, and it's painful. So I spent a couple of days profiling with Lighthouse and also looking at real user timing, which was honestly my favorite part because the numbers were so different from what I expected. I found three payment scripts loading up front, all blocking the page. I deferred two of them and lazy-loaded the card form so it only pulls in when someone actually gets to that step. That got us down to about 1
Got it, so you got it down to about 1.8 seconds or so? What was the actual number you hit?

Yeah, about 1.8 seconds, so roughly a 40% drop from the 3.1. Honestly I'm a little wary of quoting it too precisely, since the number moves depending on which tool you run and whether the phone's on Wi-Fi or a shaky LTE connection. I ran it a bunch of times, and I think 1.8 was the typical result on mobile, and the real-user numbers were in the same range. It's funny, because the first time I saw the Lighthouse report I thought I'd messed up the setup, and I spent like twenty minutes re-running everything before I trusted it. My roommate says I do that with everything, like I'll recheck the milk expiration date three times. Anyway, the short answer is about 1.8 seconds on mobile, down from about 3.1.
Makes sense. And after you made those changes, did you measure whether it actually affected user behavior—like, did people complete checkout more often, or spend less time on the page?

Honestly, I don't know, and I don't want to make something up. My part was getting the load time down, and I did the profiling and the script changes, but I didn't own the funnel analytics. I think the product side tracks checkout completion, and I'm pretty sure someone was looking at it, but I never sat down and compared before and after numbers for it myself. It's a little embarrassing, because I know I'd spend twenty minutes rechecking a Lighthouse score and then not check that. My manager would be the better person to ask whether anyone measured conversion after the change. What I can say for sure is that the page got about 1.3 seconds faster on mobile, and I'd want to see the behavior data before I claimed it helped people finish checkout.

I appreciate that honesty. So in your first month on the job, if you were working on something like that again, how would you approach it differently to make sure you're connecting the dots between the technical change and the actual business outcome?

Honestly, I'd try to figure out the business question before I touched any code. Last time I jumped straight into profiling because load time was the thing I could measure, and I got really into the Lighthouse stuff. In my first month I'd sit down with whoever owns the checkout funnel and ask what they're trying to move, whether that's completion, drop-off on the card step, or something else. Then I'd make sure we agree on how we'd measure it before and after, so we're not scrambling to figure out the baseline once the change is already live. It's kind of like when I was TAing and a student would ask me to check their code. My first move was always to ask what they expected it to do. I'd probably also set up a little checklist for myself so I don't end up with a great speed number and no idea whether it mattered. Anyway, that's what I'd do differently, and I'd want to know from you how the team usually tracks that kind of thing.

Good instinct. We'll talk more about how we work, but I'm glad you're thinking about it. Let me shift gears a bit. You also mentioned a payments dashboard you built in React for the support team. Tell me about that—who actually used it, and what were they doing before you built it?

Sure, so the payments dashboard was for the support team, and there were six people on it who used it every day. Before that, they were basically working out of a spreadsheet that someone exported every morning, and whenever they needed to look up a refund, they'd be digging through rows and cross-checking columns. It was slow and kind of error-prone, and honestly I think a couple of them had built their own little workarounds that nobody else really understood. I built the React front end, and a senior engineer on the team built the API that the dashboard pulls from, so I want to be clear about that split. The main thing it changed was refund lookups, which used to take around five minutes and now take under one. I remember the first time one of the support people used it live, she kind of laughed and said it felt like cheating, which was a nice moment. Oh, and the spreadsheet had this weird color-coding system that I had to reverse-engineer, which was a whole thing on its own. Anyway, that's the gist of it.
Nice. So you built the front end, the senior engineer built the API. What was the hardest part of your piece—the React part—and how did you solve it?

Honestly, the hardest part wasn't really the React code. It was figuring out what the support team actually needed to see. The spreadsheet had all these columns, and some of them were clearly important, but a few people had their own shorthand for things, and the color-coding thing I mentioned was a big piece of that. So I spent a bunch of time sitting with two of them, watching them look up refunds, and writing down where they hesitated. My first version was honestly too busy, with everything on one screen, and one of them just said "I don't need that" about half of it. I had to cut a lot
And then what did you do after that feedback?

Oh, right, sorry, I got distracted by the color-coding thing. So after they told me that, I went back through the screen with them and asked which fields they actually touched during a refund lookup. Most of it turned out to be stuff they only needed once in a while, so I moved those behind a expand button and made the default view just the search box and the couple of fields that matter for a decision. I also had to check with the senior engineer on the API side, because a couple of the fields I wanted to hide were still being pulled, and we agreed on which ones to keep in the response. Then I had one of the support people try a few real cases while I watched, and she went through them way faster than the first version, which was a relief. I think I also spent an embarrassing amount of time nudging spacing and fonts after that, which my roommate would say is the same recheck-everything thing I do. Anyway, the short version is I cut the screen down to what they used, and then I watched them use it to make sure I was right.
Good. Let me ask you about the Campus Eats app. You said it had about 1,200 weekly users. How were you counting that—what does a weekly user actually mean in that context?

So a weekly user, for the Campus Eats number, was a distinct account that placed at least one order in a given week. We pulled that straight from the database, and the 1,200 figure was from October. I want to be careful, though, because there's a version of that number people throw around that counts people who opened the app, and that's a different thing. We weren't counting app opens, and I don't think we were counting logins either. I'm pretty sure one of my teammates set up the query, and I remember us arguing a little about whether to count accounts or unique phones, since some people had two accounts. Honestly, I went and checked the query more than once, which, yeah, my roommate would say is the same thing as always. The short answer is distinct accounts with at least one order in a week, measured in October.
Got it. So you built this with two other people. What was your piece of it—what did you personally own?

Okay, so there were three of us building Campus Eats, and I did the ordering backend. That meant the part that takes an order, talks to the payment provider, and saves everything to the database. The other two handled the front end and the menu and restaurant side of things. I'd say the ordering backend was the piece I was most responsible for, and it's also where the hardest problem lived. People would double-tap the "Pay" button, and sometimes they got charged twice. That was honestly kind of scary once we noticed it. I ended up adding idempotency keys, so if the same payment request comes in twice, the system recognizes it and doesn't charge again. I'm still a little proud of how that turned out, even though it took longer than I wanted. Anyway, that's my piece, and I'm happy to go deeper on any of it.
That double-charge problem sounds rough. Walk me through how you figured out that idempotency keys were the right solution. Did you consider other approaches first?

Yeah, that one was rough, and I'll be honest that I didn't come up with idempotency keys in some brilliant flash. When we first saw the double charges, my gut was to just disable the button after the first tap, which seemed like the obvious fix. Then I realized that doesn't really solve it, because a slow network can make the app look like nothing happened, so people tap again, or the request retries on its own and the button state doesn't help at all. I spent a couple of days reading through the payment provider's docs, which, to be fair, I'd been avoiding because they're long and kind of dry, and that's where I found the idempotency key stuff. The idea is you generate a unique key for each order attempt and send it along, so if the provider sees the same key again, it returns the original result instead of charging twice. I also looked at doing a lock on the server side, and I think I was leaning toward that for a while because it felt more familiar. But a lock can get messy if the first request hangs or crashes halfway, and the key approach handled retries more cleanly. Honestly, I also remember going back and forth with a teammate about where to generate the key, client or server, and we landed on generating it when the user starts checkout so retries reuse the same one. Anyway, that's the rough path, and I'm happy to get into the details of how we stored the keys if you want.

No, that's clear. One thing I'm curious about though—you mentioned you were TAing an intro programming course over the summer. Your resume shows that overlapping with the internship. How did that actually work? Were you doing both at the same time?

Yeah, they overlapped, and honestly it was more manageable than it sounds on paper. The TA job was about four hours a week, all remote, and I did it in the evenings, so the internship stayed my main thing during the day. The tricky part was switching gears. I'd be debugging a checkout issue at like two in the afternoon, then at seven I'd be answering questions about loops in a discussion thread. I kept a notebook where I wrote down anything I'd promised to follow up on, because my brain was basically full by the end of the week. One student in particular kept failing anything with loops, and I ended up spending about three weeks drawing out traces on paper with them, step by step, over video. It was slow, but they passed the midterm, which was a great feeling. Anyway, I'd say it was a lot to juggle, but the evening schedule was what made it work.
That's good detail. So with that student who was struggling with loops—what changed for them? Was it just the repetition, or did you figure out a specific way of explaining it that clicked?

Honestly, it was a mix of both, but I think the thing that clicked was slowing way down. My first instinct was to explain loops the way I'd learned them, which was basically "the loop goes back to the top until the condition is false," and that made sense to me but clearly not to them. So we just started tracing. I'd have them write the variable values on a piece of paper, one row per pass through the loop, and they'd fill in what they thought would happen before we ran it. Sometimes they were right and sometimes they weren't, and the wrong ones were actually the useful part, because you could see exactly where their mental model broke. By about the third week they'd start predicting the trace before I asked, which was the moment I knew something had changed. I'm not totally sure whether it was the paper or the fact that they stopped being afraid to guess, but they passed the midterm, and they told me afterward that the tracing was what made it make sense. Anyway, I still have that notebook somewhere, and I think it's the best teaching thing I've done.
That's a solid example. Before we wrap up, I want to ask you something broader. Tell me about a time you failed—something that didn't go the way you hoped.

Hmm, yeah, I've got one. The first version of the support dashboard was kind of a mess. I was so focused on making sure nothing from the spreadsheet got lost that I just dumped everything onto one screen, like I was trying to prove I'd covered every column. I was pretty proud of it for about a day, which is funny now. Then I sat down with one of the support people to watch her use it, and she looked at half the screen and said, "I don't need that," very politely. My first reaction was a little defensive, because I'd put a lot of work into it. But she was right, and it was the kind of feedback that stings because you can't really argue with it. I had to cut a lot and rethink the whole layout, which took longer than I'd planned. I think what I took from it is that I'd been building for complet
I hear you cutting off there. What did you take from it? What would you do differently next time?

Yeah, sorry, I was mid-sentence and kind of drifted. What I took from it is that I'd been building for completeness instead of for the person actually using the screen. I was so worried about dropping a column from the spreadsheet that I forgot the goal was making a refund lookup faster, and those aren't the same thing. Next time, I'd spend more time with the people who'll use it before I build anything, even just watching them work for an hour, and I'd show them a rough version early, like a sketch or a clickable mockup, so the feedback comes before I've sunk a week into it. I'd also try to be less attached to the first version, which is harder than it sounds when you've been staring at the same screen all day. I'm glad she was blunt with me, honestly, because it was way more useful than being told it looked good.
That makes sense. Last thing—why do you want this kind of role? What's drawing you to it?

Honestly, a lot of it is that I liked the checkout and dashboard work because it felt like it directly touched people. With the dashboard, a support person could go from five minutes to under one, and that's a pretty clear before and after. With checkout, I got to see that a technical change could make a real difference for someone on a bad connection. I'm still early, and I want to get better at connecting the technical work to whether it actually helps the business, which, as I said earlier, is the part I'm still learning. I also like being on a team where I can ask questions and learn from people who've been doing this longer. I think fintech is interesting because the stakes are real, like with the double-charge problem, where getting it wrong means real money and real trust. And I'll be honest, I like that a startup gives you more chances to own things, even if it's a little chaotic. Anyway, that's the main pull for me.
Got it. Do you have any questions for me?
Yeah, just one, if that's okay. How does the team usually check whether a technical change actually moved a business number, like checkout completion, after it ships?

Good question. We have a product analytics person who owns the instrumentation, and engineers usually pair with them before shipping to agree on what we're measuring. Then we run it for a week or two and look at the data. It's not perfect, but it's way better than guessing. We also have a pretty active Slack channel where people post wins and breakage, so you get feedback fast. It's something we're still iterating on, honestly.

Thanks for taking the time today, Alex. We'll be in touch soon. Good luck with everything.

Sounds like you figured it out, at least for that stretch.

verdicts.notes: Strength: good probing on the checkout measurement method and on idempotency keys, plus both practice questions were asked and the candidate was invited to ask questions. transcript.text: Hi, thanks for coming in. Did you find everything okay today?

Yeah, thanks, everything's good. Honestly the parking situation was a little rough, I ended up circling the lot behind the science building for like ten minutes, which is funny because I almost took the bus, but my roommate said it'd take forty minutes so I drove, and then I got here and realized I'd left my water bottle in the car, so I was kind of a mess for the first five minutes. But I found the building fine, and the front desk person was really nice about pointing me to the right floor. Thanks for asking, I appreciate it.

Ha, yeah, parking here can be rough. Glad you made it up okay though.

So, tell me a bit about yourself—what's brought you to software engineering, and what have you been working on recently?

Sure, so I'm a junior CS major, and I got into it kind of by accident, honestly. I was originally thinking about becoming a pharmacist, and I took Intro to Programming mostly because it fit my schedule, and then I just kept finding myself staying late in the lab trying to get things to work. Which is maybe why I ended up TAing that same class later, which was a lot of fun, and also a good excuse to keep thinking about code every week. Right now I'm a software engineering intern at a fintech startup, and most of my time goes to the checkout flow and some internal tools. The biggest thing I've done there is work on checkout performance. Mobile load was around 3.1 seconds, and I profiled it, found three payment scripts loading up front, deferred two of them, and lazy-loaded the card form, and it got down to about 1.8 seconds. My manager had pointed me toward the scripts, so I did the digging and made the change. I also built a React dashboard that replaced a spreadsheet our support team had been exporting every day, and I did the front end while a senior engineer built the API. Refund lookups went from about five minutes down to under one, which the support folks seemed to like. Outside of work I've also built a food ordering app for campus, and I did the ordering backend there.

That's great context. I'm curious about the checkout work you mentioned—you said you got it down from 3.1 seconds to 1.8. How are you measuring that time? Like, what tool or method are you using to confirm that improvement?

Good question. So I used Lighthouse for most of it, which is the Chrome tool that runs a page in a simulated mobile setting and gives you a performance score and load timings. I ran it a bunch of times before and after, because one run can be noisy, and I kept the same throttling settings so the comparison was fair. I also looked at real-user timing, which is basically data from actual sessions on phones, since a lab test can look great and still not match what customers see. Honestly the real-user side is what convinced me the change was real, because it showed the same kind of drop across the sessions, not just in my test runs. I think the profiling in the browser dev tools was where I spent the most time, just watching the waterfall and seeing the payment scripts block everything early on, which is kind of satisfying when you finally spot it. Oh, and I should say, my manager had pointed me toward the scripts as a starting place, so I did the investigating and the actual changes, but the direction came from them. Anyway, happy to dig into any of those numbers if you want more detail.

No, that makes sense. You did the legwork and validated it both ways, which is smart. I'm glad you mentioned the real-user data—that's the one that matters most.

So you built this Campus Eats app and you said you did the ordering backend. How many people actually used that, and what was the hardest part of building it?

Yeah, so the number is about 1,200 weekly users, and I want to be precise about that because it's easy to inflate. It's distinct accounts that placed at least one order in a given week, and I pulled that straight from the database back in October. I think the app itself was pretty popular for a campus thing, and honestly, a lot of it came from the dining hall lines being brutal, so people just wanted a faster way to order. There were three of us who built it, and I took the ordering backend, which is the part that handles carts, orders, and the payment handoff. The hardest problem was double charges. People would double-tap the Pay button, especially on slow connections, and the app would send two requests, so some students got charged twice. It was really frustrating to debug at first, because it only happened sometimes and I couldn't reproduce it reliably on my own phone. What fixed it was adding idempotency keys, so the backend recognizes a repeat of the same payment attempt and doesn't process it again. Once I got that in, the double charges stopped, and I remember feeling way more relieved than I expected. Anyway, happy to go deeper on how the keys work if you're curious.
That's a solid catch and a good fix. When you say you added idempotency keys—was that something you knew about going in, or did you have to figure out how to implement it?

Honestly, I'd heard the term before, but I didn't really know how it worked until I was stuck on the double charge bug. I remember going down a bit of a rabbit hole, reading a payments provider's docs, and there was this whole section on it. The basic idea is that the client generates a unique key for each payment attempt and sends it along with the request, and the server stores that key with the result. If the same key shows up again, the server just returns the stored result instead of charging again. The part I had to figure out myself was where to generate the key, because if the app makes a new one on every tap, it doesn't help at all. So I ended up creating it when the user opens the checkout screen, and reusing it for that attempt. I also had to think about what happens if the first request actually succeeded but the response got lost, which is kind of the scary edge case. Anyway, I think that's the part I'm still most proud of from that project, even if it was a small change in the end.

That's really good thinking—you understood not just what to do but why it matters. 

Let me shift gears a bit. You mentioned you're a TA for Intro to Programming. Can you tell me about a student who was struggling, and what you actually did to help them?

Yeah, so I TA'd Intro to Programming, and I ran weekly labs for about 40 students, which was honestly the best part of my week. Most of them were pretty quick, but there was one student who kept failing the loop problems, and I could tell it was really getting to them. I'd been through the same thing myself, so I knew the feeling of staring at a for loop and having no idea what it's doing. Anyway, I ended up meeting with them one-on-one, and what worked was drawing out traces on paper, like writing down the variable values line by line as the loop ran. We did that for about three weeks, and I kept having them predict what would happen before they ran anything. By the time the midterm came around, they passed it, which was a big deal for them. I think the thing I'm proudest of from that is they stopped being scared of loops. Also, the TA gig was only about four hours a week, remote, in the evenings, so it fit around everything else pretty well, which is probably why I could commit to those extra sessions.
That's good. So you traced through it with them by hand on paper. Did anything surprise you about what they were struggling with once you dug in, or was it pretty much what you expected?

Honestly, it was a little different from what I expected. I figured it would be something obvious, like not knowing the loop syntax, but the syntax was fine. What got them was that they kept thinking the loop body ran once and then the loop was "done," like it was a single step instead of something that repeats with the variables changing each time. My roommate says I explain everything with a whiteboard, and I think I was doing the same thing, so I kind of stumbled into this without planning it. Once we wrote out the values line by line, they could see the counter going up and the total building, and I think that was the moment it clicked. Their face changed, which was a pretty great moment. I'm not totally sure I'd have caught it that fast if I hadn't just been through the same confusion in my own intro class. Anyway, do you want to know how I set up the sessions, or are you more interested in what I'd change about it now?

No, that's helpful. I'm curious though—you're interning at a fintech startup now. Why'd you want to move into that kind of role rather than, say, staying with more education-focused stuff or something else entirely?

Yeah, so that's a fair question, and honestly I didn't go into fintech on purpose at first. I was kind of looking at a bunch of different internships, and I'd been thinking about the pharmacy track before I switched, so I wasn't sure what I wanted. The startup had a posting that mentioned checkout and payments, and I was like, okay, that sounds like it's real stuff that real people use every day, which is kind of what got me hooked on the campus app too. Also, the TA work was awesome, and I'd love to keep doing some teaching someday, maybe on the side or through something like developer education, but right now I want to get better at building things that are actually in production. I think fintech is interesting because the stakes are high, like after the double charge thing I got really into making sure payments don't go wrong. Anyway, I'm still figuring out long term, but that's where my head's at right now.

That makes sense. You're drawn to the stakes and the real-world impact.

I want to ask you something different now. Tell me about a time you failed at something, or when something didn't work out the way you planned.

Sure, so there's a bunch of stuff that comes to mind, honestly. The one that sticks with me is from the Campus Eats project, back when we were first trying to get the ordering flow working. I had this plan where I'd build the whole backend first, all the endpoints and the database schema, and then hook up the front end at the end. I was really proud of how clean the schema looked, and I spent maybe two weeks on it. Then when my teammate actually tried to connect the app, the response shapes didn't match what he'd built against, and we spent most of a week untangling that. It was kind of embarrassing, because I'd been so focused on doing it "right" on my side that I never checked in with them. I also think I was a little too stubborn about the schema, and I didn't want to change it once I'd already polished it. We ended up agreeing on the API contract up front after that, and everything went faster. Anyway, I think that's probably the biggest lesson I took from it, which is to talk to the people on the other side of the work early, even when you feel like you're not ready to show anything yet.
That's a good one. So you didn't talk to your teammate until after you'd already built it all out. What would you do differently if you were starting a similar project today?

So honestly, the first thing I'd do is sit down with whoever's on the other side of the work and agree on the API contract before writing any real code. Like, what the endpoints are, what the request and response shapes look like, what the error cases are. I'd write it down somewhere we both can see, even if it's just a shared doc or a quick OpenAPI file, because when I think back, half the problem was that we each had a picture in our heads and they didn't match. I'd also keep the schema looser at the start, since I got attached to mine and that made me resist changing it when we needed to. And I'd probably push a really rough version to the front end early, even if it's just stubbed data, so we'd catch mismatches in a day instead of a week. My roommate would say I'd also draw the whole flow on a whiteboard first, which, fair. Anyway, I think the big change is just being less precious about my part and more willing to show it half done.

That's practical. Sounds like you learned from it.

I noticed on your resume that your TA role and your internship both happened in summer 2026. How did that overlap work?

Yeah, so it was a little tight, but it worked. The TA job was only about four hours a week, and it was remote, in the evenings, so I'd usually do the grading and check-ins after I got off work. Honestly, the evenings were the part I had to protect, because I'd get back from the office around six and my brain was pretty fried, so I'd make a cup of coffee and just sit down and go. My roommate thought I was crazy for taking on anything extra, but I really liked the students, so it was worth it. The internship was mostly during the day, and I'd sometimes have a meeting that ran long, which was the only real conflict. If I had to name what made it work, it's that the TA hours were small and predictable, so I could plan around them. Anyway, I did get a little burned out
You got a little burned out—what happened there?

Yeah, it was mostly me doing too much at once and not being great about it. The TA hours weren't really the problem, since four a week is pretty small. It was more that I kept saying yes to extra stuff, like the one student I was meeting with every week, and then the internship had a few weeks where the checkout work ran late, so I'd be on a call until seven and then still have to get my head into TA mode. I didn't really sleep great for a bit, and I noticed I was getting short with people, which I didn't like. My roommate basically told me to pick one thing to stop doing, and I ended up just being more strict about keeping Sunday off. It got better

That's fair. Sounds like you figured it out, at least for that stretch.

Let me ask you one more thing before we wrap up. You've done billing tests at the internship—what was that work actually like, and what did you personally write?

Sure, so the billing tests were a good chunk of my time, and I want to be careful about what I actually did versus what the team did. The coverage on the billing service went from about 38% up to about 61%, which sounds great, but it was a team effort. I personally wrote the tests for the invoice proration module, which was around forty tests, and two of my teammates handled the rest of the coverage. Proration was honestly the fun part, because there are so many edge cases, like mid-cycle plan changes, rounding, and what happens when someone downgrades right before a billing date. I kept finding little assumptions in the code that I had to write down before I could test them. It was kind of nerve-wracking, since billing bugs are the kind of thing that cost real money, so I was pretty careful. I also remember spending a while on one test that turned out to be wrong, not the code, so I learned to double-check my expected values against the spec. Anyway, I'm happy to walk through a couple of those edge cases if you want.

No, that's clear. You owned the proration piece and you were careful about it because the stakes are real.

Before we wrap up, do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, I do, just one. What does a typical week look like for someone in this role, especially how much of the time is spent on new work versus keeping existing stuff running?

Good question. Honestly, it depends on the sprint, but I'd say it's usually around 60-70% new features or improvements, and the rest is bugs, maintenance, and supporting other teams. Some weeks you're heads down building something, other weeks you're context-switching more. It also depends on seniority—early on you get more pairing and code review, which eats some time but teaches you a lot. Anything else?

Um, I think that covers it for me. That 60 to 70 percent split sounds about right for a team that's shipping, and I like that you pair early on, since I'm still pretty new to reading other people's code. Honestly I'd probably want more of that than I'd admit in an interview. I'm also going to try to remember my water bottle this time, because I left it in the car earlier and I'm still a little annoyed at myself about it. Anyway, thanks so much for your time today, I really appreciate it, and I hope I get to hear how things go.
Ha, yeah, grab that water bottle on the way out. Thanks for coming in, Alex. We'll be in touch soon, and good luck with everything.

That's a good example of debugging discipline.

verdicts.notes: Strength: the interviewer asked for concrete baselines, measurements and personal ownership (checkout baseline, delay measurement, coverage, who implemented idempotency), and it covered both practice questions. Weakness: it often evaluated answers ("good catch", "solid", "good example of debugging discipline"), skipped the Payments dashboard, and didn't push back on the vague first-month answer or the timing answer.

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for coming in. Did you find everything okay today?

Yeah, everything's good, thanks for asking. Honestly the building was a little tricky. I came in from the north side, and the badge reader at the side entrance was being weird, so I had to wait for someone to let me in. Then I got lost on the third floor because all the hallways look the same, and I ended up asking a guy with a coffee who turned out to be from facilities, not your team. He was nice about it though. Oh, and I had to stop for coffee too because I barely slept last night, so if I seem a little slow, that's why. But yeah, I'm glad I made it, and thanks for having me.

No problem at all—glad you made it through the gauntlet. The building layout definitely takes some getting used to. Well, you're here now, so let's dig in.

So, looking at your background—you've got the internship at the fintech startup, the TA work, some projects—what drew you to this kind of role, working in software engineering?

Yeah, honestly I think it started in my intro programming class, which, funny enough, is also where I ended up TAing later, so it's kind of a full circle thing. I remember being totally lost for like the first month, and then one afternoon something just clicked, and I got this rush from making a program do exactly what I wanted. My roommate is a music major and he always says he gets that same feeling from playing a chord progression right, so I think I'm just wired for that kind of puzzle. The fintech internship was the first time I got to work on something real people depend on, which is a different kind of pressure. Like, when I was working on checkout, I cared a lot about how long the page took to load, and I kept thinking about people on bad cell service trying to buy something. I guess that's what pulled me toward this kind of role, wanting to build stuff that's actually useful to people, and maybe I'm still figuring out exactly what kind of engineer I want to be. Sorry, that was a bit of a wander.

No, that makes sense. That shift from the classroom click to building something real—that's a good thread.

Let me dig into that checkout work a bit. You mentioned cutting the load time by 40 percent. What was the baseline you were starting from?

Yeah, so the baseline was about 3.1 seconds on mobile, which was the number from Lighthouse and also from real-user timing, so it wasn't just a lab thing. Going from that to about 1.8 seconds is where the 40 percent came from. My manager actually pointed me toward the scripts, which I think was a good call, because I'd been staring at image sizes for like two days and getting nowhere. So I profiled the page, and there were three payment scripts loading up front before anything else. I deferred two of them and lazy-loaded the card form, since most people don't even get to that part until they're ready to pay. It's funny, I was kind of nervous about touching the payment stuff at all, since it's the part where if you break something, people can't buy anything. I did a lot of testing on a throttled connection to make sure it actually felt faster and didn't just look faster on paper. Anyway, is there a specific part of that you wanted me to go deeper on?
No, that's solid. I'm curious though—when you deferred those two scripts, how did you decide which ones to defer versus which one to lazy-load? What was the trade-off there?

Yeah, good question, and I'll be honest, part of it was just looking at what each one did. So there were three payment scripts, and one of them was actually needed for the page to render the total and the button, so that one couldn't really wait. The other two were more like fraud-check and analytics stuff, which I figured could load after the page was already usable. Deferring those meant they still ran, just a bit later, and I had to double check that nothing depended on them being there at first paint. The card form was different because it's a big chunk and most people never even scroll to it until they're ready to pay, so lazy-loading made sense there. The trade-off I worried about was a little delay before the card form appears if someone taps pay fast, so I tested that on a slow connection too. Honestly I'm still not 100 percent sure I got the split right, and my manager asked me the same thing in review, so I think it's worth a second look. Also, the fraud script thing reminded me of a late-night debugging session where I thought the whole page was broken, and it turned out I just had the wrong staging cache, which is a whole other story.
That's fair. So when you tested on the slow connection and saw that little delay before the card form appeared—did you measure that? Like, how much delay are we talking about?

Honestly, I didn't put a hard number on it, which I probably should have. I ran the throttled tests in Chrome dev tools, and I was watching the timeline and just looking at when the card form showed up after tapping the button. It was noticeable on the slow setting, but it didn't feel broken, and I didn't want to over-engineer it. I think I was also kind of stuck on the first part of the problem, and the card form was the less scary piece. My roommate, the music major, would say that's like practicing the hard chord change but not really timing the rest. If you asked me for a number, I'd say I'd want to pull the real-user timing data before I quoted anything, because I don't want to guess in an interview. That's actually one of the things my manager flagged, so I'd want to go back and measure that properly.

Got it. That's a fair instinct to pull real data rather than guess.

I want to shift gears for a second. You mentioned on your resume that you improved test coverage across the billing service. What was the coverage before and after, and what did you personally write?

Yeah, so coverage went from 38 percent to 61 percent across the billing service. What I personally wrote was the tests for the invoice proration module, which was about 40 tests. Two of my teammates did the rest of the coverage work, so I want to be clear about that, because the 61 percent is a team number, not mine. Proration was a good place for me to start, since it has a lot of edge cases, like mid-cycle plan changes and rounding, and I spent a lot of time working through those by hand on paper before I wrote the test cases. Honestly that's kind of how I approach most things, I like sketching it out first, which I also do when I'm helping students with loops. Anyway, I think the proration tests are the part I'm most proud of, because they caught a couple of rounding issues that would have been annoying to find in production.
Nice. So those rounding issues—did you find them yourself while writing the tests, or did they already exist in the code?

Hmm, honestly, I want to be careful there, because I said "caught" a bit too quickly. The rounding edge cases came up while I was writing the tests, since I was working through mid-cycle changes by hand on paper and the numbers didn't always land where I expected. But whether those were actual bugs already sitting in the code, or whether I was just misreading what the spec wanted, I don't want to guess in an interview. I'd have to go back through the ticket history and the PR comments to be sure. It reminds me of a time a student in my section swore the autograder

Fair enough. Let me ask you something different. Tell me about a time you actually failed at something—either in the internship or the TA work or one of your projects. What happened, and what did you learn from it?

Yeah, a failure question, okay. The one that comes to mind first is the Campus Eats thing, though it's more of a near miss than a full failure. We were building the ordering backend, and users would double-tap the Pay button, so sometimes they got charged twice. That was really stressful, because nobody wants to be the person whose code double-charges people. I'd been treating it as a frontend problem at first, like maybe the button just needed to disable faster, and that didn't fully fix it, because the request could still go through twice on a slow network. What actually fixed it was adding idempotency keys on the backend, so the second request gets recognized as a repeat and doesn't charge again. I learned that you can't really rely on the UI to protect you from duplicate requests, and that the server has to be the one that enforces it. I also learned to think about the failure path before the happy path, which I'm still getting better at. Honestly I think about that bug a lot now, and it's a good example of why I like working on payments code even though it scares me a little.

That's a good catch on your part—shifting from frontend to backend. So when you realized the button disable alone wasn't working, what made you think to look at the server side? Was that your idea, or did someone point you there?

Honestly, I don't remember exactly who said what first, and I'd rather not claim it was all my idea when it was a team effort. It was a bunch of us on a call trying to figure out why the double charges kept happening, and somebody said something like, the button can't be the only thing stopping this, which I think was the real turning point. I was pretty stuck on the frontend, mostly because that's where I'd been spending my time, and I kept tweaking the disable timing like it was going to magically fix a network problem. Once the idea of idempotency keys came up, I went and read a few payment provider docs to understand how they handle repeated requests, and that's when it clicked for me. There's a whole side story
Got it. So once you understood the idempotency key approach, did you end up implementing it yourself, or did someone else on the team take that?

Yeah, I did end up implementing it, since I was the one on the ordering backend, so the server side was mine. I'll be honest, though, it wasn't a solo thing. The other two builders were in the same codebase, and we talked through where the key should live and how long to keep it around, so I wouldn't call it a one-person fix. What I actually wrote was generating a key for each payment attempt and having the backend check whether it had already seen that key before it sent anything to the payment provider. I also had to figure out what to return when a repeat came in, because the first request might still be in progress, and that part took me a while to get right. I tested it by hammering the endpoint with repeated requests on a throttled connection, which is kind of the same habit I had with checkout. Oh, and that's the part where I spent an entire weekend convinced the bug was in the database, when it turned out I'd just forgotten to clear a test key. Anyway, yeah, the implementation was mine.
That's a good example of debugging discipline. Let me ask you this—in your first month on the job here, how would you approach getting up to speed on a codebase you've never seen before?

Okay, so I think I'd start by picking one real user flow and following it through the code, kind of like how I approached the checkout page. With checkout, I didn't read the whole frontend first. I just followed what happened when someone loaded the page, and that showed me where the time was going. So I'd want to do the same thing here, maybe start with a small bug or a small ticket so I have a reason to touch the code. I'd also read the existing tests, because they usually tell you what the original authors thought was important, and the proration tests taught me that the edge cases are where the real logic lives. I'd try to find the person who knows the messy parts and ask them a few specific questions, not "how does this work," but more like "why is this done this way." I'd probably keep a running doc of what I figure out, since I tend to forget things if I don't write them down. And honestly, I'd be asking a lot of questions in the first couple we
Makes sense. Before we wrap up, I want to circle back to something on your resume. Your TA role and the internship overlap in summer 2026. How did that work timing-wise?

Yeah, that one's pretty simple, thankfully. The TA job was only about 4 hours a week, and it was remote and in the evenings, so it mostly sat outside the internship hours. I'd check in with the professor or the course staff on the schedule each week, just so nothing slid, and I kept a shared calendar so the office hours and the grading didn't pile up on one day. Honestly the bigger juggling act was my commute, because I was taking the bus in and some days the timing was rough, but the evenings were easy to protect. So the short answer is it worked fine because the TA hours were light and at night, and I never had to pick one over the other.
Got it. We're nearly out of time here, so let me ask—what questions do you have for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, just one, if that's okay. What does a typical first month look like for someone new on the team, like what would you expect me to have shipped or learned by the end of it?

Good question. Honestly, the first month is mostly about getting oriented and shipping something small—nothing that's going to move the needle by itself, but something that gets you comfortable with the process, the codebase, how we work together. Could be a bug fix, could be a small feature. By the end of month one, I'd hope you've got a sense of how decisions get made here, who knows what, and where the rough edges are in the code. If you've shipped something and you're asking good questions, that's a win for me.

Any other questions?
No, I think that's everything for me, thanks. That was a really helpful answer, and it makes me more excited about the role. Thanks for taking the time to talk with me today.
Great. Thanks for coming in, Alex. We'll be in touch soon with next steps. Good luck with the rest of your semester.
