transcript.text: Hi, thanks for coming in. Did you find everything okay today?

Yeah, everything's good, thanks for asking. Honestly the trip over was kind of a mess, I took the bus instead of driving because I didn't want to deal with parking near the building, and the bus was ten minutes late, so I was sitting there refreshing the map thinking I'd be late for sure. But I made it, and the lobby has this really nice coffee machine, which I'm now a little bit obsessed with. Anyway, yes, all good, and thanks for having me.

Ha, glad you made it and found some good coffee. Those buses can be unpredictable. Well, we're glad you're here.

So, tell me a bit about yourself—your background, what you've been working on, that kind of thing.

Sure, so I'm a junior in CS, and I've been doing a software engineering internship at a fintech startup this year, which has been a lot of fun, honestly, although I'm still figuring out how much of it I actually understand versus how much I just nod along to. Before that I did a bunch of random stuff in school. The thing I'm probably most proud of is a food ordering app for campus, Campus Eats, that around 1,200 people use every week. I was one of three people building it, and I did most of the ordering backend, which is where the hardest problem was. People kept double-tapping the Pay button and getting charged twice, so I ended up adding idempotency keys so repeat requests don't create a second charge. I learned a ton from that one, mostly that users will tap things in ways you never planned for. At work I've been on the checkout page, and I got mobile load time down from about 3.1 seconds to around 1.8. My manager pointed me toward the scripts, and I did the profiling and the changes, which was basically deferring a couple of payment scripts and lazy-loading the card form. I also built the React front end for a payments dashboard the support team uses now, which replaced a spreadsheet they were exporting every day. Oh, and I TA'd an intro programming course, which I'd recommend to anyone, because explaining loops to someone who's stuck is the best way to figure out whether you understand them yourself.
That's a solid overview. I want to dig into a couple of those. Let's start with Campus Eats—you mentioned 1,200 weekly users. How are you measuring that number?

Oh, good question, and honestly I should have been clearer about it earlier. It's distinct accounts that placed at least one order in a given week, and I pulled it straight from the database back in October. Which means it's not counting people who just opened the app and browsed the menu, and it's not counting anyone twice if they ordered four times that week. I remember we argued a bit about that definition in our team chat, because one of the other builders wanted to count any login, and I was like, no, that's going to make us look way bigger than we are. We went with orders, which I think is the more honest number. Also, October was kind of a weird month for us because of midterms, so I'm not totally sure how steady it is week to week. If you want, I can pull up the exact query I ran, or we can get into how the idempotency keys work, since that's the part I spent the most time on.

I appreciate the detail there. So you were pretty intentional about how you defined it, which is good. Let me ask you this—you mentioned the double-tap problem with the Pay button. Walk me through how you actually figured out that was happening and what you changed.

Yeah, so that one was kind of a mess to track down, and I'll be honest, I didn't figure it out right away. A few people in our beta group messaged us saying they got charged twice, and my first reaction was that it had to be the payment processor doing something weird, because that felt like the less embarrassing explanation. I spent like a whole afternoon going through the processor's logs, which, if you've never done that, is a special kind of boring. Eventually I noticed that the two charges were usually a second or two apart, and the order IDs were basically the same, which made me think the app was sending the request twice. And then I looked at the button handler and realized nothing was disabling it after the first tap, so someone double-tapping on a slow connection would just fire off two requests. Which, honestly, is pretty normal for a student app, because we weren't thinking about it. So the fix was idempotency keys: the client generates a unique key for each payment attempt, and the backend checks if it's already seen that key before it creates a charge. If it has, it just returns the original result. I also disabled the button after the first tap, which helps the user experience, but the idempotency key is the part that actually guarantees you don't get charged twice, because the button alone doesn't stop retries after a network timeout. I think that's the part I'm proudest of, mostly because it was the first time I had to think about a bug where the user did something totally reasonable and the system still broke.

That's a really good breakdown. So you owned that end-to-end—you dug into it, found the root cause, and fixed it the right way, not just the quick way. I'm curious, when you look back at it now, is there anything about how you approached it that you'd do differently?

Honestly, yeah, the biggest thing is that I wasted that whole afternoon blaming the payment processor. I really didn't want it to be our fault, so I kept digging through their logs when I should have just looked at our own button handler first. My roommate, who's way more chill about this stuff, basically said "check your own house first" and I kind of rolled my eyes, but he was right. I also think I should have written a test that simulates a double tap and a timeout retry before I called it done, because right now it's more like I reasoned my way to it and hoped it worked. We did end up testing it manually, but a repeatable test would have been better. And I probably should have asked the beta testers for their exact timestamps earlier, since that's what made the pattern obvious once I finally got them. Oh, and I'm
You're good, take your time.

Sorry, I got distracted there. I was going to say I'm also kind of a bit of a perfectionist about this stuff now, which is funny because at the start I was just happy it worked. Honestly the thing I'd change most is my instinct to blame whatever's outside my code first, like the processor, or the bus, or the coffee machine if I'm being ridiculous. My roommate keeps joking that I'd blame the Wi-Fi for a bad commit. So if I were doing it again, I'd check our button handler and write that double-tap test on day one, instead of spending the afternoon in someone else's logs. Then I'd know in five minutes whether it was us. That's probably the lesson I took most seriously from it, more than the idempotency key stuff itself.

Fair enough. Let me shift gears a bit. You mentioned the checkout page work at your internship—you cut load time from 3.1 seconds down to 1.8. How are you measuring that, and what was the first thing you tried?

Okay, so for measuring it, we used Lighthouse for the lab numbers, and then real-user timing from our analytics so we could see what people on actual phones were getting. Lighthouse is great for repeatable tests, but it runs on a fake setup, and the real-user numbers are what made me believe it was a problem. Honestly the first thing I did was not very glamorous. My manager pointed me toward the third-party scripts, and I was like, okay, but I'd never profiled a page before, so I spent a day just watching the network waterfall and seeing what loaded when. That's when I saw there were three payment scripts loading up front before the page even showed anything useful, which was kind of wild once I noticed it. Then I deferred two of them and lazy-loaded the card form so it only pulls in when someone actually gets to that step. That got us from about 3.1 seconds to about 1.8 on mobile. I still wonder
What would you do differently if you were starting that project over today?

Honestly, probably start by setting up the measurement before touching anything, because I kind of jumped in with Lighthouse and the waterfall and didn't write down a clear baseline first. I'd also ask my manager more specifically which scripts he thought were the problem, since he pointed me in the right direction and I spent a day rediscovering it. And I'd check whether the card form lazy-load broke anything on slower connections, because we tested it mostly on decent Wi-Fi in the office, and I'm not totally sure how it behaves when someone's on a bad signal on the train. Oh, and I'd probably have looped in whoever owns the payment vendor integrations sooner, since deferring those scripts is the kind of thing that can cause weird edge cases if you don't know the vendor's loading expectations. That's the part I'm least sure about, honestly, so I'd want someone who knows that side to look at it with me.

That's thoughtful. So you spotted a real problem but you're also aware of the gaps in how you validated it. That's good. Let me ask you this—tell me about a time you failed at something, either at school or at work.
Okay, a failure... so, the TA job. I was the TA for intro programming, and early on one student kept getting stuck on loops, and I kept explaining them the same way
I'm following—keep going.

Yeah, so I kept explaining loops the same way, just louder and slower, like that was going to help, and honestly it didn't. The student would nod, say "okay," and then get the next problem wrong. I was getting frustrated, and I think they were too, and I remember thinking maybe I just wasn't a good teacher. Eventually I stopped talking and grabbed some paper, and we drew out the traces by hand, line by line, tracking what the variables were doing on each pass. It took about three weeks of doing that, and it was slow, and I'm not going to pretend it was some big breakthrough moment. But they ended up passing the midterm, which I was honestly pretty relieved about. The thing I took from it was that my explanation wasn't the problem, my approach was, and I should've tried a different method sooner instead of repeating the same one harder. Oh, and the TA job was only about four hours a week, remote, in the evenings, so I was juggling it with the internship, which is its own story.
Got it. So you figured out that repeating the same thing wasn't working and you switched tactics. Did you change how you approached other students after that, or was it just this one person?

Good question. Honestly, it changed how I did most of the rest of the job. After that student, I started asking people to walk me through their own trace before I said anything, because half the time I could see where they were going wrong just by watching them do it on paper. Some of the other TAs thought that was overkill, and one of them told me it was slow, which, yeah, it was, but I didn't have a better answer for why it worked. I also got a bit more careful about checking whether someone actually understood or was just nodding along, which I'm definitely still bad at myself, as I mentioned. I think the thing I'd say is that I got more patient, though I'm not sure it was patience so much as just being willing to stop and try something else. And if I'm being honest, the course was also during the same semester I was figuring out the internship, so my evenings were kind of a blur, and I probably didn't reflect on it as much as I should have at the time.

Makes sense. So you learned something and applied it, but you're also saying you were stretched thin that semester. Speaking of which, I noticed your TA role and the internship overlapped in summer 2026. How did you manage both at the same time?

Yeah, so the TA job was only about four hours a week, and it was remote and in the evenings, so on paper it didn't clash with the internship that much. Honestly, the thing that made it tight was less the hours and more the timing of my brain. Some days the internship ran late, and I'd finish a call, grab something quick to eat, and then have to get my head back into explaining recursion to someone. My roommate thought I was crazy for not just dropping one of them, but I really liked the TA work, and I didn't want to quit in the middle of the semester. I also got pretty good at blocking off the same evening slots every week so I
Sorry, go ahead.

Oh, right, sorry. I was going to say I got into the habit of blocking the same evening slots every week, so the TA stuff felt like a fixed appointment and not something I had to squeeze in. My calendar looked like a mess, with little colored blocks everywhere, and my roommate said it looked like a hospital schedule. Some weeks the internship would run over, like when a deploy went sideways, and then I'd be doing the TA session on a bowl of cereal with my camera off. That's honestly where I learned that the hours weren't really the issue. It was switching between two kinds of thinking, debugging a payments flow and then walking someone through a loop. So the short answer is I kept it structured and didn't let either one bleed into the other too much. I'm not sure I'd call it managing it well, though, because I think I was just stubborn about not quitting.
Fair enough. So you stuck it out partly because you didn't want to quit mid-semester. I'm curious—why do you want this kind of role? Like, what draws you to software engineering?

Yeah, so, honestly, I think what draws me in is that moment when something finally clicks, like when the double-charge bug stopped being a mystery and became a specific line in a button handler. I like that software gives you that feeling a lot, where you can be confused for days and then suddenly it makes sense, and you can usually check it. I also really like building things people actually use, which is maybe why the Campus Eats stuff stuck with me, even though it was messy. There's something about seeing a thousand-plus people open an app you wrote and not think about it. The fintech work is a big part of why I'm excited about this, because payments are high stakes and kind of unforgiving, and I like that kind of pressure, most days anyway. I'm still figuring out what kind of engineer I want to be, like whether I end up more on the backend or the frontend side, but I think I want to keep working on things where getting it right matters. Also, I've been on a lot of buses lately, so I've had time to think about this, which is ironic given how the ride over went.
That makes sense. Alright, we're almost out of time here. Do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, I do, just one. What does a typical week look like for someone starting on the team, like how much of it is building new stuff versus fixing things that are already in production?

Good question. Honestly, it depends on the sprint and what's on fire, but a rough split is maybe 60-70 percent on new features or improvements, and the rest is bugs, on-call rotation stuff, and code review. First month or two you'd probably skew a bit more toward the on-call and review side while you're getting up to speed, but we don't throw you in the deep end. It's a real team, so you're not alone with it.

Do you have anything else?

Nope, I think that covers it for me, thanks. That split sounds about right, honestly. I'd rather learn the codebase by fixing stuff and reading reviews than get dropped into something huge, so the first couple months sound good to me. Thanks for your time today, I really appreciate it.
Great, thanks for coming in and for the thoughtful answers. We'll be in touch soon with next steps. Good luck with the rest of your semester, and thanks again.

Honestly, I don't think we did a proper before-and-after measurement, and I'd rather say that than make something up. Hold on—when you say checkout was taking three seconds, how were you measuring that? Like, was that a real user metric or a lab measurement?

Did you do any testing before shipping that to production? Like, how confident were you that you weren't breaking something?

Yeah, we did some testing, though I'd call it more careful than thorough. I ran the checkout flow end to end on a few devices and a staging build, including the card form loading late, because that was the part I was worried about. Honestly, I wasn't fully confident, and I kept refreshing the staging page like it might suddenly break. Honestly, the proration tests are the work I'm proudest of from that internship.

I remember staring at the failing output for a while, convinced I'd messed up my math, so I went back through my spreadsheet line by line, which took forever. My roommate was getting frustrated with me because I kept saying "one more check" over dinner. But my numbers were right and the code was wrong. It was rounding at a different step than the spec said, so the error only showed up on certain split amounts. I didn't dig into how long it had been happening in production, and I'm honestly not sure. I flagged it to my manager and the fix was pretty small, but that's kind of the point of proration tests, right? The bugs are small, but they add up across a lot of invoices.
Makes sense. So you also built a payments dashboard in React that the support team used—what was that replacing, and what did you personally build?

Sure, so the dashboard was replacing a spreadsheet the support team was exporting every day. Got it. And did you talk to the support team directly to understand what they needed, or was that all through the senior engineer?

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for coming in. Did you find everything okay today?

Yeah, all good, thanks for having me. Honestly I almost didn't find the building, because the parking garage on that side is a maze, and I ended up circling the block twice behind a delivery van. Oh, and I grabbed a coffee from the place downstairs, which is kind of a dangerous move for me because I get jittery, so I'm hoping I don't talk too fast. Anyway, I'm really glad to be here, and I appreciate you guys fitting me in.

Ha, well, the coffee gamble—I respect that. We'll just keep it conversational, no need to rush anything.

So let's start with the basics. Walk me through your background a bit. Where are you coming from, and what's brought you to this point?

Sure, so I'm a junior in CS, and I've been at it for about three years now, which honestly feels like both forever and no time at all. I got into it kind of by accident, I was originally going to do pre-med, took an intro programming class to fill a requirement, and then I spent the whole semester way more excited about the homework than the chemistry. My roommate says I talked about it nonstop after that, which is probably true. Right now I'm doing a software engineering internship at a fintech startup, which is a pretty good place to be, though the office coffee machine is a whole other story. I also TA the Intro to Programming course, which I do remotely in the evenings, about four hours a week, so it fits around classes and the internship pretty well. Before that I'd mostly been doing little side projects, and I built a food ordering app for campus with two other people, which was a lot of fun, and that's really what made me want to do more of this kind of work. So yeah, that's kind of the arc, from pre-med dropout to, hopefully, someone who builds stuff people actually use.

That's a good arc. I like that you found something that actually grabbed you.

So you're doing both the internship and the TA role right now—how are you managing the two at the same time?

Honestly it's been a bit of a juggling act, but a manageable one. The TA job is only about four hours a week, and it's remote and in the evenings, so it doesn't clash with the internship during the day. The tricky part is that the evenings are also when I'm trying to do my own coursework, and my roommate has very strong opinions about me sitting at the kitchen table with my laptop at ten at night. I also have to be pretty disciplined about the TA stuff, because one student in the class was really struggling with loops, and we spent about three weeks drawing out traces on paper together. That took more time than the official hours, and I had to make a point of not letting it bleed into the rest of my week. I'd say the internship is what I'm really prioritizing right now, but the TA job keeps me sharp on fundamentals, which I think helps more than I expected. Anyway, that's kind of how it's been working so far.
That makes sense. Let me dig into the internship a bit more. I see on your resume that you cut checkout page load time by 40%. What was the baseline there, and how did you measure it?

Okay, so the baseline was about 3.1 seconds on mobile, which, honestly, my phone was the worst offender, because it's the one I always test on and it's basically a potato. We measured it two ways: Lighthouse for the lab numbers, and real-user timing from the actual app, since a lab test can look great and real people on bad signal still wait forever. My manager pointed out that the scripts might be the problem, and I'll admit I was kind of skeptical at first, but then I profiled the page and found three payment scripts loading up front before anything else. We deferred two of them and lazy-loaded the card form, so it only loads when someone actually gets to the payment step. That brought it down to about 1.8 seconds. I know I'm rambling a bit, sorry, I get excited about page load stuff more than I probably should. The main thing I'd say is that I did the profiling and the change, but the idea to look at the scripts
No, that's good detail. So your manager suggested looking at scripts, you profiled it, found the culprit, and made the change. What would you do differently if you were starting that project over?

Honestly, probably the first thing I'd do differently is set up the measurement earlier. We were kind of scrambling to get the baseline right, and I spent a while going back and forth between Lighthouse and the real-user numbers before I trusted either one. I think if I did it again I'd write down exactly how each number was collected before touching any code, which sounds boring, but it would've saved me a couple of confusing days. I'd also probably ask the people who own each of those scripts what they're actually for before deciding which ones to defer, because I mostly went off what the page looked like and what the timing said. There's a podcast I've been listening to about engineering postmortems, and one guy says the best projects are the ones where you write the failure modes down
That's thoughtful. When you say you'd ask the script owners before deciding which ones to defer—did you end up talking to them after you'd already made the change, or did you just kind of go ahead?

Honestly, I mostly just went ahead. I looked at what each script was doing on the page and what the timing showed, and I deferred the two that didn't seem needed up front. I didn't really go talk to the people who owned them first, which in hindsight is the part I'd change. I think I was a little nervous about slowing things down, and my manager had already pointed me at the scripts, so I kind of ran with it. Looking back, I was lucky nothing broke, because a payment script can matter in ways that don't show up in a load-time chart. I still think the speed win was real, but I'd want to ask first next time. That's probably the biggest lesson I took from the whole thing, honestly, more than the performance stuff itself.
Fair enough. Let me ask you about the billing tests you worked on. The resume says you improved test coverage across the billing service. What was the coverage before and after?

Yeah, so coverage went from 38% to 61%, which is a pretty big jump, though I want to be clear that a lot of that was the team's work, not just mine. I wrote the tests for the invoice proration module, which was about 40 tests, and two of my teammates handled most of the rest of the service. Proration is the part of billing that's honestly kind of nerve-wracking, because if you get the math wrong, someone gets charged for the wrong number of days and then you're in a support ticket for a week. So I spent a lot of time on edge cases, like mid-cycle upgrades and leap years, which I probably spent too long on. I also learned that coverage percentage is a pretty blunt number, because you can hit a high number with tests that don't really check much. So I tried to make sure the proration tests actually asserted on the amounts instead of just making sure the function ran without crashing. That's kind of what I'd want to talk about more, if we get to it.
I want to understand your piece of it better. Of those 40 tests you wrote for proration, what was the hardest one to get right?

Okay, so the hardest one was a mid-cycle upgrade that also crossed a billing boundary, which sounds way more dramatic than it was. Basically the customer switches to a more expensive plan halfway through the month, and the proration has to figure out how many days were on the old plan versus the new one, and then account for the fact that the invoice period doesn't always line up with the calendar month. I kept getting the amounts off by a day or so, and at first I thought my expected values were wrong, which I spent an embarrassing amount of time on. Turns out I was counting the days inclusively in one place and exclusively in another, and the code was right and my test was wrong, or the other way around, I honestly don't remember which by the end of it. I ended up writing out the calculation by hand on a notepad, the same way I did with the student who was stuck on loops, which I think is just my thing now. What finally helped was pinning the expected amount to a specific cents value instead of a rounded dollar figure, so a one-day error would actually show up. Anyway, that's the one that kept me up. There's also a funny story about a leap year test I wrote, but I'll spare you.

Got it. So you found the bug by being precise about what you were asserting on. That makes sense.

Let me shift gears. Tell me about a time you failed at something.

Oh, that's a good one to ask, because the Campus Eats app has a story I'm not totally proud of. We were a three-person team, and I built the ordering backend, so when people started reporting they'd been charged twice, that was my code. The cause was pretty dumb in hindsight: if someone double-tapped the "Pay" button, which people do constantly when an app feels slow, the request went through twice. I'd been so focused on getting the happy path working that I never really thought about what happens when the same action fires two times. My roommate, who uses the app way more than I do, is the one who first mentioned it, and I remember feeling kind of sick reading the messages. The f
What did you do after you found out?

Honestly, the first thing I did was panic a little and check whether anyone had actually been charged twice, because that's real money and real people. We pulled the order logs and found a handful of duplicate charges, and I went through each one and refunded them, and I told the other two builders what had happened instead of quietly patching it. Then I fixed the actual problem by adding idempotency keys, so each payment request gets a unique key and the backend recognizes a repeat and doesn't process it again. I also disabled the button after the first tap on the frontend, but that was more of a band-aid, because the real protection had to be on the server. I'll admit I didn't think about any of that until after it happened, which is kind of the whole lesson. I also remember being annoyed that my roommate was the one who caught it, but honestly, that's the reason it got fixed fast. Anyway, that was probably more than you wanted, but that's the story.
No, that's useful. So you caught it, refunded people, and fixed it with idempotency keys. Looking back, what would you do differently from the start?

Honestly, the big thing is I'd treat payments as the place where you think about failure first, not last. I was so focused on getting the happy path to work that I never asked what happens if the same request shows up twice, and with money that's a really bad question to skip. So from the start I'd design the payment endpoint with idempotency keys, and I'd write a test that fires the same request two or three times and checks that only one charge goes through. I'd also sit down with the other two builders and list out the ways things could go wrong, like slow networks, retries, and people tapping buttons, before we wrote any code. It's kind of like what I said about the postmortem stuff, where you write the failure modes down first. My roommate keeps joking that I should make a checklist for everything, but for payments I think she's right. Anyway, that's what I'd change.
Makes sense. Let me ask about the payments dashboard you built in React. Who actually used it, and what were they doing before you built it?

Right, so the dashboard was for the support team, which is six people, and before we built it they were basically living in a spreadsheet that got exported every day. Whenever someone wanted to look up a refund, they'd have to find the right export, search through it, and hope the data was current from that morning. That could take around five minutes per lookup, which doesn't sound terrible until you multiply it across a whole team and a whole day. I built the React front end, and a senior engineer built the API underneath it, so I want to be clear that I wasn't doing it alone. Once it was live, refund lookups dropped to under a minute. I remember one of the support people saying it was the first time she didn't have to keep a second tab open for the spreadsheet, which was a nice moment. I also spent a lot of time going back and forth with them about which fields they actually needed, and honestly I think that conversation mattered more than the code. Anyway, that's the gist of it.
When you say you built the React front end, what specifically did you build? Like, what components, what did you have to figure out on your own versus what the senior engineer kind of handed you?

Okay, so the main screens were a search page where you could look up a refund by customer or order ID, a results table, and a detail view that showed the refund history and status for a single transaction. I built those components and the state handling around them, so things like loading states, what happens when a search returns nothing, and keeping the filters in sync with the URL so people could bookmark a search. The senior engineer had already set up the API, and I think the auth and the basic data-fetching layer were mostly done when I got to it, so I was mostly consuming endpoints that already existed. The part I had to figure out on my own was the table, because the support team wanted to sort and filter by a few different fields at once, and I got a little lost in how to keep that performant with a few thousand rows. I ended up talking through it with the senior engineer, and honestly a lot of what I learned was from watching how he structured the API responses. I think I also made a couple of UI choices that were probably wrong, like a modal I later wanted to turn into a regular page, but the support team seemed happy enough. Anyway, that's the rough breakdown.
Got it. So you built the components and state handling, and the senior engineer had the infrastructure in place. What's the one thing you'd do differently if you were building it again?

Honestly, the big one would be talking to the support team even more before I wrote any components. I did some of that, but I mostly went off the fields they told me they needed, and I didn't really watch them use the spreadsheet in real time. If I had, I probably would've figured out the sorting and filtering needs earlier, instead of getting stuck on the table later. I also think I'd push for a quick pass on performance with realistic data sizes from the start, not once I was already lost in it. I did end up asking the senior engineer a lot of questions, which was helpful, but I'd rather have asked them before I was halfway through. My manager has a line about how the cheapest time to fix a design is before anyone's built it, and that stuck with me. So yeah, more time with the actual users up front, and more early testing with real data volume.
That makes sense. We're nearly out of time here, so let me ask—why do you want this kind of role? What draws you to it?

Yeah, so honestly, what draws me to this kind of role is that I like building things where somebody on the other end actually depends on them. The payments dashboard was the first time I really felt that, because the support team went from a spreadsheet to something that saved them real time every day, and that felt way better than a class project that gets graded and then forgotten. The Campus Eats stuff pushed the same direction, except it was more of a gut check, since it taught me that when money is involved you really have to think about what goes wrong before anything goes wrong. I also like that fintech has that kind of stakes built in, and I think the proration work was a good example of why I enjoy it, even though it made me want to throw my laptop at one point. I'm still pretty early, so I'm trying to figure out how to get better at the stuff I keep messing up, like asking people what they need before I start building. That's kind of why this role appeals to me, because it sounds like the kind of place where I'd get to learn that from people who've been doing it longer. Sorry, that got a little long. The short version is I want to build things that matter to real people, and I want to do it somewhere I can keep learning.
That's a good answer. Do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, one quick one: what does a typical week look like for someone starting on the team?

Good question. Honestly, the first week or two is a lot of onboarding—getting your environment set up, meeting the team, understanding how we ship things. After that, you're usually paired with someone on a small project to get your bearings, something with real impact but not mission-critical. By week three or four, you're usually carrying a piece of a larger project alongside someone more senior. The pace picks up pretty fast, but we try to make sure you're not drowning.

Thanks a lot for taking the time today. We'll be in touch soon, and I appreciate you being thoughtful and honest about the stuff you've done. Good luck.

Thanks, that's really helpful, especially the part about not drowning. I appreciate you guys making the time today, and I'm glad I got to talk through all of this. Have a good rest of your day, and I'll look out for the email. Oh, and I hope the coffee downstairs is better than the one I got this morning.
Ha, I'll take that as a warning. Take care, and we'll be in touch.

I think I'd also disable the button as soon as it's tapped, so there's a visual cue that something's happening, and I'd make sure the server checks for an existing order before it creates a new charge. My roommate says that's the same logic as proofing bread: you don't just hope it rises once, you build in a check at every step. There's probably a part of me that wanted to ship it faster, too, and I'd tell myself to slow down on anything touching money. I also would've asked a senior engineer to review the payment path specifically, instead of assuming it was fine because the happy path worked. Anyway, that's what I'd do differently, and I'm still a bit embarrassed that it took a teammate to find

Got it. So you'd build in the safeguards upfront instead of after testing. That makes sense.

Let me ask you this—why are you interested in this kind of role? What draws you to it?

Yeah, I think what draws me to this is that fintech is where software touches real money and real people's bills, so the stakes feel higher in a way I actually like. My internship was the first time I got to work on something like that, and I found that I liked caring about the details, like the card form loading order or making sure a payment doesn't go through twice. I also like that a lot of the work is about making things faster and less confusing for people who just want to pay for their food or their rent and move on. I'm not totally sure yet whether I want to stay on the payments side long term or end up somewhere else, but I'd like to keep learning how these systems hold up under pressure. Also, I should mention the TA job I had this year was four hours a week, remote, in the evenings, so I'd have time to keep that up alongside a role like this, if that matters. Anyway, that's a big part of why I'm here.
That's helpful context. Just to clarify—you mentioned the TA role was this past summer. How did that overlap with your internship at the fintech startup?

Yeah, I think I mixed up my timeline a little there, sorry. The TA job and the internship overlapped, so I was doing both at the same time. The TA role was only about four hours a week, remote, and in the evenings, so it fit alongside the internship without too much trouble. There was one stretch where a student kept getting stuck on loops, and I sp
What ended up changing for that student? Like, did they get unstuck, and if so, what actually helped?

Yeah, they did get unstuck, which was honestly the best part of the job. The student kept tripping up on loops, especially figuring out when the loop stopped, and they'd just stare at the screen. I ended up sitting down with them for about three weeks and we drew out traces on paper, like a table with a column for each variable, and we'd walk through each iteration by hand before running anything. At first it felt slow, and I kept thinking about my internship backlog, and I may have been eating a sad granola bar the whole time. But once they started predicting what the loop would print before running it, something clicked, and they passed the midterm. I think the paper part
Did you keep using that same approach with other students who were stuck, or was it something specific to them?

Mostly it was just that one student, honestly. I didn't really have a set method I took to everyone. The class had around 40 students and I was doing weekly labs, so most people were fine with the regular office hours and the autograder feedback. This one student needed more hands-on time than I could give the whole room. If another student had come to me stuck on loops, I'd probably try the paper traces again, since it worked, but I'd want to see if the problem was the same first. I did notice some people just wanted the answer quickly, and I'm not sure that's the same thing as learning it. Anyway, I think that's the honest answer. I don't want to make it sound like I had a big teaching philosophy when really I just sat there with one person for a few weeks.
Fair enough. Let me ask you about the payments dashboard you built at the fintech internship. Who actually used that thing day to day?

Yeah, the dashboard was for the support team. There were six people on it, and before that they were basically exporting a spreadsheet every day and digging through it by hand to find refunds. I built the React front end, and a senior engineer built the API that fed it. The main thing it changed was refund lookups, which went from around five minutes down to under one. I remember one of the support folks saying it was the first time her morning didn't start with a spreadsheet, which was nice to hear. Honestly, the API side was way beyond what I could have done alone, so most of the credit there goes to my senior engineer. Anyway, that's who used it and what it did.
So you built the front end—what was the hardest part of that, technically speaking?

Hmm, honestly, the hardest part was less about React itself and more about getting the front end to line up with the API my senior engineer was building at the same time. We were working on it in parallel, so there were a few times I'd build a screen around what I thought the data looked like, and then the response would come back a little different. I spent a lot of time with the browser dev tools open, just looking at the raw responses and trying to figure out why a field was empty. It was a bit tedious, but it taught me to ask a lot more questions before I start building. I also had to make the lookup feel fast enough that the support team would actually trust it over the spreadsheet, which I think mattered more than any single bug. I don't want to overstate my part, though. If you want the real technical details on the API side, he'd be a much better person to ask than me.
That makes sense. Quick one—before you built the dashboard, what exactly were the support team doing with those spreadsheets? Like, what was the workflow?

Yeah, I'm going to be honest that I didn't shadow them for a whole day, so I'm piecing this together from what they told me and from the setup I saw. As I understood it, every day someone on the team exported a big spreadsheet of transactions, and then they'd search through it by hand whenever a customer asked about a refund. That usually meant finding the customer's order, checking whether the refund had gone through, and sometimes cross-checking a second tab. I remember one of them had a color-coding system she'd built herself, which was clever but also kind of a sign of how much manual work it was. It's funny, my roommate and I were just talking about how people build these elaborate workarounds without anyone asking them to. Anyway, the short version is that they were doing a lot of searching and double-checking, and that's what the dashboard was meant to replace. If you want the exact steps they followed, one of the support leads would be a much better source than me.
Got it. We're running short on time here, so let me ask—do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?

Yeah, I do, and I'll keep it short since you're pressed for time. What does a typical week look like for someone in this role, especially how much of it is building new things versus keeping existing systems running?

Good question. It's probably 60-40, new features to maintenance and support. You'd get some sprint work on the product side, but you're also on call for bugs and customer issues, especially if you're touching payments or checkout. The team's small, so you get ownership pretty quickly, but you're not totally alone—there's a senior engineer and a product manager you'd be working closely with.

Anything else?
Yeah, just one more. What does the first few months look like for someone new, like what would you want me to have figured out by the end of it?

By month three, I'd want you to have shipped at least one small feature end-to-end, know the codebase well enough that you're not asking where things are every day, and have a sense of who your go-to people are for different kinds of questions. Also, honestly, I'd want to see that you can take feedback without getting defensive. That matters more than being perfect early on.

Alright, I think we're good. Thanks for taking the time today, Alex. We'll be in touch either way within the next week or so.

Thanks so much, I really appreciate you taking the time today. That's helpful to hear, especially the part about feedback. I'd rather learn from someone who's been doing this longer than pretend I've got it all figured out. I'm looking forward to hearing from you, and thanks again for having me.
You got it. Take care, and safe travels on that bus.

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for coming in. Did you find everything okay today?

Oh, yeah, everything's good, thanks for asking. Honestly, the campus parking situation this morning was a bit of a nightmare. I circled the lot behind the engineering building for like fifteen minutes, and I'm pretty sure I saw the same maroon Civic go around with me the whole time, which is kind of funny in a sad way. Then I found the building, and the security guy at the desk was super nice, he asked if I was here for the interview and I said yes, and he said good luck, which, I don't know, made me feel a bit better. I actually had a coffee on the way, so I'm fully awake now, so that's good too.

Ha, yeah, parking here is rough. But glad you made it and you're caffeinated. That's half the battle.

So let's jump in. Can you walk me through your background a bit? Just take me from where you started through to now.

Sure, yeah. So I started out kind of unsure about computer science, honestly. I took Intro to Programming my first year mostly because it fit my schedule, and then I ended up loving it, which surprised me. My professor that year had this habit of starting every lecture with a bad joke, and I still think about them sometimes when I'm debugging. Anyway, I ended up being a TA for that same class, which was four hours a week, remote, in the evenings, so it worked around my other stuff. One student kept failing loops, and I spent about three weeks drawing traces on paper with them, and they passed the midterm, which was honestly the most satisfying thing I've done. Last year a few friends and I built a food ordering app for campus, and I did the ordering backend. It got to around 1,200 weekly users, which I was pretty proud of. The hardest bug was people double-tapping Pay and getting charged twice, so I added idempotency keys to fix it. Now I'm a software engineering intern at a fintech startup, and that's where I've been working on the checkout page. I got the mobile load time down from about 3.1 seconds to about 1.8, mostly by deferring some payment scripts and laz

Got it. So you've got a good mix of things going on. Let me dig into the fintech internship a bit, since that's your most recent work.

You mentioned cutting the checkout load time down pretty significantly. What was the baseline you started with, and how were you measuring that time in the first place?

Yeah, so the baseline was about 3.1 seconds on mobile. We used Lighthouse for the lab runs, and then we also had real-user timing from the production app, which is what I trust more, because Lighthouse runs on a fake throttled phone and real people are on all kinds of connections. Honestly, I didn't love that part at first. I spent a whole afternoon fighting with the analytics setup because it kept reporting weird numbers, and I was convinced I'd broken something, but it turned out a timing event was firing twice. My manager had mentioned looking at the scripts, so I did the profiling, and there were three payment scripts loading up front on every page. I deferred two of them and lazy-loaded the card form, since most people don't even reach it until the last step. That got us to about 1.8 seconds. Sorry, I think I went a bit long there. Was there a specific part of the measurement you wanted me to go deeper on?
No, that was helpful. You mentioned your manager suggested looking at the scripts — what would you have done differently if they hadn't pointed you in that direction?

Honestly, I think I would have been a lot slower to get there. Left to myself, I probably would have started by squinting at the Lighthouse report and going straight to the biggest-looking warnings, which for a lot of pages are images and unused CSS. Those are the things everyone tells you about, so I'd have assumed that was the problem. My roommate is always saying I trust the first thing that sounds right, and that's kind of what I'd have done here. It's a bit embarrassing, but I'd have spent a day or two on image compression before I looked at what was actually blocking the page. Once my manager said to look at the scripts, I could open the waterfall and see that three payment scripts were all loading before anything else on every page, which was the real problem. So I guess what I'd do differently now is look at the waterfall first, before I start guessing at fixes.
That makes sense. So when you first joined the fintech team, what did you work on in your first month or so? How did you get ramped up?

Yeah, so the first few weeks were mostly getting my dev environment working, which took longer than I'd like to admit. The repo had some setup steps that weren't in the README, and I spent most of a Tuesday going back and forth with a teammate who was super patient about it. My manager paired me with someone on the checkout team for the first couple of weeks, which helped a lot. I was reading through the codebase, and honestly the payments side is pretty intimidating, there's a lot of stuff you can't just poke at because it touches real money. I also sat in on a few standups and kept a running list of questions in a notes doc, which I think annoyed nobody. Eventually I got into the checkout page work, which is where the load time stuff came from. I also did some smaller tickets around the same time, mostly UI cleanup, and that's how I got comfortable with the deploy process. I think by the end of the first month I could actually ship something without someone holding my hand, which felt like a big deal.
That's good context. You also have the payments dashboard on your resume — can you tell me about that one?

Yeah, the dashboard was one of my favorite things to work on. Honestly, it started because I got a little obsessed with the support team's spreadsheet. Every day they exported a big CSV from the billing system, and they'd sort and filter it by hand, and one of them had a color-coding system that only she understood. My roommate's dad does something similar with his tax receipts, so I kind of get it. Anyway, the goal was to replace that spreadsheet with a React dashboard for the six people on support. A senior engineer built the API it pulls from, and I built the front end, which was mostly figuring out what they actually needed to see. The biggest win was refund lookups, which used to take about five minutes each and now take under one. I think what I'm proudest of is that I sat with two of the support folks while they used it, and I changed a bunch of things based on what they got stuck on. Sorry, I went a little long. Did you want me to get into how we handled the data syncing, or more about the React side?
No, that's useful. So you built the front end — what specifically did you build yourself versus what the senior engineer owned?

Yeah, so the split was pretty clear. The senior engineer built the API, and that included how the data got pulled from the billing system, so I honestly can't speak in much detail about the backend internals. I did everything in the React front end, which meant the screens the support team actually looked at every day, the search and filter stuff that replaced their spreadsheet sorting, and the refund lookup view, which is the part that got faster. I also handled the state management and how the pages talked to the API, which was a bit of a learning curve for me since I'd only done small React projects before. My roommate kept telling me to just use whatever library was trendy, but I went with the simplest thing that worked, which was mostly the senior engineer's suggestion anyway. If you want, I can tell you more about the parts I'd do differently now, because there's definitely a few things I'd change.
Sure, what would you change?

Honestly, the biggest thing I'd change is that I'd write more tests for the front end from the start. I mostly checked things by clicking through them, and that worked fine for a six-person team, but a couple of times a filter broke after a change and I didn't catch it until someone on support told me. My roommate has this whole speech about how tests are just you talking to your future self, and I used to roll my eyes at that, but he's right. I'd also handle loading and error states better. Early on, if the API was slow, the screen just sat there blank, and the support folks would hit refresh and make things worse. And I'd have pushed harder to see the daily workflow before building anything, because I ended up rebuilding a couple of views after I sat with them. So if I did it again, I'd start with the support team's actual day, then build the smallest version, then add tests as I go.
That's fair. Let me ask you this — you've got the TA role and the internship both listed for summer 2026. How did those overlap, or did they?

Yeah, they did overlap a bit, but it wasn't a big deal. The TA job was four hours a week, remote, and it was in the evenings, so it basically slotted into whatever else I had going on. I think the thing that made it work was that I could do the tutoring over video or on a shared doc, so I didn't have to commute anywhere. My roommate jokes that I was the only TA who could also be found at a standup in the morning, which, fair. Honestly, I'd double-check the exact dates on my resume before
Got it. So you're managing both pretty well at the time. Let me ask you something different — tell me about a time you actually failed at something, or something that didn't go the way you hoped.

Yeah, sure. The one that comes to mind is the first version of the campus food app. Before we added idempotency keys, we just had the Pay button fire a request, and when people double-tapped it, they got charged twice. Honestly, I didn't see it coming, because in testing I was the only one using it, and I never double-tapped. Two of our first users messaged us about it in the same afternoon, and one of them was pretty upset, which I totally understood. We refunded everyone that day, and I spent the next couple of nights reading about how payment APIs handle retries, which is how I landed on idempotency keys. The fix itself wasn't that hard once I understood it. What stuck with me is that I'd been testing the happy path and calling it done. Now I try to think about what a stressed-out or impatient user would do with the thing before I ship it. Anyway, that's the one that stung the most.
That's a good one. So what would you do differently if you were building that payment flow again from scratch, knowing what you know now?

Honestly, the first thing I'd do is put idempotency keys in from day one instead of bolting them on after people got charged. I'd generate a key on the client when the checkout screen opens, send it with every payment request, and have the server treat repeat requests with the same key as the same payment. I'd also disable the Pay button as soon as it's tapped, which is the obvious frontend fix, but I'd still keep the server-side check, because the button isn't the only way a request can get sent twice. My roommate, who is an actual ethics-and-tech nerd, would probably also say to think about what happens when a request times out, because the user doesn't know if it went through, and you have to handle that state on purpose. Looking back, I'd also write tests that simulate double-taps and flaky network calls before I ever shipped, since I was the only person testing and I never tried to break it. So yeah, keys from the start, a disabled button, and a test that taps Pay three
Makes sense. So shifting gears a bit — why do you want this kind of role? What's drawing you to this work?

Honestly, I think it started with the dashboard. Watching the support team spend their days in that spreadsheet, and then seeing refund lookups go from about five minutes to under one, made me realize how much I like building things that real people use every day. My roommate's always joking that I get weirdly excited about boring stuff, and he's not wrong. Payments are also a good fit for me, because after the double-charge thing in my campus app, I've become a bit obsessed with how money moves through software and what happens when it goes wrong. The checkout work at my internship has been the most interesting part so far, since every millisecond there affects whether someone actually finishes buying something. I like that the stakes are real but the problems are concrete, so you can usually tell whether you fixed something. I also want to work somewhere that takes engineering seriously, where you're expected to measure things and not just guess, which is basically what I learned from the load time project. So that's what's pulling me toward this, I think. Sorry, I can keep going if that's too much.

No, that's good. I've got a couple more things I want to cover. You mentioned running labs as a TA for 40 students — was there a student who stands out to you, or a moment where you felt like you really made a difference?

Yeah, there's one student who really stands out. He kept failing the loops problems, and I could tell he was getting frustrated, honestly kind of embarrassed about it. So instead of just re-explaining the syntax again, I sat down with him and we drew out traces on paper, step by step, tracking the variables on each iteration. We did that for about three weeks, which was more time than I'd planned to give one student, but it just kind of happened. And then he passed the midterm, which was honestly the most satisfying thing I've done. My roommate says that's the same thing I do with debugging, just with more pencil. Anyway, I think the part I'm proudest of is that he stopped being scared of loops. I don't know, it's kind of a small thing, but it felt big to me. Sorry, I know that's a bit of a tangent from the fintech stuff.
No, that's useful to know. One more thing — you mentioned the billing tests on your resume. What did you actually work on there?

Yeah, so the billing service tests were one of those things where I got to contribute but wasn't really driving it. Coverage went from about 38% to 61%, and I wrote the tests for the invoice proration module, which was around 40 tests. Two teammates covered the rest of the billing code. Proration is a fun one to test, honestly, because there are so many edge cases, like mid-cycle plan changes and rounding, and I spent a good chunk of time just working out what the right answer even was before I could write the assertion. My roommate says I've basically turned every problem into a spreadsheet, which might be true. I felt pretty good when the coverage number moved, but the part I was happier about was catching a couple of rounding bugs while writing those tests. Sorry, I got a little into the weeds there.

No, that's exactly what I wanted to know — what you personally wrote. So you had 40 tests for that one module. Before you started, did you have a sense of what the coverage baseline was for that specific module, or was it all bundled together?

Honestly, I don't think I had a clear number for that specific module before I started. The coverage report we looked at was for the whole billing service, so I saw the 38% for the service as a whole, not for proration on its own. I'm not sure whether the report broke it down by module, and I didn't go digging for it at the time. I mostly just opened the proration file, saw that it had almost no tests, and started from there. My roommate would probably say that's very on brand for me, just diving in and figuring out the gaps as I go. If you want, I can look at the numbers again, but I'd rather not guess at a percentage I don't actually remember.
Fair enough. Do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, just one. What does a typical week look like for someone on the checkout team, like how much of it is new feature work versus fixing things and watching metrics?

Good question. It's pretty balanced, honestly. Most weeks you're splitting time between shipping something new — usually a small feature or an optimization — and then keeping an eye on the metrics to make sure it's working as expected. We also spend time on tech debt and test coverage, which sounds like something you care about. You'd be paired with a senior engineer for the first few weeks, similar to what you had at your internship.

Thanks for coming in today, Alex. We've got what we need. You'll hear from us early next week.

Thanks so much, I really appreciate you taking the time. That answer about the checkout team sounds great, and the pairing thing is good to hear. I'll look out for the email early next week. Have a great rest of your day, and thanks again!
You too. Take care.

I deferred two of them and lazy-loaded the card form, so it only loads when someone gets to that step.
Got it. So you deferred two of the three. What about the third one—why did that one stay up front?

Fair enough—I appreciate that you didn't guess. Just trying to understand the trade-offs you made. So after you made those changes, how did you actually measure that the page got faster? Did you look at the same metrics again, or did you do something different?

I used the same tools both times, Lighthouse and the real-user timing data, so I could compare like with like. Before the changes, mobile load was about 3.1 seconds. After, it was about 1.8. I reran Lighthouse on the same mobile setup and checked that the real-user numbers moved in the same direction, so I wasn't just seeing a good run in the lab.
That's solid—1.8 from 3.1, so roughly a 40% improvement. Did you ship that change, and if so, did you see the real-user numbers actually move after it went live?

Yes, it shipped. I watched the real-user numbers after release, and they moved in the same direction as the lab results, so it wasn't just a good Lighthouse run. I'd still want to look at a longer window before calling it settled, since one week of data can be noisy.
Makes sense. Did you do anything else on the checkout page after that, or was that the main win there?

That was the main change. I did some smaller cleanup along the way, but nothing else that moved the load time in a meaningful way. If you want the exact list of follow-up commits, I'd have to check the history, since I don't remember every small change off the top of my head.
No need to dig into the details. So you also built that React dashboard for the support team. Tell me a bit about what that replaced and what you actually built versus what the team did.

So the dashboard replaced a spreadsheet the support team was exporting every day. They'd pull the data together by hand, and the dashboard lets them look up refunds directly instead.

On my part, I built the React front end. A senior engineer built the API the dashboard talks to, so I was working against that. It's been good to see the support team actually using it day to day.
How many people on the support team are using it, and how often are they hitting it? Do you have any sense of that?

I don't have solid usage numbers, so I'd rather not guess. The support folks were the ones using it day to day, and the best feedback I got came from sitting with them and watching how they worked. That taught me more about building for non-engineers than any metric would have. Is there something specific about adoption you're trying to understand?

Just trying to get a sense of the impact. Sounds like you got good qualitative feedback at least. Let me shift gears a bit—you've got a lot going on. You're interning, you're TAing, and you built that Campus Eats app. How are you managing all of that, and which one takes up most of your time?

Honestly, the internship takes the most time. It's the one with real deadlines and people counting on me. The TA job is only about four hours a week, and it's remote and in the evenings, so it fits around everything else. I'd say the TA work actually keeps me grounded, because explaining loops to someone who's stuck makes me slow down and check my own understanding.

Campus Eats was more of a project I did with two other builders, and I did the ordering backend. It's not something I'm juggling day to day the way I am with the other two. The main thing I've learned about managing all of it is to be honest with myself about what I can actually finish in a week.

That makes sense. On the TA side—you mentioned running labs for about 40 students. Tell me about a time when one of those students was really stuck, and what you actually did to help them get unstuck.

Sure. There was one student who kept failing the loop problems. They understood the syntax fine, but they couldn't tell what the code would actually do step by step.

So for about three weeks, we'd meet and I'd have them trace the loop on paper. We'd write out the variables and update them line by line, and they'd predict the output before we ran anything. At first they kept skipping steps, so I'd ask them to say out loud what the counter was at each pass. Slowly they started catching their own mistakes before I pointed them out.

By the midterm they passed. What stuck with me is that the problem wasn't really loops. It was that they didn't have a reliable way to check their own thinking, and that's something I had to relearn myself when I was a student.
That's a good example. Did you change how you ran the labs after that, or was it just working with that one student?

Mostly it was just that one student, but I did start suggesting the paper tracing to other people who seemed stuck on loops. I didn't overhaul the labs or write anything formal. I just got more in the habit of asking, "Can you tell me what the variable is after this pass?" before jumping in with the answer.
Makes sense. So shifting gears again—you also improved test coverage on the billing service at the internship. What was the coverage before, and what did you actually write?

I wrote most of the tests for the invoice proration module. Proration is easy to get subtly wrong, like mid-cycle plan changes and rounding, so I spent a lot of time on edge cases. Two teammates covered the rest of the service.

As for the coverage numbers, I don't want to quote them from memory and get them wrong. What I remember is that the proration tests taught me a lot about how billing logic fails, which mattered more to me than the percentage itself.
Fair. So when you were writing those proration tests, what was the hardest edge case you ran into, and how did you figure out how to test it?

The hardest one was a mid-cycle upgrade. If someone switches plans partway through a billing period, the daily rate has to be split across two plans, and the rounding can leave the total a cent off depending on how the days fall.

To figure out how to test it, I first worked out by hand what the invoice should come to, day by day, and wrote that down as the expected value. Then I compared it with what the
Yeah, go ahead.

...compared it with what the code actually produced. When they didn't match, I traced through the rounding step by step until I found where the cent was going. Once that was clear, I wrote a few variations around it, like upgrades on the first day, the last day, and a leap-year month, so the test wasn't just passing for one lucky setup.
Good. Quick question—when you found that rounding issue, did you fix the code yourself, or did you surface it to someone else?

I flagged it to my teammate who owns the billing module, and we went through it together. I wasn't going to change core billing logic on my own without someone who knows that code reviewing it. I did put the fix up as a suggestion in the pull request, and they took a look at it before we merged anything.
Makes sense. So I want to ask you something else before we run out of time. Tell me about a time you failed at something—what happened, and what did you take from it?

Probably the Campus Eats payments bug. When I first wrote the ordering backend, I didn't think about what happens if someone double-taps "Pay." The request would go through twice, and users got charged twice. I'd tested the normal flow and assumed that was enough.

Fixing it meant adding idempotency keys so the server could recognize a duplicate request and not process it again. That part was fairly straightforward once I understood the problem. The bigger lesson was about how I was testing. I'd been checking the happy path and not asking what a user might do that I hadn't planned for. Now, with anything that moves money, I try to list the ways a request can go wrong, like retries, timeouts, and double taps, before I call it done.
That's a solid lesson. And why do you want to work on backend infrastructure and platform reliability? What draws you to that kind of work?

I think it's the moment when something I built has to hold up under real use. With the double-charge bug, the normal flow worked fine. It was the retries and double taps that broke it, and that really stuck with me. I like thinking about what happens when things go wrong, not just when they go right.

The checkout work was similar. The slowness came from things I wasn't expecting, like scripts that had nothing to do with the checkout itself. Finding that kind of hidden problem is satisfying, and I think it's the same instinct behind reliability work: figure out what's really happening under the surface.

I'm also drawn to it because it's the part of the system people don't notice when it works. If payments just go through and nobody gets charged twice, that's the goal. I'd like to get better at building things that way.
That makes sense. We're almost out of time here, so let me ask—do you have any questions for me or the team?

feedback_leaks.quote: Thanks for being thorough and honest in your answers—I appreciated that.
