verdicts.notes: Strength: the interviewer asked pointed baseline and measurement questions on the checkout and dashboard claims, and it covered both practice questions and the candidate's questions. Weakness: it dropped the unanswered 40% baseline after the candidate dodged it, and it did not press for numbers on the dashboard. It also leaked evaluative praise ("good lesson", "sounds solid", "thorough and honest"), and it barely touched the billing tests.

transcript.text: Hey, good to meet you. How's your day been so far?

Hey, good to meet you too! My day's been pretty good, thanks for asking. I had a slow start, then got into a groove after lunch. Honestly I'm a little nervous, but I've been looking forward to this one. How about you, how's your day going?
Can't complain, thanks for asking. Busy but good. Well, I'm glad you're here. So, what drew you to this role? What kind of work are you looking to do?

I'm really drawn to fintech because the stakes feel real. When a checkout page is slow or a payment goes through twice, actual people feel it, and I like that kind of pressure. I've been doing an internship at a fintech startup this year, and that's where I found I enjoy the frontend and the payment-flow side the most. I want to keep building things that people depend on every day, and I'm hoping to go deeper on the reliability and performance side of that. This role seemed like a good place to do that, especially with a team that's already shipping payments work.
That makes sense. You mentioned cutting checkout page load time by 40% during your internship—what was the baseline there, and how did you actually measure that improvement?

Honestly, the measurement side is hard to quantify. It was messy, and I learned more from the process than from any single figure. What stuck with me was how much time I spent just figuring out what was slowing things down. Once I started profiling, the problem looked very different from what I'd assumed. Can I ask what your team usually uses to track performance, like page speed or real-user timing?

We use a mix of synthetic benchmarks and real user monitoring, so we see both the lab numbers and what customers actually experience. But I'm curious—when you started profiling and the problem looked different from what you assumed, what did you actually find? What was the first thing you changed?

Mostly that it wasn't the code I'd been poking at. I'd assumed the slowness was in our own rendering, but when I profiled the mobile page, the bulk of the waiting was third-party payment scripts loading up front, before anything else. My manager had pointed me toward the scripts, and that was the right call. The first change was deferring two of them so they didn't block the page, and then lazy-loading the card form so it only loaded when someone actually needed it. I was surprised how much of the problem was just what was loading first, and not anything fancy.
Got it. So you deferred the scripts and lazy-loaded the form—did you own those changes end-to-end, or were you working with someone else on the implementation?

Yeah, I owned it. My manager pointed me toward the scripts as a place to look, but I did the profiling myself, then made the changes and tested them. It was a small enough scope that I could handle the whole thing, though I did run it by my manager before it went out. Is there a particular part of the process you want to hear more about?
No, that's helpful. Let me ask you this—in your first month here, if you joined the team, how would you approach getting up to speed on the payments codebase?

Honestly, I'd start small and go with what's in front of me. I'd read through the code for the one or two flows I'd be touching first, instead of trying to take in the whole repo at once. Then I'd find the tests and run them locally, because they usually show how the code is supposed to behave better than the docs do. I've done that on the billing service, writing tests for the invoice proration module, and it helped me get a feel for the edge cases.

I'd also want to sit down with someone on the team for an hour or so and ask them what's bitten them before. That's usually where the real gotchas are. And I'd pick a small, low-risk bug or ticket early on, so I get comfortable with the deploy and review process without the pressure of something big. Does your team have a good onboarding doc, or is it mostly learning by doing?

It's a mix—we have the basics written down, but yeah, a lot of it is learning by doing and leaning on the team. That approach sounds solid.

Let me shift gears a bit. Tell me about a time you failed or something didn't go the way you planned.

Yeah, I've got one from my Campus Eats project. I was on the ordering backend, and we had a bug where people who double-tapped "Pay" got charged twice. I hadn't really thought about that case when I wrote the payment flow. Once we saw it, it was a bit embarrassing, but it was also the hardest problem I've worked on.

I ended up adding idempotency keys so repeated requests for the same order couldn't create a second charge. What stuck with me was that I'd been testing the happy path, and I didn't think enough about what happens when a user does something unexpected. Now I always ask what happens if this request runs twice, or fails halfway through.
That's a good lesson. When you found out about the double-charge bug, how did you discover it? Was someone on the team catching it, or did a user report it?

It was a user report that got us looking at it. Once we had the details, we dug into the logs and reproduced it by tapping "Pay" twice really fast. Looking back, I should have caught it before anyone else did. Since then I've made a habit of asking what happens if a request runs twice, even on small features.
Fair. So with the idempotency keys—was that something you implemented yourself, or did you work with someone else on that fix?

Yeah, I wrote the fix myself. I was on the ordering backend, so the idempotency key logic was mine. I did check the approach with my teammates before merging, since the payment flow touches a few other pieces, and they gave me some feedback on the edge cases. But the implementation and the testing were on me.
Makes sense. You also mentioned running labs as a teaching assistant for Intro to Programming with about 40 students. What was the hardest part of that role for you?

The hardest part was patience, honestly. Most of the students were fine with the lab exercises, but one kept struggling with loops. They'd get the syntax, then freeze when the loop had to actually do something across several iterations.

What finally helped was sitting down and drawing out the trace on paper, tracking the variables line by line with them. We kept at it for about three weeks. It was slow, and I had to resist just giving them the answer. I learned that explaining the same idea three different ways is sometimes what it takes. They ended up passing the midterm, which felt great.
That's patient work. Did you follow up with them after that, or was it mostly just those three weeks of lab time?

Mostly just those three weeks, honestly. I was a TA for a lot of students, and the role was only about four hours a week, remote, in the evenings, so I didn't have a lot of spare time for one-on-one follow-up outside the lab. I did check in with them a couple of times before the midterm, and they seemed more confident by the end. I'd like to think they kept that momentum after the course, but I don't really know. Is there something specific about how you'd handle mentoring students that you're curious about?
Not really—I was just curious how much you stayed connected. Let me ask you about the payments dashboard you built at your internship. Who actually used it, and what was it replacing?

The support team used it. It replaced a spreadsheet they'd been exporting every day, which was a pain. I built the React front end, and a senior engineer built the API behind it. Honestly, the best part was watching the team start using it without much training. What made the biggest difference, I think, was how fast refund lookups became, and I really liked seeing that change how their day went.
How fast are we talking? Like, what was the workflow before, and how much faster did the dashboard make it?

Honestly, it's hard to put an exact number on it. The old way was a daily export, then searching through rows to find the right customer and order, and that could take a while depending on how messy the data was that day. The new version was just a search box and a results view. What I remember most is that people stopped dreading refund requests. I'm curious how your support team handles refunds now. Is it mostly a self-serve thing, or do they still go through engineering for some of it?
It's a mix. But I want to circle back—when you built that dashboard, how did you know what to build? Like, did you talk to the support team first, or did someone hand you a spec?

Mostly I sat with the support team and watched them work. I wanted to see where they got stuck in the spreadsheet, not just what they said they wanted. The senior engineer had already scoped the API, so my job was figuring out what the screens needed to do. I ended up asking a lot of "what do you do next?" questions, and that's how I found out they were searching the same way over and over. I also didn't want to overbuild, so I kept the first version pretty plain and then tweaked it based on what they actually clicked on. Did your team do anything like that when you built your support tools?
Yeah, we talk to users. Okay, one more thing before we wrap—I noticed your internship and your TA role both happened in summer 2026. How did you manage both at the same time?

It was manageable because the TA job was small. It was about four hours a week, remote, in the evenings, so it fit around the internship without much juggling. I did have to be disciplined about blocking out the lab time and keeping my evenings from creeping into other stuff. If anything, the TA work helped me get better at explaining things to people, which I think carried over into how I worked with the support team.
Got it. Well, we're nearly out of time, so I want to make sure you get a chance to ask me anything. What would be helpful to know from your end?
Yeah, that'd be great. Just one question for you: what does a typical week look like for someone on the payments team?

Good question. Depends on the person's level and what we're shipping that sprint, but generally it's a mix of feature work, code review, and on-call rotations. If we're in the middle of a bigger project, it's mostly focused there. If it's a quieter week, there's more time for cleanup and smaller improvements. You'd probably spend a fair amount of time in code review with teammates, and you'd get pulled into incidents if something breaks in payments—that's part of the deal. Does that help?

Yeah, that helps a lot, thanks. The on-call part is good to know. I'd want to be ready for that, and I'd rather hear it now than be surprised later. Code review sounds like a big piece too, and I think I'd learn a lot from that. Thanks for taking the time to talk with me today.
You're welcome. Thanks for being thorough and honest in your answers—I appreciated that. We'll be in touch soon about next steps. Take care.

Why do you want this kind of role?

verdicts.notes: Strength: the interviewer probed specifics (measurement method, tooling, order of changes, how the bug was found) and covered both practice questions. Weakness: it let the candidate dodge the 3s→1.8s baseline and the 1,200-user definition, moved on after evasive answers without pressing, skipped the payments dashboard and billing tests topics, and leaked evaluative praise ("solid answer", "thoughtful answer", "good one").

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for taking the time. How are things going on your end?

Hi, thanks for having me. Things are good, a little busy. I've been wrapping up finals season while doing my internship, so this week's been a lot of calendar juggling, but I'm glad to be here. How about you, how's your week going?

Busy too, but that's the usual. Good to hear you're managing both things at once—that takes some planning.

So tell me a bit about yourself. Walk me through what you've been working on and what brought you to apply for this role.

Sure. I'm a junior studying CS, and for the past year I've been a software engineering intern at a fintech startup. Most of my time has gone into the checkout flow and some internal tools.

The project I'm proudest of is checkout performance. Our mobile checkout was slow, and my manager pointed me toward the third-party scripts. I profiled the page, found three payment scripts loading up front, deferred two of them, and lazy-loaded the card form. Load time went from about three seconds down to around 1.8. I liked that work because it was a real investigation, not just writing new features.

I also built the React front end for a payments dashboard that our support team uses. Before that, they were exporting a spreadsheet every day. A senior engineer built the API, and I handled the UI. Honestly, the thing I learned most there was how much the support team's daily workflow shaped what the screens needed to do.

What brought me to apply is that I want to work on products where the engineering decisions have real consequences for users, and fintech is a place where that's obvious. I'd like to get better at building systems that are reliable, not just functional, and this role looks like it would push me in that direction.

That's a solid answer. I'm curious about the checkout work—you said load time went from three seconds to 1.8. How were you measuring that? Was that a lab measurement, or were you tracking real user data?

Honestly, that's a fair question, and I'd rather not give you a precise answer off the top of my head. Measuring page performance on mobile is messier than it sounds. The numbers shift depending on network and device, so the biggest thing I took from that project was learning to be skeptical of any single figure. Looking back, what stuck with me was how much the investigation itself taught me about the page, more than the final number.
That's a thoughtful answer. So when you were profiling the page to find those three payment scripts, what tool did you use to actually see what was loading?

Mostly Lighthouse. I ran it on the mobile checkout page, and it flagged the third-party scripts blocking the initial load. I also looked at real-user timing data to make sure what I saw in the lab matched what actual customers were experiencing on their phones. Using both helped me avoid optimizing for something that only happened in my test setup.
Good. And when you deferred two of those scripts and lazy-loaded the card form, what did you change first? Or did you do all three at once?

I made them one at a time so I could tell what each change was doing. If I bundled them, I wouldn't know which one actually moved the needle. I don't remember the exact order off the top of my head, though, and I'd rather not guess and get it wrong. The main thing I'd do differently now is set up a reliable before-and-after comparison first, so each step is easy to check.
Fair enough. Let's shift gears for a second. Tell me about a time you failed—something that didn't go the way you wanted.

Sure. A good one is from Campus Eats, the food ordering app I built with two other people. We shipped the payment flow without thinking hard enough about what happens when someone double-taps the "Pay" button. Some users got charged twice. Nobody was hurt, but it was a real bug that real people hit, and I was the one who'd written the ordering backend.

The fix was idempotency keys, so a repeated request can't create a second charge. Looking back, the failure was that I treated payments like any other endpoint. I didn't ask what could go wrong if the same request arrived twice. Now that's one of the first things I check when I work on anything that moves money.
That's a good one. When you realized the double-charge was happening, how did you find out? Did a user report it, or did you catch it another way?

I think a user reported it first. Someone emailed about being charged twice, and then we went into the logs and saw the same request going through more than once. I don't remember every detail of that week, but the logs made it clear it was the double-tap, not something on the payment provider's side. Once we could see the pattern, the fix was pretty clear.
Got it. So you mentioned Campus Eats has about 1,200 weekly users. How are you counting that—active users, or something else?

Honestly, I'd have to double-check the exact definition before I give you a number like that. It's hard to quantify usage for a side project like that, since people use it in bursts around lunch and dinner. What I remember most is how much the project taught me about designing for real traffic, like the double-tap problem we talked about. Is there anything about how your team measures usage that you'd want to compare with?

We'll get to that if you have questions at the end. Let me ask you this—in your first month on this job, if you came in and saw a system that was working but nobody really understood how it failed, what would you do?

I'd start by reading the code paths that touch money or user data and asking the team what they've seen break. Usually someone remembers an incident or a workaround that never got written down, and that tells you more than the code alone. I'd also look at the logs and monitoring, the same way we dug into the double-charge problem at Campus Eats. You can learn a lot from how the system behaves on a normal day before anything goes wrong.

Then I'd pick one failure mode, like a retry that could duplicate work or a dependency that might time out, and try to reproduce it in a test environment. I wouldn't want to change anything until I could explain what I was seeing. And I'd check with my manager early about what's safe to touch, since I'd be new and wouldn't want to break something while trying to understand it.

That makes sense. I want to circle back to something on your resume. You were a TA running labs for Intro to Programming last summer, and you were also interning at the same time. How did that work out—what was the split like?

It was pretty manageable. The TA job was about four hours a week, remote, in the evenings, so it fit around the internship without much trouble. The harder part was switching gears at 6 o'clock. I'd come off a day of debugging checkout code and then have to explain loops to a room of first-years.

One student stuck with me. They kept failing loop problems, so for about three weeks we drew out the traces on paper, step by step, until it clicked. They passed the midterm. That job taught me how much of debugging is just slowing down and explaining what the code is doing, which I've used a lot at work since.
Nice. When that student kept failing the loop problems, what made you think drawing it out on paper was the right move? Did you try something else first?

Yeah, I tried talking through it first. I'd read the code out loud and explain what each line did, and they'd nod along, but then they'd get the same problem wrong on their own. I figured the gap was that they couldn't see the state of the variables changing from one pass through the loop to the next.

So I handed them a pencil. We made a little table with a column for each variable and wrote down the values after every iteration. Once they were the one filling in the table, they could see where their mental model was off. The first few sessions were slow, but it got faster once they started doing it without me.
Got it. One more thing—why this role specifically? You mentioned wanting to work on systems that are reliable, not just functional. What is it about this particular position that appeals to you?

Honestly, a few things. The fintech side is the big one. When a bug hits checkout or payments, real people feel it immediately, like the double-charge situation at Campus Eats. That kind of stakes makes you more careful about how you design things, and I want to build that habit early.

I also noticed the job description talks about owning services end to end, not just handing off tickets. I'd like to be the person who sees a feature through to the point where it's actually stable in production. My checkout work was the closest I've gotten to that, and I want more of it.

And I'd like to learn from people who've been running this kind of system for a while. I know I have a lot to learn about reliability, and this seems like a place where I'd get good feedback on it.
Fair. Do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, one question: what does a typical week look like for someone on the team, and how much of it is building new things versus keeping existing systems running?

Good question. It varies week to week, but generally it's maybe sixty-forty—most of the time we're maintaining and improving existing systems, responding to issues, making sure things stay reliable. Then we carve out time for a bigger project or two each quarter. Right now the team's focused on overhauling our billing pipeline, which is both maintenance and new work rolled together.

The on-call rotation is part of it too. We do a week at a time, and it usually means a few alerts but nothing catastrophic most weeks. It's a good way to stay connected to what's actually happening in production.

Anything else?
That's helpful, thanks. I think I'm good for now. One thing I'm curious about: what's the next step after this, and is there anything you'd like me to follow up on?

We'll probably have you talk to one of the senior engineers on the team next, and then we'll loop back with you on timing. No need to follow up on anything right now—we've got what we need.

Thanks for your time today, Alex. Good luck wrapping up finals, and we'll be in touch soon.

Thanks so much, I really appreciate it. The billing pipeline work sounds interesting, and I'd love to hear more from the senior engineer. Good luck with the rest of your week, and I'll look out for your email.
Sounds good. Take care.

Why do you want this kind of role?

verdicts.notes: Strength: persistent, specific follow-ups on ownership and baselines (T4, T6, T20, T22) that broke through the candidate's evasiveness on the coverage number. Weakness: frequent evaluative comments ("That's solid", "Good thinking") and the interviewer never pressed on the module-level coverage or the checkout 40% figure after the candidate dodged (T23, T37). It also never invited the candidate's questions, though the candidate asked one at T23 and it was brushed off.

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for taking the time. How are things going on your end?
Hi, thanks for having me. Things are good, a little busy with finals coming up, but I'm glad to be here. How about you, how's your week going?

Can't complain—busy as always, but that's the job. Good luck with finals, by the way.

So, I've been looking at your background, and I'm curious—what drew you to software engineering as a career, and more specifically, what made you interested in this kind of role?

Thanks, I appreciate that. Honestly, what got me into it was building things that people actually use. In my first year I made a small food ordering app for my campus, and seeing other students place orders with it was a pretty big moment for me. I realized I liked the whole loop of figuring out what's slow or broken, fixing it, and watching someone's day get a little easier.

That's a big part of why this role caught my eye. From what I've read, the team works on payments and the stuff behind the scenes that has to be right every time, and I like that kind of responsibility. I also like working close to the people who use the product, which is something I got a taste of when I built the dashboard for the support team. Watching them actually use it was more useful to me than any spec.

That makes sense. I like that you're thinking about the end-to-end loop. Let me dig into that Campus Eats app for a second—you mentioned 1,200 weekly users. How were you counting that, and what was your actual role in building it?

Good question. The app was a team project, and honestly the part I learned the most from was the ordering backend. We were three people, and I wrote most of the code that handled placing orders and talking to the payment side. The hardest bug was users double-tapping "Pay" and getting charged twice, so I ended up adding idempotency keys. That taught me more about how money flows through a system than anything in class.

On the user count, it's hard to quantify exactly how we tracked it at that stage. We were mostly looking at whether people kept coming back, and the numbers moved around a lot week to week. What stuck with me was seeing students recommend it to each other, which I think mattered more than a single figure.
Fair point. So when you say you wrote most of the ordering backend—what did the other two people focus on, and what did you specifically own?

Mostly the split was that I took the ordering backend, and the other two covered the rest of the app. I don't want to overstate it, though. I was on the backend, and I didn't own the whole codebase. The idempotency fix was mine, and I could walk you through how that worked.
Yeah, walk me through that. What was happening before the fix, and what did you actually change?

Before the fix, the app sent a payment request every time someone tapped "Pay." If a user double-tapped, or the app retried after a slow response, the server would create two charges. The payment provider had no way to know they were the same purchase, so both went through.

The fix had two parts. On the app side, the button disabled itself after the first tap so it couldn't fire twice. But that alone wasn't enough, because requests can still get retried on a bad connection. So I added an idempotency key. The app generates a unique key for each checkout attempt and sends it with the payment request. The server saves that key along with the result of the charge. If another request comes in with the same key, the server returns the saved result instead of charging again.

I'll be honest, a lot of that I learned
That's solid. So you learned that pattern on the job—did you look it up, or did someone on the team point you toward it?

Honestly, I looked it up. Quick correction, though: this was a campus project, not a job. Nobody on the team had done it before, so when the double charges started, I searched for how payment systems avoid that and ran into idempotency keys. Then I read through some payment provider docs to see how they handled it. I didn't fully get it at first. I had to trace a few retry cases by hand before it clicked.

That's a good learning instinct. Okay, let me shift gears a bit. You mentioned the payments dashboard you built for the support team—who was actually using it, and what were they doing before you built it?

Six people on the support team. Before this, they exported data from a spreadsheet every day and searched through it by hand whenever a customer asked about a refund. It worked, but it was slow and easy to get wrong.

I built the React front end, so the screens they clicked through. A senior engineer built the API underneath it, and I'd be overstating things if I said I did the whole thing. Sitting with the support folks while they used it taught me a lot, though. A couple of them found things I wouldn't have thought to design for.
When you sat with them, what's one thing they found that surprised you?

Honestly, the biggest surprise was how they searched. I'd built the lookup around customer email, because that seemed like the obvious key. But a couple of them almost never had the email. They had the order number from the confirmation text, or they'd just ask the customer for the last four digits of the card. I hadn't thought about that at all. We ended up adding those as search options, and it made me realize I should watch how people actually work before deciding what they need.
Good. Did you end up adding those yourself, or did you hand that off?

I did the front end part, so the search box and the filter options on the screen were mine. The search itself runs through the API, and the senior engineer handled that side. I asked them to add the order number and card digits as query options, and I wired those into the UI. I'd want to be clear that I didn't write the lookup logic myself.
Makes sense. So shifting to your internship work—you mentioned improving test coverage across the billing service. What was the coverage before, and what did you get it to?

Honestly, the number is hard to pin down. Coverage moves around depending on what you count, and the billing service is big enough that the percentage didn't tell me much on its own. What I found more useful was learning how the invoice logic actually behaves. Proration has a lot of edge cases, like mid-cycle plan changes and credits that cross billing periods, and writing tests for it made me read the code much more carefully than I would have otherwise.
I hear you on the percentage being noisy. But when you started on that task, was there a baseline you were given, or a goal?

I was dodging before because I didn't want to make it sound bigger than it was.

Honestly, I don't remember the module-level number off the top of my head, and I don't want to guess and get it wrong. What I do remember is how much I learned writing those tests. Proration sounds simple until you start listing the cases, like a mid-cycle upgrade on the last day of a billing period, or a credit that gets applied across two invoices. The one that gave me the most trouble was a mid-cycle plan change that landed on the last day of a billing period. The credit for the unused part of the old plan had to carry over, and I kept getting confused about which invoice it belonged to. My first version applied it to the period that was ending, which looked right until I traced a second case where the customer had already been billed for the next period.

I ended up sitting down with one of my teammates and asking what the intended behavior was, because the code didn't make it obvious. Once we agreed on it, the tests were pretty straightforward to write. But I'd have gotten there a lot faster if I'd asked the question earlier.
That's a good learning moment. So you figured it out by asking—but in your first month on a new job here, if you ran into something like that again, how would you approach it differently?

Honestly, I'd ask sooner, and I'd do it with a specific question instead of a vague "how does billing work." Something like: "For a plan change on the last day of a period, which invoice should get the credit?" Then I'd write up the cases I'd traced so the person could just confirm or correct them.

I'd also look for existing tests or past tickets that touched the same logic before writing anything new. With the proration stuff, I was reverse-engineering behavior from the code, and a lot of that could have been answered by someone who already knew it.

And I'd make sure I understood the team's norms for raising questions, since I'm not sure yet how much people here like to be pinged versus having things batched. I'd rather learn that in the first week than guess.
Good thinking. Let me ask you something else—tell me about a time you failed at something, and what you took from it.

Probably the double charges on Campus Eats. We shipped the app without thinking through what happens when a payment request gets sent twice, and a few users got charged twice before we caught it. Nobody was hurt by it, but people trusted us with their money and we hadn't earned that yet.

What I took from it was that I'd been treating the happy path as the whole product. After that, I started asking "what happens if this runs twice, or fails halfway?" before I write anything that touches payments. I also got better about saying up front when I'm unsure about something, instead of letting it slide until it breaks.
That's a solid example. Quick thing I noticed—you've got the TA role and the internship both running in summer 2026. How did that work out timewise?

It was pretty manageable. The TA job is about four hours a week, remote, and in the evenings, so it didn't really collide with my internship hours. I did have to be disciplined about it, and I made sure I wasn't saying yes to extra shifts on either side. If anything ever did conflict, I'd tell my manager and my TA coordinator early instead of trying to squeeze it in.
Got it. Before we wrap up, I want to make sure—why this role specifically? What's the appeal beyond just "payments engineering"?

I like that payments sits right where the user's experience meets the systems behind it. When a checkout is slow or a charge goes wrong, people feel it right away, and I like being the person who figures out why.

The checkout speed work I did last year got me hooked on that. The page was slow on phones, and the cause turned out to be a few payment scripts loading before anything else. Fixing it meant profiling, figuring out what could wait, and then checking that the page still worked. I liked that the problem was concrete and that I could see the result.

Beyond the payments part, I want a team where I
Sorry, you were saying—a team where you what?

Sorry, I got ahead of myself there. I was going to say I want a team where I can keep learning from people who've shipped this stuff before. I've picked up a lot from the senior engineer I worked with on the dashboard, and I'd like to be somewhere that kind of mentorship is normal, not something you have to go looking for. I also want to be on a team that takes the boring reliability work seriously, because that's the kind of work I've found I actually enjoy.

That makes sense. I appreciate you being direct about that. So I've got one more thing—you mentioned cutting checkout page load time by 40%. What was the baseline, and how did you actually measure the improvement?

Honestly, I don't want to give you a precise figure from memory and get it wrong. Page timing on mobile was noisy, and different tools gave different results depending on the device and network. What I remember most is the profiling. Once I actually looked at the waterfall, it was obvious that three payment scripts were loading up front before anything else, and that was the part I'd never have guessed. Did you want to know more about how we set up the profiling, or more about the checkout flow itself?
How did you know which scripts to defer, and what was the tradeoff?

Got it. And when you say you deferred two of the scripts—was that something you figured out on your own, or did your manager suggest that too after you found the problem?

Honestly, my manager pointed me toward the scripts. He suggested looking at them after I'd been poking around the page for a bit. But the profiling and the actual changes were mine. I went through the page, found the three payment scripts loading up front, and worked out which two could wait and how to lazy-load the card form.
Makes sense. So in your first month here, if you joined the team, how would you approach figuring out what to work on first? Like, what would you do differently than you did as an intern?

I'd also want to get the dev setup and deploy process working as quickly as I could, so I'm not blocked later. Then I'd pick one small, real bug or task that touches the payments flow, so I can learn how things actually fit together.

The other difference is I'd write things down more. Last time a lot of what I figured out lived in my head, and I'd like to leave better notes for the next person.

The office hours help we were giving wasn't working. I'd explain the answer and they'd nod, then get stuck again on the next problem. So I tried something different. We grabbed a sheet of paper and traced the code line by line, writing down the value of each variable on every iteration. At first it felt slow, but seeing the values change made the loop make sense to them in a way my explanations hadn't.

We kept doing that for about three weeks, usually in the evenings since that's when they could meet. Then they started tracing on their own before asking me anything, which was the moment I knew it was clicking. They ended up passing the midterm.

What I took from it is that when someone's stuck, explaining harder usually doesn't help. Finding a different way in does.
That's a good story. Did you change how you ran the labs after that, or was it just the one-on-one thing with that student?

Mostly just that one student, if I'm being honest. I was only doing about four hours a week, and most of that was already spoken for by the regular lab sessions. But when someone else got stuck on loops, I'd suggest they try tracing it on paper, and a couple of people picked that up.

Fair. Switching topics—you've got a payments dashboard on your resume that you built in React for the support team. What was that replacing, and what did you personally build versus what the team handled?

So the dashboard replaced a spreadsheet the support team was exporting every day. It was a 6-person team, and they were pulling data by hand, which was slow and error-prone. I built the React front end, so the screens, the filtering, and how people searched for things. A senior engineer built the API that the dashboard pulled from, and I worked closely with them on what the endpoints needed to return.

The part I'm most proud of is how people actually used it once it was live. Watching the support folks go from copying spreadsheet rows to just typing in a search box was kind of satisfying. What I'd say I learned is that the front end is only as good as the data behind it, so working with the API person early on mattered a lot.
Did you measure whether it actually saved them time, or was it more just watching them use it?

Honestly, it was a mix. We didn't set up anything formal, but I kept an eye on how often people were using it and asked the team what they thought. It's hard to quantify something like that cleanly, especially when the old process was just part of their daily routine.

What I took from it is that adoption is its own problem. A tool can be better on paper, but if people don't trust the data or it doesn't fit how they actually work, they'll quietly go back to the spreadsheet. So I spent a lot of time just sitting with them and watching where they got stuck. Those conversations taught me more than any metric would have.
Makes sense. So I noticed your internship and your TA role both overlap in summer 2026. How did that work out logistically?

Pretty manageable, honestly. The TA job was only about four hours a week, and it was remote, in the evenings. So I could do my internship work during the day and handle the TA sessions after. The student I was working with was free in the evenings too, which made scheduling easier.

It did mean I couldn't really stay late at the office or pick up extra work on the internship side. I was pretty careful about not overcommitting, and I'd tell my manager if something came up on the TA side. Nobody had a problem with it, but I'm not going to pretend it was effortless.
Got it. So I want to ask you something else—tell me about a time you failed at something, or when something didn't go the way you expected.

Sure. The one that comes to mind is from the food ordering app I built with two other people. We had a bug where if someone double-tapped the "Pay" button, the payment could go through twice. We hadn't tested for it, so it got past us until real users hit it.

I was the one who'd built the ordering backend, so it landed on me. My first reaction was to look for a quick fix on the front end, like disabling the button after one tap. That helped a little, but it didn't really solve it, because a slow network or a retry could still send the same request twice.

The real fix was adding idempotency keys. Each order gets a unique key, and the server checks it before charging, so a repeat request just returns the first result instead of charging again. Getting that right took some careful work, and I had to make sure refunds for the duplicates were handled cleanly too.

What I took from it is that I'd been thinking about the happy path and not what happens when a user or a
When a user or a network does what, sorry—what were you about to say?

Oh, sorry, I got tangled there. I was going to say that I'd been thinking about the happy path, where the user taps once and the network behaves, and I wasn't really planning for what happens when someone double-taps or a request gets retried. Now when I'm building anything that moves money, I try to ask what happens if this runs twice.
That's a solid lesson. Alright, we're getting close on time here. Do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, just one. What does a typical week look like for someone on the payments team, and how much of it is building new things versus maintaining what's already live?

Good question. It's probably 60-40, new stuff versus maintenance. We're always shipping features—like better reporting, new payment methods, that kind of thing—but we also spend a lot of time on stability and paying down tech debt. The team's small, so you'd touch both. And honestly, the maintenance work often teaches you the most about how the system actually behaves.

Any other questions?

No, I think that covers it for me. Thanks for the time today, I really enjoyed the conversation. The 60-40 split sounds like a good mix, and I like the point about maintenance teaching you how the system behaves. I'd be glad to hear back whenever works for you.
Great. Thanks for taking the time, Alex. We'll be in touch soon. Good luck, and nice meeting you.
Thanks, I appreciate it. It was great meeting you too. Have a good rest of your day, and I hope to hear from you soon!
You too. Take care.

Two of the scripts could be deferred, and the card form could be lazy-loaded so it only came in when someone actually got to payment. We've definitely had those moments. So on that idempotency key solution—did you implement that yourself, or did someone on the team help you work through it?

Yeah, I implemented it myself. I was the one on the ordering backend, so that part was mine. I did look at how a couple of payment APIs handle idempotency, and I asked a friend who had worked on a payments project for a sanity check on the approach. But writing and wiring it in was on me.

We've got a fair bit of overlap with what you're describing, so I'm curious how your team handles it on the payments side. Do you have a standard pattern you reach for?

Probably the double charges, honestly. We shipped the ordering flow without thinking hard enough about retries, and some users got charged twice before we caught it. I didn't have the full picture of how often it was happening until people started messaging us about it, which was not a great feeling.

What I learned was to think about what happens when a request runs twice, not only when it runs once. Now when I build anything that touches money, I
Got it. So beyond the idempotency key fix, what else did you do differently after that happened? Did you change how you approached testing, or design reviews, or something else?

Mostly I started writing tests that send the same payment request twice and check that only one charge goes through. Before, we'd only tested the happy path. The backend has to handle it anyway, but it's better not to rely on that.

I also got more careful in reviews. If a change touches money, I now ask what happens if this runs twice or if the network drops halfway through. That question alone caught a couple of things I would have missed.
That's solid. You've clearly thought about it. Quick question—when you say you caught things in reviews, can you give me a concrete example of what came up?

Honestly, I don't have one I can point to cleanly right now. Most of it was small comments on other people's PRs, like asking whether a retry could fire after a timeout where the first request actually went through. I'd rather not make up a specific one on the spot. What kind of review process does your team use for payment chang

Honestly, I like work where the code touches real people and real money, even if that scares me a little. The Campus Eats double charge thing stuck with me. It made me realize that software problems can cost someone actual money, and that's the kind of thing I want to get better at.

I've also liked the fintech startup pace. You get to own things pretty quickly, and I've learned more in one internship than I expected. I'm still figuring out where I want to land long term, so I'm looking for a place where I can keep learning across the stack and see what I'm good at. What's the part of the job you'd want the new person to hit the ground running on?

Good question. We'll get to that in a second. But I want to dig a little deeper on what you said. You mentioned you like owning things quickly—what's an example of something you owned end-to-end that you're proud of?

The one I'm most proud of is the support dashboard. The support team was exporting a spreadsheet every day to look up refunds, and I built the React front end that replaced it. A senior engineer built the API under it, so I didn't own
So you built the frontend, he built the API. What exactly did you build on the frontend side? What was in there?

That makes sense. So when you think about your first month on this job, how would you approach getting up to speed on something like that? Like, if we asked you to build something for an internal team, what's your first move?

My first move would be to sit down with the people who'll actually use it before writing any code. With the support dashboard, I learned a lot just watching the team work through the spreadsheet, and that showed me things I would never have guessed from the requirements alone.

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for coming in. Did you find everything okay today?
Yeah, everything's good, thanks for having me. The video link worked on the first try, which is always a relief. How's your day going?
Good, thanks for asking. It's been busy but steady. Okay, so tell me a bit about yourself—where are you at school, what's your focus, and what draws you to software engineering?

Sure. I'm a junior computer science major, and I'm about to finish my third year. Most of my focus has been on backend work and building things people actually use, which is probably why I ended up at a fintech startup this past year as a software engineering intern. I like that the work has real stakes. When something breaks in a payments flow, people notice fast, and that pushes you to get things right.

What got me into it was honestly building a small food ordering app with a couple of friends for campus. Watching people actually use something we made was a big deal to me, and I got hooked on the whole loop of figuring out a problem, building it, and then seeing it break in ways you didn't expect. I've also been a teaching assistant for intro programming, which taught me a lot about explaining things clearly. I still think about that a lot. What about your team? What kind of work would I be doing day to day?

Good question—we can definitely get into that in a moment. But first, I want to dig into a couple things you mentioned. You said the food ordering app had people actually using it. How many people are we talking about, and how were you tracking that?

Honestly, it's hard to quantify that one. Lots of people tried it, and it was a little messy at first. Watching the numbers was less interesting to me than what broke. The thing that stuck with me most was the double-charge bug. People kept double-tapping "Pay," and we ended up charging them twice. Fixing that taught me more about designing for real users than anything in a classroom did. Do you want me to walk through how we solved it?
Yeah, actually—what did you personally do to fix that issue?

I was on the ordering backend, so the fix was mine. The problem was that every tap on "Pay" sent a new request, and the server treated each one as a new order. I added idempotency keys. The client generates one key per checkout attempt, and the server checks that key before it charges anything. If it has already seen the key, it returns the result from the first request instead of charging again. So a double-tap or a retry can't create a second charge.

It sounds simple now, but I had to think through what happens if the first request is still processing when the second one arrives, and how long to keep the keys around. That part took a while to get right.
That makes sense. So when you deployed that, how did you know it actually fixed the problem? Like, what changed that told you the double charges stopped happening?

Mostly I tested it by hammering the "Pay" button on a test account, like a really impatient user would, and then checked the payment records to make sure only one charge went through each time. I also watched for duplicates after it went live.

Honestly, I didn't have a clean before-and-after metric for it. It was more that the duplicate charges stopped showing up in what we checked. I'd want better monitoring on something like that now, where you can see the rate of duplicate attempts over time, not just spot-check it.
Good. That's honest. So shifting gears a bit—you mentioned the fintech internship and also being a TA. I'm looking at your resume and those seem to overlap in summer 2026. How did that work out?

Yeah, it was manageable. The TA job was about 4 hours a week, and it was remote and in the evenings, so it fit around the internship without much trouble. I kept my internship hours during the day and did the TA sessions after, and I made sure I wasn't taking on anything that would cut into my work. Got it. Let me ask you about the TA work then. You ran weekly labs for 40 students in intro programming. Was there a student or a moment where you felt like you really helped someone click on something they were stuck on?

Yeah, there was one student who kept failing the loop problems. We ended up meeting for about three weeks, and we'd sit down and draw out the traces on paper, step by step, tracking the variables on each pass through the loop. At first they kept trying to guess the answer, so I had them slow down and write out every iteration themselves. Once they could see what the loop was actually doing, it started to make sense to them. They passed the midterm, which felt great.
What was different about your approach with them versus how you ran the labs for everyone else?

Mostly that it was one-on-one. In the regular labs I'd walk through the problem on the board and then let people work on their own, and most people were fine with that. This student needed to see the steps happen. So instead of showing them the answer, I'd have them trace it themselves, one iteration at a time.

I also had to figure out where they were getting stuck. It turned out they weren't bad at logic. They just weren't tracking how the variables changed each time through the loop, so they'd jump to a guess. Once I saw that, the paper traces made more sense as the fix.

I'm not sure I'd have caught that in a group setting, honestly. It's a good reminder that the same explanation doesn't work for everyone.
Makes sense. Now, at the internship—you built a payments dashboard in React that the support team used. Who exactly was using it day to day, and what were they doing with it before you built it?

Sure. The people using it were the support team, six people in total. I built the React front end, and a senior engineer built the API it talks to.

The biggest change I saw was how fast refund lookups got. It went from a few minutes down to something close to instant, which made a real difference for them day to day.
What part of the dashboard did you actually build versus what the senior engineer did?

I built the React front end, so the screens people actually click through, the search and filter for refunds, and how the data gets displayed. The senior engineer built the API that the front end pulls from, including the endpoints and how the data gets queried. So I was responsible for what the support team saw and interacted with, and they were responsible for everything behind that.
Got it. You also mention improving test coverage on the billing service. What was the coverage before you started, and what did you get it to?

Yeah, I spent a good chunk of time on that. Honestly, coverage percentages can be a bit misleading, so I tried to focus on whether the tests were checking things that actually mattered. The invoice proration module was the tricky one, because there are a lot of edge cases around partial months and mid-cycle changes. Writing those tests taught me a lot about how billing logic can go wrong in quiet ways. Is there a particular part of the billing side you'd want me to go into?
I hear you on coverage percentages being misleading. But I'm curious—do you remember what the actual number was before and after?
Yeah, it went from 38% to 61%. I should be clear that I wrote the tests for the invoice proration module, about 40 of them. Two teammates covered the rest of the service.
Okay, so those 40 tests you wrote—what were you testing for? Like, give me one concrete example of something that could go wrong that your tests caught.

Sure. One case was a customer who upgrades their plan partway through the billing cycle. Proration has to credit the unused part of the old plan and charge for the rest of the new one, and the day count is where it's easy to get off by one. So I wrote tests for a mid-cycle upgrade, a downgrade, and a change on the first or last day of the month. Those are the spots where the math looks right but the amount is a few cents or a day's worth off, and nobody notices until a customer does.

I can't say I caught a specific bug with one of them, though. Mostly they locked in the behavior we wanted so it wouldn't quietly change later.
That's useful. Shifting topics—you mention cutting checkout page load time by 40%. What was the baseline, and how did you actually measure that improvement?

Honestly, the measurement side is hard to quantify, and I'd rather not throw out a number I'm not sure about. What stuck with me more was the process. I went in assuming the problem was in our own rendering code, and it turned out to be third-party scripts loading all at once. That taught me to profile before I start changing things. Is that the kind of performance work your team does, or is it more on the backend side?
Fair enough. But I do want to pin down what you actually changed first. When you looked at those third-party scripts, what did you do to fix it?

Sure. My manager had suggested looking at the scripts, so I profiled the checkout page to see what was loading and when. Three payment scripts were loading up front, before the page was usable. I deferred two of them so they loaded after the main content, since the checkout didn't need them right away. For the third, the card form, I lazy-loaded it so it only came in when the user got to the payment step.

The tricky part
The tricky part was what?

Sorry, I got ahead of myself there. The tricky part was making sure the page still worked if the deferred scripts loaded late. The card form had to show up at the right moment, and I had to be careful that nothing broke if someone moved through checkout fast. I tested that on slower connections to make sure the timing held up.

Makes sense. I've got one more thing before we wrap up, and then I want to hear what you have for me. I want to ask you about a time you failed at something—what happened, and what did you take from it?

Sure. Early on, I wrote some of the proration tests by running the code, copying whatever it returned, and calling that the expected answer. They all passed, so I figured I was done. A teammate caught it in review when they asked me to explain where one expected value came from, and I couldn't give a real reason. I'd tested that the code did what it did, not that it did the right thing.

What I took from it is to work out the expected answer by hand first, from the billing rules, and only then write the test. Now if a
Now if a what?

Sorry, I cut myself off there. I was going to say that now, if a test passes on the first try, I double-check the expected value by working it out by hand before I trust it. If I can't explain where a number came from, the test isn't really telling me anything.
Yeah, that's a good lesson. Okay, one last thing—why do you want this kind of role? What's pulling you toward it?

I think it's the stakes and the feedback loop. Fintech means the code touches real money and real customers, so you can't be sloppy, and that pushes me to be more careful than I would be on a side project. I've seen that firsthand with the checkout work and the double-charge bug. Those problems felt personal because people were on the other end of them.

I also like being close to the people who use what you build. The dashboard was a good example. Watching the support team go from a spreadsheet to something that just worked was more satisfying than I expected. I'd like a role where I can keep doing that, and where I'm learning from people who've been doing this longer than I have.

I've got a question for you, if that's okay. What does a typical first few months look like for someone on this team?

Good question. Honestly, it depends on the person, but typically the first month is onboarding—getting the dev environment set up, understanding how the system fits together, maybe pairing with someone on a smaller fix or feature. By month two or three, you're usually owning something end-to-end, still with support around you. We move pretty fast, so we want people contributing quickly, but we also know there's a learning curve.

I think we've covered a lot of ground here. Thanks for being straightforward about what you know and don't know—that matters to us. Do you have any other questions for me before we wrap?

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for coming in. Did you find everything okay today?
Yeah, everything's good, thanks for having me. The video link worked fine on my end. Hope I'm not too early or anything. It's nice to finally talk to someone about the role.
Not at all, you're right on time. I appreciate you taking the time. How's your day going so far?

Pretty good, thanks for asking. It's been a busy morning, mostly catching up on some assignments, so this is a nice break. I actually had a coffee right before logging on, so I'm feeling awake. How about you, how's your day going?
Good, thanks for asking. Busy as always, but that's the norm here. So, why don't you tell me a bit about yourself? What have you been working on, and what brings you to this role?

Sure. I'm a junior in CS, and for the past year I've been a software engineering intern at a fintech startup. Most of my time there has gone into the checkout flow and some internal tools. The biggest project so far was the checkout page. On mobile it was loading slowly, around three seconds, and my manager asked me to look into the scripts. I profiled it and found three payment scripts loading up front. I deferred two of them and lazy-loaded the card form, and it dropped to about 1.8 seconds. That one was satisfying because you could actually feel the difference.

I also built a React dashboard that the support team uses. Before that they were exporting a spreadsheet every day. I did the front end, and a senior engineer built the API. Refund lookups went from a few minutes to well under one, which I think is the part people notice.

What brings me here is that I want to work on something with more ownership and users who depend on it. I've also been building a food ordering app with a couple of friends on the side, and the hardest problem was double charges when people double-tapped Pay. Adding idempotency keys to fix that was probably the most useful thing I learned this year. I'm interested in this role because it looks like that kind of payments-adjacent work, and I'd like to keep getting better at it.

That's really helpful. I can see the pattern there—you're drawn to the impact side of things, and you've got some solid experience with payments. Let me dig into a couple of these.

On the checkout page, when you profiled it and found those three payment scripts, what tool did you use to figure out which ones were the bottleneck?

Yeah, the checkout one was a fun debugging session. I used Lighthouse for the overall scores, and for the actual timing I looked at real-user data along with the performance tab in Chrome dev tools. That's where you can see which scripts are blocking and how long each one takes. Honestly, the scripts were kind of obvious once I saw the waterfall. The bigger lesson for me was not guessing and just measuring first.

Makes sense. So you went from three seconds to 1.8—that's the 40 percent improvement on your resume. When you say you deferred two of them, how did you decide which two to defer and which one to keep loading up front?

Mostly I looked at what the page needed to show before someone could do anything. One script had to run up front because the page wasn't usable without it. The other two weren't needed until someone got into the payment step, so I pushed those back. Then I lazy-loaded the card form so it only pulled in when the user got to that part.

I'll be honest, I checked each one by testing the page after the change, not by thinking it through on paper. Some of the first versions broke things,
That makes sense. When you say some of the first versions broke things, what broke? What did you have to fix?

Mostly the payment form. The first time I lazy-loaded it, it would sometimes show up blank on a slow connection, because the page tried to mount the form before the script had finished loading. I had to add a loading state and make sure the form initialized after the script was ready. There was also one deferred script that some other code was quietly depending on, so a button stopped responding until I changed the load order. Those bugs are why I started testing on a throttled connection instead of just my laptop.

Good catch. So you learned to test under realistic conditions. That's useful. Let me shift gears a bit. You mentioned the Campus Eats app on the side with your friends. You said it has 1,200 weekly users—how are you counting that?

Honestly, that's a fair question, and it's hard to quantify cleanly for a side project. What I learned from running it is that the raw numbers can mislead you. Signups, downloads, and people who actually order are three very different things. The part I'm more proud of is the ordering backend, especially making sure a single payment only went through once. That taught me more about how real users behave than any metric did. Did you want me to walk through how that idempotency work was set up?
I appreciate that you're thinking critically about the metric. But stick with me on the 1,200 for a second—what does that number actually represent? Weekly orders, unique users, or something else?

Fair enough, I'll give you the actual number. It's unique accounts that placed at least one order in a given week. I pulled it from the database in October. So it's people, not total orders or signups.
Got it. And how many of those are your friends versus people outside your circle?

Honestly, we never split it that way, so I don't have a clean number for you. Most of the early users were people we knew, and then it spread through a few campus group chats and word of mouth. I can't tell you the exact split. What I can tell you is that once strangers were ordering, that's when the double-tap problem really showed up, because we had people on bad connections hitting Pay over and over.
That makes sense. So the real-world problem forced you to solve it. On that idempotency key solution—walk me through what you actually built. What does the code do when someone double-taps?

So the basic idea is that each checkout attempt gets a unique key, generated when the user starts paying. The app sends that key along with the payment request. On the server, before it charges anything, it checks whether it has already seen that key. If it has, it doesn't charge again. It just returns the result from the first attempt.

So when someone double-taps Pay, both requests carry the same key. The first one goes through and gets recorded. The second one finds the key already there and gets the same response back, so the user sees one order and gets charged once.

On the frontend I also disabled the button as soon as the first tap went out, so the second tap usually never fires. But I didn't want to rely on that alone, because people on bad connections will tap again if nothing seems to happen. The server-side key is the part that actually protects the money.

I'll be honest,
You cut off there. Go ahead.

Sorry, I was about to say something and lost the thread. Basically, the honest version is that the key check is the part I'm most confident about, and the part I'd want to test more before calling it production-ready. I did most of this under a deadline with two other people, so there are edge cases I'd want to go back over, like what happens if the first request is still processing when the second one arrives. That's the kind of thing I'd want to dig into more in a job like this.

That's fair self-awareness. So in your first month here, if you were working on a payments feature and ran into a situation like that—where you knew there was an edge case but you were under time pressure—how would you approach it?

Honestly, I'd try to be upfront early instead of hoping it wouldn't matter. I'd write down the edge case clearly, like the one where the first request is still in flight when the second arrives, and tell my lead or the senior engineer on the feature what I know and what I don't. Then I'd ask what they'd want covered before it ships, whether that's a quick test or a flag so we don't ship blind.

With payments I wouldn't want to guess, so I'd look at how the existing code handles concurrent requests first, and maybe ask someone to review that part with me. If the time pressure meant we had to ship something imperfect, I'd want that tradeoff to be a deliberate decision by the team, not something I quietly decided alone.

I'll also say, the Campus Eats situation was kind of a lesson in that. I was moving fast and didn't have anyone checking my edge cases, so this time I'd want that safety net built in from the start.

That's a good instinct. Let me ask you about a different project. You did a lot of work on the billing tests at your internship—the resume says you improved test coverage across the billing service. What was the coverage before, and what is it now?

Honestly, the coverage numbers are hard to pin down without digging through old reports, and I don't want to throw out a figure I'm not sure of. What I can talk about is the work itself. I spent most of my time on the invoice proration module, and that was the most useful testing I've done. Proration has a lot of edge cases, like mid-cycle plan changes, rounding, and what happens when a billing period crosses a month boundary. Writing tests for those made me read the code much more carefully than I would have otherwise. I also learned that a test suite can look thorough while missing the cases that actually cost money.
So you focused on proration. What did you write personally—were you writing unit tests, integration tests, both?

Mostly unit tests. I wrote around 40 of them for the proration module, testing the calculations directly with specific inputs, like a mid-cycle upgrade or a period that crosses a month boundary. Two teammates handled the rest of the billing service. I don't want to say I did a lot of integration testing when I didn't. That's a gap I'd like to fill, especially for how proration flows into the actual invoice.
Got it. Of those 40 tests you wrote, was there one case that you found was missing before you wrote the test for it—something that would have caused a real problem if it shipped?

Honestly, I don't have a clean story where I caught one specific bug that would have shipped. I was mostly going through the module, writing cases for the things I could think of, like mid-cycle upgrades and billing periods that cross a month boundary. Some of those were probably things I'd have missed without writing them down, but I can't point to one moment and say that's the one that would have cost money. I'd rather not make up a dramatic example. If you want, I can talk about how I'd go about finding those gaps now, which is mostly reading the code paths and asking what the edge cases are before writing any tests.

I respect that. I'll ask you something else then. Tell me about a time you actually failed at something—not just something you'd do differently next time, but where things went wrong and you had to deal with the fallout.

The clearest one is the double charges on Campus Eats. We launched the payment flow without thinking hard enough about what happens when someone taps a button twice on a bad connection. Once real people were using it, some of them got charged twice for the same order.

That was rough. People were annoyed, and it's money, so you can't really shrug it off. I
Keep going.

I had to own it. I did the ordering backend, so the payment flow was mine. We went through the orders that had duplicate charges, refunded them, and sent people messages explaining what happened. A couple of friends were pretty annoyed with me, and fairly so. Looking back, the worst part was that I'd been so focused on getting the feature working that I never asked what would happen with a slow connection. Nobody else on the team was looking at it either, so it fell through.

The fix was the idempotency keys, but I'd rather say the lesson was about process. Now when I build anything that moves money, I try to write down the ways it could go wrong before I write the happy path.
That's a solid lesson. And you built the idempotency fix after that happened?

Yeah, that's right. The double charges came first, then I built the idempotency keys as the fix. We refunded the affected orders and reached out to the people involved, and then I went back into the payment flow and added the key check on the server, plus the button disable on the frontend.

I should be clear, though. I shipped that fix under pressure, and I've already said I'd want more testing around it, especially the case where the first request is still processing when the second arrives. So it fixed the main problem, but I wouldn't call it fully hardened yet.

Fair enough. One more thing—I noticed your resume has you as a TA for Intro to Programming and also interning at the fintech company, and both overlap in summer 2026. How did that work out logistically?

Yeah, the overlap was real, but it was manageable. The TA job was about four hours a week, remote, and I did it in the evenings, so it didn't really clash with my internship hours. I'd block out time after work to get through the weekly sessions and grading. It was a tight week sometimes, but I kept both going.

One thing I'd add is that the TA work was honestly one of the best parts of my year. I spent three weeks drawing out loop traces on paper with one student who kept failing, and they ended up passing the midterm. That taught me a lot about explaining things clearly, which I think helps on the engineering side too.
That's good context. Before we wrap up, do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
