transcript.text: Hey, good to meet you. How's your day been so far?
Hi, good to meet you too. My day's been pretty good, thanks for asking. I had a slow start with coffee, but I'm glad to be here. How about you, how's your day going?

Good, thanks for asking. Busy as always, but I'm looking forward to chatting with you. So, Jordan, why don't you walk me through your background a bit? Where are you coming from, and what's brought you to apply for this role?

I'm a business major, and for the past year I've worked as a sales associate at an outdoor gear store. Before that I got my start on the sales floor, and alongside school I've been treasurer for a campus club. Both of those jobs taught me a lot about working with customers and handling money responsibly, which is why this role caught my eye. I'm looking for a place where I can use those skills in a more structured way and keep growing. What drew me to this position in particular was the focus on customer relationships, since that's the part of my work I enjoy most.

That makes sense. So you mentioned you were a top seller at the outdoor gear store—three months in a row, right? Walk me through what you actually did differently compared to your coworkers to get to that spot.

Yeah, I ranked first out of nine associates from June through August. What set me apart was that I changed how I opened conversations. Instead of walking people straight to products, I'd ask what trip they were planning first. If someone said they were heading into the mountains for three days, I'd know to talk about layering and water filtration instead of just pushing whatever was on sale. My add-on sales ran about 1.9 times the store average, and I think that came from people feeling like I was helping them plan rather than selling to them.
That's a concrete example. How did you actually measure that 1.9x number? Was that something the store tracked, or did you calculate it yourself?

The store tracked it. Our monthly sales reports showed add-on numbers for each associate, and I compared mine against the store average. The 1.9 times figure came from those reports, not from a calculation I did on my own.
Got it. And when you were asking those questions upfront—like about the trip they were planning—did any customers push back or seem annoyed by that approach?

Yeah, a few did, especially the ones who came in already knowing exactly what they wanted. Someone would say they just needed a headlamp and wanted to pay and go. I didn't push it. I'd say something like, "Sure, here's the one I'd recommend," and grab it. Most of the time, though, if I asked one quick question, people opened up and ended up buying more because they actually needed it for what they were doing. I learned to keep the questions short and to back off quickly if someone seemed impatient.
Makes sense. So you also trained four new hires on the sales floor. How did you actually go about training them? Walk me through what that looked like.

Sure. When new hires started, I shadowed each one for their first two shifts. I'd stay close enough to see how they greeted customers and handled questions, but I let them watch me work first. After that, I flipped it: they led the sales conversations while I stood back and watched, then I gave them feedback on the way out. I kept the feedback specific, like "you asked a good question about the trip, but you jumped to price too fast." Three of the four hit their first monthly sales target, which felt like a good sign that the approach worked.
How did you know the training actually worked for the one person who didn't hit that target? What was different with them?

Honestly, I don't have a clear answer for that. I didn't follow up with them in as much detail as I should have, so I can't say for sure what was different. If I'd been doing it again, I'd sit down with them after the first month, ask what felt hard, and look at which part of the sales conversation they were struggling with. I'd rather tell you I didn't fully figure that out than make up a reason.
Fair enough. Let's talk about the customer complaint side. You mentioned handling escalated customer returns. Give me a specific example of one that was tough—what happened and how did you handle it?

Sure. A customer came in wanting a full refund on a tent they'd already used a lot, and it was past our return window. Our policy wouldn't cover a refund, so I didn't just say no. I looked into whether the brand's warranty could cover a repair, found that it could, and walked them through setting it up. They left a positive review afterward, which I was glad about, since they'd come in pretty frustrated.
What did the customer say when you first told them the return was outside the window? How did that conversation start?

I don't remember the exact words, and I'd rather not make up a quote. What I do remember is that they were pretty frustrated and clearly expected a refund. I let them finish explaining, then said that I couldn't do a refund since it was past the window, but that I could check whether the warranty covered the tent. That shifted the conversation from "no" to "let's see what we can do," and once they saw there was a real option, they calmed down.
That's helpful. Did you ever have a return situation where you couldn't find a workaround and it just ended badly?

Yeah, there was one. A customer wanted to return a jacket that had clearly been worn through a season, and the warranty didn't cover wear, so there wasn't a repair or replacement I could offer. I explained the policy, tried to point them toward a store credit option, and they still left unhappy. It stuck with me, because I wanted to fix it and couldn't. Looking back, I could have explained the policy earlier in the conversation instead of letting them build up expectations, so next time I'd set the limits sooner and be clear about what's possible right away.
Got it. You were also treasurer for a campus club and managed a twelve-thousand-dollar annual budget. Tell me about a time you had to make a hard call on what to fund or what to cut.

Sure. The $12,000 came from student government, and the hardest call was the end-of-year banquet. It was budgeted at $3,000, but we had a competition coming up where a few members needed travel money to attend. I looked at the numbers and decided to cut the banquet down to $1,200 so we could fund the travel. Some members were disappointed about the banquet, so I explained the reasoning openly at a meeting and kept the event simple, with food and a short awards section. The travel went through, and I think being upfront about why I made the cut mattered more than the cut itself.
What would you have done differently if you'd realized earlier in the year that you couldn't fund both at full levels?

That's a good question, and honestly, I think I should have caught it sooner. I was looking at the budget month by month, but I didn't map out the competition travel costs against the full year until later. If I'd sat down at the start of the year and listed every big expense, including travel, I'd have seen the squeeze coming.

So I'd set a rough plan early: what the travel would cost, what the banquet would cost, and what we'd need to save each month to cover both. That way I could have talked to the members about tradeoffs in the fall instead of making a cut close to the event. Members would have had more time to plan, and I could have looked for a sponsor or fundraiser for the travel earlier too.
You mentioned securing three local sponsors for the spring event. How did you actually find those sponsors and pitch them?

I started by emailing about 25 local businesses, and honestly, most of those went nowhere. Maybe a handful wrote back at all. So I changed tactics and started walking into shops with a one-page flyer that listed the event, who'd be coming, and what each sponsor would get in return. Those in-person visits worked much better. I ended up with three yeses, a bike shop, a cafe, and a bank branch, worth $2,400 combined.
What was different about the ones who said yes versus the ones who didn't respond to the email?

I honestly can't point to one clear difference. I didn't track the emails in detail, so I don't have a clean comparison. What I can say is that the three who said yes were places where I could talk to someone face to face. Once I was in the room, I could explain the event in a minute, hand them the flyer, and answer questions right then. An email is easy to ignore, and I think that's what happened with most of them.

I'd rather not guess at more than that. If I ran the same outreach again, I'd keep a simple log of who I contacted, how, and what they said, so I could see the pattern instead of relying on my memory.
That's smart. I want to ask you about something else—tell me about a time you actually failed at something. What happened, and what did you take away from it?

Sure. The clearest one for me was the jacket return I mentioned earlier, but I think a better example is the new hire who didn't hit their first monthly target. I trained four people, and three of them hit it, but I didn't follow up closely with the fourth. I assumed that since I'd done the same shadowing and feedback with everyone, it would work out. It didn't, and I didn't catch it until the month was already over.

What I took from it is that the training plan is only half of it. You also have to check in on each person and look at their actual numbers early, not wait until the end. Now I'd sit down after the first couple of weeks, ask what feels hard, and look at which part of the sales conversation they're struggling with. That's the step I skipped, and I should have done it.
Makes sense. So why this role specifically? You mentioned earlier that customer relationships drew you, but what is it about this particular position that made you want to apply?

I'm not totally sure what this role's day-to-day looks like yet, so I'd rather not pretend I know every detail. What I do know is that the work I've enjoyed most, at the gear store and with the club, is the part where you're figuring out what someone actually needs and helping them get there. Whether it's a customer planning a trip or a sponsor deciding if an event is worth backing, I like being the person who makes that connection.

I also want a job where I can build on those skills in a more structured way. I've learned a lot by trial and error, like the sponsor emails and the training follow-up I missed, and I'd like to work somewhere that gives more room to plan things out and learn from people who've done it longer. That's a big part of why this role interests me.
Got it. Well, we're nearly out of time here, so let me ask—do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yes, one question. What does a typical first few months look like for someone in this role, and how do you usually check in on how new people are doing?

Good question. Typically the first month is onboarding and shadowing—you'll work closely with someone on the team to learn our processes and meet clients. By month two, you're starting to own some smaller projects or accounts with support. We check in weekly one-on-ones for the first three months, then move to biweekly. It's pretty hands-on early on, which most people find helpful.

Any other questions?

No, I think that answers most of what I was wondering. The weekly check-ins sound really useful, especially given how much I've learned from following up late on past work. Thanks for your time today. I've enjoyed the conversation, and I'd be glad to hear more about next steps.

Great. Thanks so much for taking the time to talk with me today, Jordan. I really appreciated hearing about your specific examples—the way you approach customer conversations, how you've thought through what didn't work, and your honesty about where you'd do things differently. We'll be in touch within the next week or so with next steps. Take care.

Mostly it came down to one habit. Before I showed anyone a single product, I'd ask what trip they were planning. Once I knew that, I could suggest the add-ons they'd actually use, like the right layer or a water filter, and not just whatever was on sale. Over June to August my add-on sales ran about 1.9 times the store average, and that's why I ranked first out of nine associates each month.

My manager would go over those in our monthly check-ins, so I knew where I stood. I also tracked my own attach rate in a notebook during the shift, mostly to see whether the trip question was actually changing what people bought. It was, which is why I kept doing it.
I like that you were measuring it both ways. So when you were training those four new hires on the sales floor, did you teach them that same approach, or did you do something different?

Yeah, I taught them the trip question first, since that was the thing that worked for me. But mostly I was teaching by doing it with them. We still had a celebration, just a smaller one, and the team went to the competition.

Honestly, I don't have a clean answer for you. I'd have to check the results before I say how we placed, and I don't want to guess in an interview. I also figured a local business is more likely to say yes to someone standing in the shop than to a message in their inbox. I didn't know that for sure going in, I just tested it, and the in-person approach got three yeses where the emails got none.
Got it. Let me ask you this—tell me about a time you failed. Not the fourth hire you mentioned, but something where things didn't go the way you wanted.
(long pause)
Take your time.

Sure. Okay, one that comes to mind is the cold emails to the 25 local businesses. I sent them out expecting a decent response, and most of them just went nowhere. So I stopped and went in person with the flyer, and that's what got the three sponsors. I'd say the lesson for me was to notice a method isn't working early and switch, instead of polishing something that isn't landing.

That's a reasonable take. But I want to push back a little—is that really a failure, or is that just a pivot that worked out? What's an actual time where you tried something, it didn't work, and you couldn't fix it?

That's a fair push. You're right that the sponsor story is more a pivot than a true failure, since I did get the yeses in the end.

A real one that comes to mind is the refund request on the used tent. A customer wanted their money back, but the return was well past the window, and our policy didn't allow it. I offered to walk them through a repair under the brand's warranty. They took it, and they left a positive review. But I'll be honest, the first thing I said made things worse before I found a fix, and I didn't reach for an alternative soon enough. That's something I'd do differently: look for the options sooner when a customer is already upset.

I don't remember the exact words, and I don't want to make up a quote. It was accurate, but it came across as a closed door, and the customer took it as me not caring about their problem. Looking back, I should have started by asking what they were hoping to get out of the tent, instead of leading with what I couldn't do.
That's a useful reframe. Okay, last thing before we wrap up—why do you want this kind of role? What's pulling you toward it?

I want a role where I can see clear results from my work, and where I'm working with real numbers and real people. Retail showed me I'm good at figuring out what someone actually needs, and the treasurer job showed me I like owning a budget and making the hard trade-offs. What pulls me toward this role is the chance to combine those two things, and to keep learning from the kind of feedback I got on the sales floor, where you can tell fast whether your approach is working.
Makes sense. Do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?

Um, yeah, mostly I just tried to check in more. Like, keep an eye on how they were doing during shifts instead of just waiting to see. I don't think I did a great job of that the first time, honestly.

Um, yeah, I think I'd check in earlier, like in the first few days instead of waiting until the end of the month. I'd also ask them more often what's been hard, so I'm not just guessing. I think that would've helped a lot, honestly.

Um, yeah, I mean, the competition was kind of the main reason the club exists, so it felt like it should come first. The banquet is nice, but people mostly go for the event itself. I didn't love cutting it, though.

Um, yeah, I talked to the other officers first, and we kind of went back and forth on it. I didn't really run it by the whole club before we decided, though. When you say you trained four new hires on the sales floor, walk me through what that actually looked like. How did you train them?

Sure. Honestly, I did most of it myself, so I'll walk you through my part. For each new hire, I shadowed them for their first two shifts. I'd watch how they greeted customers and handled questions, and I'd jump in if something was off. After that, I had them lead the sales conversations while I stood back and watched. Then we'd talk through what went well and what they'd change.

Three of the four hit their first monthly target, which I was happy about. The one who didn't was still picking up the product knowledge, so we spent more time on that.
That's helpful. When you say you'd jump in if something was off—give me a concrete example. What's one thing you saw a new hire do wrong, and how did you correct it in the moment?

Honestly, I don't have one specific moment I can point to cleanly, and I don't want to make up a story. The most common thing I'd step in on was a new hire jumping straight to products without asking what the customer was planning. If I saw that happening, I'd usually wait for a natural break, then ask the customer the trip question myself to get the conversation back on track. Afterward, I'd go over with the new hire why that question changes what you should show someone.

Fair enough. So you'd model the right behavior and then debrief. Did you ever follow up with them later to see if they'd actually started doing it that way on their own, or was it more of a one-time conversation?

Honestly, it was mostly a one-time thing. I did the shadowing and the debrief after their shifts, and I was around on the floor, so I'd see them on other shifts. But I didn't set up a formal check-in to see if they kept the trip question habit. I can't tell you how many of them were still doing it a month later. If I ran it again, I'd schedule a quick follow-up at the two-week mark and ask them directly what's working.
That makes sense. Let me ask you this—tell me about a time you failed or something that didn't go the way you wanted it to.

Sure. The sponsorship push for our club's spring event didn't start well. I emailed about 25 local businesses, and most of them never answered. Cold emails just weren't working. I was getting frustrated, and I realized I was sending the same pitch over and over and hoping it would land.

So I changed the approach. I printed a one-page flyer with what the event was, who'd come, and what a sponsor would get, then started walking into shops and asking for the person who handled community stuff. That worked a lot better. We ended up with three sponsors: a bike shop, a cafe, and a bank branch, worth about $2,400 total.

What I took from it is that the first attempt failed because I didn't think about what the other person need

Got it. So you learned that a personal ask beats a mass email. Out of curiosity, why did only three sponsors say yes after you switched to the in-person approach? What was the barrier for the ones who turned you down?

Honestly, I don't know the reasons for most of the no's, and I don't want to guess and pass it off as fact. A few places just didn't have budget for sponsorships that season, and I think some were busy or didn't see the club as a priority. But I didn't write down what people said, so I can't tell you which reason came up
That's fair. Let me ask you this—why are you interested in this kind of role? What's drawing you to apply?

Mostly because I like the part of the job where you figure out what someone actually needs and help them get there. That's what I liked about the store, and it's also what I liked about sponsorship work. Once we stopped pitching everyone the same way, the conversations got a lot better.

I'm also finishing my business degree this year, so I want a role where I can use that on real problems, not just study them. I don't know much about this position yet, though, so I'd like to hear what the day-to-day looks like before I say more.

That's a good point. We're almost out of time, so let me tell you a bit about what we're looking for, and then I want to hear what questions you have.

This role is focused on working with clients to understand their business challenges and help shape solutions. A lot of it is listening, asking good questions, and then owning the follow-through. You'd be learning on the job, but you'd own your own projects pretty quickly.

What questions do you have for me?

That sounds like a good fit with what I've been doing, especially the asking-questions-first part. Thanks for laying that out.

I do have one question: what does a typical first 90 days look like for someone starting in this role?

Good question. Honestly, the first month is mostly learning—shadowing clients, sitting in on calls, understanding how we work and what our actual problems are. After that, you'd start owning smaller projects with support, and by month three you'd be running your own client work with a mentor checking in. It's not a ton of hand-holding, but you're not thrown in alone either.

Anything else?

Thanks, that's really helpful. I think the shadowing and then taking on smaller projects sounds like a good way to learn. One last thing: what's the biggest thing you'd want someone in this role to get better at in their first six months?

I'd say ownership. Being able to see what needs to happen next and actually doing it without waiting to be told. It's the biggest gap we see in people early on.

Well, I appreciate your time today. Thanks for being thoughtful and honest about what you know and don't know. We'll be in touch soon about next steps.

Thanks so much for the time today, and for walking me through the role. Ownership makes sense to me as the thing to build. I'd like to get better at spotting the next step before someone has to ask. I look forward to hearing from you about next steps.
Great. Take care, and good luck with finals.
Thanks, I appreciate that. Good luck with the hiring, and thanks again for the chat. Have a good rest of your week!
You too. Bye, Jordan.
Bye, thanks again!
(Call ends)
Thanks, bye!
(The interview is complete.)
Take care!
(End of interview.)
Thanks again, have a good one!
(The call has ended.)
Thanks again, bye!
(Interview concluded.)

practice_questions.question: Tell me about a time you failed.
Why do you want this kind of role?

verdicts.notes: Strength: the interviewer probed the metrics and the sponsorship story persistently (1.9x measurement, fourth hire, flyer pitch) and covered both practice questions and the candidate's questions. Weakness: it never asked what the candidate personally did when they said "we" (T9, T11, T25), skipped the customer complaint topic, and over-dug the sponsorship answer (T16–T22). It also gave a mild evaluative comment at T14.

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for coming in. Did you find everything okay today?
Yeah, all good, thanks for having me. Finding the building was easy, and the video link worked fine on my end. I'm glad to be here.
Great, glad to hear it. So, Jordan, I've got your resume here. Before we dive in, what drew you to this kind of role?

I think what drew me in is that I like seeing a plan actually work with real people. At the outdoor gear store, our team got really good at figuring out what customers needed before we ever pitched anything, and I liked how fast that felt when it clicked. And on the club side, we had to make money decisions that affected a lot of people, which made me want more of that kind of work. This role looks like it puts those two things together, so that's what got my attention.

That makes sense. So you're drawn to that mix of understanding people and making decisions that have real impact. Let me dig into one of those a bit. You mentioned being top seller at the outdoor gear store for three months running. What were you actually doing differently that got you there?

Honestly, the biggest thing was that I asked what trip people were planning before I showed them anything. Someone walks in wanting a jacket, and I'd ask where they were headed and what the conditions would be like. That changed what I recommended, and people usually ended up buying more because the stuff actually fit what they needed. My add-on sales ran about 1.9 times the store average, and I ranked first out of nine associates from June through August.
Got it. So you were asking better questions upfront and that drove more add-ons. How did you know the 1.9 times number, and how were add-ons actually measured in the store?

Honestly, the store's monthly sales reports showed it. Our manager pulled numbers by associate each month, so we could see who was ranked where and how many add-ons were attached to each sale. I'd have to double-check the exact formula, since I didn't track that part myself, but the rankings and the comparison to the store average came straight from those reports.

That's fair. So the store was already tracking it, and you could see where you stood. Did you talk to the other associates about what you were doing, or did anyone ask you how you were getting those numbers?

Yeah, a few of us talked about it. Our team had a loose habit of sharing what was working on the floor during slow stretches, so the trip-first question came up pretty naturally. A couple of the other associates started trying it too, and we'd compare notes on what customers said. I wouldn't say it was a formal thing, just a team that wanted to get better together.
Nice. You mentioned training four new hires on the sales floor. What did that training actually look like, and how did you know it was working?

So we set up a pretty simple process for the new hires. Each one got shadowed for two shifts, where we'd watch how they greeted customers and asked questions. Then we flipped it, and they led the sales conversations while we stayed close by to jump in if needed. We kept it hands-on because that's how the trip-first approach really sticks.

How we knew it was working was pretty concrete. Three of the four hit their first monthly sales target, which was a good sign the process was getting them up to speed.
What about the fourth person? Did they not hit the target, or what happened there?

Honestly, that one didn't hit the first target. I don't want to guess at the reason, because I didn't follow that person's numbers after the first month. What I can say is that we looked at it as a team, and the question we asked was what they needed more of, not whether the training itself was the problem. If I were doing it again, I'd check in earlier with anyone who was struggling, instead of waiting for the monthly numbers to tell us.
That's a fair reflection. Let me shift gears for a second. Tell me about a time you actually failed at something.

Sure. The sponsor search for the club's spring event is the one that comes to mind. We emailed about 25 local businesses, and the cold emails mostly went nowhere. Only three said yes: a bike shop, a cafe, and a bank branch, worth $2,400 total. Honestly, the emails were the part that wasn't working, and we were slow to notice that.

What turned it around was walking in with a one-page flyer. Once people could see the event and what their business would get out of it, the conversations went a lot better. The lesson I took from it is that I should have tested the approach on a few businesses before sending out 25 emails. Now I try a small batch first and adjust before scaling up.
So you sent 25 cold emails before you realized the approach wasn't landing. When you switched to the one-page flyer and walked in, how many more sponsors did you end up getting?

I don't have a clean split for that. In total we got three yeses, the bike shop, the cafe, and the bank branch, worth $2,400. Some of those may have come from emails before we changed approach, so I don't want to claim the flyer got all three. What I can say is that the in-person visits with the flyer had a much better response rate
Got it. So you landed three sponsors total for that spring event. Walk me through what you actually did in those in-person visits with the flyer. What was the pitch like?

So the pitch was pretty simple. We'd walk in with a one-page flyer that laid out the spring event, who'd be coming, and what a sponsor would get out of it, like their name on the flyer and a mention at the event. We kept it short, because most owners were busy and didn't want a long sales speech.

Honestly, I'm not sure I can say exactly what each conversation sounded like. The team had a rough script, and we'd check in afterward about what landed. I'd rather not make up a play-by-play of one visit when I don't remember the details that precisely.
Fair enough. Of the three that said yes, do you remember anything specific about one of those conversations? Even just what the owner's concern was or what seemed to matter most to them?

I don't have a specific conversation I can walk you through, and I don't want to make up an owner's concern. What I can say is that the three places that said yes were a bike shop, a cafe, and a bank branch, so they were pretty different businesses. As a team, we noticed the flyer helped most when we could show the owner exactly what they'd get, like their name in front of the crowd. But I can't tell you which of those points mattered to which owner.
Understood. Let me ask you this—if you were starting this sponsorship search from scratch on day one of a new job, what would you do differently from the jump?

I'd start with a small test batch, maybe five or so businesses, before committing to 25 emails. We'd send a couple of versions, see what got replies, and then decide. I'd also get the flyer ready before reaching out at all, since that's what ended up working. And I'd go in person sooner. Cold emails were the slow route, and the walk-ins gave us the real answers faster.
Makes sense. Shifting to the club treasurer side—you managed a $12,000 annual budget. Tell me about a specific decision where you had to choose what to fund and what to cut.

The hardest call was the end-of-year banquet. We had the budget from student government, and the banquet was planned at $3,000. The team needed money for travel to a competition, so we decided to cut the banquet down to $1,200 and put the difference toward getting people to the competition.

It wasn't an easy choice, because people like the banquet and it's the one event everyone sees as a reward. We talked through it as a group, and the competition seemed like the thing that would help the club the most that year. We still kept a smaller version of the banquet so people had something to celebrate.
How did you know that the competition was actually the right priority over the banquet? Like, what made you confident that was the call?

Honestly, I wouldn't say we had a hard number that proved it. It was more of a judgment call. The competition was a chance for the club to show up as a team and get visibility, and the banquet is a nice night but it's a one-time thing. We looked at what the budget could realistically cover and asked which option would do the most for the club that year.

I was also pretty upfront with the group that the banquet would be disappointing for some people. We didn't want to act like cutting it was painless, so we kept a smaller version to make sure people still had something to celebrate.
We're almost out of time, so I want to make sure I get your questions in. What would you like to know from me about the role or the team?
Sure, I'd love to know what a typical first 90 days looks like for someone in this role.

Good question. Honestly, the first month is a lot of listening and learning the systems we've got in place. You'd be shadowing the team, understanding our processes, and getting to know the customers and what they actually care about. By month two, you'd start owning some smaller projects on your own while we're still close by. And by month three, you'd have a clearer sense of where you can make an impact and what you'd want to tackle next.

Anything else?
Thanks, that helps. One more: how do you usually measure success for someone in this role after the first year?

We look at a mix of things—how well you're owning your projects without needing constant check-ins, how the team and customers respond to working with you, and whether you're actually moving the needle on the goals we set together in month one. It's not just one metric. It's judgment and impact.

Well, I really appreciate your time today, Jordan. Thanks for being thoughtful with your answers and for coming in. We'll be in touch soon.
Thanks so much for the time today. I enjoyed the conversation, and I appreciate you walking me through the role. I'm looking forward to hearing back.
Great. Take care, and have a good rest of your day.

It also asked the failure question. Weakness: it never pushed back on repeated "don't quote me" non-answers, such as the target figure and the budget breakdown. It also skipped the "why this role" question and never invited the candidate's questions, and it gave small evaluative comments at T2, T8 and T18.

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for coming in. Did you find everything okay today?

Yeah, yeah, everything's good, thanks for asking. Honestly the video call link was a little weird at first, it kept asking me to update something and I almost didn't get in, and then I remembered my roommate had this same issue last week with a different app, so I just clicked through. I actually left my apartment about twenty minutes early because the bus near me has been running late lately, and I'd rather be early than scrambling. Anyway, I'm glad to be here, and I appreciate you taking the time to meet with me today.

Good thinking on the timing. Better to be early. Well, I'm glad you made it through the tech stuff and we're here now.

So let's start with the basics—walk me through your background. How'd you end up where you are today?

Sure, yeah. So I'm a business major, junior year, and I've been working part time at an outdoor gear store on the east side for about a year and a half now. Honestly I kind of fell into it. I needed a job that worked around my classes, and I'd always liked hiking, so I figured I'd rather be around stuff I actually care about than stock shelves at a big box place. It's a small store, maybe nine of us on the sales side, and the manager is great, though she's always reorganizing the tent section, which drives everyone a little crazy. Somewhere in there I got more into the selling side, and then I ended up running the money side of my campus club too, which is how I got into the budgeting stuff. I'm trying to figure out whether I want to go into retail management or something more on the finance side, so this kind of interview is part of that process for me.
That makes sense. And which club is that?

It's the outdoor rec club, which is kind of a funny fit since I'm basically a business major who just happens to like hiking. We do weekend trips and a few bigger things over the year, and I took over as treasurer because the last person kind of disappeared in the middle of the semester, and nobody else wanted to deal with the spreadsheets. My econ professor, Dr. Hanley, actually told me I should put it on my resume, which I thought was a weird thing to get excited about, but here we are. The club's got around twelve active members, maybe more on paper. Anyway, it's the student org that gets the most of my free time, so yeah, that's the one I'm talking about.

Got it. So you inherited that role mid-semester and had to jump in. Let me ask you about the retail side first since that's where most of your time is.

You were top seller three months in a row. What were you doing differently than the other folks on the floor?

Okay, so that's June through August, and honestly I didn't think about it as a competition at the time. I was just doing my own thing. My trick, if you want to call it that, is that before I show anybody anything, I ask where they're headed. A lot of people walk in thinking they need a tent or a jacket, and then you find out it's a three-day trip in the rain, or they're taking their kid on a first overnight, and suddenly the conversation is about what they actually need. I'm also kind of nosy, which helps. My manager jokes that I'd ask a stranger on the bus where they're going, and she's not totally wrong. Anyway, the add-ons were the part that moved the numbers. Things like a better sleeping pad, or a headlamp, or the stove fuel they forgot about. I was selling those at about 1.9 times the store average. So the short version is I ask about the trip first, then I suggest the stuff that makes the trip work. Honestly it's pretty simple, and I think most people just don't slow down enough to ask.
That's a solid approach. So when you say 1.9 times the store average on add-ons—how did you know that number? Were you tracking it yourself, or did your manager pull that for you?

Yeah, so my manager pulls the monthly reports, and she shares the attach-rate numbers with the whole floor, which is a little awkward sometimes because everyone can see where they land. I didn't keep my own spreadsheet or anything, I just kind of looked at the board in the back office every couple weeks. Honestly I was surprised when I saw it, because I wasn't really counting, I was just talking to people about their trips. I think the reports break it down by associate and by category, so the add-on number was on there next to my name. I'm pretty sure that's how it works, but don't quote me on the exact formatting, since the software they use is kind of clunky. Anyway, that's how I knew, and I was pretty happy about it, even if the tent section is still a mess.
Fair enough. And you won that top seller spot three months straight. Did anything change after August, or did something else happen?

Honestly, not really anything dramatic. Once fall semester started my shifts got shuffled around, and I was picking up a lot more evening hours, so I wasn't on the floor during the times I used to be. I'm not sure I'd even call it a change, more like the schedule just moved. Oh, and the manager asked if I'd help with new hires around then, which is kind of funny because I'd never trained anyone before. I think she figured I was the one who talked to customers the most, so I guess I was the logical pick. My roommate says I'm always the person people ask for directions too, so maybe it's just a me thing. Anyway, that training thing ended up being a bigger part of my fall than the sales numbers, and I can tell you more about it if you want.
Yeah, let's talk about that. You trained four new hires. Walk me through how you actually did that—what did a training session look like?

Sure. So the way it worked, and I'll try not to go on forever about it, is I shadowed each new hire for two shifts first. On the first shift I'd basically just follow them around and watch them talk to customers, which honestly was a little awkward for everyone, including me. My manager had this thing where she always said you learn more by watching than by reading the handbook, and I kind of agree, though the handbook is also really long and has a section on tent stakes that nobody has ever read. Anyway, on the second shift I'd hang back and let them run the floor while I jumped in only if they got stuck. Then after that, they led and I just watched. Three of the four hit their first monthly target, which I was pretty happy about, though the fourth person is now doing really well in the bike department, so I think it worked out for everybody.
So three of four hit their first monthly target. What was the target, and how did you know the fourth person wasn't going to make it before they moved to bikes?

Yeah, so the target was the store's monthly sales goal for new associates, and I don't remember the exact dollar figure off the top of my head, sorry. I think it was something like a per-person number the manager set based on the first few months, but don't hold me to that. As for the fourth person, honestly I didn't really know they weren't going to make it until pretty late. They were a little quieter on the floor than the others, and I kept thinking they'd find their rhythm, and then the month was almost over and they were behind. I'm not sure whether it was the schedule or just that the fourth person wasn't as into the outdoor stuff as the rest of the group, but when the bike department had an opening they asked to move over, and my manager said yes. Which, I mean, I think that's a fine outcome. I wasn't keeping a count of who was on track, so I can't tell you the exact week it became clear, but that's what happened.
Got it. So looking back, is there anything you'd do differently with that fourth person if you were training them again today?

Yeah, that's a good question, and I've actually thought about it a bit since. I think the big thing is I waited too long. I kept assuming they'd come around, and I was pretty hands-off after the first two shifts because I didn't want to hover, which is probably a bit of a me thing, since I'm so used to just doing my own thing on the floor. So if I did it again, I'd check in more often, maybe a quick two-minute chat after every shift just to ask what felt hard that day. My manager does something like that with her own group, I think, though honestly she also has a whole color-coded tracker that I've never fully understood. I'd also ask the new person more directly what they're into, the way I ask customers where they're headed. Like, if they didn't care about camping, maybe bikes was the right place for them from the start, and I could've figured that out earlier instead of after a month of them being behind. So yeah, earlier check-ins and asking more questions. Oh, and I'd probably stop calling it a "fourth person" in my head. They were a real person with their own thing going on, and I think I treated them like the odd one out.

That's thoughtful. Now let's shift gears a bit. You managed a twelve-thousand-dollar budget as club treasurer. Walk me through how you approached that—what were the big buckets, and did you have to make any tough calls?

Sure, so the twelve thousand came from student government, which was kind of a surprise, because I thought I'd be scrambling for money the whole year. When I took over midway through the semester, the first thing I did was dig through the old spreadsheets, which were honestly a mess. Some of the categories didn't even match the receipts, and I spent a whole weekend trying to figure out what "misc" meant. My econ professor, Dr. Hanley, keeps saying I should build a proper budget template, and I keep saying I will. Anyway, the biggest bucket by far was travel for the weekend trips and the bigger competition, and the end-of-year banquet was the other big one. The tough call was the banquet. It had been sitting at three thousand dollars, and people really like it, but there was a competition coming up where we needed travel money, so I cut the banquet down to twelve hundred. Some members were pretty annoyed, and one of them asked me in a group chat whether I was "trying to make the club boring." I got why they were upset, and I still think it was the right call for the people actually going to the competition, but I wish I'd talked to everyone
Hold on—so you cut the banquet from three thousand to twelve hundred. What did that three thousand actually cover? What were you cutting?

Okay, so the three thousand was basically the whole end-of-year thing, the venue, the food, and some kind of awards stuff. I don't have the exact line-item breakdown in front of me, and honestly the old spreadsheet was so messy I'm not sure everything was categorized the same way. I think the venue was the biggest piece, and there was catering, and a bunch of small stuff like decorations and printed certificates, which Dr. Hanley would probably say we could've done digitally. When I cut it to twelve hundred, I kept the basic dinner and a space to sit down and cut back on the fancy parts. Some people were like, why does it matter if there's a slideshow or not? And I get that. But the competition travel was going to be a lot more expensive than people realized, like hotel rooms and gas for three vehicles, plus entry fees. So I went with the banquet being smaller and the travel being covered. I'm not 100 percent sure I got every number exactly right on the breakdown, so if you want the precise split I'd want to double-check the old budget file before I quoted you anything.
Fair. So you made that call—smaller banquet, more travel money. Did you talk to the club members before you made the decision, or did you just announce it?

Honestly, I'd like to say I talked to everyone first, but that's not really what happened. I floated the idea in our group chat, mostly to see what people thought, and a couple of people replied, but it wasn't really a discussion. The competition was coming up fast and the travel money had to be locked in, so I kind of made the call and then explained it after. Looking back, that's the part I'd change. The reply about making the club boring stung a little, mostly because I felt like I was the one doing the boring work of keeping the money straight. Oh, and Dr. Hanley told me later that a short poll would've taken five minutes and saved me a lot of grief, which, yeah, he's right. So now when I have a call like that, I try to post the numbers first and give people a day to react before I lock it in.
Makes sense. You mentioned you also secured three local sponsors for the spring event. How did you find them, and what was your pitch?

Yeah, so the sponsors were a bit of a grind, and I'll admit the first approach didn't work at all. I sent cold emails to about twenty-five local businesses, and the replies were basically silence or a polite no. Then I kind of got frustrated and thought, okay, what if I just walk in? So I made a one-page flyer, nothing fancy, with a little photo from one of our weekend trips, a short paragraph about who we are, and what a sponsor would get, like a logo on the event shirts and a shout-out at the event. Then I started going into shops in person, which was honestly kind of nerve-wracking, and some of them were really nice about it. Three said yes: a bike shop, a cafe, and a bank branch. Between them they came to about twenty-four hundred dollars, which was a good chunk of what we needed for spring. The bike shop was probably the easiest, since they already knew a couple of our members. The bank took the longest, because they had to run it past someone at corporate, and I think I sent that person about four follow-up emails, which I'm not proud of, but it worked out.
So the cold emails didn't work, but walking in did. What do you think the difference was? Like, why did showing up in person land three sponsors when the emails didn't?

Yeah, I've thought about that a lot, actually. I think part of it is that an email is really easy to ignore. You send it, and it sits in someone's inbox between a vendor invoice and a newsletter, and it's super easy to just not reply. When you walk in, the person's standing right there, and it's a lot harder to say no to somebody's face, especially when they're friendly about it. Also, I kind of think the flyer helped, because it gave them something to look at while we talked, and they could see the photo from the trip and get a sense of who we were. My roommate says I'm too good at small talk, which probably helped too, because I'd usually end up chatting with the owner about hiking or whatever they were into before I even brought up the club. Oh, and the cafe owner actually told me she used to be in a hiking group in college, so that kind of sealed it. I don't know if that's the real reason or I just got lucky with who was working those days, but I think showing up and being a real person with a real flyer made a difference.
That's helpful. One more thing on that—of the three that said yes, did any of them push back on what you were asking, or did you have to negotiate anything with them?

Not really pushback so much as a few questions. The bike shop asked whether the logo would go on the shirts or the banner, and I honestly had to check with the club before I could answer, which I should've done before I walked in. The cafe wanted to know how many people usually show up to the event, and I didn't have a great number, so I said something like "around forty, maybe more," which I'm pretty sure was an okay guess. The bank was the one that actually made things slow. They had a whole approval process, and the person I was working with kept saying they needed to check with corporate about what kind of sponsorship they could do, so I ended up going back and forth on the wording for a few weeks. I don't think I really negotiated the amount, though. Everybody who said yes was kind of fine with the basic package I put on the flyer, and I think the bank ended up with a slightly smaller logo spot than they wanted, but I'd have to double-check the agreement to be sure. Honestly the hardest part was just not giving up on the bank while I waited. Oh, and the cafe owner also asked if she could bring some of her pastries to the event, which I thought was a really nice bonus.

Nice. So you've been handling customer stuff on the sales floor too—escalated returns and complaints. Tell me about a time when something went really wrong with a customer, and walk me through how you handled it.

Yeah, so one that stands out was a customer who came in wanting a refund on a used tent. The problem was it was past the return window, and I think they'd been using it for a while and it had a tear in the rainfly. They were pretty frustrated, and honestly I got why, because nobody wants to feel stuck with a tent that failed on them. My first instinct was to just say no, because the policy is pretty clear about the window, and the manager is always saying we don't want to be pushovers. But then I kind of thought about it, and I remembered the brand has a warranty program for defects, so I asked if they'd be open to getting it repaired through that instead of a refund. I had to look up the warranty terms in the back, which took a few minutes, and I think the customer was a little skeptical at first, because they wanted their money back. I also ended up explaining that the repair route would probably be faster than a refund anyway, since the brand handles it directly. They agreed, and a few weeks later they left a positive review, which honestly surprised me, since I didn't think I'd made anybody happy that day. I'm not totally sure the review mentioned me by name, but it said the staff was helpful, so I'll take it.
So you didn't give them the refund they wanted, but you found them another path. How did you know about the warranty program? Was that something you'd learned, or did you just think to look it up?

Honestly, a bit of both. I didn't have it memorized, so I did have to look it up in the back, but I'd seen the warranty info in the binder once when I was going through the returns stuff with the manager, and it stuck in the back of my head. I think the tent was a brand we carry a lot of, so it wasn't totally new territory. Ugh, I can never remember which brands have the lifetime stuff and which ones are just a set number of years, so I always have to check. Anyway, I think the real thing is I didn't want to just say "sorry, policy," because that's the answer that makes a customer walk out angry. So I was kind of digging for something I could actually offer them. I'm not sure I'd call it clever, more like I was annoyed at the idea of sending someone out the door with nothing. My roommate says I'm weirdly stubborn about that kind of thing, which, fair.
Got it. Let me ask you something else. Tell me about a time you actually failed at something—where things didn't go the way you wanted and you didn't have a good workaround.

Okay, so the one that comes to mind is the fourth new hire I trained, because that one didn't really get fixed. I did the whole shadow-then-lead thing with them like I did with everybody else, and I kept telling myself they'd find their groove. Honestly, I was so caught up in how the other three were doing that I didn't notice how behind this person was until the month was almost over. My roommate says I have a bad habit of assuming things are fine if nobody's yelling, which is kind of true. By the time I realized it, there wasn't much time left to try anything. They ended up moving to the bike department, which is a good place for them, but I didn't really solve the problem. It just
So you realized too late. Looking back now, what would you actually do differently in that first week or two if you could go back?

Okay, so the first thing I'd change is I'd stop waiting for the monthly numbers to tell me how someone's doing. By the time the month was almost over, it was already too late to fix much. So in that first week or two, I'd sit down with the new person for a few minutes after each shift and just ask what felt hard that day, and I'd also ask what they actually care about, like whether they're into camping or more into bikes, the same way I ask customers where they're headed. I think I'd also be more honest with myself. I kept telling myself they'd come around, and that was really me avoiding an awkward conversation. My manager probably would've told me to just talk to them sooner, and honestly she'd be right. I also think I'd ask the manager early what she's seeing from her side, since she's got that color-coded tracker thing, even if I still don't fully get it. Anyway, that's the plan. Can I ask one quick question now, or is that for later?
Sure, go ahead.

practice_questions.question: Tell me about a time you failed.
Why do you want this kind of role?

verdicts.notes: Strength: the interviewer kept pulling a rambling candidate back on track with pointed follow-ups on measurement, readiness criteria, pitch and budget decisions, and it asked both practice questions. Weakness: it skipped the customer complaint topic and never pushed on vague answers about motivation or the first-month plan. It also leaked mild evaluative praise ("solid example", "good lesson") and cut the candidate off at T17 without noticing.

transcript.text: Hey, good to meet you. How's your day been so far?

Hey, good to meet you too, thanks for making time. My day's been pretty good, honestly. I had a bit of a rush this morning because the bus was late, which is so typical for this route, and I ended up grabbing coffee from the place by the library that always gets the order wrong, but it was fine. I actually made it here a few minutes early, so I've been sitting in my car going over my notes, which, be honest, is a little nerve-wracking. My roommate keeps joking that I'm going to recite my whole resume back to you, so I'm trying not to do that. Anyway, how about you? Has your day been busy?
Ha, yeah, I get that. It's been a solid day on my end, thanks for asking. Alright, so let's dig in. Tell me a bit about yourself—what brings you here, and what's your background?

Sure, happy to. So I'm finishing up a business degree, and I'm at the stage where I want to get real experience in something beyond classes. My background is mostly two things. The first is retail. I've been working as a sales associate at an outdoor gear store for about a year now, which I honestly picked up because I like being outside and I figured I'd be good at talking to people about hiking boots and sleeping bags. The second is on campus, where I'm the treasurer for one of the student clubs. That one's a bit of a funny story, because I didn't really expect to end up with the money side of things. Anyway, I think those two together are what I'd bring here. I'm curious what the role looks like day to day, if you don't mind me asking.

I'll tell you more about the day-to-day in a bit. But first, I'm curious about the retail side. Your resume mentions you were a top seller for three months in a row. What were you doing differently than the other folks on the floor?

Oh, good, I was hoping you'd ask about that one. Honestly, I don't think I was doing anything magic. It was more that I kind of stumbled into a habit. The store was slammed that summer, and the guys on the floor would grab a customer and start pulling down tents and stoves right away, which I totally get because that's what you're supposed to do, right? But I noticed people would look at the first three things and kind of glaze over. So I started just asking what kind of trip they were planning, like, is it one night or a week, are you going to be carrying everything on your back, that kind of thing. It sounds obvious now, but people really like being asked. Then I'd only show them stuff that fit that trip, and I'd throw in a small add-on, like a better pad or a headlamp, because if you're going to be out for four days you're going to want it. My add-on sales ended up being around 1.9 times the store average, which I was pretty proud of, though my manager probably would've said it was the summer crowd. What about you, is that kind of consultative approach something you look for in people?
That's a solid example. So when you say your add-on sales were 1.9 times the store average—how did you actually measure that? Was your manager tracking it, or did you figure it out yourself?

Good question, and honestly, I'm not a numbers person by nature, which is kind of ironic given I ended up as a club treasurer. The store runs everything through a point-of-sale system, so every transaction gets logged with the items in it. Our manager, Dana, pulled a report at the end of each month that showed sales by associate, and she'd sometimes break it down by how many items were on each receipt beyond the main purchase. I think that's where the 1.9 times number came from, but I'm going from memory on the exact way she calculated it. I remember her waving the printout at the break room and saying something like, "Jordan, you're either a genius or you've been stealing headlamps." I'm pretty sure she was joking, mostly. Anyway, I didn't build a spreadsheet or anything like that myself, so if you want the precise methodology, Dana would be the one to ask. Does your company track something like attach rate, or do you look at it differently?

We do track it, yeah. I appreciate the honesty about going from memory. Let me ask you this—when you were training those four new hires on the sales floor, how did you actually train them? Walk me through what that looked like.

Yeah, I figured you'd track it, it's pretty standard. So with the training, it wasn't a formal program or anything. Our store didn't really have one, so when the new people came in, the manager would just kind of point at whoever was free and say, "Go show them the ropes." I got that job a few times, and honestly I think it's because I was the one who didn't mind repeating myself. The way I did it was, I'd shadow each new hire for their first two shifts, just following them around and watching. I'd mostly stay quiet, except if they were about to tell someone something wrong about a product, which happened with a sleeping bag temperature rating once and that was a whole thing. After the two shifts, I'd flip it, and they'd lead the customers while I stood back and watched. Then I'd give them feedback on the way home, which I did in the parking lot a lot, because there's a coffee place next to the store that I'm pretty sure has a sad, unclear sign on the door. Three of the four hit their first monthly target, and the fourth one ended up being great too, just a little slower to get going. Is that kind of hands-on approach how your team onboards people, or do you have something more structured?
That's helpful. So out of curiosity—how did you know the three were actually ready to be on the floor solo? What were you looking for?

Good question, and I think I was mostly going by gut feel, which I'm not sure is the best answer but it's the honest one. The main thing I watched for was whether they could figure out what a customer actually needed without me jumping in. Like, could they ask the trip question without it sounding like a script, and did they listen to the answer or just keep talking about the product they liked? I also paid attention to how they handled it when a customer pushed back, because that happens constantly with people who are spending a lot of money on a tent. One of the new hires was super quick with product knowledge but kind of rushed people, and I was worried about that for a while. My roommate says I overthink everything, and she's probably right, but I'd rather have someone slow and right than fast and wrong. Honestly, I also just asked them how they felt, because if they were nervous, they usually weren't ready yet. Do you guys have a set checklist for that, or is it more of a manager's call?
It's a mix, but I hear you. Let me shift gears a bit. Tell me about a time you actually failed at something—didn't go the way you wanted.

Oh, that's a good one to ask, because I've definitely had those. Honestly, the one that comes to mind is from the club, with the spring event sponsors. I thought I'd be smart and just email local businesses, which seemed efficient, and I sent out about 25 of them. It was kind of a grind, because every time I sent one I'd second-guess the wording, and I think I rewrote the first one like four times. Most of them just never answered, which I should have expected, but I took it personally anyway. I was sitting in the library one afternoon, which is where I do most of my thinking, and the guy at the next table was literally reading a flyer for a bake sale, and it hit me that maybe nobody reads email anymore. So I printed a one-page flyer and just started walking into shops. That's what actually worked, and I ended up with three yeses, a bike shop, a cafe, and a bank branch, worth about $2,400 total. So the failure was really me thinking the easy channel would work. Does that kind of thing come up a lot in your work, or is it more of the other way around?
That's a good lesson. So you got three sponsors in the end—that's what's on your resume. When you were walking into those shops in person, what was your pitch like? How'd you actually convince them?

Yeah, the pitch was a bit of a mess at first, honestly. I'd practice it in the car and then freeze the second somebody looked up from the register. What ended up working was pretty simple. I'd walk in, ask for whoever handled community stuff or the manager, which sometimes took a few tries because at the cafe the manager was in the back, and I had this whole thing where I'd almost leave before she came out. Then I'd hand over the one-page flyer and kind of just talk through it. The flyer had the event date, roughly how many students were expected, and what the sponsor would get, like their logo on the banner and a shout-out at the event. I tried to keep it short, because I figured busy shop owners didn't want a lecture. The bike shop was actually the easiest, because the guy there had been a student years ago and he just said yes before I finished. The bank branch took the longest, they wanted to check with someone at corporate, which I thought was going to kill the whole thing. I think what helped was that I wasn't asking for a huge amount, and I was honest that it was a small club with a small budget. Do you usually have people pitch sponsors like that at your company, or is it more of a formal partnership process?

We handle it differently, but I appreciate the detail. Quick follow-up—you mentioned you were honest about the small budget. Did you have a number in mind when you walked in, or did you feel them out first?

Honestly, I had a rough idea in my head, but I didn't lead with a number, mostly because I didn't want to sound like I was haggling in a store. I'd gone in thinking about what the club actually needed for the spring event, and I'd sort of worked backward from that. The problem is I'd also been eating a lot of granola bars in the library that month, so my sense of what things cost was a little skewed. Anyway, what I did was describe the event, say how many students we'd probably get, and then let them tell me what they could do. The cafe manager actually brought up a number first, which was a relief, and I just said that sounded great. Between the three of them it came to about $2,400, which felt like a win for a club that

Got it. Let me ask you about the budget side of things. You mentioned you manage a $12,000 annual budget as treasurer. Walk me through a decision you had to make there—something where you had to cut or fund something and it wasn't obvious which way to go.

Oh, that one was rough. So the twelve grand comes from student government, which gets split across all the clubs, and every year you have to justify it to a room of people who mostly want free pizza. Our club had this end-of-year banquet that everybody loves, and it was eating about three thousand of the budget. Then the team got invited to a regional competition, and the travel costs were going to be way more than what we had left. I remember sitting in my car in the parking garage, which is where I go when I need quiet, going back and forth on it for like an hour. Honestly, I think my roommate was the one who finally said, "Nobody remembers the banquet, but they'll remember going to nationals," which is maybe an overstatement, since it was a regional thing. In the end I cut the banquet from three thousand down to twelve hundred, and that covered the travel. People were grumpy about it, and I had to send a pretty awkward email. But the team went, and I think it was the right call. Do you guys have a similar tension with your own budgets, or is that more of a finance-team thing?
That's a real tradeoff. So when you sent that email about cutting the banquet, how did people actually react? Did you get pushback?

Yeah, there was some pushback, mostly from people who'd already started planning what they were going to order for the banquet. A couple of members replied to the email pretty quickly, and one of them basically asked if I could just find the money somewhere else, which, I wish I could have. I rewrote that email so many times that I think I ended up overexplaining it, and I'm pretty sure I included a paragraph about the student government funding rules that nobody asked for. Honestly, I think the thing that helped most was that I didn't hide the numbers. I put the actual totals in the email, what the banquet cost, what the travel cost, and what was left. A few people came up to me in the hallway after the next meeting and said they got it, even if they didn't love it. Oh, and my roommate says I should have just done it over coffee instead of email, but I think she's just mad she didn't get to go to the banquet either. Anyway, I learned to explain tradeoffs before people find out about them, which I guess is a useful thing to know for a job like this one.
That makes sense. So why are you actually interested in this role? What's drawing you to it?

Honestly, I've been thinking about that a lot since I saw the posting. I'm trying to figure out what I want after graduation, and I keep bouncing between wanting to stay close to customers and wanting to do more with the numbers. My roommate thinks I'm overcomplicating it, and she might be right, because she also thinks I should watch fewer cooking shows at midnight. Anyway, the retail job taught me that I like figuring out what someone actually needs, and the treasurer job taught me that I can handle a budget and explain tradeoffs to people who are annoyed with me. This role seems to sit right where those two things meet, which is why it caught my eye. I'll be honest that I don't know the company as well as I'd like yet, so I've been reading up on it on the bus, which is a fun way to get motion sickness. What I'd really like is a job where I'm still talking to people every day but I'm also responsible for the results. Is that something people in this role end up doing, or is it more of a behind-the-scenes kind of job?
That's fair. We'll get into the day-to-day in a second. But let me ask—in your first month here, if you got the job, what would you actually focus on? How would you spend your time?

Good question, and I've thought about it a little, though I'll admit I'm guessing since I don't know the team yet. My first instinct would be to spend the first week or two just listening. I'd want to sit in on conversations with customers or whoever the main users are, and figure out what they actually struggle with. That's basically what I did with the new hires at the store, shadowing them before I let them run anything, so I'd probably do something similar here. I'd also want to get my hands on whatever numbers the team already tracks, because I'd rather understand what's being measured before I try to change anything. I know that's a bit of a cautious answer, and my roommate would say I'm overthinking it again, but I'd rather learn the ground before I start pushing on it. Around week three or four, I'd want to pick one small thing I could improve and actually follow through on it, so I'd have something concrete to show. Oh, and I'd probably want to ask a lot of questions in the first few days, which I hope nobody minds, because I tend to ask about everything. Honestly, what does the first month usually look like for someone in this role?
We'll walk through that more once you're onboarded. I'm nearly out of time here, so let me ask—what questions do you have for me about the role or the team?
Sure, just one for now. What does success look like for this role at the six-month mark?

That's a good question. Honestly, it depends on where the team is at when you start, but generally we're looking for someone who understands the core workflows, can handle some of the day-to-day independently, and has spotted at least one or two things we could be doing better. We don't expect perfection early on—we're more interested in good judgment and ownership. Does that help?

Yeah, that helps a lot, thanks. Understanding the workflows and being able to handle some of the day-to-day on my own sounds reasonable, and I like the part about spotting things to improve. I'd probably be pretty nervous about that first stretch, but I think I'd rather be slow and careful than rush into something I don't understand yet. Honestly, I appreciate you being straight about not expecting perfection, because I'd be hard on myself if you did. I'm really glad I got to meet you today, and I hope the conversation was useful on your end too. Is there anything else you need from me before we wrap up?

No, I think we're good. I appreciate you taking the time today, and thanks for being thoughtful and honest throughout. We'll be in touch soon about next steps. Good luck with the rest of your semester.
