verdicts.notes: Strength: the interviewer followed the resume topics well, asked both practice questions, and caught the sponsor-count confusion (T18), which made the candidate clarify. Weakness: it never asked about the club budget, which was a listed topic. It also let the vague "why this role" and "first month" answers go without follow-up, and it gave mild evaluative paraphrases such as "That's fair. You knew what success looked like."

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for coming in. Did you find everything okay today?

Yeah, all good, thanks for having me. Honestly I almost missed the turn off the main road because the construction on Fulton is still a mess, and I got here a little early, so I sat in my car for like ten minutes listening to this podcast about, uh, how honey gets made, which is way more interesting than it sounds. My roommate always says I'm too into random stuff like that. Anyway, the building's easy to find once you're inside, and the front desk person was really friendly, so yeah, everything's fine.

Ha, well I'm glad you made it through the construction gauntlet. And hey, honey production is legitimately fascinating—there's a lot of logistics involved.

So tell me a bit about yourself. What's been on your plate the last couple years, work and school-wise?

Oh, thanks, yeah, the logistics thing is what hooked me, the bees are basically running a whole supply chain. Okay, so about me. I'm a business major, almost done, and I've been working part time at an outdoor gear store for a while now, which is honestly the best job I've had because I get to talk about hiking and camping all day. I've also been treasurer for one of the campus clubs, which mostly means I'm the person everyone asks where the money went. Juggling those two plus classes has been a lot, but I like being busy, I think. There's also this professor who keeps telling me I should go into finance, and I keep saying I'll think about it, and then I go back to the store. So yeah, sales and the club budget are probably the main things I'd point to.

Got it. So you've got sales experience and you're managing money for the club. Both seem pretty hands-on.

Let me dig into the sales side first. Your resume says you were top seller three months in a row. What were you actually doing differently than the other folks on the floor?

Okay, so the honest answer is I didn't really do anything fancy, I just kind of ask people questions first. Before I show anybody a single product, I ask what trip they're planning, and that sounds obvious, but a lot of people on the floor just start pulling down jackets. It reminds me of my cousin's wedding last year, where the DJ asked everyone what songs they liked before he played anything, and the dance floor was packed all night. Anyway, once someone tells me they're going somewhere like the Smokies in October with a bad sleeping bag, the add-ons pretty much suggest themselves, like a better pad, a headlamp, that kind of thing. My add-on sales ended up being about 1.9 times the store average, which I only know because my manager posts the numbers on a whiteboard in the break room, and I'm pretty sure that whiteboard is the only thing in the building anyone actually reads. I ranked number one out of nine associates from June through August. I think the main thing is I'd rather know what someone needs than just try to close them fast, but I'm still figuring out how much of it is me and how much is just that I really like talking about hiking.

That makes sense. So you're listening first, and the add-ons are a natural outcome of that conversation rather than a hard sell.

When you trained those four new hires on the sales floor, did you pass along that same approach, or how did you go about training them?

Yeah, I think I did pass it on, though I didn't really sit them down and lecture them about it, which is probably what a real trainer would do. Mostly I just shadowed each of them for two shifts, so I'd be standing right there while they helped customers, and I'd jump in if something got weird. Then after those two shifts I'd flip it, and they'd lead while I watched from the back, which felt awkward for everybody at first, including me. It reminds me of when my little brother tried to teach me to parallel park in his old Civic, and he kept saying "just feel the car" like that helped at all. Anyway, I think it's important to let people struggle a little, because you learn way more from fumbling a conversation than from watching someone else nail it. Three of the four hit their first monthly target, which I was pretty happy about, though the fourth one was honestly a great person who just really didn't like upselling, and I'm not sure I'd have changed that for her.
Okay, so you were hands-on with them for a couple shifts, then flipped it. How did you know whether the training actually stuck? Like, what were you looking for when you watched them lead?

Mostly I was watching whether they asked the trip question before grabbing anything off the wall. That's the big one for me, because if they skip it, everything after is guesswork. I also listened for whether they let the customer finish talking, or whether they cut in with a "this one's great" the second someone mentioned a trail. It's kind of like that cooking show my roommate and I got hooked on, where the judges can tell in the first bite whether someone actually tasted their own food. Anyway, I didn't have a checklist or anything. I just noticed when someone had that moment where they stopped reciting features and started asking follow-up questions, and I'd write a quick note afterward. The three who hit their first monthly target were the ones who got there pretty fast. The fourth one was asking good questions too, she just wasn't comfortable pushing an add-on once she knew what someone needed, so I think the training stuck for her in the parts that mattered to her.

That's fair. You knew what success looked like and you watched for it.

Let me shift gears. Your resume mentions you handled escalated customer returns. Can you walk me through a specific difficult one and what actually happened?

Yeah, sure, there was one that stuck with me. A guy came in wanting a full refund on a tent he'd bought a while back, and it was past the return window, so the answer at the register was no. He got pretty worked up, which, honestly, I get, because it's not fun to feel like you got stuck with something. It reminds me of when my landlord tried to keep my deposit over a scratch on the floor that was already there when we moved in, and I spent a whole afternoon with the lease printed out, which, looking back, was kind of a mess. Anyway, I didn't want to just repeat the policy at him, so I asked what the problem with the tent was. Turned out it had a broken pole section, and I was able to set up a repair through the brand's warranty, which the store could process, so he didn't have to ship it anywhere himself. He wasn't thrilled that it wasn't a refund, but he took the repair, and he left the store a positive review afterward, which my manager actually pointed out on the whiteboard. I guess the main thing I took from it is that when someone's mad, the policy is usually not what they're mad about, so it helps to find the real problem first.

So you went past the stated policy and found a workaround that actually solved his underlying problem. Did you check with a manager before you offered the warranty repair route, or did you just propose it on the spot?

Good question. I did check, sort of. Our manager was on the floor, just a few feet away at the cash wrap, so I kind of waved her over and said, hey, this tent has a busted pole, can we run it through warranty? And she said yeah, go for it, which was nice because I didn't have to hunt her down. Honestly it reminds me of the time I asked my professor for an extension and he said "sure" before I even finished the sentence, and I was so relieved I almost forgot what I was asking for. Anyway, I'd say I didn't really propose it totally on my own, more like I checked in fast before I offered anything. I think that's the right move, because if you promise something the store can't do, you've made the situation worse, and then the customer is mad at you and the policy both.

Makes sense. You checked before you committed.

Let me ask you this—tell me about a time you actually failed at something. Not a near-miss, but something that didn't go the way you wanted.

Okay, so the one that comes to mind is the sponsorship thing for the club's spring event. I figured I'd just email local businesses, and I sent out 25 emails, which felt like a lot of work at the time. I got three yeses, a bike shop, a cafe, and a bank branch, worth about $2,400 total, but the other 22 basically went nowhere, and a couple didn't even write back. It reminds me of when I tried to get a group chat going for a study session and nobody answered until I just showed up at the library with snacks. Anyway, I finally got it through walking into some of the shops with a one-page flyer, and that worked way better than the emails. The part that bugged me was that I should have tried in person from the start, since I'd already learned from the store that people respond better when you're standing in front of them. I guess the lesson I took is that I was so focused on doing it efficiently that I picked the method that was easiest for me instead of the one that would act
I hear you cutting yourself off there. Take your time.

Oh, yeah, sorry, I kind of lost my train of thought there. What I was going to say is that I picked the method that was easiest for me, which was email, instead of the one that would actually work, which was walking in. And honestly, it's kind of embarrassing that it took me 22 ignored emails to figure that out. But I think that's the thing I'd want people to know about me, that I can be pretty stubborn about doing things the efficient way until it clearly doesn't work. Anyway, once I switched to the flyers, I got the rest of the sponsors pretty quickly, so I guess it was a fail that turned into something useful. Also, the bike shop owner was super nice and asked if I was going to be at the next club meeting, which I wasn't, but I said I would be.
So you got three sponsors total from the in-person approach, or three plus the original three from email?

Wait, let me get this straight, because I think I muddled it earlier. It's three total. Three businesses said yes: the bike shop, the cafe, and the bank branch, and together they came to about $2,400. I sent out 25 emails, and those mostly went nowhere, so I'm not counting six. When I said I got the rest quickly, I was probably just talking about the flyer visits, which is where the three yeses came from. It's kind of like when my roommate says she "basically" finished a whole season of a show in one night, and then you find out she means the first two episodes. Anyway, that's why the bike shop guy's question about the club meeting stuck with me, because it felt like the first time someone actually wanted to

Got it, so three sponsors total from the in-person visits. That's clear.

Why do you want this kind of role? What's drawing you to apply here?

Honestly, a lot of it comes down to the stuff I've been doing already. I like that sales here seems to be about figuring out what someone actually needs, which is the part I've always liked most at the store, and I'd like to get better at it on a bigger scale. It also reminds me of my grandpa, who ran a hardware store for thirty years and used to say the best salesperson is the one who sends you home with the right screw, not the most expensive one. I'm not sure that's a perfect fit for this job, but it's kind of how I think about it. The club budget stuff is probably the other piece, since I've gotten pretty into making numbers make sense for people, even though my professor keeps saying I should be in finance. Anyway, I looked at what the company does and it seemed like the kind of place where people actually talk to each other, which matters to me more than I expected. So yeah, that's basically what's pulling me in.
That's helpful. One more thing—if you started here in the first month, what would you actually focus on? Like, what's the first thing you'd want to get right?

Okay, so the first thing I'd want to get right is just learning how things actually work here, which sounds boring but I think it matters. I'd probably spend the first couple weeks mostly listening, like I did when I started at the store, where I'd just follow people around and see how they handled customers before I tried anything myself. It's kind of like when I started the club treasurer job and I had no idea where the receipts were kept, and I spent an entire Saturday in a storage closet with a flashlight, which in hindsight was not the best use of a weekend. Anyway, I'd want to figure out who the people are I'd be working with, what the real priorities are, and what the team considers a good month. I'd also want to avoid the mistake I made with the sponsors, where I picked the method that was easiest for me instead of the one that works. So my honest answer is: learn how this place actually runs before I try to change anything.
Makes sense. Well, I appreciate you walking through all that with me. Do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, just one, if that's okay. What does a typical week look like for someone in this role, especially in the first few months?

That's a good question. Honestly, the first month or two is a lot of onboarding and shadowing, kind of like what you described doing with your trainees. You'll be paired with someone on the team who'll walk you through how we handle things, what our processes are, that kind of thing. After that, it's a mix of client interaction and internal projects—some weeks are busier than others depending on where we are in the cycle. You'd also be in a few standing meetings where we talk through what's working and what isn't. It's not glamorous, but it's structured enough that you're not flying blind.

Any other questions?

Nope, that's all I've got. That actually sounds pretty good, the shadowing part especially, since that's how I'd want to learn too. Thanks so much for your time today, I really enjoyed talking with you.
Great, I'm glad. Thanks for coming in, Jordan. We'll be in touch with next steps early next week. Have a good one.

feedback_leaks.quote: I appreciate you being straight about that.
Thanks for being thoughtful and honest through all of this.

Why do you want this kind of role?

verdicts.notes: Strength: covered all five resume topics and both practice questions, with good probing on the sales metric (T6), the complaint (T12), and the sponsorship failure (T22, T24). Weakness: several feedback leaks ("solid example", "fair self-awareness"). The interviewer also let vague or rambling answers pass (T9, T19, T29) and never asked about the budget decision's results or the follow-up on the training numbers. It also asked "why this role" twice (T2, T28).

transcript.text: Hey, good to meet you. How's your day been so far?

Hey, good to meet you too, thanks for having me. My day's been kind of a mess, honestly. I almost missed the bus this morning because I was up way too late finishing a case study for my marketing class, and the professor who assigned it, Dr. Halvorsen, has this habit of changing the rubric the night before it's due, so I'm still a little annoyed about that. Then I got here and realized my camera was pointed at the ceiling for like five minutes before I fixed it, so I'm sure that made a great first impression. Anyway, I'm doing okay now, a little coffee-fueled, and really glad to be talking with you today.
Ha, well you're here and the camera's working now, so we're good. Coffee's a solid choice. So tell me—what drew you to this role?

Thanks, I'll take the win. Honestly, what got me looking at this kind of role was my job at the outdoor gear store. I work there about twenty hours a week, and my commute is this long bus ride that always runs late, so I've gotten really good at reading a book in the forty-minute window. Anyway, the part I actually like is talking to people when they're planning something big, like a first backpacking trip or a winter camping setup. I've found that if I ask someone where they're headed before I show them anything, they end up buying stuff they actually need, and that's how I ended up ranking first among nine associates for June through August. I think I want a job where that kind of conversation is the whole point, and it sounds like yours is.

That makes sense. So you're saying the conversation piece is really what hooked you on this work. When you say you ask them where they're headed first—what's an example of how that changed what they actually bought compared to what they might have grabbed otherwise?

Okay, so there was this couple who came in looking at a cheap two-person tent, the kind with the bright orange rainfly that everyone grabs off the shelf. Before I showed them anything, I asked where they were headed, and it turned out they were going to the coast for a week, with a lot of wind and sand, which, honestly, I didn't know until they said it. That changed the whole conversation, because the tent they were holding would've been miserable out there. I walked them toward a sturdier one with a lower profile and a better stake setup, and I also mentioned a footprint and a tarp for the sand, which they hadn't thought about. Obviously I'm not going to claim I'm some kind of genius, and some people just want the tent they came in for, which is fine. But that kind of question is why my add-on sales ended up around 1.9 times the store average over those summer months. I think that's the thing I'm most proud of, that people leave with stuff
That's a solid example. So when you say your add-on sales were 1.9 times the store average—how'd you actually measure that? Like, did the store track it for you, or did you figure that out yourself?

Good question, and honestly I should be a little careful here. The store tracks sales by associate, so the numbers came from the monthly reports the manager shared at the team meeting. I didn't pull that together myself. My manager would show the add-on rate for each person, and mine was around 1.9 times the store average for June through August. I don't have the exact spreadsheet in front of me, but that's what the report showed.

Um, I'll also say, the team meetings were in this little back room that smelled like the camp stove demo, so I'm not sure I'd trust my memory of every detail, but the ranking and that multiple were what stuck with me. If you want the exact figures, I could ask my old manager for the summary, though I'd guess they'd be happy to send it to you if you ever need a reference.
Fair enough. I appreciate you being straight about that. So beyond the numbers, what do you think you were actually doing differently than the other eight people on the floor?

Honestly, I think the biggest difference was that I was slower at the start than some of the other people on the floor. A couple of the guys would walk up to someone, point at the tent they'd been looking at, and start listing features, which is fine, but I kind of hate that. It reminds me of my roommate's cousin who sells gym memberships and does the whole pitch before you've even sat down. I'd usually just ask the question, then wait, and sometimes that awkward silence is the whole trick. I also think I got a little obsessed with the second item, so if someone bought a tent, I'd ask what they'd be sleeping on or whether they'd need something for rain, the way Dr. Halvorsen always asks "and then what?" after every answer in class. Some days it worked great, and some days people just wanted to get out of there, which is totally fair. So I guess the difference was mostly that I cared about the trip more than the sale, and I'm not totally sure that's a skill you can teach, but I'd like to find out. Did you want me to talk more about how I'd handle that with a new team?
I might come back to that. But first—you mentioned handling escalated customer returns on your resume. Can you walk me through a specific time that was tough, and how it actually turned out?

Yeah, that one's a good story, though I should say it wasn't exactly fun while it was happening. A guy came back with a tent he'd used for, I think, two summers, and he wanted a full refund. The problem was that he was about three weeks past our return window, and he was pretty convinced that his tent should count anyway. I get why he was frustrated, and honestly, I was a little stressed, because my manager was on a call in the back and the line was getting long behind him. Anyway, I didn't want to just say no and send him off angry, so I looked at the tent and checked what the brand's warranty covered, since a lot of their gear has lifetime coverage on things like zipper or pole failures. Turned out the damage he was describing was a pole sleeve that had torn, which the warranty did cover, so I offered to start a repair claim instead of a refund. He wasn't thrilled at first, mostly because he wanted cash back and didn't want to wait, but I walked him through what the repair would look like and how long it usually took. He ended up taking it, and a few days later the store got a positive review from him, which, to be fair, is not something I expected. So the lesson I took from that is that people usually aren't angry about the policy itself, they're angry that nobody's tried to find them a yes. Do you want me to tell you about

No, that works. So in that moment, when he first pushed back on the return window—walk me through what you were thinking. Did you know the warranty angle right away, or did you have to figure that out on the fly?

Honestly, I didn't know the warranty angle right away. My first thought was basically, oh no, he's three weeks out and I'm going to be the one who has to say no. I could feel the line behind him getting longer, and my manager was still on that call in the back, so I kind of panicked for a second and just stood there with the tent in my hands.

Then I remembered there's this laminated card by the register, the one with the warranty coverage list, and I'd looked at it during training because I was kind of nerdy about the gear. So I pulled it out and started scanning, and I'm pretty sure I was also half-listening to the guy complain about his kid's soccer schedule, which had nothing to do with anything. Anyway, the card said pole and zipper failures were covered, and when I actually looked at the tent, the sleeve had torn near one of the joints. That's when it clicked.

I'll be honest, I didn't have a clean plan. I just tried to keep him talking and not get defensive, and the warranty thing kind of showed up as I went. I think that's the part I'd want to be better at, because a more experienced person probably would've known the policy cold and wouldn't have needed the card.
That's fair self-awareness. So when you first started at the store, how did you actually learn all that stuff? Like, who trained you, and what did that look like?

Okay, so training at the store was kind of a mix of formal and totally informal, which I actually liked. There was a senior associate named Dana who did the first couple of shifts with me, and she was super patient, but she also had this habit of just handing me a tent and saying "okay, sell me this" while she pretended to be a customer. I was terrible at it the first few times. I kept listing features like the gym-membership guy I mentioned earlier, and she'd just laugh and ask me where I was going to camp. That's basically where I got the "ask where they're headed" thing from, honestly, though I've probably made it my own since.

There was also a binder, which I'm pretty sure nobody read except me, and a bunch of product videos the brand put out, some of which I watched on the bus, because, again, the bus. The warranty card by the register was in the binder section too, which is why I knew it existed. I think it was about a week before I felt like I actually knew what I was doing, and maybe a month before I stopped second-guessing every answer. Dana said I'd figure out the rest by just doing it, which annoyed me at the time, but she was basically right.

Do you want to hear about the store's returns policy, or should we get back to the bigger picture?
Let's keep going with the bigger picture. You mentioned on your resume that you trained four new hires on the sales floor. How'd you approach that, and how'd you know it actually worked?

Yeah, the training thing. So, I'll admit I was kind of nervous about it, mostly because I'd just been Dana's trainee a few months before, and it felt weird to suddenly be the one showing people where the binder was. My approach was pretty simple, honestly. I shadowed each new hire for two shifts, so I'd just stand a few feet back while they helped customers, and then I'd jot down notes on the back of a receipt, which I still have somewhere, I think. After that, I flipped it, so they'd lead and I'd watch, and I'd only jump in if someone was about to get in trouble with a warranty question or a sizing mess. I also had them do the "where are you headed" thing with me pretending to be a customer, like Dana did with me, because that's the part that's hard to learn from a binder.

As for knowing it worked, the simplest measure was the monthly target. Three of the four hit their first one, which I was pretty happy about. The fourth one, a guy who was really into climbing gear, struggled a bit at first, mostly because he was so knowledgeable he'd overwhelm people, so I had to coach him on slowing down. He got there in his second month, though, so I'd call that a win too. I'm not totally sure how much of it was me and how much was just them being good at the job, and I'd be lying if I said I had some big formal evaluation. But three out of four hitting target in their first month felt like a decent sign.

Do you want me to go into how I'd set that up with a team here, or was there something specific about the numbers you wanted to dig into?
No, that's helpful. Let me ask you this—if you were training someone here in your first month, what would you do differently than what you did at the gear store?

Honestly, I'd write more of it down, and not on the back of a receipt. I still have that receipt somewhere, and I'm pretty sure half of it is just grocery math from my own bag. Dr. Halvorsen would probably call that a rubric problem. For a new hire, I'd make a simple checklist for the first two weeks, with stuff like the warranty rules, the return window, and the top five tents people ask about, so nobody has to guess what good looks like. I'd also check in with them more often than I did. I mostly left the climbing guy alone until he was already struggling, and I should have asked him earlier what felt hard. I'd probably sit down with each person after their second shift, too, instead of just watching quietly from a few feet back like a creepy plant. And I'd do a quick debrief after every shift, five minutes, nothing formal, just what went well and what they'd try next. I think the biggest thing is that I'd want them to know what they're aiming for before they start, not figure it out from a binder nobody reads. Does that sound like
Yeah, that makes sense. So you've talked a lot about things going well—the sales, the training, the customer who left a good review. Tell me about a time you actually failed at something.

Oh, man, a failure. Okay, so the one that comes to mind is the sponsor thing for the club. I was treasurer and we needed money for the spring event, so I emailed about 25 local businesses. Honestly, the emails mostly went nowhere. I think I sent the same generic message to everyone, and it read like a form letter, which, looking back, it kind of was. Maybe a couple people replied, and then I just got quiet.

What finally worked was printing a one-page flyer and walking into shops in person. Three of them said yes: a bike shop, a cafe, and a bank branch. Together that came to about $2,400, which was good, but I kept thinking about how much time I'd wasted on the emails before I tried anything different. I should've tested it on five places first instead of blasting all twenty-five. Also, I know the bike shop owner is a friend of my roommate's cousin, so, yeah, the gym-membership guy would be proud of me for once.
So when you walked in with the flyer—what was different about that pitch compared to the email?

Honestly, the biggest difference was that I could actually see the person's face. With the emails, I was basically shouting into a void, and nobody knows who you are when you're just a name in an inbox. When I walked in, I could say "hey, I'm the treasurer for the outdoor club at school, and we're doing a spring event," and then I could watch whether the owner was interested or just being polite. The flyer helped too, because it was one page, so they could glance at it while we talked and didn't have to read a whole pitch. It had the event date, what the club was, and what a sponsor would get, like a logo on the banner or a shoutout at the event. I also stopped asking for some vague "support" and asked for a specific amount, which made it easier for them to say yes or no. The cafe owner actually asked me two

Right. So the email was generic, and the in-person version was specific and you could read the room. When you think back to those twenty-five emails that didn't work—what would you do differently if you were doing that part over?

Honestly, the first thing I'd change is that I'd test it on five places before sending twenty-five. I think I got excited, copied and pasted the same message into a bunch of inboxes, and then just sat there refreshing my email like that was going to change anything. My roommate, who is way more organized than me, would have made a spreadsheet with a column for each business and a column for whether they replied. That would have shown me in about a day that the emails weren't working. I also would've tried to find a name for each email, instead of sending to some generic info address, because I'm pretty sure a few of them went straight to the spam folder. And the subject line was honestly kind of boring, which I didn't think about until way later, when Dr. Halvorsen made us rewrite a cold email for our marketing class. So yeah, if I did it over, I'd start small, make it personal, and walk in sooner.
Got it. So you managed a twelve-thousand-dollar budget as treasurer. Walk me through a time you had to make a tough call on what to fund or cut.

Okay, the budget was honestly the part of treasurer I was most nervous about. The $12,000 came from student government, and I spent a lot of time that first week staring at the spreadsheet the last treasurer left, which was mostly color-coded cells and one tab called "misc" that I never fully figured out. My roommate says I should have just asked the last treasurer for coffee, and she's probably right. Anyway, the hardest call was the end-of-year banquet. It was budgeted at $3,000, and we had a team that needed travel money for a regional competition, which was a big deal for a few of the members. I know banquets are the fun part, and I got some pretty grumpy messages in the group chat, which I still think about. So I cut the banquet down to $1,200, which meant a simpler venue and no sit-down dinner, and I moved the rest toward travel. The thing I'm still a bit torn about is that I didn't ask people what they'd want before I made the call, so I'd probably do that part differently now. But the team went to the competition, and the banquet still happened, just smaller. Do you want me to talk about how I'd handle budget conversations with a bigger group?
No, that's helpful. Before we wrap up, I want to ask—why do you want this kind of role specifically? And I know you touched on it earlier, but is there anything else?

Yeah, I did touch on it, but I think the honest answer is a little bigger than the sales floor. I like jobs where I'm talking to people about something they care about, and the gear store is the closest I've gotten to that so far. When I'm treasurer, I'm kind of doing the same thing, just with budgets and sponsors instead of tents. The flyer thing with the bike shop owner was the best part of that whole semester, even though it was also pretty nerve-wracking. I also want to be somewhere that actually gives you feedback, because my roommate's cousin, the gym-membership guy, has been doing the same pitch for three years and nobody ever sits him down to tell him what's not working. I'd like to grow in a job where someone checks in on me, and where I can help other people get better at the stuff I figured out by trial and error. And honestly, I'm a business major, so I'd like to see how this kind of work connects to the bigger picture, not just the daily stuff. I think I'd be a good fit because I care about the why behind a
That makes sense. We're running pretty close on time here, so let me ask—do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, I do, just one. What does a typical week look like for someone in this role, especially in the first few months?

Good question. In the first few months, you'd spend a lot of time shadowing the team and learning our processes—kind of like your training at the gear store, but we'd be more structured about it. You'd probably spend two to three days a week with different people on the floor, then gradually take on your own work. We check in weekly, so you'd have regular feedback built in, which I think aligns with what you mentioned. By month three, you'd be running your own projects, but you'd still have support. It's not a sink-or-swim place. Does that sound like what you were looking for?

Yeah, that sounds really good, especially the weekly check-ins. That's honestly the part I was hoping to hear, because I learned most of what I know at the store from Dana, who would just hand me a tent and make me pretend to sell it to her. Two to three days a week shadowing people sounds about right to me. I'd rather spend my time watching how good people do the job than reading some binder, though I'll admit I still have a soft spot for that binder at the store. My roommate keeps telling me I should have asked more questions in my first interview, so I guess I'm doing that now. Anyway, yes, it sounds like what I'm looking for. I'd be excited to learn more about how the team handles those first few months, and thanks for taking the time to talk with me today.
You're welcome, Jordan. Thanks for being thoughtful and honest through all of this. We'll be in touch soon about next steps. Good luck, and take care.

I appreciate you being straightforward throughout this—especially about what you actually know versus what you'd need to verify. That matters.

verdicts.notes: Strength: the interviewer probed claims well (measurement of the 1.9x figure, whether the sponsors actually paid, how training was judged) and covered both practice questions and the candidate's questions. Weakness: it never asked about the customer complaint topic, it repeatedly gave evaluative praise ("I appreciate the honesty", "useful lesson"), and it didn't push on the vague "why this role" answer or the thin company knowledge.

transcript.text: Hey, good to meet you. How's your day been so far?

Hey, good to meet you too, thanks for making time for this. My day's been pretty good, honestly, kind of a slow start. I had to get up early because my commute is a mess right now, the bus takes forever and there's this one stop where it always seems to sit for like ten minutes with no explanation, so I've been trying out a podcast about urban planning to make it bearable. Anyway, I got a coffee from the place near campus, which was great, and then I spent most of the morning going over my notes for this interview. How about you, has your day been busy?

Oh, you know, the usual—back-to-back calls. But I'm glad you're here. So tell me a bit about yourself. Walk me through, you know, what you've been doing the last couple years and what brings you here today.

Sure, happy to. So I'm a business major, almost done, and for the last couple of years I've mostly been juggling two things: a job on the sales floor at an outdoor gear store and being treasurer for one of the clubs on campus. The store job is actually how I got into this, because I didn't expect to like selling so much. My manager there is a big hiking person, and she kept telling me that selling camping stuff is really just listening to people figure out where they're going. The club thing started as a favor to a friend who didn't want to do the money side, and I ended up really liking it, even though I had no idea what I was doing at first. I spent a lot of time with a spreadsheet and a very patient professor, Dr. Alvarez, who I swear answers emails faster than anyone I know. Anyway, I'm here because I want something where I can use both of those, the people part and the numbers part, and this role seemed like it could be that mix. So that's the short version, I think. I can go into specifics on any of it if you want.

That's helpful. I like that you ended up liking something you didn't expect. So you mentioned being top seller at the store three months in a row—what were you doing differently that made that happen?

Thanks, yeah, it surprised me too. Honestly, the thing that changed it was pretty simple. Before I showed anybody anything, I'd ask what trip they were planning, and that's a weird question to lead with at a store, but people almost always light up when you ask it. My manager, the hiking one, had been saying that for months, and I kind of rolled my eyes until I tried it. Funny story, there was this guy who came in for a headlamp and ended up walking out with a whole backpacking setup, a water filter, and a stove, because he'd been planning a trip to Utah and didn't even know he needed a stove. I think the add-on stuff ended up running about 1.9 times the store average, which I still can't believe, but a lot of it was just asking one more question and then listening. It's kind of like the bus, honestly, if you just pay attention to where people are headed, the rest sort of takes care of itself. Anyway, that's the main thing. Was there a particular part of the sales side you wanted me to get into?

No, that makes sense. So when you say your add-on stuff was running 1.9 times the store average—how was that measured? Like, was that something you tracked yourself, or did your manager pull that number?

Good question, and honestly I'd want to be careful not to oversell it. I don't think I tracked it myself. The store runs monthly sales reports, and my manager showed us the rankings at a team meeting, so I'm pretty sure that's where the numbers came from. I didn't ask her exactly how she calculated the add-on part, and I don't want to guess and get it wrong in front of you. The ranking I'm confident about, because it was number one out of nine associates from June through August. The 1.9 figure is the one I'd double check before I'd call it a hard number. Funny, the team meeting was in the back room with the bad fluorescent light, and everyone was squinting at a printout, so I'm

That's fair. I appreciate you being straight about what you actually know versus what you'd need to verify. So when you were the top seller those three months, did your teammates ever ask you how you were doing it, or did anyone pick up on what you were doing?

Yeah, a couple of people asked, and it was kind of funny because some of them just assumed I had a secret sales technique. Honestly, it was mostly the question about the trip. One of the other associates, who's been there a while, tried it for a week and told me it felt awkward at first, but then customers started opening up to him. I don't think anyone was competitive about it in a bad way, which was nice, because the store can get a little tense when the monthly board goes up. We had a whole thing going where people would leave sticky notes on the register with tips, and I left a few too, mostly about how to handle people who say they're just browsing. Anyway, I think what I'd say is that the best part was seeing the team pick it up, more than the ranking itself, though I still got a little thrill seeing my name at the top of the list. So yeah, people noticed, and a couple of them actually started doing it, which I'll admit felt pretty good.
That's good. You mentioned training four new hires on the sales floor—how did you actually train them? Like, walk me through what that looked like.

Sure, so it was pretty hands-on. For each new hire, I basically shadowed them for two shifts, just following them around the floor and watching how they talked to people. I'd jot stuff down on my phone, like where they lost a customer or where they nailed it. Then for the next part, they'd take the lead and I'd just stand back and watch, which was honestly the hardest part for me, because I kept wanting to jump in. There was this one guy, really nice, who kept asking customers about the price of stuff before asking where they were going, and I had to gently tell him to flip that order. It reminded me of when Dr. Alvarez made us do group presentations, and I was the one who kept trying to take over the slides. Anyway, three of the four hit their first monthly target, which I was pretty happy about, though I'd say the fourth one was still figuring things out, and honestly that's probably on me as much as on her. Did you want me to talk about how I'd approach training on a different kind of team, or something else?
No, that's useful. So you said three of the four hit their first monthly target—how did you know the training actually worked? Like, what were you looking for to tell you it stuck?

Good question. Honestly, the simplest answer is that I looked at their numbers at the end of the month, same as everyone else on the floor, since the store posts targets and the monthly sales reports. Three of the four hit their first target, so that was the main signal. But I'd be lying if I said I had some fancy way of checking whether it stuck. I mostly just kept an eye on whether they were asking the where-are-you-headed question on their own, without me standing there. When I'd catch one of them doing it during a shift, that felt like the real win. The fourth one, I'm not totally sure what was going on. I think she was more nervous with customers, and I probably should have spent more time with her before stepping back. Anyway, I'd want to check with my manager on the exact numbers before I'd call it a hard result. Does that answer what you were getting at?
Yeah, that does. So you managed a twelve-thousand-dollar budget as club treasurer—what was the hardest call you had to make with that money?

Oh, that's a good one. The hardest call was cutting the end-of-year banquet. We'd budgeted about three thousand for it, and it's the one event everyone actually shows up for, so nobody wanted to touch it. But we also had a competition coming up that needed travel money, and the travel was the part that would make or break whether anyone on the team got to go. I kept thinking about it on the bus, which is where I do most of my thinking now, and that stop where it sits for ten minutes gave me plenty of time to stare at the spreadsheet on my phone. Dr. Alvarez, who I keep mentioning, told me to stop trying to make everybody happy and just lay out the tradeoff, so I did. In the end we cut the banquet down to twelve hundred, which meant a smaller room and a lot fewer appetizers, and we used the difference for travel. People grumbled a little, but a couple of them told me afterward it was a good call, and the team got to the competition. Honestly, I'd still say it was the hardest thing I did with that money, just because it was people's favorite part of the year. Is that the kind of call you were asking about, or did you mean something more on the
No, that works. I'm curious—when you presented that tradeoff to the club, how did you actually make the case? Like, what did you say?

Honestly, I didn't give some big speech. I put the numbers on one page, the banquet at three thousand, the travel cost for the competition, and what we had left in the budget, and I said we couldn't fully fund both. I think the thing that helped was that I didn't pretend it was painless. I said something like, we can keep the banquet as is and some people might not be able to go, or we can shrink the banquet and everybody gets to the competition. Dr. Alvarez had us do a case study in one of her classes where the answer was basically "name the tradeoff out loud," and I think that stuck with me more than I expected. I was also nervous, because the room was mostly people who'd been looking forward to the banquet for months, and one guy had already started planning his outfit. Anyway, we voted, and it passed, but I'd say the reason it passed was that people could see the math and didn't feel like I was hiding something. Did you want to know how I'd handle that kind of pushback again, or more about the budget itself?
No, that's clear. So you also secured three local sponsors for the spring event—how did you actually find them and pitch them?

Yeah, so the sponsor thing was a bit of a grind, and honestly the way I figured it out was mostly by failing first. I started by emailing about twenty-five local businesses, which felt efficient at the time, and I think I got maybe one reply that was even remotely interested. The cold emails just mostly disappeared into the void. Then I switched to walking in with a one-page flyer, which sounds old-fashioned, but it worked way better. I'd go in during a slow part of the afternoon, which at the cafe near campus meant about two o'clock, and just ask for the manager. The flyer had what the event was, who would be there, and what the sponsor would get, like a logo on the banner and a shoutout at the start. I ended up with three yeses: a bike shop, a cafe, and a bank branch. Together they came to about twenty-four hundred dollars. I'd say the bank branch was the hardest, because the person I talked to had to check with corporate, and I spent a week refreshing my inbox like it was a bus schedule. Anyway, the in-person thing is what I'd tell anyone to do, though I'd still double-check the exact dollar figure with the club's records before quoting it as final.
That makes sense. And when you walked in with the flyer, what would you say to the manager when you first got there? Like, what was your opening?

Okay, so my opening was pretty basic, honestly. I'd walk up to the counter, smile, and say something like, hi, I'm Jordan, I'm the treasurer for the student club at the college, and we've got a spring event coming up. Then I'd ask if the manager had a couple minutes, which at the cafe was usually fine around two o'clock, because the lunch rush was over and nobody was in line yet. I'd hand over the flyer and let them look at it for a second before I said anything else, which felt awkward at first but I think it helped. The first few times I tried talking over them while they were reading, and that didn't go well. There was this one place where the manager was carrying a stack of cups, and I just said I could come back, and she actually told me to go ahead, so I ended up talking to her while she stacked. Anyway, I'd keep it short, mention the one or two things the sponsor would get, and then ask if they'd be open to talking more. Honestly the best part was not trying to sell too hard, which is maybe the same lesson as the store, just asking people where they're headed and listening.
Got it. So you mentioned you'd want to double-check the dollar figure with the club records—did those three sponsors actually come through, or did something fall through?

Yeah, so, good question, and I want to be careful here. All three said yes, the bike shop, the cafe, and the bank branch, and that's the part I'm confident about. The bank was the one that took forever, because the branch manager had to run it past corporate, and I think I checked my email about four times a day that week. Whether the money actually landed in the account is a different question, and honestly I'd have to look at the club's records to tell you. I was the treasurer, so you'd think I'd know, but I was juggling a lot that spring, and the banner and the shoutouts were the parts I was tracking more closely. I'd want to pull the ledger and confirm each payment before I'd tell you the full twenty-four hundred is in hand. I can also check with the event coordinator to make sure the logos made it onto the banner, since that was part of the deal. Is that the kind of follow-through you were asking about?
I appreciate the honesty. So let me ask you this—thinking back on the sponsorship push, what didn't work? Like, beyond the cold emails, was there anything else you tried that flopped?

Yeah, honestly the cold emails were the big one, but there were a couple of smaller things too. I tried a version of the flyer that was way too busy, with a whole paragraph about the club's history and a little map of the campus, and nobody read past the first line. One manager actually said, "I just need to know what you want from me," which was fair. I also went to one place on a Friday afternoon, thinking it'd be quieter, and it was packed with a line out the door, so I ended up standing awkwardly by the door for twenty minutes before I just left and came back the next week. Oh, and I once tried to pitch a sponsor over text because I got their number from a friend, which was a mistake, because I think it came across as kind of random. The stuff that worked was keeping it simple and showing up in person at the right time. Anyway, I learned more from those flops than from the wins, which is probably the most honest thing I can say about that whole stretch. Do you want me to dig into any of those, or is that enough on sponsors?
No, that's helpful. Let me ask you something different. Tell me about a time you actually failed at something—not just a learning moment, but a real miss.

Oh, that's a harder one to answer. The fourth new hire at the store is the one I think about. She didn't hit her first monthly target, and I was the one who'd set up her training. I did the two shifts of shadowing with her like everyone else, but then I stepped back way too early, because I wanted to prove I could let go, the way my manager had kept telling me to. I didn't notice she was getting more nervous with customers until it was already a pattern. My manager pulled me aside and asked what I'd seen, and I kind of got defensive, which I'm not proud of. I was reading this book about coaching on the bus, and there's a line about how you don't hand someone the wheel until they've practiced in the parking lot, and that really stuck with me. So now I'd spend more time with someone like her before I step back. I don't think it was a disaster, but it was a real miss, and I'd rather own it than pretend I had it handled.
That's fair. So when your manager pulled you aside, what did that conversation actually look like? Did she tell you what she'd noticed, or did she ask you questions?

Honestly, it was a fairly short conversation, and I don't remember every word, so I'd be guessing if I gave you a transcript. She started by asking how the training had gone, and I think she asked a couple of questions first, like what I'd been seeing on the floor and whether I'd noticed anything with the new hire. I remember feeling my face get warm, which is a weird thing to notice when you're standing next to a rack of rain jackets. She didn't come in with a long list of complaints, which I appreciated, but she was clear that the new hire was struggling and that I'd been the one shaping her early training. I said something about how I thought she was doing fine, and looking back, that was me trying to protect myself more than actually paying attention. The bus ride home that night was one of the longer ones, since that stop was stuck again, and I spent the whole time thinking about what she'd asked me. So she mostly asked questions and let me work it out, which in h
Yeah, that's a useful lesson. So thinking about this role we're talking about, why do you want it? Like, what drew you to apply?

Honestly, it's the mix I keep coming back to. The store taught me I like the people side, figuring out what someone actually needs and then helping them get there, and the club taught me I like the numbers side, where you have to make a call and then live with it. I didn't expect to care about both, but this role looks like it sits right in the middle. I read the job posting a few times on the bus, and the part about working with teams and tracking results stood out, because that's basically the stuff I've been doing without a title for it. There's also a practical thing, which is that I'm about to graduate and I want to work somewhere I can keep learning, not just run the same routine. I'd also like to see how a bigger organization handles the kind of tradeoffs I dealt with on a smaller scale, like the banquet thing. Anyway, that's the honest version. I'm sure there's more specific stuff about the company I should have looked up better, so I'd want to hear more about what the day-to-day looks like before I'd say I fully understand the fit.
That makes sense. We're almost out of time, so let me ask—do you have any questions for me? About the role, the team, anything else?
Yeah, one quick one: what does a typical first few months look like for someone in this role?

Good question. Honestly, the first month is mostly getting to know the team and the systems—who does what, how decisions actually get made versus how they're supposed to. Second month, we'd probably have you running point on a smaller project or two so you can see how things move. By month three, you'd be taking on more ownership. It's a team that values people who ask questions and aren't afraid to say when something doesn't add up. Does that help?

Yeah, that helps a lot, thanks. The part about asking questions and saying when something doesn't add up is good to hear, since that's kind of how I ended up in the banquet situation anyway. I'd want to know a bit more about what those smaller projects look like in month two, and whether the team usually gets together in person or mostly online. I'm also curious how you've seen people do after that first three months, but I can wait for the next conversation if that's easier. Either way, thanks for the time today, I really enjoyed talking with you.

Those are all fair questions, and we can dig into those next time if we move forward. I appreciate you being straightforward throughout this—especially about what you actually know versus what you'd need to verify. That matters. Thanks for taking the time today, and we'll be in touch soon.
Thanks so much, I really appreciate you taking the time. It was good talking with you, and I'm looking forward to hearing from you soon. Have a great rest of your day.
You too, take care.

practice_questions.question: Tell me about a time you failed.
Why do you want this kind of role?

verdicts.notes: Strength: the interviewer probed measurement and baselines (T6, T10, T22) and pushed past a weak failure answer (T26) to a real one. Weakness: it never asked about the Customer complaint topic, it ended with "You did great" (T36), and it gave a "That's a good one" evaluation at T28. It also dug repeatedly into already-complete answers.

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for coming in. Did you find everything okay today?

Yeah, everything's fine, thanks for asking. Honestly the video link took me a minute to find, because I had two tabs open and one of them was my professor's grading portal, which, don't ask, long story involving a late submission and a very patient TA. Anyway, I got a coffee on the way, which I probably shouldn't have because now I'm a little wired, so if I talk fast that's why. The commute was actually not bad, the bus was on time for once, which felt like a sign. So yeah, all good, and I'm happy to be here.

Ha, well I'm glad the bus cooperated. And hey, coffee's never a bad call before an interview.

So let's jump in. Walk me through your background a bit—how'd you end up where you are now, and what are you looking to do next?

Thanks, yeah, I'm definitely going to be a little jittery for the next hour. So, background. I'm a business major, and honestly I picked it kind of by accident, because I took an intro econ class and a professor kept making jokes about spreadsheets that I found weirdly funny. I've been working at an outdoor gear store for about a year and a half, which is how I ended up loving sales, mostly because people come in excited about a trip they're planning and it's fun to help them figure out what they actually need. I also got roped into being treasurer for my campus club, which I thought would be a boring title but turned out to be real money decisions. I'm looking for something where I can do both, the customer side and the numbers side, which I know sounds kind of vague, but that's the honest version. Also my roommate is convinced I should go into real estate because I can talk to anyone, so I'm still figuring that part out.

That makes sense. So you've got the sales experience and the finance side from the club—that's a good mix.

Let me dig into the sales piece first. You were top seller at the outdoor gear store for three months in a row, right? What were you actually doing differently than the other people on the floor?

Yeah, June, July, and August, I ended up at number one out of nine people on the floor. Honestly, it reminds me of the time I tried to get into a rock climbing gym and the guy at the desk asked me three questions before he even handed me a form, and I thought, oh, that's just good customer service. So anyway, the thing I started doing was asking people what trip they were planning before I showed them anything. Like, are you going somewhere wet, is it a two-night thing or a two-week thing, do you have a pack already. Most of the other associates would grab a tent off the wall and start talking features, which is fine, but people would just nod and walk around. When I asked first, I could usually tell what they'd actually need, and they'd also add on stuff like the stove or the rain shell without me pushing too hard. My add-on sales ended up being about 1.9 times the store average, which my manager pointed out in one of those awkward little check-ins, but I think it's mostly just because I was curious about what people were doing. Sorry, I think I wandered a little, but that's the short version of what I did differently.

No, that's helpful. So you asked questions first instead of leading with the product. When you say your add-on sales were 1.9 times the store average—how was that actually measured? Did your manager pull that number, or did you track it yourself?

Oh, my manager pulled it, not me. I don't think I was tracking anything on purpose, which is kind of funny, because I'm the treasurer who's supposed to care about numbers. It came from the store's monthly sales report, the one that breaks down add-ons per associate, and she showed it to me during one of those check-ins where she's trying to be encouraging but also a little bit like, what are you doing over there? I think she was comparing my add-on rate to the store average, which I'm pretty sure was just the average across all nine of us. I remember being surprised, because I thought I was just chatting with people. There's a whole thing about how the reports are set up, and I honestly don't know every detail of how they calculate it, so if you want the exact method, my manager would be the one to ask. But that's where the 1.9 came from.

Got it. That makes sense—so your manager flagged it, and it stuck with you. 

You also trained four new hires on the sales floor. How did you actually train them? Walk me through what that looked like.

Yeah, training four new hires, that was a good one. So the store had a few people starting around the same time, and my manager asked if I could help get them up to speed, which I said yes to before I really thought about what that meant. My approach was pretty simple. I shadowed each new person for two shifts, so I'd be right next to them on the floor, mostly just listening to how they talked to customers and jumping in if something was off. Then after the second shift, I'd flip it, and they'd lead while I stood back and watched. It's kind of like when you're learning to drive and your parent sits in the passenger seat, except nobody's gripping the handle, I hope. Honestly, the hardest part was not jumping in too fast, because my instinct was to just grab the customer and do it myself, which obviously doesn't help anyone learn. Three of the four hit their first monthly target, which I was really happy about. The fourth one was still getting comfortable with the tech specs, and honestly, that's a thing I'm still not great at myself, so I probably wasn't the best person to coach that part.
So three of the four hit their first monthly target—what was the target, and how did you know the training actually worked versus just them being naturally good at sales?

Honestly, I'd have to check the exact number for the target, because my manager set those and I was mostly focused on the people. I think it was the standard first-month goal for new associates, but don't quote me on the figure. As for whether it was the training or just them being natural salespeople, I can't say for sure, and I'm not going to pretend I proved it. Two of them had sold stuff before, one at a restaurant, the other at a phone store, so they had some experience. The fourth was brand new to retail, and honestly, she's the one who made me think the training mattered, because she went from nervous to pretty confident in about three weeks. Hmm, I'm not sure that's a fair comparison, though. It's like my roommate says about her plants: you can't tell if the fertilizer worked or if the sun just showed up that week. What I can say is that everyone got the same two-shift setup, so if there's a difference, it's probably in how fast they got comfortable, not in whether they could sell at all. Sorry, that got a little philosophical. Would it help if I went back to how I'd track

No, that's fine. I get it—hard to isolate the variable when there's a lot going on.

Let me shift gears. You managed a twelve-thousand-dollar budget as club treasurer. Tell me about a decision you had to make where you couldn't fund everything—what did you cut, and why?

Okay, so the budget. Quick clarification first, because I think people assume I raised the money, and I didn't. The twelve thousand came from student government, and my job was basically to make it stretch across the whole year without anyone yelling at me. The hardest call was the end-of-year banquet. We had it planned at about three thousand dollars, which sounds like a lot until you remember that a big chunk of our members were going to a regional competition, and travel was the thing that actually decided whether people could go at all. I remember sitting in my dorm lounge with a spreadsheet open and a bag of pretzels, and I kept going back and forth. I ended up cutting the banquet down to twelve hundred, which meant a cheaper venue and a lot less food, and I moved the rest to travel. Some people were pretty annoyed, and one member told me the banquet was the only fun thing we did all year, which, fair. But I thought about it like the store, where you'd rather someone spend on the tent they'll actually use than the fancy extra they'll never touch. So yeah, I'
That makes sense. When you cut the banquet budget, how did you decide what to keep versus what to go? Like, did you just pick a venue, or did you talk to people first?

Honestly, mostly I looked at the spreadsheet first, then I talked to a few people, which I should've done earlier. My co-treasurer would have been the obvious person to run it past, but she was dealing with her own midterms that week, so I kind of ended up making the call on my own and then texting people the plan. I did ask a couple of the members who were going to the competition what the travel costs looked like, mostly because one of them had already booked a bus and I didn't want to be the person who said no after she'd paid. For the banquet, I went through what we'd actually spent the year before, which was a lot of pizza and a rented room nobody used the whole time. So I figured we could get a smaller room, cheaper food, and still have people show up. Oh, and this is a side note, but my roommate thinks I should've just asked the whole club to vote, which, in theory, sure, but a vote on a banquet budget is how you end up with a DJ nobody asked for. Anyway, I kept the things that made the club work, like the competition travel and the basic room, and cut what I thought people would miss least. Does that answer it, or do
Yeah, that helps. Sounds like you learned something from doing it solo—what would you do differently if you had to make that same call again?

Honestly, the big thing I'd change is talking to people before I made the call, not after. I texted the plan once I'd already decided, and that's backwards. Even a quick group message asking "what would you actually miss?" would have given me better information, and it might have calmed down the people who felt blindsided. The banquet member who said it was the only fun thing we did all year, I wish I'd heard that before I cut it, not after. I'd also want to check the actual travel numbers with the competition group earlier, so I wasn't guessing. It's kind of like the store, where I'd ask a customer a few questions before grabbing a tent off the wall. I did the asking part on the sales floor, but I skipped it with the club, which is funny because it's the same skill. My co-treasurer also said afterward that she would have liked a heads up, so yeah, that's the lesson. I'd still make the same cut, I think, but I'd make it with people, not just a spreadsheet and a bag of pretzels.
Fair enough. So you mentioned you secured three local sponsors for the club's spring event. How'd you actually find those sponsors, and what was your pitch?

Okay, so sponsors. I started by emailing about twenty-five local businesses, which sounds like a lot of work, and it was, but I was pretty proud of how organized my spreadsheet was. The emails mostly went nowhere. I got a couple of "maybe next time" replies and a lot of silence, which is honestly what I expected from cold emails. My roommate says nobody reads email anymore, and she might be right, because she also thinks nobody reads anything with a subject line. So I switched to walking in with a one-page flyer, which felt awkward at first, like I was a kid selling cookies for a school trip. But it worked way better. The flyer had the event date, who we were, what the sponsor would get, like a logo on our shirts and a shout-out at the event, and a rough idea of what the club would do with the money. Three places said yes: a bike shop, a cafe, and a bank branch. Between them it came to about twenty-four hundred dollars. The bank was the hardest one, because they needed to check a bunch of things first, and
What didn't work? You said the emails mostly went nowhere. Did you learn anything from that that made the in-person pitch better?

Honestly, the emails didn't work because they were easy to ignore. I'd write a nice paragraph, hit send, and then nothing, or a "maybe next time" that really meant no. I didn't keep a close count of which emails got which response, which is kind of ironic for a treasurer, so I can't give you exact percentages. What I did notice is that when I walked in, people had to look at me and say something, and that's harder to brush off. It reminded me of the store, where a customer who's standing right there is way more likely to buy than one who's scrolling on their phone. The flyer helped too, because it was something they could keep on a desk or stick on a bulletin board after I left. I also got better at keeping it short. In the emails I'd write three paragraphs about the club's history, and nobody needs that. With the flyer, I just said who we were, what they'd get, and when the event was, and then I stopped talking so they could ask questions. Sorry, I think I might be overexplaining, but yeah, the in-person version was the one that got a y
No, that's helpful. Out of the places you walked into, how many actually said yes versus how many turned you down?

Honestly, I don't have a clean count for the walk-ins, and I know that's a weird thing to say as a treasurer. I was mostly going door to door with the flyer after the emails flopped, and I didn't write down every place I stopped in, so I'd be making up a number if I gave you one. What I can say for sure is that the three yeses were the bike shop, the cafe, and the bank branch, and together they came to about twenty-four hundred dollars. The bank was the one that made me sweat, because they wanted to check a bunch of stuff before they'd commit, and I spent about two weeks just following up with the same person. Most of the other places said no, or said they'd think about it, which in my experience usually means no. Oh, and my roommate says I should've kept a little tally on a sticky note, which, yeah, she's not wrong. If you want the real ratio, I'd have to dig through my notes, and I'm honestly not sure I kept them that well. But the three yeses are the part I'm proud of, because they came from people I had to actually look in the eye.
Got it. So you didn't track the conversion rate, but you got three yeses. Tell me about a time you failed—something that didn't work out the way you wanted.

Okay, a failure. The first one that comes to mind is the cold email campaign for sponsors, which I honestly thought would be the easy part. I sent emails to about twenty-five local businesses, put a lot of effort into the wording, and then mostly heard nothing. My roommate says that's just how email works now, and she might be right, but at the time I felt kind of dumb, like I'd wasted a whole weekend on something that was never going to work. Also, I'm pretty sure the coffee
So you pivoted to the in-person approach after that flopped. But I'm asking about a real failure—something where you couldn't recover or where it actually had a cost. Did anything like that happen?

Hmm, yeah, I think the banquet is the closest thing to a real failure, even though the travel part worked out. I cut it without asking anyone first, and a couple of members felt blindsided, which made the whole thing feel worse than it needed to be. One person told me the banquet was the only fun thing we did all year, and I didn't really have an answer, because she was right. My co-treasurer also told me afterward she wished she'd heard about it sooner, and that stung a little, since we're supposed to be a team on this. I don't think the decision itself was a disaster, since the competition group got to go, but I definitely lost some goodwill with people I still have to see every week. Honestly, my roommate says I should've just put it to a quick vote, and I'm still not sure she's wrong. Anyway, that's the one I think about, because it cost me something real, even if it wasn't a total meltdown.

That's a good one. So you lost some goodwill and your co-treasurer felt left out. If you were starting that club role over, what would you do differently in your first month to avoid that kind of thing happening again?

Okay, first month, starting over. The biggest thing is I'd sit down with the co-treasurer in week one and just ask her how she likes to handle money decisions, because we never actually set that up, and I think we both assumed the other one would handle the big stuff. I'd also get the full picture of the year early, like what the competition travel was going to cost, what the banquet had cost before, and what members actually cared about, so I'm not finding out halfway through. Honestly, I'd send a short message to the whole club asking what they'd want to protect in the budget before I built anything. It's kind of like the store, where I ask what someone's planning before I start pulling stuff off the wall. I did that well on the sales floor and then skipped it in the club, which is still a little funny to me. And I'd keep a running spreadsheet with notes on every decision, including who I talked to, so if someone asks why, I can show them. Also, I'd probably drink less coffee before I make budget calls, but that's a separate issue.
Fair enough. So why are you looking for this kind of role? What's pulling you toward it?

Okay, why this kind of role. Honestly, it's the mix I keep bumping into. On the sales floor, I like that moment when someone walks in unsure and walks out knowing exactly what they need for their trip, and that feels good in a way I didn't expect. Then with the club, I got hooked on the money side, even though I thought it would be boring, and I liked figuring out how to make twelve thousand dollars stretch. The banquet thing taught me that the numbers are only half of it, though, because the people part is what makes a decision stick. So I'm drawn to a role where I'm talking to people and also working with numbers, and where I'd be expected to check in with the team before making a call, not after. My roommate keeps saying I should go into real estate because I can talk to anyone, and I'm not totally ruling that out. But what I'm really looking for is a place where I can keep learning on both sides, and where I'm not the only one holding the budget. Sorry, that got a little long, but yeah, that's the honest version.
That's helpful. Do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, one question. What does a typical first few months look like for someone starting in this role, and who would I be working with most day to day?

Good question. So the first few months are really about getting up to speed on our systems and meeting the team. You'd be paired with someone in the department for the first month or so, then moving into your own projects pretty quickly. Day to day, you'd be working with a small team of three or four people in your area, plus touching base with other departments depending on what you're working on. It's collaborative—we don't do a lot of solo work here. Beyond that, I think once you're further along in the process, you'd get a clearer picture from the team lead.

Thanks for taking the time today, Jordan. We've got what we need, and we'll be in touch soon about next steps.

Thanks so much, I really appreciate you taking the time. And sorry if I was a little all over the place today, that coffee was doing a lot of talking. I'm looking forward to hearing from you, and thanks again for the info about the team. Have a great rest of your day!
Ha, no worries at all. You did great. Take care, and we'll talk soon.

You've got good instincts around ownership and impact, and I like that you're thinking about what you'd be good at versus what you're just okay at.
