verdicts.notes: Strength: the interviewer asked concrete follow-ups on the budget, top-seller and sponsorship answers, including verifying the 1.9x figure, and covered both practice questions. Weakness: it skipped Training new hires and Customer complaint, left the vague closing answers (T17, T19) unprobed, and gave several evaluative comments (T4, T6, T22, T24).

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for taking the time. How are things going on your end?

Oh, hi, yeah, no, thanks for having me. Things are good, honestly. It's been kind of a hectic week, I had two finals back to back on Tuesday and Wednesday and I think I survived mostly on iced coffee and that one gas station granola bar, which, don't recommend. My commute over here was a little rough too, the bus was late and I ended up sitting next to a guy who was eating a whole rotisserie chicken with his hands, so that was an experience. But I'm glad we could make this work, and I'm pretty excited to talk about the job, so, yeah, thanks for asking.

Ha, okay, I appreciate the honesty. Gas station granola bars and rotisserie chickens on the bus—sounds like you've earned a good coffee after that. Well, I'm glad you made it here. So, tell me a bit about yourself. What brings you to this point, and what are you looking for in your next role?

Ha, yeah, the coffee is happening as soon as we're done. So, um, I'm a business major, almost done, and I've kind of been doing two things at once for the last couple years. Mostly I work at an outdoor gear store, which is a great job if you like talking to people and don't mind being asked about hiking boots forty times a day. My manager says I'm the guy who knows the trails, but honestly I just ask people where they're going first, because that changes what they actually need. I also got elected treasurer for my campus club, which sounded like a small thing until I realized I was in charge of twelve thousand dollars of student government money, and that was kind of terrifying. What I'm looking for next is a place where I can use both, the sales side and the money side, and maybe actually be responsible for something bigger than my own shifts. I think that's what I'm after, anyway, and I'm not totally sure yet what that looks like, which is probably why I'm here.

That makes sense. So you've got exposure to both sides—customer-facing and managing resources. I like that you're thinking about what responsibility actually means. Let me dig into one of those a bit more. You mentioned managing the twelve thousand dollar budget as treasurer. Walk me through a specific decision you had to make with that money. Was there something you had to say no to, or a tradeoff you faced?

Yeah, okay, so the budget thing. The twelve thousand actually comes from student government, so it's not like I'm sitting on my own pile of cash, which I kind of wish people understood. Anyway, I've got this spreadsheet that I'm pretty sure I built wrong the first time, and I spent a whole Sunday color-coding it, which my roommate found hilarious. The hardest call was the end-of-year banquet. It was budgeted at three thousand, and the club was also trying to send a team to a regional competition, and travel for that was not cheap. Everybody loved the banquet, and I felt bad cutting it, but I ended up dropping it from three thousand to twelve hundred and putting the rest toward travel. The banquet still happened, just with pizza and a much shorter speech from the president, and honestly I think people had more fun than they would have at a fancy dinner. So that's the tradeoff, I guess, you can't fund everything, and you have to pick what the money is actually for.

That's a solid example. So you made a call that the competition mattered more than the fancy dinner. How did you know that was the right priority, though? Did you check with anyone, or was that your call to make?

Honestly, it was kind of my call, but I didn't want it to feel like a random call, you know? So I went back and looked at what the club had actually voted on at the start of the year, and the competition was the thing people had signed up for. The banquet was more of a nice-to-have, which is hard to say out loud when everybody's excited about it. I also remember my econ professor saying something like, "Money is a statement of priorities," and I thought that was kind of dramatic at the time, but then I was staring at my spreadsheet going, oh, okay, he's right. I did talk to the president before I sent the numbers around, mostly so she wasn't blindsided, and she was more relieved than anything, because she'd been dreading the banquet planning. So I guess the way I knew was that the goal was the thing I was trying to protect, and the banquet was just one way to celebrate it.

Got it. So you anchored it back to what the club actually committed to doing. That makes sense. Let me shift gears a bit. You mentioned being a top seller at the outdoor gear store three months in a row. What were you doing differently that made that happen?

Oh, yeah, the top seller thing. Honestly, I think a lot of it was just that it was summer, and the store gets slammed in June, and there were nine of us on the floor, so if you just show up and answer questions you're going to do fine. Anyway, that's kind of a cop-out answer, so the real thing is I started asking people what trip they were planning before I showed them anything. My coworker Dev thought it was weird at first, because he'd just walk people straight to the tents and the jackets. But if someone's going car camping near a lake, they need totally different stuff than someone doing a three-day hike with a heavy pack, and it's way easier to sell something useful when you know that. I also got really into knowing what the add-ons were, like the cheap stove fuel or the extra water filter, because people always forget that stuff and then they're annoyed later. I think my add-on sales ended up being about 1.9 times the store average, which my manager mentioned in a meeting, and I was kind of embarrassed because I was eating a pretzel at the time. Reminds me, I really need to get a real lunch before my next shift, because that pretzel was not a meal. So yeah, the big thing is I stopped selling products and started figuring out the trip first.

So you flipped it—figure out what they actually need, then sell them that. And you tracked the add-ons, so you had a number for it. How did you know the 1.9 times figure was real, or did your manager just tell you that?

Yeah, so my manager pulled the numbers from the register system, and she showed me the report after the meeting, which was kind of a relief because I didn't want to be the guy who just felt good about himself. Basically it compares each associate's add-on attachment rate against the store average for the month, and mine was around 1.9 times the average for the summer. I didn't keep a personal log or anything, which I probably should have, because now I'm kind of guessing at how I'd explain it if someone asked me to prove it line by line. But the report is what she showed me, so I trust it more than my memory. Also, I just realized I'm still hungry, so if my stomach growls at some point, that's the pretzel talking.

Fair enough. So your manager had the data to back it up. That's good. Now, I want to ask you about something else. Tell me about a time you actually failed at something, or something didn't go the way you planned.

Okay, yeah, so the sponsorship thing for the spring event. That one's a little embarrassing, but also kind of useful. Our club needed sponsors to cover part of the event, and I figured I'd be efficient about it, so I wrote one email and sent it to about 25 local businesses. Basically I was sitting in the library, and the library has these weird motion-sensor lights that turn off if you sit still too long, which, relatable. Anyway, most of those emails just didn't go anywhere. I got a couple of polite "not right now" replies and a lot of nothing. So I printed a one-page flyer, with the event details and what sponsors would get, and I just started walking into places. A bike shop, a cafe, and a bank branch said yes, and together that came to about $2,400. The honest lesson is that I thought a clean email would be en
Hold on—so the email blast didn't work, but walking in with a flyer did. What was different about that approach? Why do you think showing up in person made the difference?

Yeah, so, um, I think it's mostly that an email is really easy to ignore. You send it, it sits in some inbox between a newsletter and a parking ticket, and nobody has to do anything. When I walked in, the person behind the counter had to actually look at me and make a call right then, which is kind of uncomfortable for them but also means they can't just let it slide. The flyer helped too, because it was one page, so they could read it in like thirty seconds while I was standing there. The bike shop owner actually said he liked that I'd come by because he gets pitched all the time by people who never show their faces. I'm not sure that's a universal rule, though. The bank branch was a little different, they had to kick it up to someone, so I had to follow up twice, which, if you're thinking about the follow-up thing, I'd say that's the part people skip. Also, my stomach is definitely making noises right now, so sorry about that.
No worries at all. So you learned that showing up matters, and follow-up matters too. Did you try anything else that didn't work, or was it mostly the email and then the flyer approach?

Mostly it was just the email and then the flyer, honestly. I did try calling a couple of places first, but I got stuck in phone tree hell at one of them, and the other person just said to send an email, which, yeah, I had already done. So I figured I'd skip the middle step and go straight to the door. I also thought about asking my roommate's dad, who owns a plumbing company, to sponsor us, but I felt weird asking him for money, so I didn't. Looking back, that was probably a mistake, because he probably would have said yes. The bank was the one place I really had to push, because the first person I talked to said they'd have to check with corporate, and I'm pretty sure I got a little too comfortable just waiting by the front desk. Anyway, I think the main thing I'd do differently is ask for help sooner instead of trying to do everything myself, which is kind of a theme for me. Sorry, I think my stomach just made a noise that you definitely heard.
Ha, we're almost out of time, so let me ask you this before we wrap up. Why do you want this kind of role, specifically? What are you looking for that you're not getting right now?

Yeah, so, um, I think what I'm not getting right now is the chance to own something that goes beyond my own shifts. At the store, I'm really good at what happens between me and a customer, but once I walk off the floor, I don't see whether the decisions I'm making actually add up to anything. The treasurer job was the closest I've come to that, and I liked it way more than I expected, even though I was basically sweating over spreadsheets on Sunday mornings. I'd like a role where the sales side and the money side are connected, so I can see how a good conversation with a customer turns into revenue and then into something I can plan around. Also, I'm kind of a nerd about trip planning, so I'd probably be happiest somewhere that cares about getting the details right for the people you're serving. I don't have it all figured out, and I know I'd need to learn a lot, but I'd rather be the person who has to ask for help on something real than the person who's coasting on something easy. Sorry, my stomach is now staging a protest, so I'm going to need that real l
I get it. Well, I've got a couple more minutes if you have any questions for me about the role or the team.
Yeah, sure, I do have one. What does a typical week look like for someone in this role, like how much of it is hands-on with customers versus working through numbers or reports?

Good question. It really depends on the level, but for someone starting out, I'd say it's probably 60, 70 percent customer-facing or project work, and the rest is reporting, planning, that kind of thing. You're not going to spend your whole day in a spreadsheet, but you'll definitely need to be comfortable with data. The role also requires some ownership—you're not just executing tasks, you're thinking about what moves the needle. Does that sound like the mix you're looking for?

Yeah, that mix sounds pretty good, honestly. I'm more of a people person than a spreadsheet person, but the treasurer thing taught me that the spreadsheet is what keeps you from doing something dumb with other people's money. So having the numbers be part of the job, not some separate thing I have to remember to do on Sunday mornings, would actually help me. The 60 to 70 percent part is interesting, because at the store that's basically my whole day, and I like that it's not all just answering questions. I'd want to know how much of the project work is planning something new versus fixing something that's already broken, because I think I'd be better at the first one. Also, my stomach is making a sound right now that I'm going to blame on the bus guy with the rotisserie chicken. Anyway, yeah, that sounds like the right direction for me.

Ha, fair enough. Well, I think we've covered a lot of ground. You've got good instincts around ownership and impact, and I like that you're thinking about what you'd be good at versus what you're just okay at. We'll take everything you've shared and get back to you within a few days with next steps. Sound good?

Yeah, sounds good, thanks so much for the time. Honestly, I really appreciate you hearing me out, even with the stomach noises. I'm looking forward to hearing back, and I'll be the one who actually answers the email quickly, unlike my sponsorship emails. Have a good rest of your day, and I'm going to go find that real lunch now.
Perfect. Good luck with the rest of your day, and enjoy that lunch. Take care, Jordan.
Thanks, you too. Take care, and I'll keep an eye out for that email.
Will do. Bye.
Bye, thanks again!
You're welcome!
Thanks again, have a good one!
You too!
Thanks, bye!
Bye!
Bye, take care!
Take care!

feedback_leaks.quote: Thanks for being so candid about what's worked and what hasn't—that's really helpful.

practice_questions.question: Tell me about a time you failed.
Why do you want this kind of role?

verdicts.notes: Strength: the interviewer kept good control with a rambling candidate, asking specific follow-ups on the top-seller, training and budget stories (including the pointed question about whether members were consulted) and covering both practice questions. Weakness: the customer complaint topic was never raised, and the interviewer let the vague answer at T9 pass without asking for specifics. There were also minor evaluative remarks ("Good question", "that's really helpful").

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for taking the time. How are things going on your end?

Oh, hi, yeah, thanks for having me. Things are good, honestly, it's been kind of a busy week. I've been juggling finals prep with a couple of shifts at the outdoor gear place, which, if you've ever tried to study for an accounting exam while someone is asking you whether a sleeping bag is rated for January, you know it's a whole thing. My roommate also keeps leaving the coffee maker on, so I've been up earlier than I'd like. Anyway, I'm glad we could get this scheduled, because the job posting honestly caught my eye right away.
Ha, yeah, that's a lot going on at once. Glad you made it work. So tell me a bit about yourself—walk me through how you got to where you are now, and what's drawing you to this role.

Sure, so I'm a business major, junior year, and I've kind of bounced around a bit, which I think is maybe a good thing? I started out thinking I'd do something in finance, then I got a job at the outdoor gear store near campus because I needed money and I figured I'd be bored. I was not bored. The store is one of those places where people come in and have no idea what they need, and you end up asking them where they're headed, and it turns out most of them just want to not die of hypothermia on a weekend hike. Anyway, I got pretty into it, and I ended up being the top seller for three months straight, June through August, out of nine associates. My main thing is I ask what trip they're planning before I show them anything, and that seems to help, because my add-on sales were around 1.9 times the store average. I also ended up training four new hires, which was kind of a big deal for me. I shadowed each of them for two shifts, then had them lead while I watched, and three of the four hit their first monthly target. The fourth one is still working on it, and honestly I think she's going to be fine. On the campus side, I'm the treasurer for a club, and I manage a twelve thousand dollar budget, which came from student government. The hardest call I had to make was cutting our end-of-year banquet from three thousand down to twelve hundred so we could fund travel for a competition. That was rough, but I think people understood. I also got three local sponsors for our spring event, which, to be fair, took a lot of emails that mostly went nowhere, and then walking in with a one-page flyer ended up working way better. As for this role, I'm drawn
Sorry, go ahead—what draws you to this role?

Oh, no, you didn't interrupt, I just got lost in my own sentence there. Honestly I was trying to think of how to say it without sounding like I memorized something. My professor, Dr. Alvarez, keeps telling us to have a real answer for this, and I always feel like I'm failing at that. Anyway, what draws me to this role is that it's the kind of work where I'd be dealing with actual people and also numbers, which is the combo I've kind of stumbled into. At the store, I like it when someone walks in confused and walks out with exactly what they need, and at the club, I like seeing a budget actually turn into a trip or an event. I think this role sits right in the middle of those two things, and I'd like to see if I can be useful on both sides instead of just one.

That makes sense. So you've gotten a taste of both—people and the numbers side. Let me dig into one of those experiences a bit more. You mentioned being top seller for three months, and you said add-on sales were about 1.9 times the store average. Walk me through a specific customer interaction where that approach really worked—what did you do differently than maybe someone else would have?

Okay, a specific one. I think it was a Saturday in July, and it was slammed, which is how I know it was July, because everyone's trying to get their gear before the weekend. A guy came in looking at rain jackets, and the usual move is to just walk him to the rack and start pointing at things. But I asked him where he was headed, and he said he was doing a three-day trip in the Cascades, which, I'm not going to pretend I've done that, but I've been to a couple of those trailheads and I know the weather there can be brutal. So that changed the conversation completely. Instead of telling him about the jacket's waterproof rating, I asked whether he'd be sleeping in a tent or a hut, because that affects what layers matter. He ended up buying the jacket, plus a base layer and a small pack liner he hadn't even been thinking about. And honestly, I think that's the whole trick, because people trust you more when you're asking about their trip instead of trying to sell them something. I'm sorry, I got distracted there, my commute is about forty minutes on the bus and I always think about that trailhead th

No, that's helpful. So in that case, you asked about the trip first, and that led to the base layer and the pack liner. How did you know those were the right things to suggest? Was it just experience, or did you have some kind of framework you were using?

Honestly, it's mostly experience at this point, but I do have a rough mental checklist, and I'm not sure I'd have called it a framework until someone asked. It's basically: where are they going, how long are they out, what's the weather likely to do, and where are they sleeping. Once you know those, the add-ons almost pick themselves. If someone's out for three days, a base layer matters more than a fancy jacket because they'll be sweaty and cold at the same time, which is miserable. And a pack liner is one of those things people don't think about until their gear is soaked on day two. I learned a lot of that from our store manager, who would stand next to me on the floor and say "ask about the trip, then ask about the sleep." Oh, and the bus I take is always late on Tuesdays, so I've had a
Got it. So you picked up that framework from your manager. When you trained those four new hires, did you pass that same framework along to them, or did you teach them differently?

Yeah, I passed it on, pretty much word for word at first, because that's what I was taught and it's easy to remember. But the thing I figured out pretty quickly is that a checklist only gets you so far, and people kind of need to see it happen before it sticks. So with each of them I shadowed for two shifts, just standing back and watching how they talked to people, and then I'd say something like, "okay, you ask about the trip, and what did you want to ask about next?" And then they'd lead and I'd just watch. One of them, Priya, was really quiet at first, and she was worried she'd sound like she was interrogating people. So I told her to think of it less as questions and more as just being curious about where someone's going, which honestly sounds kind of obvious now. She ended up being one of the ones who hit her first monthly target. The other two were a little more natural with people, so they mostly needed me to help them not rush the product part. Three of the four hit their first target, and the fourth, Marcus, is still getting there, but he's the one who's best at remembering people's names, which I think matters more than people give it credit for. Also, I've been meaning to say, my roommate finally fixed the coffee maker, so that's one thing off my mind.

That's good. So you adapted your teaching based on what each person needed—Priya needed a different framing than the others. How did you know that approach was actually working? What were you measuring?

Mostly I was going by the monthly numbers, honestly, which is the obvious thing to look at. Three of the four hit their first monthly target, and that felt like the clearest sign. But I'll be real, the numbers come in at the end of the month, so by the time you see them it's too late to do much about it. So on the floor I was watching for smaller stuff: did they ask about the trip before they walked someone to the rack, did they get the customer to talk, did the customer leave with more than they came in for. And if someone was rushing the product part, like Marcus or the other one, I'd notice that pretty quick because the add-on stuff falls off. Priya was a different case, because she was so nervous about sounding pushy that she wasn't asking much of anything at first, so I was looking for her to actually ask one real question per customer, even if it was clunky. Once she started doing that, her add-ons went up, and I could see her getting more comfortable, which, you know, is the part I kind of cared about most. Oh, and I also started keeping a little notebook at the register, which sounds nerdy, but it helped me remember which customers came back, and honestly that's where I first noticed Marcus was great with repeat people, which I did not expect. Anyway, I think that's the honest answer, it's a mix of numbers and just watching them work.
Makes sense. Let me shift gears a bit. Tell me about a time when something didn't go the way you wanted—a failure or a setback. What happened?

Okay, so the big one that comes to mind is the sponsors for the club's spring event. I figured it would be easy. I sat down one night and emailed 25 local businesses, and I was pretty proud of the email, I'd rewritten it like four times. Almost none of them answered. I think I got maybe a couple of "not right now" replies and a lot of nothing, which was kind of demoralizing, because I'd put in a whole evening. Our treasurer job is partly about getting money in, not just tracking it, so I was worried I'd look bad to the club. Then I was talking about it with my friend who works at a coffee place, and she said people in small businesses don't check their email much but they'll talk to you if you show up. So I printed a one-page
So you changed your approach after that email didn't work. What was different when you actually walked in with the one-pager?

Okay, so the flyer was basically the same info as the email, just on one page with a logo spot and a little table showing what a sponsor would get, like banner space and a shout-out at the event. The big difference was that I was standing in front of a person instead of hoping someone would open an inbox. I went to maybe a dozen places over two afternoons, and most of them were kind of busy, so I'd say something like, "Hey, I'm with the student club, do you have two minutes?" and then hand them the page. The bike shop owner actually asked me how many students would be there, which I didn't know exactly, so I had to say I'd get back to him, and that felt awkward but he said yes anyway. The cafe was easy because my friend's coworker sort of knew me already. The bank branch took the longest, I had to wait around for a manager, and I think I was sweating through my shirt, which is the most honest thing I can say about that. Three yeses total, worth
So you got three sponsors. What would you do differently if you had to do it again?

Honestly, the first thing I'd change is the order. I spent a whole evening on those 25 emails, and I should have just gone to the businesses in person from the start, because that's what actually worked. The bike shop guy asking how many students would show up really stuck with me. I didn't have that number, and I should've had it before I walked in, so I'd get a head count from the event committee first. I'd also bring a couple of sample sponsor banners, because the flyer was fine but people kept asking what things looked like. And the bank took forever, so next time I'd call ahead and ask for the manager's name, which would've saved me like an hour of sitting there. Oh, and this is kind of a side note, but my professor, Dr. Alvarez, said something in class about how the cold outreach is always the least efficient part of any sales job, and I think I just didn't want to believe her. Anyway, that's the honest answer, I'd just go in person sooner and come in more prepared.

Got it. You mentioned the club budget earlier—you cut the banquet from three thousand down to twelve hundred. Walk me through that decision. What else were you weighing at the time, and how did you land on that number?

Okay, the banquet. That one was rough, because people really look forward to it, and it's kind of the only time everyone in the club is in the same room without a meeting agenda. We had the competition coming up, and the travel costs for the team were the thing we couldn't really skip, since a few people had already committed to going. So I sat down with the board and we went through every line item, which took way longer than I wanted, and the banquet was the biggest one that wasn't tied to something we'd already promised. I was also thinking about the twelve thousand from student government, because they'd want to see that we used it on the stuff that mattered most to members, not just on the stuff that was fun. I didn't want to cut it all the way, though, because I think people would've been pretty upset, so we landed on twelve hundred for a smaller dinner, which kept the tradition alive. I remember the treasurer's job being way more about saying no than I expected, and honestly that was the hardest part, not the math. Oh, and I think someone asked if we could do a potluck instead, which I thought was a great idea, but we were already past the point where we could plan that well. Anyway
So you kept some version of the banquet because you thought it mattered to people. Did you actually talk to members before you made that call, or did you just decide with the board?

Honestly, no, not really, and I think that's a fair thing to push on. I went to the board first because the travel money had to be locked in before the competition deadline, and I was kind of in a hurry. I talked to a couple of people who'd committed to the trip, and they were fine with it, but I didn't do a proper survey or ask the wider club what they'd rather have. That's what I'd do differently now. A quick poll or even a message to the whole list would have told me whether people cared more about the dinner or the travel, and maybe I'd have found out the potluck idea was the thing everyone wanted. I wasn't being lazy, I just didn't think about it until after, when someone brought up the potluck. So the honest answer is I made the call with the board, and I probably should've asked members too, even if it added a day or two.
Fair. So if you were starting as a treasurer in a new club tomorrow, what would you do in that first month to figure out how to handle money the right way?

Okay, so the first thing I'd do is sit down with whoever handled it before me, if they're around, and just ask for the whole picture, not only the spreadsheet. Like, where does the money come from, what's already been promised, and what got people complaining last year. I'd also want to see the bank statements myself instead of trusting a summary, because I learned pretty fast that a budget on paper and what actually left the account can be two different stories. Then I'd probably do what I should have done with the banquet, which is send a quick message to the whole club asking what they care about most, so I'm not guessing. I'd also set up a simple tracker, nothing fancy, that I'd check every week, because the end of the month is too late to catch a problem, same as with the sales numbers. And honestly, I'd want to get in front of the board early about the stuff I'd have to say no to, since that was the part that surprised me most. Oh, and I'd make sure whoever's on the student government side knows what I'm doing, because they're the ones signing off on the twelve thousand, and I'd rather they hear it from me first. Anyway, I think that's a pretty solid first month, though I'd probably adjust once I actually saw the books.

That's thorough. One more thing before we wrap up—why does this kind of role appeal to you? I know you touched on it earlier, but I'm curious what specifically about this job, or this company, made you apply.

Honestly, the posting kind of caught me because it mentioned working with clients and also keeping the books tight, and those are the two things I keep ending up doing without planning it. I was going to say something more polished, but my roommate was yelling about the coffee maker again, so I lost my train of thought for a second. Dr. Alvarez always says that the best jobs are the ones where you can't fake your way through the middle, and I think this one is like that, because you'd be talking to people all day and also answering for the numbers. At the outdoor store, the part I like most is when someone comes in totally lost and leaves with exactly what they need for their trip. At the club, it's watching a budget turn into an actual trip or event that people remember. I think what appeals to me about this role is that it would let me keep both of those going instead of choosing one. And I'll be honest, I'd like to find out what the day-to-day really looks like, because I'm a lot better at learning by doing than by reading a job description.
That makes sense. So do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, just one, if that's okay. What does a typical week look like for someone in this role, and what's the first thing you'd want a new person to get good at?

Good question. So a typical week is probably a mix—you'd spend maybe half your time talking with clients, understanding what they need, troubleshooting problems when things go wrong. The other half is internal: reconciling accounts, reporting to leadership, making sure we're tracking where money is going. The first thing I'd want someone to get good at is listening to what a client actually needs versus what they think they need, because that changes how you help them. Beyond that, just getting comfortable with our systems and learning who does what on the team. Fair enough?

Yeah, that makes sense, thanks. The listening part is kind of what I was getting at with the trip questions at the store, so that lines up. I'm guessing the internal half is where the numbers stuff gets real, and I'm curious how much of that is shared with the client side, like whether the people you help ever see the reports. Anyway, that's a great answer, and I really appreciate you walking me through it. I'm excited about the chance to find out more.

Great, I'm glad. Well, I think we've covered a lot of ground today. Thanks for being so candid about what's worked and what hasn't—that's really helpful. We'll be in touch in the next week or so with next steps. In the meantime, good luck wrapping up finals and those shifts.

Thanks so much, that means a lot. I really appreciate you making the time, and I enjoyed talking through all of it. Good luck with the rest of your week too, and I'll keep an eye out for your email. Oh, and if the coffee maker thing ever comes up again, I'll take it as a sign I should be up early anyway. Talk soon, and thanks again.
Ha, sounds good. Take care, Jordan.

feedback_leaks.quote: You're being honest about what you remember and what you don't, which I appreciate.
That makes sense. You're watching for the behaviors that matter, not just the numbers.

verdicts.notes: Strength: the interviewer asked concrete follow-ups that checked how the numbers were measured, asked for a specific example, and asked what the candidate would do differently. It covered both practice questions and invited the candidate's questions. Weakness: it never asked about the customer complaint topic, it let a few vague or cut-off answers pass, and it gave small evaluative remarks such as "You're being honest... which I appreciate."

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for taking the time. How are things going on your end?

Oh, things are good, thanks for asking. Honestly it's been a little hectic, I'm not gonna lie. I pulled an all-nighter on Tuesday for a group project, which was not my best decision, and then I had to take the bus over this morning because my car's been making this weird clicking noise. My mechanic thinks it's the battery, but he also said it could be something else, so I'm just kind of waiting on that. Anyway, I'm really glad to be here, and I've been reading up on your company, which is pretty interesting. Did you want to start with the background stuff, or should I just jump in?

Ha, yeah, car trouble is never fun. But glad you made it here. Let's just dive in—no need to overthink it.

So what drew you to this kind of role?

Yeah, totally. So honestly, the reason I got into this is kind of a funny story. I was working the floor at an outdoor gear store last year, mostly because I needed the paycheck and I like being outside, and I didn't expect to like the selling part as much as I did. I started noticing that the people who came in usually had a trip in mind, like a weekend hike or a first camping thing, and they were kind of overwhelmed by all the options. So I started asking them what they were planning before I showed them anything, and that seemed to help a lot. I ended up being the top seller for three months in a row, which surprised me, and I was doing about twice the add-on sales of the store average. That kind of made me realize I like figuring out what people actually need, which is why this role caught my eye. Also, my roommate says I talk about this too much, so feel free to tell me if I'm rambling.

No, that's helpful. So when you say you were doing twice the add-on sales of the store average, how was that actually measured? Like, were you tracking it yourself, or did the store give you those numbers?

Good question, and honestly I should be clear about it. I didn't keep a spreadsheet or anything like that. I think the numbers came from the store's monthly sales reports, but I'd want to double-check that before I said it for sure. It's kind of funny, because the first time I saw the comparison I thought it was a mistake. My manager had printed out the reports and pointed at a line that said my add-on rate was around 1.9 times the store average, and I was like, wait, really? My coworker Dev kept saying that the reports were the only thing anyone ever really looked at, which is how I knew they were the official source. I was ranked first out of nine associates from June through August, so the add-on number was part of why. If you want
Got it, that makes sense. So you were ranked first overall for those three months—what do you think you actually did differently than the other eight people on the floor?

Okay, so the main thing was the question I asked first. Before I'd show anybody anything, I'd ask what kind of trip they were planning, like where they were going, how long, and whether they'd be carrying their own stuff. And I know that sounds obvious, but a lot of the other guys on the floor would just walk people straight to the tents and start listing features. I think it was because they wanted to get to the sale faster, which, funny enough, is kind of the opposite of what happens. Once someone tells you they're doing a three-night trip with a four-year-old, you already know what to pull off the wall, and they trust you more. There was also this one guy, Marcus, who I think just liked talking gear more than anybody, so he'd sometimes lose people in the details. I'm not saying I was some genius, I just listened a little longer than everyone else did. Sorry, I think I drifted there. So, yeah, the question first, and then the recommendation, and that was basically it.
That's clear. So when you recommended something after they told you the trip details, how did you decide what to actually show them? Like, walk me through one specific example.

Okay, a specific one. I had a guy come in a few weeks before the summer rush, and he said he was going up to a lake for a long weekend with his girlfriend, and they'd be hiking in about three miles and then camping. So I asked a couple more things, like whether they were planning to carry everything themselves and what the nights were going to be like, because it was supposed to get cold up there. He said they'd be out in early June and it could drop to near freezing, which, honestly, I didn't expect him to know. That changed what I pulled, because a summer bag that's fine for July would have left him freezing. So I showed him a warmer bag, a lighter two-person tent since they were carrying it, and a small stove, and I explained why each one mattered for that specific trip. He kind of joked that I was overdoing it, and I said it's a lot cheaper to be warm than to cut the trip short. He bought the bag and the tent,
Did he buy the stove too, or just the bag and tent?

Honestly, I don't remember for sure, and I don't want to make something up in an interview. I think he got the bag and the tent, and I want to say the stove was a maybe, but I was also kind of in the zone with the customer, so I might be mixing him up with someone else. That's the kind of thing I'd check if I were looking at the sales log, which, now that I think about it, is actually how I'd want to track it: which items went with which trips. It's kind of like how I'm feeling about my car right now, where I'm not sure it's the battery until the mechanic tells me. If he didn't take the stove, I'd guess it's because he already had one from a buddy, which happens a lot with camping stuff. Sorry, I think I wandered again. What I'm pretty sure about is that the trip details drove what I showed him, and that's

No, that's fair. You're being honest about what you remember and what you don't, which I appreciate.

Let me shift gears a bit. You also trained four new hires on the sales floor. Walk me through how you actually trained one of them—what did that look like?

Yeah, sure. So with the training, I kind of fell into it, honestly. The store was swamped one summer and they hired four people in about two weeks, and my manager asked if I could show them the ropes. The way I did it was I shadowed each new hire for two shifts. So for the first shift I basically just stood next to them while they dealt with customers, and I'd jump in if they got stuck, which happened a lot with the tent poles and the sleeping bag ratings, because those are confusing when you first see them. Then on the second shift I'd let them lead and I'd just watch from a distance, and afterward we'd grab a coffee from the place across the parking lot and I'd tell them what worked and what didn't. One of them, Priya, was super nervous at first, and she ended up being one of the better sellers, which made me really happy. Three of the four hit their first monthly target, which I think is a decent result. The fourth one, I'm not totally sure what happened with him, but I think he left the job for a different job pretty quickly, so I can't really take credit for that one. I also think the coffee part was the most useful thing, because people open up more when they're not standing on the floor. Anyway, that's basically how it went, and I'm happy to talk more about any part of it.
When you gave them feedback during the coffee, what's one specific thing you told someone they should do differently?

Oh, that's a good one. I think the big thing I kept coming back to was the trip question. One of the new hires, I don't want to say his name since I'm not totally sure he'd want me talking about him, would jump right to the tents the second someone walked in. Customers would tell him something, like they were going to a campground with their kids, and he'd nod and keep listing features. So over coffee I told him to hold off for a second and ask one or two questions first, like how long they'd be out and whether they were carrying everything. I also said it's fine if the customer doesn't know the answer, because that tells you something too. He kind of pushed back at first and said it felt slow, which, yeah, I get, the coffee place across the lot is also slow. But a couple of shifts later he told me a customer had actually thanked him for not rushing them. I honestly think that one change did more than anything else I told anyone, but I'm not sure how much of it was me and how much was just him getting comfortable on the floor. Anyway, do you want me
That's helpful. So how did you know the training actually worked? Like, beyond the three hitting their monthly target—what made you feel like they were ready to be on their own?

Good question. Honestly, the monthly target was the easiest thing to point to, but it wasn't really what I was watching for. What I looked for was whether they'd start asking the trip questions without me reminding them. Like, on the second shift, when I was standing back, I'd watch to see if they went to the customer first or to the tents first. If they were asking where someone was headed and how long they'd be out before they grabbed anything, I figured they'd got it. Priya was the one who made that really obvious to me, because she started doing it on her own and didn't even seem to think about it, which is kind of how you know something's clicked. The other thing was how they handled it when a customer didn't know what they needed. The new hires who could stay calm and ask a couple more questions, instead of panicking and pushing the most expensive thing, I felt good about. I also liked it when they came back to me after a rough customer and asked what they could have done differently, because that meant they were thinking about it themselves. I don't have a formal checklist or anything, it was more of a gut feeling from watching them over those two shifts. Oh, and the one who left, I still wonder if I missed something in those first couple of shifts, but I don't really know, and I guess that's fair to admit.

That makes sense. You're watching for the behaviors that matter, not just the numbers.

Let me ask you this: tell me about a time you failed, or something that didn't go the way you wanted.

Yeah, sure, I've had plenty of those, which is probably a good sign that I'm actually trying stuff. The one that comes to mind most is from the club, when I was treasurer. We had a big end-of-year banquet planned, and I had it budgeted at around three thousand dollars, which seemed fine on paper. Then the club got invited to a competition out of town, and travel for the team was going to cost a lot more than we'd planned for. I had to figure out where the money was going to come from, and the only real option I could see was cutting the banquet down to about twelve hundred. Honestly, I felt bad about it, because a few people had already been talking about it like it was going to be a big night, and I was basically the one telling them it was going to be smaller. I did it, and the team got to go, which was the main thing, but I'm not sure I communicated it as well as I could have. I think I should have brought the people who were planning the banquet in earlier, instead of just making the call and then sending the update. I also feel like the way I handled it was a little rushed, which is kind of how I handle a lot of things when there's a deadline, including, honestly, that group project I mentioned at the start. Anyway, that's the one I think about. It's a decent example of me making the call, and then realizing afterward I should've involved people a bit more. Sorry, that was a bit of a ramble, but I think I've got the gist out there.

No, that's useful. So when you say you should've involved the banquet people earlier—what would you actually have done differently? Like, what's the first step you'd take if you faced that same situation again?

Yeah, good question, and I've actually thought about this one a bit since. Honestly, the first thing I'd do is sit down with whoever was running the banquet before I made any decision, even if it's just a quick call. I'd lay out the numbers, like, here's what the competition travel costs, here's what we have, and here's the gap. Then I'd ask them what they'd want to keep, because maybe it's the food, or maybe it's the venue, and maybe we can cut the decorations and the band but still do a sit-down dinner. I think that would've gotten us to a smaller banquet that people were actually okay with, instead of me just announcing it. I also would've given myself a day or two before deciding, because I was rushing because of the deadline, and I think that's where I went wrong. I'd still probably end up cutting it to around twelve hundred, since the travel had to happen, but I'd have a better shot at getting people on board. Also, the banquet planners were a couple of people I'd known since freshman year, so I should have just texted them sooner. Anyway, that's basically what I'd do differently.

Makes sense. You'd bring them in early and give yourself a little more time.

You mentioned securing three local sponsors for the club's spring event. How did you actually find those sponsors and pitch them?

Yeah, so this one was kind of a grind at first. I started by emailing about 25 local businesses, which seemed like the efficient way to do it, and honestly it mostly didn't work. I think I got maybe a couple of replies that were just "thanks, not right now." My roommate said I should stop emailing and just go in person, which sounded kind of annoying to me, because I hate walking into places cold. But I tried it anyway, and I made a one-page flyer with the event date, what the money would go toward, and what the sponsor would get, like a logo on the poster and a shout-out at the event. I'd walk into a place during a slow part of the afternoon, ask for the manager, and just give them the flyer and a two-minute pitch. That worked a lot better. We ended up with three yeses: a bike shop, a cafe, and a bank branch, and together they came to about $2,400. The bank was the hardest one, because they had to check with corporate first, and I think I
What would you have done differently with the bank, or what did you learn from that one taking longer?

Yeah, the bank was a slog. They had to run it past corporate, and I kind of assumed a yes from the branch manager meant it was basically done, so I didn't follow up for a while. Then I realized it was sitting in some approval queue, and I had to keep checking in, which felt awkward but I think it was necessary. Honestly, what I'd do differently is ask on day one who actually has to approve it and how long that usually takes. That way I'd know the timeline up front instead of getting surprised. I also think I should've given the branch manager something they could forward internally, like a short summary email on top of the flyer, so they weren't stuck explaining it from memory. The cafe and the bike shop said yes right there, which made me kind of lazy about the bank, I guess. Oh, and the bank was also the one that wanted the logo in a specific size, which took a couple of back and forths. So yeah, mostly I learned to ask about the approval process early and make it easy for someone to pass the pitch along.
Good. So out of the 25 emails you sent initially, you got a couple of "not right now" replies. What do you think didn't work about the email approach compared to walking in?

Honestly, I think the big thing is that an email is really easy to ignore. You send it, it sits in some inbox between a supplier invoice and a newsletter, and nobody has to make a decision about it. When I walked in, the manager had to actually look at me and say yes or no, and that made a difference. I also think I was sending the same generic message to 25 places, so it kind of read like a mass email, even though I tried to personalize the first line. The flyer was the other piece, because it gave people something they could hold and pass along. Looking back, I probably should have tested the walk-in approach on two or three places first, instead of spending a whole week on emails. My roommate still thinks I'm too stubborn about things, and maybe he's right, but I'd say the in-person visit was the thing that actually got me the sponsors. Also, I should be honest that I'm not sure of the exact number of replies I got, so don't quote me on that part.
Fair enough. We're getting close on time here, so let me ask: what questions do you have for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, sure, I've got one. What does a typical week look like for someone in this role, especially in the first few months?

Good question. So the first month or two, you'd be onboarding—learning our systems, meeting the team, understanding how we work. You'd probably shadow a couple of people, sit in on some meetings to see how we operate. After that, it depends on the specific position, but you'd be taking on your own projects pretty quickly, with support from whoever's managing you. Some weeks are quieter, some are hectic. It's not a sales floor, so it's different from what you're used to, but it's still customer-focused in its own way. Does that help?

Yeah, that helps, thanks. Shadowing for the first month or two sounds pretty familiar, honestly, since that's kind of how I trained the new hires at the store, so I'd like that. I'm curious what the customer side looks like in this role, since you said it's different from the floor. Is it more account management, or more about working with internal teams? Sorry, I think I've got a couple of other questions bouncing around in my head, but I'll stop there and let you go.

Ha, no, that's fine. It's a mix of both, honestly—you'd be working with internal teams to solve customer problems, so it's less face-to-face selling and more problem-solving behind the scenes. But the core skill is the same: listening to what people actually need and figuring out how to help.

Well, I really appreciate you taking the time today. You've given me a lot to think about, and I enjoyed hearing about your experience. We'll be in touch in the next week or so with next steps. Sound good?

Yeah, that sounds great, thanks so much for your time today. I really enjoyed the conversation, and the part about listening to what people actually need is kind of the thing I keep coming back to, so that's encouraging to hear. Sorry if I rambled a bit here and there. I'll look out for your email in the next week, and if there's anything else you need from me before then, just let me know. Have a good rest of your day, and I hope the rest of your week goes smoother than mine did with the car.
Ha, I appreciate that. Good luck with the car—hope it's just the battery. Take care, Jordan.

feedback_leaks.quote: which from what you've said today, sounds like your style anyway.

Why do you want this kind of role?

verdicts.notes: Strength: covered all five resume topics plus both practice questions, with sharp follow-ups on measurement (T6) and the fourth trainee's shortfall (T20). Weakness: gave no follow-up on several vague answers (T9, T13, T17), never pressed on the sponsorship numbers or the day-to-day ownership of the budget, and leaked mild evaluation at T28.

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for coming in. Did you find everything okay today?

Yeah, thanks, I found it totally fine. Honestly, the parking situation was a little rough. I circled the lot twice and ended up behind the building by the loading dock, which, funny story, is where I got into this whole retail thing in the first place. My roommate works at an outdoor gear shop downtown, and she's the one who got me my first shift there, so I owe her a coffee or five. Anyway, I printed out my resume twice just in case, because one time at a different interview the printer jammed and I had to kind of improvise, which I'm actually pretty good at. So yeah, everything's good, I'm just glad to be here.
Good, glad you made it. And hey, sounds like your roommate did you a solid. So tell me—what drew you to apply for this role?

Yeah, she did, she's the best. So what drew me to this role... honestly, a bunch of things. I'm a business major, and I keep saying I want to end up in something where I'm actually dealing with people and numbers at the same time, and I kind of figured out during my summer on the sales floor that I like that mix. Working the floor at the gear shop, I got really into figuring out what customers actually need, which sometimes isn't what they walk in asking for. My trick is I always ask where they're headed before I show them anything, like if someone wants a jacket I'll ask if it's for a cold rainy hike or a winter camping trip, because that changes everything. That habit is part of why I ended up at the top of the monthly sales board, which felt pretty great, though honestly my manager probably deserves some of that credit too. Anyway, I also was treasurer for my campus club and dealt with a budget, and I liked that a lot more than I expected. So when I saw this posting, it just seemed like the place where those two things, selling and managing money, could actually come together. That's the short version, I think.
That makes sense. You mentioned being top seller for a few months straight—what was different about what you were doing compared to the other people on the team?

Honestly, I'm not sure it was that different, at least not at first. Everybody on the floor knows the basics, like show the product, mention the warranty, and try to get them to add a pair of socks or a water bottle. The thing I did, which I kind of stumbled into, was just asking people where they were headed before I pulled anything off the wall. My roommate, the one who got me the job, says I'm annoying about it, because I'll stand there for like two minutes asking about someone's route and their sleeping situation. But once you know whether someone's doing a muddy overnight in April or a flat car-camping weekend, the add-ons almost sell themselves, because you're suggesting stuff they actually need. I think that's why my add-on sales ended up around 1.9 times the store average over the summer, which, don't quote me on the exact math, but that's what the manager showed us. I was ranked number one out of nine associates from June through August, and I know that sounds like a flex, but a lot of it was just that one habit done consistently. There was also a rainy Tuesday where I spent like forty minutes with one guy and he ended up buying almost his whole kit, which was kind of wild. So yeah, the difference was mostly just slowing down at the start
Got it. And how did your manager actually measure that? Like, was it just the ranking, or did they track the add-on percentage you mentioned?

Hmm, good question, and I'll be honest, I'm not 100% sure of the details on the back end. The ranking was on the monthly board in the break room, so that part was pretty visible, and it was based on total sales dollars for each associate. The add-on thing came up at a team meeting, where my manager pulled up some report from the register system and showed us how often each of us was selling a second item with the main thing. I think it's the kind of stat the system tracks automatically, but I never asked how it's calculated, which, now that I'm saying it out loud, I probably should have. My manager is pretty chill and kind of loves spreadsheets, like she once spent a whole lunch explaining to me how she'd set up the inventory counts, and I was like, okay, I just wanted my sandwich. Anyway, that's why I said the 1.9 times th
No, that makes sense. So when you're starting a new job, how would you go about learning how the numbers actually work on day one or week one?

Good question, and I think I'd start by asking the boring questions early, which honestly I'm not always great at because I like jumping straight into the fun stuff. So day one, I'd want to know exactly how the numbers get pulled, like what the reports are, who runs them, and whether the add-on rate is something I can check myself. My first job taught me that a lot of people just assume you know the system, and then you're stuck guessing for a month. I'd probably sit down with whoever handles the budget or the reporting and ask them to walk me through one real example, the way my manager did with the inventory counts, even though I was distracted by my sandwich at the time. Then I'd try to trace a few of my own numbers back to the source, just to make sure I understand them. Also, my roommate says I'm too detail-oriented about this stuff, which might be true. But I'd rather know what's behind a number than just repeat it in a meeting, and honestly that's also how I ended up doing the club budget, where I had to explain every line item to the student government people. Anyway, I think the key is just asking early and not pretending you get it when you don't.

Fair enough. Let me ask you about the club budget—you managed twelve thousand dollars as treasurer. Walk me through a specific decision you made. Was there something you wanted to fund but couldn't, or had to cut?

Yeah, there was one, and it was kind of a tough one. So the twelve thousand came from student government, and every year the club does an end-of-year banquet, which is basically the big party where everybody gets together and the officers get thanked, and it had been running around three thousand dollars. My roommate, who's in the club too, and I went to a few of the board meetings, and there was this competition coming up that a couple of our members had qualified for, and they needed travel money. Like, gas, a hotel for two nights, the entry fee. Honestly, I was kind of attached to the banquet because I went to it my first year and it was really fun, and I remember the food was good, like there was this lasagna thing, and I'm still annoyed about the lasagna. Anyway, I sat down with the spreadsheet, which my manager at the gear shop would have loved, and the math was basically that we couldn't do both at full price. So I cut the banquet from three thousand down to twelve hundred, and that covered the travel for the team. I got some pushback from a few people, and I had to explain it a couple times, but the competition was the thing that actually represented the club, so it made sense to me. Looking back, I'd probably have talked to the members earlier instead of making the call mostly on my own, because people got upset when they heard about it second-hand. But yeah, that was the hardest call I made with that budget.
That's helpful. So when you say you'd talk to the members earlier—what would that conversation have looked like, and how would you have handled it differently?

Yeah, so I think it would've been a short conversation at the start, like a quick email or a meeting before the board voted, saying, hey, here's the budget, here's the competition, here's what it costs, and here's what we're thinking about cutting. I basically should've done that with the banquet committee and the general members, since they're the ones who'd be sad about it. I kind of did the math on my own at my desk and then told people after it was decided, which is the part that made people mad. My roommate was super blunt about it, like, you didn't ask anybody, you just announced it, and she was right, even though she still got her travel covered. I'm also thinking about how the gear shop works, where if you're going to change a return policy you tell the whole floor first, because otherwise people get weird with customers. So I'd probably have done a quick poll, asked if people would rather have a smaller banquet or skip something else, and then made the call with their input. It might not have changed the outcome, but people would've felt like they had a say, which honestly matters more than I thought it would. Anyway, I'd take that lesson into any job with money involved.
Makes sense. So let me shift gears a bit. Tell me about a time you actually failed at something.

Oh, that's a fair question. The sponsor thing for the spring event is probably my best example, even though it's not a huge disaster. I emailed about 25 local businesses, and honestly I thought it would be easy, like I'd just write a nice email and people would say yes. Most of them never answered, and the few who did were polite no's. My roommate, who's apparently a professional at everything, saw me moping over my laptop and was like, why don't you just go walk in somewhere? So I printed a one-page flyer, and I went to some places near campus in person, and that's where I got three yeses: a bike shop, a cafe, and a bank branch. Between them they were worth $2,400 total, which for us was a big deal. The lesson I took from it is that cold email is kind of easy to ignore, and a real person standing in front of you with a piece of paper is harder to brush off. I still think about how many emails I sent before I figured that out, but I guess it's like
Right, so you figured it out and pivoted. But what would you do differently if you were doing that sponsorship push again from the start?

Honestly, I'd skip the email blast and go straight to the walk-ins, which, looking back, is kind of embarrassing that I didn't start there. I'd spend maybe an hour or two before I even sent anything just making the flyer really clear, like one page, what the event is, who's coming, what the sponsor gets, and a little logo spot. Then I'd map out the businesses within walking distance of campus and go in on a weekday afternoon, when managers are less slammed. My roommate says the best time is like two to four, which I think she got from her boyfriend who works at a coffee place, so I'm not sure that's reliable. I'd also ask for the owner or manager by name if I could, since the cold emails probably went to some general inbox nobody checked. And I'd probably follow up with the three yeses and say thanks in a way that made them want to come back next year. Anyway, the email thing wasn't a total waste, because a couple of the places I walked into had actually seen my email and recognized the name, which, I guess, is kind of the point of sending them in the first place.
Got it. Let me ask you about training—you trained four new hires on the sales floor. How did you actually train them, and how did you know it worked?

Okay, so the training part is actually pretty simple, which is kind of funny because I made it sound like a bigger deal on my resume. The way it worked was, I shadowed each new hire for two shifts, just walking around with them and seeing how they talked to people. Then I flipped it, and they led while I stood back and watched. My roommate, who somehow ends up in every story I tell, says I hovered like a nervous parent during those first sessions, and she's probably right. I also used to bring whatever I was eating on break, which one of the new people said was the best part of training, so I'm not sure what that says about me. As for how I knew it worked, the main thing was the monthly target. Three of the four hit their first monthly target, and the fourth one was honestly a little behind but got there the next month, so I counted that as a win too. I also kept asking them what they'd ask a customer at the start, because that was the habit I was trying to pass on, the where-are-you-headed question. It's not a perfect measure, and I'd want more data before saying it's a proven system. But it seemed to stick, and that felt good.
When you say the fourth person was a little behind, what does that actually mean? Like, how far behind, and what did you do about it?

Honestly, I don't remember the exact number, and I should've written it down. It was close enough that I wasn't worried, but I can't tell you if it was a few percent or a bigger gap. What I did was kind of low-key. I sat down with her after a shift, and we looked at which customers she'd been talking to and where she was losing people. I think she was jumping into the product too fast, like she'd grab a jacket before she knew where the person was going, which is exactly the habit I'd been trying to teach. So we did a couple of shifts where she only asked questions for the first few minutes, and I stood a little farther back. My roommate would say I was still hovering, and she'd probably be right about that. Then the next month she hit the target, and she messaged me a picture of a plate of tacos to celebrate, which I still think is the best outcome. Anyway, I'd want a proper tracking sheet next time instead of just going off memory.
Fair. So let me ask you about a customer complaint. Your resume says you handled escalated returns. Give me a specific example—what happened, and what did you do?

Yeah, so there was one that stuck with me. A guy came back with a tent he'd bought a while ago, and he wanted a full refund, but he was past the return window by a couple of weeks. He was pretty frustrated, and I could tell he felt like he was getting the runaround. My manager was off that day, and I was the one at the counter, and my roommate, who was in the store that afternoon to buy trail mix, later told me I got this weird look on my face like I was doing math in my head, which I guess I was. Anyway, I couldn't just hand over the money because it was outside policy, so I looked at what the brand's warranty covered. The tent had a zipper issue and a pole sleeve that was tearing, and the warranty would cover repairs for that kind of wear. So I offered to get it sent in for repair through the warranty, and I walked him through the process and said I'd follow up with him on the status. He wasn't thrilled at first, but he took it, and a few weeks later he left a positive review that specifically mentioned the warranty help. I think what I took from it is that when the policy says no, you can still look for the option that actually solves the problem. I did have to check with the store manager afterward to make sure I wasn't overstepping, and she was fine with it, which is also a good thing to know for next time.
So when you checked with your manager afterward, what did she say, and did that change how you'd handle something like that in the future?

Yeah, so when I went to her afterward, she was actually pretty chill about it. I kind of expected her to be like, you can't do that, but she said the warranty route was the right move and that I should've just gone ahead, which felt good, honestly. She did point out that next time I should write down the exact warranty claim number and the timeline in the notes, so nobody's confused later about what got promised. Any other questions?

Thanks for the time today, I really appreciate it.
