transcript.text: Hi, thanks for coming in. Did you find everything okay today?
Yeah, everything's good, thanks for having me. Finding the place was easy, and the video link worked fine on my end too. I'm glad to be here.
Great, glad to hear it. So, why don't you tell me a bit about yourself—what brings you to this conversation?

Sure. I'm a business major finishing up this year. For the past couple of years I've balanced a part-time job on the sales floor at an outdoor gear store with being treasurer for a campus club. I like work where I'm talking with people and then seeing the numbers move, which is a big reason I'm interested in this role. I'm looking for a place where I can keep building on that, and I think my retail and money-management experience fits pretty well with what you're hiring for.
That makes sense. So you mentioned the numbers moving—when you were at the outdoor gear store, what kind of numbers were you tracking or trying to move?

Mostly sales, I guess. I was on the floor at the store, so I was trying to help people walk out with the right gear. Honestly, a lot of what I learned was about the conversation itself. I started asking people where they were headed before I showed them anything, and that changed how the whole sale went. It's hard to quantify how much that helped, but it's the thing I'd bring here.
Got it. You mentioned you were the top seller there for three months in a row—how did you know that was actually happening? Like, how was that measured?

Oh, the manager posted stuff at the end of each month, so you could kind of see where everyone landed. I didn't really watch it that closely, though. What stuck with me more was how much I had to adjust for different customers. Some people know exactly what they want, and others just need someone to ask the right questions. Figuring out which one you're dealing with is probably the part I got better at the most.
That's helpful. So when you say you adjusted for different customers—can you walk me through one specific sale where you had to do something different than usual to land it?

Sure. A guy came in one Saturday wanting a jacket, and he kind of waved at the rack and said, "Just show me what you've got." Normally I'd start pulling options, but I asked him where he was headed first. Turned out he was doing a shoulder-season hike with a bunch of rain forecast. So instead of the jacket he'd pointed at, I grabbed a lighter shell and a pair of gaiters and explained why they'd matter in that weather. He ended up buying the whole setup, and he came back a few weeks later to say it kept him dry. Honestly, that was the moment I realized that asking questions first usually gets you a better sale than the one the customer walked in planning.
That's a good example. When you look back at your time there, is there a moment where you didn't handle something the way you would now—something that didn't go the way you wanted?

Yeah, there's one that comes to mind. A customer wanted a refund on a used tent, but the return window had already passed. I told them no refund was possible, and they were pretty frustrated. Looking back, I should have asked what had actually gone wrong with the tent before I said anything about the policy. I ended up finding a repair option through the brand's warranty, and they seemed happier once they had a path forward. They even left a good review. But I'd want to lead with curiosity about the problem next time, not with the rule.
That's honest. And you did end up handling the escalation—what made you think to dig into the warranty angle after you'd already said no?

Honestly, I was stuck on the policy at first. The refund window was closed, and I'd already said no, so I was trying to figure out what I could still offer without overstepping. My manager was off that day, so I couldn't just check with anyone. I remembered the brand had a warranty program for defects, so I asked the customer whether the tent had failed, like a broken pole or a ripped seam. Once they described it, the warranty looked like a real option. It's not something I'd have thought of if I'd just stuck to the return policy.
Makes sense. So you also trained four new hires on the sales floor—walk me through how you actually did that. What did that look like day to day?

Sure. Honestly, I didn't have a formal training program, so I kind of made it up as I went. When a new hire started, I'd shadow them for their first two shifts, just watching how they talked to customers and where they got stuck. Then I'd flip it, and they'd lead while I stood nearby and jumped in if something went sideways. Nobody really walked me through it either, so I was figuring out what worked by trial and error.

Three of the four of them ended up hitting their first monthly target, which I was pretty happy about. The one who didn't was still getting comfortable with the products, and honestly, I think I could have spent more time on that with him. What I'd do differently now is set up a clearer checklist for the first week so nobody has to guess what good looks like.
How did you know whether the training actually stuck? Like, what told you that those three people were ready to be on their own?

Mostly I could just tell from watching them. By the second or third shift, they'd stop checking with me before every move. They started asking customers where they were headed without me prompting them, which was the big thing I'd been trying to get across.

With the three who hit their targets, it was the little stuff. They'd catch when someone was looking at the wrong product and redirect without making it awkward. Honestly, I think it's hard to say for sure, because a month is a short window and some of it was just them getting lucky with the customers that came in.
Fair enough. On the club side, you managed a twelve-thousand-dollar budget as treasurer. Was there a time when you had to make a tough call about what to fund or what to cut?

Yeah, there was one. The hardest call was the end-of-year banquet. People really wanted it, but we also had a competition coming up, and the travel for that was going to be a big expense. I had to decide which one mattered more to the club.

Honestly, what I took from it was how much people care about things that feel like traditions, even when the money's better spent somewhere else. So I spent a lot of time explaining the tradeoff to people instead of just announcing the decision. I think that's something I'd still do, though it's hard to say how much it actually changed how people felt about it.
What did you end up doing—did you cut the banquet entirely, or did you find another way?

We didn't cut it entirely. We scaled it way back, like a smaller dinner with a lot less of the extras, so there was still something for people to look forward to. The rest went toward the competition travel. I think that compromise was what made it easier to accept, though some people were still pretty bummed about it.

Got it. So shifting gears a bit—you mentioned you're interested in this role partly because you like seeing the numbers move. Why this kind of work specifically? What draws you to it over something else?

Honestly, I like that it's close to people. In retail, you can see right away whether something clicked for a customer, and I find that satisfying. Numbers are the other half for me. When I was treasurer, I liked that a budget is basically a set of choices about what matters, and you can see how those choices play out over a semester. I'm not sure I've figured out exactly what I want long-term, but work where I'm talking with people and also making sense of the money side seems like a good fit for where I am right now.
That makes sense. One more thing—tell me about a time you actually failed at something, not just a moment where you adjusted on the fly. What happened?

Yeah, the sponsorship push for the club's spring event. At first I just sent a bunch of cold emails to local businesses, figuring that's how it's done. Most of them went nowhere. I'd hear back from maybe one out of every several, and even then it was usually a polite no. I kept sending more emails, which honestly was the wrong move. I was treating it like a volume problem when it was really a approach problem.

What changed things was going in person. I made a one-page flyer, walked into a few shops, and talked to the owners directly. That worked a lot better. A few of them said yes right there, and I got sponsors I'd never have landed over email.

What I learned is that I was hiding behind the email instead of just showing up. It was uncomfortable to walk in cold, but people responded to seeing someone in person.
How many sponsors did you end up securing that way, and what was different about the pitch when you showed up in person versus the email?

Honestly, I'd rather talk about what changed in the pitch, because that's the part I learned the most from. The emails were pretty generic. I was basically asking for help and listing what the club was about. In person, I could show the flyer, say what I thought the business would get out of it, and answer questions right there. It felt a lot more like a conversation than a request.

As for how many came through, it's kind of hard to pin down. A few of them were definitely yeses, and the whole experience taught me more than the count did.
I hear you. Just to close that out though—you said you secured three sponsors total for the event. How many of those three came from the in-person approach?

Okay, fair question. I sent out 25 emails and got three yeses, from a bike shop, a cafe, and a bank branch. Together they came to about $2,400 for the event. I didn't keep a clean record of which of the three came from email and which from walking in, but the emails were mostly dead ends, and the in-person visits are what turned things around. I should have been tracking that from the start.
We're nearly out of time here, so let me ask—what questions do you have for me about the role or the team?
Sure, just one. What does a typical first few months look like for someone starting in this role?

Good question. You'd spend the first month or so getting up to speed on our systems and meeting the team. After that, we'd have you start owning some smaller projects—nothing huge, but things where you can see the impact pretty quickly. By month three, you'd be running something more substantial. We like people to have a sense of ownership early, so we move pretty fast.

Anything else?

Sounds good, that gives me a clear picture. I think I'd like the pace. I've been pretty hands-on in my past roles, so being trusted with real work early on would suit me. Thanks for your time today. I appreciate you walking me through it.
Thanks, Jordan. I appreciate you being thoughtful and honest about your experience. We'll be in touch soon with next steps. Take care.

That makes sense. So you've got sales experience and you're managing money for the club—that's a solid mix. When you say you figured out you like working with people more than expected, what was it about the retail side that surprised you?

Honestly, I walked in thinking it'd be mostly about stocking shelves and ringing people up. What surprised me was how much of the job is just figuring out what someone actually needs. Lots of people come in for a jacket or a tent and have no idea what they're walking into. Once you get them talking about where they're headed, the whole conversation changes. I found I actually enjoy that part, the puzzle of it.

That's a good observation. So you're naturally curious about what people actually need. I noticed on your resume you were the top seller three months in a row. What were you doing differently from the other associates to hit that?

Mostly it came down to one habit. Before I showed anybody anything, I'd ask where they were headed. Like, "What trip are you planning?" Someone who says they're doing a three-day backpacking loop in wet weather needs a totally different conversation than someone car camping at a lake. Once I knew that, I could point them to stuff that actually mattered for their trip, and they usually ended up buying more because it made sense to them.

I think a lot of the other people on the floor were jumping straight to product, which is understandable. I just found that slowing down up front made the rest easier.
That's a smart approach. How did you know it was actually working? Like, what was the metric that showed you were the top seller?

Honestly, the best way I knew was just seeing how the month ended up. You get a feel for it on the floor, like which conversations turn into a bigger basket and which ones don't. I was paying attention to that pretty closely, and I learned a lot from the slow months too. Some days I'd try something and it would flop, and that taught me more than the good days did.

What about you? What do you look for when you're deciding whether a new hire is actually getting it?

Do you know what your actual sales numbers were, or how management measured that?

Yeah, fair question, and I should have answered it straight the first time. It was monthly sales. I ranked number one out of nine associates on the floor for June, July, and August. Makes sense. I also see you trained four new hires on the sales floor. Walk me through how you actually did that—what was your approach?

Mostly I tried to keep it hands-on. I shadowed each new hire for their first two shifts, just watching how they talked to customers and where they got stuck. Then I flipped it and had them lead while I stood nearby. I'd jump in only if they were about to say something wrong or lose a sale they really should have had.

After each shift we'd talk through it. I'd ask what felt natural and what felt awkward, because usually the thing that felt awkward to them was the thing they needed to practice. I also tried not to give them a script. The trip question I mentioned earlier worked for me, but everyone's style is different, so I wanted them to find their own version of it.

Honestly, I learned a lot from that too. Some people picked things up fast, and others needed a different angle, so I had to keep adjusting.
Did you ever have someone who really wasn't getting it, or where the training didn't work out the way you hoped?

Yeah, one of them. Out of the four, three hit their first monthly target, and the one who didn't was a good person who just wasn't comfortable yet. They were really careful with customers, maybe too careful. They'd answer questions but wouldn't ask much themselves, so the conversations stayed shallow.

I think I pushed them to copy my approach too closely at first, and that didn't fit their personality. I should have spent more time figuring out how they naturally talked to people. Looking back, I'd have changed that early instead of waiting to see if it would click.

That's a fair reflection. So that's an example of something not working out the way you wanted. Let me ask you more broadly—tell me about a time you actually failed at something, not just a learning moment but a real miss.

What I took from it was that you can't just make the spreadsheet decision. I talked to a few people before I finalized anything, explained why I was leaning the way I was, and tried to make it clear the banquet wasn't being dropped for good. I think that's what kept it from blowing up.
Did you end up cutting the banquet that year, or did you find another way?

Yeah, we went with a scaled-back version. It wasn't the full banquet anymore. We kept a smaller dinner so people still had something to look forward to, and the trip got funded. I'd say it's hard to quantify how much that mattered for the group, but I think the compromise is what made people willing to accept it.

Honestly, what I'd tell someone in my spot now is to always look for a middle option before picking between two things people care about.
Got it. Well, I think that covers a lot of ground. Before we wrap up, do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, one question. What does a typical first few months look like for someone in this role, and what would you most want to see from them by the end of that first stretch?

What matters most to us is that you're asking the right questions, listening to feedback, and not just executing tasks but thinking about why we're doing things a certain way. Does that make sense?

Yeah, that makes sense. Asking why things are done a certain way is something I try to do already, so that's a good fit. I'd want to earn that ownership by showing I can handle a small project well first. Thanks for walking me through it, and thanks for your time today.
You're welcome. Thanks for being thoughtful and honest in your answers. We'll be in touch either way within the next week or so. Good luck with finals.

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for coming in. Did you find everything okay today?
Yeah, everything's good, thanks for having me. The video link worked on the first try, which I was a little worried about. Glad to be talking with you.
Great, glad it went smoothly. So, why don't you walk me through your background for me? Just give me a sense of where you're coming from and what you've been up to.

Sure. I'm finishing up a business degree, and for most of the last couple of years I've juggled school with work. I've been on the sales floor at an outdoor gear store, which I really enjoy because you get to talk to people about what they're actually going to do with the stuff, whether that's a weekend hike or a trip somewhere. Last summer I was ranked number one in sales at the store for June, July, and August, which felt great.

On campus I've been the treasurer for a student club. That's where I got my first real taste of managing money and figuring out where it should go, and honestly it's taught me a lot about priorities. I also got to help bring on new people at the store, training a few of the newer associates, which I liked more than I expected.

I'm really looking to grow into something where I can keep building on that mix of people skills and numbers. What about you, what does the team look like day to day?
Got it. Before I answer that, I'm curious about those three months at the top of the sales rankings. What were you doing differently than the other associates to land there?

Honestly, it was mostly one habit. Before I showed anybody anything, I'd ask where they were headed. Like, "What's the trip?" Then I'd figure out what would actually hold up out there. A lot of people come in thinking they need a specific thing, and once they tell you it's a three-day trip with a lot of elevation gain, the conversation changes. It stopped feeling like a sale to me and more like helping them get ready.

I also got a lot better at suggesting add-ons that made sense for the trip, like a better water filter or a rain layer, instead of just pushing whatever was on sale. I think people could tell I was looking out for them, and they came back.

What about you? Do you have a sense of what made the top sellers on your team stand out?
That makes sense. And when you say you were ranked number one—how was that actually measured? Was it revenue, units sold, something else?

Honestly, the scoreboard stuff was never really what I focused on. I was more interested in whether the people walking out were happy with what they bought. I learned a lot from that, like how to tell when someone's about to overbuy, and I think that's been more useful than the ranking itself.

What about your team? How do you measure whether someone's doing well in a sales role?
We'll get to that. But I'm still curious—do you know what metric the store actually used when they ranked you number one those three months?

Yeah, it was monthly sales. I was first out of nine associates in June, July, and August. I also tracked add-ons, and mine ran about 1.9 times the store average, which is probably the part I'm proudest of.

That's helpful context. So you were looking at your own numbers pretty closely even if the ranking itself wasn't your main focus. I get that. 

Let me ask you this—when you trained those four new hires on the sales floor, how did you actually do that? Walk me through what that looked like.

Mostly I just tried to get them doing real stuff as fast as possible. I'd shadow each new hire for a couple of shifts, just watching how they talked to customers and where they got stuck. Then I'd flip it, and they'd lead while I stood back and only jumped in if something was about to go sideways.

The hardest part was not taking over. When someone fumbled a question about, say, sleeping bag temperature ratings, my instinct was to just grab it. But they learned more when they had to figure out the answer themselves and then I'd go over it with them after. I'd also ask them what they'd do differently, which I think helped more than me just telling them.

It's hard to say exactly how well it worked, honestly. Everyone's different, and I learned a lot about how people pick things up. What did your team do for onboarding?
How did you know they were ready to work the floor on their own? Like, what was the signal that someone had gotten it?

Mostly it was when they stopped checking with me. Early on, a new hire would glance over every time a customer asked something, like they wanted me to vouch for their answer. Once they started just handling it, asking the customer what the trip was and talking through options without looking back at me, I figured they had the basics.

I also watched how they handled the stuff that wasn't in the training manual. Someone's got a question about a tent that's been through a rough season, or a customer who's not sure about a return. If they could work through it calmly and know when to bring in a manager, that told me a lot.

Honestly, I don't think there was one clean moment. It was more of a gut sense, and I'd still check in with them after their first few solo shifts. Do you guys have a set checklist for that, or is it more of a manager's call?
That's fair. I'm going to shift gears a bit. Tell me about a time you failed at something.

Sure. Last spring I was trying to get sponsors for the club's event, and I started by sending a bunch of cold emails to local businesses. Most of them just went unanswered, and the few replies I got were polite nos. I kept sending more emails, honestly, because I figured if I sent enough something would stick. That was kind of dumb in hindsight.

What finally worked was going in person with a one-page flyer. I'd walk into a cafe or a bike shop, ask for the owner for two minutes, and show them what the club does and what they'd get out of it. A few of those conversations turned into yeses. I think the email approach failed because it was easy for them to ignore, and talking to someone face to face made it harder to say no.

So I learned to stop doing more of something that isn't working and try a different approach.
When you switched to going in person, how many businesses did you have to visit before you landed those three sponsors?

Honestly, I didn't keep a tally like that. It was more of a rhythm thing. I'd go in, have a quick conversation, and then move on to the next place, and I got a little better at it as I went. I'm not sure a count would tell you much anyway, since some places were a no in thirty seconds and others took a whole conversation.

The bigger thing I took away was how much the first couple of visits taught me about my pitch. I was leading with the club, and once I started leading with what the business would get out of it, people actually listened. Do you want me to walk you through what the flyer had on it?
I hear you. Let me ask you this—why are you interested in this kind of role? What's drawing you to it?

Mostly because it's the part of the job I've liked most so far. At the store, the best moments are when someone walks in unsure and leaves knowing they picked the right thing for their trip. I like that I get to figure out what someone actually needs, not just what they walked in asking for.

I also like that this kind of role brings together the people side and the numbers side. The club treasurer job got me into budgeting, and I found I liked the tradeoffs, like deciding what to cut when money's tight. I want to keep building both of those, and I think a sales role where you have to understand customers and also track how things are going would let me do that.

Honestly, I'm also at the point where I want something with more room to grow, where I can take on more responsibility over time.
That makes sense. You mentioned the club budget and tradeoffs—can you give me a specific example? Like, what was something you actually had to cut or fund differently because of the budget?

Yeah, the hardest one was the end-of-year banquet. We had a set amount for it, and the club also wanted to send a few members to a competition, which needed travel money. We couldn't fully do both, so I had to scale the banquet way back to free up money for the trip.

It was tough because the banquet is the one thing everybody looks forward to, and people weren't thrilled. I ended up going to members, explaining the choice, and saying the competition was a chance for the club to show what it could do. Some people still felt let down, and I get that. But the trip ended up being a good experience, and I learned that a budget decision is as much about how you explain it as the numbers themselves.
Did you ask the club what they'd rather have before you made that call, or did you decide first and then explain it?

Honestly, I decided first, and that's something I'd do differently now. I had the numbers in front of me and the competition deadline was close, so I made the call and then went to people with it. In hindsight, I should have floated the options to the club before committing. Some members would have had ideas I hadn't thought of, and it might have reduced the frustration.

What I did do was check the math with our faculty advisor before anything got announced, so at least the budget side was solid. But I'd give the club more of a say next time. Do you usually bring people into those kinds of decisions on your team, or is it more of a top-down call?
We're nearly out of time, so let me ask—what questions do you have for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, I've got one. What does a typical week look like for someone in this role, and what's the first thing you'd want a new person to get really good at?

Good question. A typical week is a mix of working with customers, tracking metrics, and collaborating with the team on strategy. A lot of it depends on the season, but you're always balancing the day-to-day with looking ahead. 

As for what matters most early on—it's judgment. Understanding your customer and knowing when to push and when to step back. Sounds like that's something you've already been thinking about.

Anything else?
Yeah, that makes sense. I like that it's about judgment and not just hitting a number. One last thing from me: what's the biggest thing you wish you'd known in your first few months here?

That's a good one. Honestly, I wish I'd known earlier that it's okay to ask for help when you're stuck. I spent my first month trying to figure everything out solo, and I left a lot on the table. The team knows way more than you do at the start, and they want you to succeed.

Well, I really appreciate your time today. You've given me a lot to think about, and we'll be in touch within the next week or so. Thanks for coming in.

Thanks so much, I really appreciate it. That's good advice, and I'll keep it in mind. I enjoyed talking through all of this, and I'm looking forward to hearing from you next week. Have a great rest of your day.
You too, Jordan. Take care.

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for coming in. Did you find everything okay today?
Yeah, everything's good, thanks for having me. The video link worked fine on my end, so no complaints there. How about you, has your day been going okay?
Yeah, it's been solid, thanks for asking. Busy but good. So, I'd love to hear about your background—walk me through your work and school experience so far, and what brings you here today.

Sure. I'm a business major, and I'm finishing up my degree this year. Most of my experience has been in two places. The first is retail. I work as a sales associate at an outdoor gear store, and that's where I've learned the most about working with customers. The second is on campus. I've been the treasurer for one of the student clubs, which means handling the budget and money side of things.

What brings me here is that I want a role where I can use both of those. I like working with people, but I also like the numbers side of things, and this role seemed like a good fit for that mix. Honestly, I'm still figuring out exactly where I want to land, so I'm really hoping to learn more about what the day-to-day looks like here.

That makes sense. So you've got customer-facing experience and you've managed money—that's a good foundation. When you say you like working with people, what is it specifically about that part of retail that's stuck with you?

I think what sticks with me is that people almost never walk in knowing exactly what they need. They usually have a trip or a problem in mind, and figuring that out is the fun part. I've found that if I ask about where they're headed before I show them anything, the conversation goes way better. They trust you more, and you end up helping them get something that actually works for them.

I also like that it's a real skill you can get better at. Every shift I'm picking up something new about how to read people and explain things clearly. It's hard to quantify how much that's helped me, but I can definitely see it in how I handle the tougher conversations now.
That's a good instinct—asking questions first. So you mentioned tougher conversations. Can you give me a specific example of a difficult customer situation you dealt with, and how you handled it?

Sure, there was one that stuck with me. A customer came in wanting a refund on a tent they'd already used. The problem was it was past the return window, so I couldn't just give them the money back. They were pretty frustrated, and I could tell they felt like they were getting the runaround.

What I tried to do was slow down and actually listen to what was going wrong with the tent. Once I understood the issue, I looked into whether the brand's warranty covered it. It did, so I offered to set up a repair instead of a refund. I explained what that would look like and how long it would take, and I was upfront that it wasn't the exact outcome they came in asking for.

They weren't thrilled at first, but they took the repair, and they ended up leaving a positive review. I think that's because they felt like someone had actually worked on their problem with them. That's probably the biggest thing I took from it: when someone's upset, they mostly want to know you're taking them seriously.
Good. So you didn't have the authority to override the return window—what made you think to look into the warranty angle instead of just telling them no?

Honestly, I didn't want to just say no and leave them stuck. Telling someone "sorry, we can't do that" is the easiest thing to say, and it usually ends the conversation on a bad note. So I started asking myself what else could actually help them.

Gear that fails on a trip is a real problem, and most outdoor brands stand behind their products for a while, even when the store's return window has closed. I'd seen coworkers mention warranty claims before, so I figured it was worth checking the brand's policy on that tent. Once I saw it was covered, it was a lot easier to make a real offer.

I'll be honest, it's hard to say exactly how much the warranty route saved the situation. What I do know is the customer left happy, and that's what I was going for.

Got it. You didn't just follow the rule—you looked for another way to solve their problem. That makes sense.

So on your resume, you also mention you were the top seller at the store for three months in a row. What were you doing differently than the other sales associates?

Mostly it came down to the question I asked first. Before I showed anyone anything, I'd ask where they were headed. If someone was going on a three-day backpacking trip in wet weather, that changes what they need a lot more than whatever's on the front display. Once I knew that, I could steer them toward things that would actually work for them, and they usually ended up buying more because it made sense for their trip.

I also tried not to rush people. Some of the other associates were quick to jump to the bestseller, which is fine, but I found people were more likely to add something on if it felt like I'd listened to them first.

I'll admit I'm not totally sure how much of it was the technique versus just having a good month. Still, that's the habit I'd bring here.
Fair enough. So when the store measured you as top seller, what were they actually counting? Was it total sales, number of transactions, something else?

Good question, honestly I don't remember the exact breakdown they used. I think it was monthly sales, but I'd rather not guess and get it wrong. What I do remember is how much I learned from the process. Watching how the best shifts played out and figuring out what made a conversation click taught me a lot more than the ranking did.
That's fair. Let me shift gears a bit. You mentioned you trained four new hires on the sales floor. Walk me through how you actually did that—what did a training session look like?

So for the most part, I'd shadow them for their first two shifts. I'd just stand back and watch how they talked to customers and where they got stuck. Then I'd switch it around and have them lead while I stayed close by. If they hesitated, I'd jump in with a quick tip, but I tried to let them figure out their own style.

After that, we'd go over what went well and what didn't. I think the biggest thing I tried to get across was the same thing I do myself: ask where someone's headed before you start pulling things off the wall. Most of them picked that up pretty fast.

Honestly, I learned a lot from it too. Explaining why I did something on the floor made me think about my own habits in a way I hadn't before.
So after you trained them, how did you know they actually got it? Did you follow up with them later, or check how they were doing on their own?

Honestly, mostly I just kept an eye on them. I'd check in now and then during shifts, and if I saw someone starting with the product before asking where the customer was going, I'd mention it. I wasn't formal about it, more like a quick "hey, how's that going?" kind of thing.

It's hard to say for sure whether they really got it, though. Some people pick things up fast and others need to see it a few times. What I did notice was that they started asking more questions on their own, which felt like a good sign. I'm still not sure I did it perfectly, but it taught me a lot about how people learn on the job.
Makes sense. So on the club side, you managed a twelve-thousand-dollar budget as treasurer. Walk me through that—what were the main things you had to decide how to spend money on?

Most of it was splitting money between regular club costs and events. Things like supplies, room reservations, and the events we ran during the year all had to come out of the same pot, so I had to decide what mattered most each term.

The hardest call was the end-of-year banquet. It's a nice tradition, but we also had members who needed travel money for a competition. I ended up cutting the banquet way down so we could cover the trip. People were disappointed, and I didn't love it, but the competition was a bigger opportunity for the members going.

I learned a lot from that. Budgets are never just about numbers. You're deciding what the club values, and you have to be able to explain those choices to people who might not like them.
That's a tough call. How did you actually present that decision to the club? Did you just tell them what you'd decided, or did you get input first?

Honestly, I did a bit of both. I didn't want to just drop it on people, so before I made the final call I asked a few members what they'd want to see happen. Some of them cared a lot about the banquet, and others were more interested in the competition, so I could tell it wasn't going to be an easy decision either way.

Once I'd decided, I explained it in the next meeting. I tried to be clear about why the competition trip won out and what the banquet would look like this year. A few people were still bummed, and I get that. But I think being upfront about the reasoning helped more than trying to make it sound like nobody lost anything.

I'm still not sure I handled every part of it perfectly. It's probably the thing I'd want to do differently if I had it to do over.
What would you do differently?

Probably I'd bring people in earlier. By the time I asked for input, I'd already done most of the math, so it felt more like I was checking in than actually letting them shape the decision. If I'd laid out the budget situation at the start of the term, people could have weighed in before anything was locked.

I'd also want to think harder about the people who were disappointed about the banquet. I explained the reasoning, but I didn't really follow up with them afterward. A quick one-on-one or a smaller event to make them feel included might have helped.
That's thoughtful. You also mention securing three local sponsors for the club's spring event. How did you actually find those sponsors and pitch them?

Mostly I started with email. I reached out to a bunch of local businesses, and honestly, most of them never wrote back. That was a bit discouraging.

What worked was going in person. I put together a one-page flyer that laid out what the event was, who would be there, and what a sponsor would get out of it. Then I walked into a few places, asked for the owner or manager, and gave them about two minutes. People were more willing to talk when they could see something in front of them and I was standing there.

The ones who said yes were a bike shop, a cafe, and a bank branch. I think they liked that it was a small local event and that the ask was clear. I still don't think I was great at it. I was pretty nervous the first few times, and I'd probably tighten up the pitch if I did it again.
What didn't work? You mentioned most didn't respond to email. Did you try anything else that fell flat, or was it just the email thing?

Mostly it was just the email. I sent a bunch of messages, and the ones I didn't hear back from outnumbered the replies by a lot. I'm not sure if they got buried or my subject lines were bad, but I didn't get much traction that way.

I did try a couple of things before I switched to walking in. I'd send a follow-up email and that didn't help much either. Once I started going in person with the flyer, it was a lot easier to get a real conversation.

I'm honestly not sure I'd call anything else a total flop. I was just figuring it out as I went.
That makes sense. So I want to ask you something different. Tell me about a time you failed—something that didn't go the way you wanted and what you learned from it.

Honestly, the sponsor outreach is the one that comes to mind. I started with email because it seemed like the efficient thing to do. I sent a lot of messages, and most of them just never got answered. I took it personally for a little while, like I was bad at this.

What I learned was that I'd been picking the easiest channel for me instead of the one that worked for them. A local shop owner is probably not checking a generic inbox for event sponsorship requests. Once I started walking in with the flyer, I could see their reaction, answer questions on the spot, and actually have a conversation. Some people still said no, but at least I knew where I stood.

I think that's carried over to other things. When something's not landing, I try to ask whether I'm making it easy for the other person to say yes, not just whether I'm putting in the effort.

That's a good lesson. And before we wrap up, I want to circle back to something you mentioned earlier. You said you're still figuring out where you want to land. Why do you want this kind of role specifically?

Good question. Honestly, what appeals to me is the mix. I like being around people and solving their problems, like I did on the sales floor, but I also like the numbers side, which is what the treasurer job pushed me into. A role that uses both feels like a place where I'd keep growing instead of just doing the same thing over and over.

I'll be honest, I'm still early in figuring out my path, so I'm not going to pretend I have it all mapped out. What I do know is that I learn fastest when I'm close to the work and getting real feedback, and that's what I'm hoping this role offers.
I appreciate the honesty. We're almost out of time here, so I want to flip it around. What questions do you have for me or the team?
Sure, I'd love to know what a typical first few months look like for someone in this role. Like, what would you expect me to have figured out by the end of the first quarter?

Good question. Honestly, the first month is mostly about understanding how we work—who the key people are, how decisions get made, what the actual workflow looks like versus what's in the job description. By the end of the first quarter, I'd want to see that you've picked up the basics on your own and you're asking smart questions about where you can add value. We're not looking for you to have solved everything, just to show good judgment about what matters and where to focus.

Do you have anything else?
Yeah, that helps a lot. One more thing: what does someone who does really well in this role usually do differently from someone who struggles?

That's a smart question. The people who do well here take ownership early—they don't wait to be told what to do. They also ask a lot of questions, but they think before they ask. And they care about understanding the "why" behind decisions, not just the mechanics of the task. People who struggle tend to just execute without thinking about impact, or they get stuck waiting for perfect information instead of making a call with what they have.

Alright, I think that's a good place to wrap. Thanks for taking the time today, Jordan. We'll be in touch soon with next steps.

Thanks so much for your time today, I really appreciated the conversation. That answer about ownership and making calls with what you have is useful, and it's something I want to work on. I'm looking forward to hearing about next steps. Have a great rest of your day!
You too, thanks again. Take care.

How did you know the training actually worked? Like, what made you confident they were ready to be on the floor solo?

Honestly, it was more of a gut thing than a checklist. I watched for when they stopped looking over at me before answering a customer, and when they started handling the awkward moments on their own. That's hard to put a number on, but it was pretty obvious.

I think I learned more from the ones who struggled, though. One of them was really quiet at first, and I had to figure out how to get her to open up without pushing. That taught me a lot about adjusting to different people. Is that the kind of situation you were hoping I'd talk about?
That's helpful context. But I'm curious—did anyone struggle after you trained them, or did they all pick it up pretty well?

Honestly, the quiet one was the one I kept an eye on. She got there, but it took her longer to feel comfortable on her own. I think the hardest part was figuring out when to step in and when to just let her get through it. I probably hovered more than I should have at first.

Everyone's got a different pace, so I try not to read too much into the first few weeks. What about you? How do you usually handle someone who's slower to pick things up?
I'll answer that in a second, but first—what would you do differently with her if you trained someone like that again?

Honestly, I'd have talked to her earlier about what she was feeling. I was waiting to see if she'd figure it out on her own, and I think that just left her stuck longer. I'd sit down after her first shift and ask what felt hardest, instead of guessing from across the floor.

I'd also give her a short list of two or three things to focus on for the week, so she had something concrete to aim for. Right now I'm not sure I did that well.
That's fair. Alright, let's shift gears. You mentioned managing a twelve-thousand dollar budget for the club. Walk me through what that looked like.

Sure. Mostly it was keeping track of where the money was going every month and making sure we didn't overspend on things we didn't need. The hard part was that everyone in the club had their own idea of what mattered most, so I spent a lot of time explaining why we couldn't do everything at once.

I learned a lot about making tradeoffs. You can't just say no and leave people hanging, so I tried to show the reasoning and give them a choice. Honestly, that's probably the skill I'm proudest of from that role. Do you want me to get into a specific decision we had to make?
Yeah, actually. Give me a concrete example of something you had to cut or a tradeoff you had to make.

Yeah, the big one was the end-of-year banquet. People really wanted it, and it was a fun night for everyone. But we also had a chance to send a few members to a competition, and the travel costs were a lot. We couldn't really do both at full size.

So I had to cut the banquet way down to free up money for the trip. Some people were pretty annoyed, and I felt bad about it. I tried to explain that the competition would help the club more in the long run, and I offered a smaller event so people still got a night together. I think it worked out, but it was a hard call to make.
How did you decide that the competition was worth more than the banquet? Like, what was your reasoning there?

Honestly, it came down to who the money was really for. The banquet was a great night, but it's a one-time thing, and everyone forgets the details a few weeks later. The competition was a chance for a few members to build skills and meet people from other schools, and that kind of experience sticks with them and can help the club grow the next year.

I also talked to a couple of the people who'd be going, and they were pretty clear about how much it meant to them. That helped me feel okay about the call, even though it wasn't popular with everyone. I still wish I'd explained the reasoning to the whole club earlier, before the decision was made. I think people would have taken it better if they'd had more time to get used to the idea.
Makes sense. So you also secured three local sponsors for the club's spring event. How did you actually find them and get them on board?

Mostly by making a list of local businesses that would fit the event. A bike shop, a cafe, a bank branch, places that had some connection to students. I started by sending emails, and honestly, most of them went nowhere. People just don't answer cold emails from a club.

What actually worked was going in person with a one-page flyer. I'd say who we were, what the event was, and what they'd get out of it, like having their name in front of a crowd of students. Walking in made it feel less like a favor request and more like a real conversation. Some places said no right away, but a few were interested once they could see what we were offering.

Is the sponsorship side something you've dealt with before?
I have, yeah. But tell me—of the ones you approached in person, how many actually came through?

Honestly, I'd say enough to make the event work. It's hard to put an exact number on it, though, because some of the conversations turned into maybe-next-semester. What I really took from it was how much the flyer helped. People could see what we were offering in about thirty seconds. How about you? Have you ever had to pitch something to a business?
I'll get to that. But walk me back—you said you secured three sponsors. Out of how many businesses did you actually pitch to in person?

Twenty-five. I emailed about 25 local businesses, and most of them never answered. The three that said yes were the ones I followed up with in person with the flyer: a bike shop, a cafe, and a bank branch. Together they came to about $2,400
Got it. So out of the 25 you emailed, how many did you actually walk into in person?

Honestly, I didn't keep a exact count of the walk-ins. I'd say I went in person to a handful, and I should correct what I said before. The 25 were the businesses I emailed. The three yeses all came from going in person with the flyer, and most of the emails
Okay, so a handful out of 25. Did any of the email-only ones ever come back and say yes?

Honestly, I don't think any of the email-only ones came back to me. I sent the emails, didn't hear much, and then I focused on the places I could walk into. So I can't say for sure that none of them ever followed up later, but nothing I'd count as a yes came from the emails alone.
Alright. One more thing before we wrap up—tell me about a time you failed, or something that didn't go the way you hoped.

Honestly, the sponsorship emails. I started with email because it felt easier, and I spent a while sending messages that mostly got no response. I should have just gone in person from the start. Once I did, things moved much faster.

I also think I was a bit fuzzy earlier when you asked about
Yeah, I noticed. No worries. So with the emails—what would you do differently if you were starting that sponsorship push over again?

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for coming in. Did you find everything okay today?
Yeah, all good, thanks for having me. Parking was easy to find, and the video link worked fine on my end. Nice to meet you.
Great, glad it went smoothly. So, walk me through your background a bit. How did you get to where you are now?

Sure. I'm a business major, and I've been working part-time at an outdoor gear store for about a year and a half. That's where I really figured out I like working with people and helping them solve a problem. Honestly, I went in thinking retail was just a job to pay the bills, and it turned into something I actually enjoy.

On campus I've been treasurer for one of the student clubs. That's been a big step for me, because it's the first time I've really been responsible for money that other people were counting on. It taught me a lot about planning and about saying no to things, which I think matters more than people expect.

Between the two, I'd say I'm pretty good at talking to people and then following through. That's kind of the thread I'd want to bring to a role like this.
That makes sense. Let me dig into the retail side a bit. You mentioned you were top seller three months in a row—what were you doing differently from the other associates to get there?

Mostly it came down to one habit. Before I showed anybody anything, I'd ask where they were headed. Like, "Are you going backpacking, or is this more for car camping?" People buy a lot more when you're solving their actual trip instead of just pointing at the shelf.

I also think I got lucky with timing. Summer is busy, so there were a lot of people coming in with a clear plan, and that made it easier to find the right stuff for them.

I'd say the biggest thing I learned was to slow down a little. The guys who were pushing hardest on the first pitch usually lost the sale, and the ones who listened first ended up buying more.
That's a solid approach. When you say you were top seller, how was that actually measured? Were you tracking revenue per transaction, total sales for the month, or something else?

Honestly, I'm not sure I'd say it was one clean number. The store looked at a bunch of things, and I think it's hard to boil down to one metric. What I remember most is how much I learned about reading people in those three months. Like, I got way better at figuring out what someone needs in the first two minutes. Is that the kind of thing you're hoping to hear about, or were you more interested in the sales process itself?
No, that's fair. I'm just trying to get a clear picture of what "top seller" actually meant in that context. Did the store post rankings, or did your manager tell you directly?

Okay, fair enough, I should just be straight with you. My manager went over the numbers with me each month. I was number one out of nine associates on monthly sales from June through August. I also had about 1.9 times the store average on add-on sales, like extra socks, a stove, or a better pack cover. I'm not sure how much of that was me versus the summer crowd, but that's the real picture.
Got it, thanks for clarifying. That add-on number is interesting—1.9 times the average. Walk me through one specific customer interaction where you sold them something they didn't come in for.

Sure. A guy came in one Saturday just wanting a new rain jacket because his old one had died. I asked what kind of trip he had coming up, and it turned out he was doing a three-day hike with his buddies and didn't have a real plan for cooking or keeping gear dry.

So I walked him through it. I asked what they were planning to eat, and when he said they'd be boiling water for dinner, I showed him a small canister stove that was light enough for the trip. Then I mentioned that the pack he was looking at would get soaked in the rain they were forecast for, so a pack cover made sense. He ended up with the jacket, the stove, and the cover. He said he was glad I asked, because he'd have shown up without the stove.

That's the kind of sale I like most, where you're helping someone not forget something. I don't think it was really a clever pitch. I just asked the right questions first.
That's a good example. Now, you also trained four new hires on the sales floor. How did you actually go about training them? Walk me through what that looked like.

Mostly I just tried to get out of their way. I'd shadow each new hire for their first two shifts, mostly watching how they talked to customers and where they got stuck. Then I'd flip it, and they'd lead while I stood nearby and jumped in only if they needed me.

I think the hardest part was not taking over. When someone fumbles a question, it's tempting to grab the product and fix it yourself, but then they don't learn anything. So I'd let them stumble a little, and then we'd talk through it after the customer left.

Honestly, I learned a lot from them too. Some of the new hires were better at making people comfortable right away than I was, so I tried to point that out when I saw it. I'd say it's hard to measure how well training went, but I felt like they got comfortable faster when I backed off earlier.
How did you know they actually got it? Like, what made you confident they could handle the floor on their own after you stopped shadowing them?

Mostly I just watched them work. By the second shift, I could tell when someone stopped freezing up every time a customer asked a question they didn't know. They'd still say "let me check on that," but they'd go find the answer instead of panicking.

I also paid attention to whether they were picking up on the customer's trip, like asking where they were headed before pulling anything off the shelf. Once I saw that become a habit without me reminding them, I felt pretty good about it.

Most of them hit their first month's goals, which felt like a good sign. But honestly, I'd say the bigger thing was that they started coming to me with questions about specific situations, not just as
What kind of questions were they asking you in that second phase?

Mostly they were about specific customers, like, "Someone wants a tent for a trip in the rain, what do I actually need to ask them?" or "A customer's pack doesn't fit right, how do I bring that up without sounding like I'm pushing a sale?" One of them kept asking how to handle people who already knew exactly what they wanted and didn't want to be questioned. That one was a good question, and we went through a few ways to read that kind of customer.

I liked that they were asking those kinds of questions, because it meant they were thinking about the customer and not just trying to get through the shift.

Makes sense. Let me shift gears a bit. You mentioned managing a twelve-thousand-dollar budget as club treasurer. Tell me about a time you had to make a hard call on that—something you wanted to fund but couldn't, or had to cut.

Yeah, the banquet was the hardest one. We had a competition coming up, and a few members needed travel help to get there. The end-of-year banquet was on the books at a pretty high level, and I had to tell the group we were scaling it way back so we could cover the trip.

I didn't love it. People were excited about the banquet, and I got some pushback. What helped was being upfront about the tradeoff. I put the options in front of everybody, what we'd gain, what we'd lose, and let them weigh in. I think people accepted it more because they could see the reasoning.

It taught me that budgeting is less about the spreadsheet and more about explaining why. I'd rather make an unpopular call and be clear about it than quietly cut things and have people find out later.
When you put those options in front of the group, what did you actually show them? Was it a spreadsheet, or how did you frame it?

Mostly it was a simple one-page sheet, not a fancy spreadsheet. I had two columns, one for keeping the banquet as planned and one for scaling it back to cover the trip, with a few lines on what each option would mean for people. I also talked through it out loud at the meeting, because I didn't want people just staring at a table of numbers and guessing what I meant.

Honestly, I think the framing mattered more than the sheet. I tried to make it clear that nobody was doing anything wrong, and that it was a choice between two good things. I'm not sure how to quantify how people reacted, but the questions they asked told me they were actually thinking it through.
Got it. Let me ask you something different. Tell me about a time you failed at something, or where things didn't go the way you planned.

Sure. The sponsorship push for the club's spring event didn't start well. I wrote to about 25 local businesses, mostly by email, and almost none of them wrote back. I was kind of annoyed, and I figured the problem was that people just don't answer cold emails.

Then I realized I was treating it like a numbers game when it was really about trust. So I printed a one-page flyer with what the event was, who'd be there, and what a sponsor would get out of it. I started walking into shops during slow afternoons and asking for the owner. That worked a lot better. I ended up with three sponsors: a bike shop, a cafe, and a bank branch.

What I took from it is that I should have tried in person from the start. Email was the easy option, and I stuck with it longer than I should have. Now if something isn't landing, I try to ask myself whether I'm using the approach that fits the situation.
When you walked in to those shops, what was your pitch like? How did you actually ask them?

Pretty simple, honestly. I'd walk in during a slow stretch, usually mid-afternoon, and ask if the owner or manager had a minute. Then I'd say something like, "Hi, I'm Jordan, I'm with the student club on campus, and we're putting on our spring event. I wanted to see if your business might want to be involved."

I'd hand over the flyer and let them read it while I talked. It had the basics: what the event was, who'd be there, and what a sponsor would get, like their name on the banner and a shout-out at the event.

I tried not to oversell. If they seemed interested, I'd ask what kind of customers they usually get, because that helped me explain why the event might be a good fit. A couple of places said no right away, and that was fine. I just thanked them and moved on.

The biggest difference from the emails was that they could see I was a real person from campus, not a form letter. I think that made people more willing to at least hear me out.
Of those three that said yes, did any of them push back on what you were offering, or ask for something different than what was on the flyer?

Not really pushback, no. The bike shop asked whether we could put their name on the water station signs, which was an easy yes. The cafe wanted to know if they could set up a table at the event, and we said sure. The bank branch was the most careful one. They wanted to check that nothing we were doing would look like they were endorsing a particular product, so I just forwarded the event details to whoever handled their community stuff, and they were fine with it.

I was a little nervous about the bank one, honestly. I didn't want to promise anything I couldn't deliver, so I told them exactly what we could and couldn't do before they committed.
Why do you want this kind of role? What is it about it that appeals to you?

Honestly, I like that this kind of job is about the people on the other side of the counter, whether that's a customer, a team, or a sponsor. Across the retail job, the club, and the sponsor stuff, the part I keep coming back to is figuring out what someone actually needs and then following through on it.

I also like that it's a place where you can keep learning. I went into retail thinking it was just a job to pay the bills, and it turned into something I actually enjoy. I'm hoping a role like this gives me that same kind of growth, plus a bit more responsibility.

What about the role itself? Is it more the day-to-day customer side, or the planning and budgeting side?
We're almost out of time, so let me ask—do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, just one. What does a typical first few months look like for someone in this role, and what would you most want them to have figured out by the end of it?

Good question. Honestly, the first month is about getting comfortable with our systems and meeting the team. By the end of three months, I'd want someone to own a project or two on their own—not just execute what's handed to them, but actually see something that needs doing and take it on. We value people who notice gaps and fill them.

Do you have anything else?
No, I think that covers it. That's a helpful answer, and it makes me want to be the person who spots a gap and takes it on. Thanks for your time today, I really appreciate it.
Great. Thanks for coming in, Jordan. We enjoyed talking with you. We'll be in touch soon with next steps. Have a good one.

verdicts.notes: Strength: the interviewer pressed on the evasive "top seller" metric (T6, T8) until the candidate gave numbers, and it covered all five topics plus both practice questions. Weakness: it missed several vague answers, including the training outcome, the budget outcome, the sponsor count (T29, where it let a dodge pass) and the "why this role" answer. It also leaked mild praise at T18 and didn't ask what the candidate personally did on the budget.

transcript.text: Hey, good to meet you. How's your day been so far?
Hey, thanks, good to meet you too! My day's been pretty good, a little busy with classes this morning, but I'm glad to be here. How about you, how's your day going?
Good, thanks for asking. Busy but moving along. So before we dive in, I'd love to just hear you walk me through your background a bit. How'd you get to where you are now?

Sure, happy to. I'm a business major, and I've been working part-time at an outdoor gear store for the past year or so. That's where I really got into sales. I like figuring out what people actually need, and outdoor stuff is fun because customers are usually excited about a trip they're planning.

On campus I've been the treasurer for one of the student clubs. That's been a good way to learn about budgeting and working with people who have different priorities. Between the two, I've gotten a lot more comfortable with both customer-facing work and handling money responsibly.

I'm still figuring out exactly where I want to go after graduation, but I know I want something where I'm working directly with people and seeing the results of what I do. What about the role you're hiring for? I'd love to hear more about what the day-to-day looks like.

Good context, thanks. We can definitely talk about the role in a bit. But first, I'm curious about the sales piece. Your resume mentions you were a top seller for three months in a row. What were you actually doing differently than the other folks on the floor?

Mostly it came down to the first two minutes. Before I showed anybody anything, I'd ask where they were headed. A lot of people walk in thinking they need a specific jacket or pack, but once you know if it's a rainy weekend hike or a three-day trip where they'll be cold at night, the recommendations kind of make themselves.

I also didn't push add-ons as a pitch. If someone's buying a tent, I'd mention the footprint or a repair kit only if it actually fit the trip they described. People can tell when you're just trying to move inventory, and they trust you more when you're clearly thinking about their trip.

Honestly, I'm still learning a lot about it. I think the big lesson was that listening matters more than having the perfect product knowledge. Does that match what you look for in a strong sales person?
That makes sense. So when you say you were top seller three months in a row, how was that actually measured? Like, was it total revenue, number of transactions, something else?

Honestly, it's a little hard to boil down to one number. I think it was mostly about monthly sales, but what I took away from it was more about how I was talking to people than the scorecard itself. Those months taught me a lot about slowing down and actually listening. Have you seen candidates who are good at that, or does it usually come out more in how they handle tricky customers?

Fair question. We'll probably circle back to that with some specific situations. But I want to stay on this for a second—when you say monthly sales, do you mean total dollars you rang up, or something else?

Yeah, it was total dollars sold each month, and I ranked first out of nine associates on the floor from June through August. I also tracked my add-on sales, and those ran about 1.9 times the store average. Looking back, I think the add-on number mattered more to me, because it showed people were actually leaving with what they needed for their trip, not just buying one item.
Got it, that's clearer. So you were tracking your own add-on rate—what made you start doing that?

Honestly, I got curious. The store's monthly reports showed sales by associate, and I noticed that the people selling the most weren't always the ones with the biggest tickets. So I started paying attention to whether I was sending people home with what they actually needed for the trip, like a repair kit or a second layer for cold nights. Tracking it helped me see whether the questions I was asking were working.
Makes sense. Okay, so I also see on your resume that you trained four new hires on the sales floor. Walk me through how you actually did that—what did that process look like?

Sure. When someone new started, I'd shadow them for their first two shifts. I'd just watch how they greeted customers and where they got stuck. Then I'd flip it, so they led the conversations while I stood nearby in case they needed backup.

After that, we'd go over what worked and what didn't. Usually it was small stuff, like asking a question too late or jumping to a product before they knew the customer's plan. I'd tell them what I noticed and let them try again on the next customer.

I also tried to make it low-pressure, since the floor can be intimidating when you're new. Honestly, I learned a lot from it too. Explaining why I asked certain questions made me realize how much of what I did was instinct, and I had to slow down and put it into words. Was there a particular part of training you'd want to see a candidate handle well?
I'll keep that in mind. But real quick—how did you actually know the training worked? Like, what told you they were ready to be on their own?

Honestly, it was more of a gut feeling than a checklist. By the second shift, they'd usually stop looking at me before answering questions, and they'd start asking customers about their trips without prompting. That told me they were getting comfortable.

It's hard to put a clean measure on "ready," though. Some people hit their stride fast, and others need a few weeks before it clicks. What I learned was to pay attention to how someone handled a customer who didn't fit the usual script, because that's where you see whether they actually understand the job.

How do you usually tell when someone on a team is ready to work on their own?

We use a mix of things—observation, feedback, and how they handle edge cases, kind of like what you're describing. Alright, shifting gears a bit. You also handled escalated customer returns. Can you walk me through a specific situation where that got tricky—like, what was the actual problem and how did you handle it?

Sure. This one stuck with me. A customer came in wanting a refund on a tent they'd used a bunch. It was past the return window, and they were pretty frustrated, so it got escalated to me.

I couldn't just say no and leave it there. I asked what happened with the tent, and it turned out one of the poles had a crack near a joint. That changed the conversation for me, because it wasn't really about the return policy anymore. It was about a product that failed on them.

So I checked whether the brand's warranty could cover it, and it could. I explained the repair option, walked them through what they'd need to send in, and was clear that it wouldn't be a refund. They weren't thrilled at first, but they went with it, and they ended up leaving a positive review about how it was handled.

What I took from it is that when someone's upset about a return, the policy is rarely the whole story. Figuring out what actually went wrong usually gets you to a better answer. Is that the kind of problem-solving you'd want in this role?
That's a solid example. So when you explained the warranty option to them, how did you actually frame it so they went from frustrated to accepting it instead of a refund?

Honestly, I mostly just tried to be straight with them. I didn't want to oversell the warranty like it was a full replacement, because that would've backfired. So I told them what the warranty covered, what it didn't, and roughly how the process would go.

I also let them vent first. They'd been dealing with a tent that failed them, and they wanted someone to acknowledge that. Once they felt heard, it was easier to talk about options.

It's hard to say exactly what tipped them over, though. I think it was seeing that I was actually trying to fix the problem and not just defend the policy. Do you think that kind of approach works in your customer-facing roles, or do you usually have more flexibility than that?

We do have some flexibility, but it depends on the situation. We'll probably dig into that more as we go. So on campus, you managed a twelve-thousand-dollar annual budget as club treasurer. What was the toughest call you had to make with that money?

Honestly, the hardest part was deciding what to cut. We had a competition coming up, and some members really needed help with travel costs. The end-of-year banquet was the obvious place to look, and it was a tough call because people liked it. A lot of the club's energy goes into that night.

I ended up scaling the banquet way back so more of the money could go toward the trip. It wasn't a popular decision at first, but I explained the reasoning to the board and the members. I think what I learned most is that budgeting is less about the spreadsheet and more about being upfront with people about tradeoffs. It's hard to quantify how much that conversation mattered, but it changed how I approach those decisions now.

Is this the kind of budget decision you'd expect someone to make on their own, or is it usually more of a team call?

Usually it depends on the scale and the role, but I appreciate you thinking about how to communicate it. One more thing on that—when you scaled back the banquet, did you get pushback from people who cared about it, and if so, how'd you handle that?

Yeah, there was pushback, mostly from members who'd been looking forward to the banquet since the start of the year. A couple of people were pretty disappointed, and one person asked me directly why we couldn't just keep it the same and cut somewhere else.

I took those concerns seriously. I went back through the budget with them line by line so they could see what else we'd already committed to. Then I asked what they cared about most in the banquet, and we kept those parts. We made it a smaller event, but we kept the awards and the group photo, which seemed to matter most to people.

I also made sure the board heard about the tradeoff before the decision was final, not after. I think that's what made the biggest difference. People can handle a disappointing call if they feel like they were part of it.

That makes sense. Alright, I want to ask you about something a bit different. Tell me about a time you actually failed at something—not a learning moment where things worked out, but where you missed the mark and it stuck with you.

Honestly, the sponsorship outreach for the club's spring event. I sent cold emails to about 25 local businesses, and most of them just went nowhere. I was pretty discouraged, because I'd put a lot of effort into writing them and felt like I was doing the right thing.

What stuck with me was realizing I was asking people to make a decision about a stranger's email. I wasn't giving them much reason to care. When I finally walked into a few places in person with a one-page flyer, the conversations went a lot better. Some of the businesses that said yes were the ones I'd emailed and never heard back from.

It bugged me that I didn't figure that out sooner. I'd assumed the emails were the efficient route, but I hadn't tested whether they actually worked. Now I try to check my assumptions earlier, especially when I'm putting time into something that isn't getting results.
Fair point. So when you did walk in with the flyer, what was actually different about that pitch that made them more likely to say yes?

Mostly, they could see that a real person was asking. In an email I was just a name in an inbox, but when I walked in, they could talk to me and ask questions right away.

The flyer helped too. It was one page, so I could say what the event was, who'd be there, and what a sponsor would get, all in a minute. A busy owner can take that in while standing at the counter.

I also tailored it a bit for each place. A bike shop cares about different things than a cafe or a bank branch, so I'd lead with whatever would matter to them. I hadn't really done that in the emails.
Makes sense. So you secured three sponsors that way. How many of those three came from places you'd already emailed and gotten no response from?

Hard to say exactly, honestly. I was more focused on what I learned from the whole process than on keeping a tally of which emails got which replies. What stuck with me was that the in-person visits made the difference. Have you ever had to go back and change your approach halfway through a project like that?
Sure, happens all the time. Alright, last thing before we wrap up—why do you want this kind of role? Like, what's drawing you to it?

Honestly, I want something where I'm working directly with people and can see what my effort actually does. Retail showed me I like that feeling of helping someone leave with exactly what they need, and I'd like to build on that with more responsibility. From what you've described, this role seems to involve that kind of problem-solving with customers, plus some of the judgment calls I've been making with budgets and returns. That mix is what appeals to me.
Got it. We're almost out of time, so I want to make sure you get a chance to ask me anything. What do you want to know?
Yeah, I'd love to know, what does a typical week look like for someone in this role?

Good question. It really depends on the position, but generally it's a mix of customer-facing work, some internal problem-solving, and collaboration with the team.
