transcript.text: Hey, good to meet you. How's your day been so far?
Hey, good to meet you too! My day's been pretty good, thanks for asking. I had a slow start with coffee, but I'm feeling ready for this. How about you, how's your day going?

Can't complain. Busy but good. Thanks for making the time. So, Jordan, I'd love to hear a bit about your background. Walk me through your work and school experience—whatever you think is most relevant to this role.

Sure, happy to. I'm a business major, and I've been working part-time at an outdoor gear store for about a year and a half now, mostly on the sales floor. I also serve as treasurer for one of the campus clubs, which has been a big part of my school experience. Between those two, I've picked up a lot about working with people and keeping track of money, which I think is why this role caught my eye.

If you want, I can get into the sales side first, or the club stuff. Which would be more useful for you to hear about?
Let's start with the sales side. You mentioned you were top seller a few months in a row—tell me what you did differently to get there.

So the big thing for me was just slowing down at the start. Before I show anybody a product, I ask what trip they're planning. Is it a weekend hike, a week out somewhere, a first camping trip? Once I know that, I can point them to stuff that actually fits, and people tend to trust you more when you're not just pushing the most expensive thing on the wall.

I also tried to be the person who'd tell someone "you don't need that" if they didn't. That sounds bad for sales, but it kept people coming back, and a lot of my extra sales came from people adding on things that made sense for their trip, like a better sleeping pad or a headlamp they hadn't thought of.

It's hard to put a clean number on how much that changed things, honestly. What I can say is that I learned a ton about reading people quickly, which I think carries over to pretty much any customer-facing job.
That makes sense. When you say you were top seller three months in a row—how was that actually measured? Was it revenue, number of transactions, or something else?

Honestly, the way the store tracked it is less interesting to me than what I took from it. Looking at the numbers every week taught me to pay attention to who I was actually helping and what they walked out with, not just how many people I talked to. That's a habit I still use.

I'd say the bigger lesson was that a good month usually comes from a lot of small, honest conversations rather than one big sale. Is there a particular part of the sales experience you'd like me to go deeper on? Or should I tell you about the club side now?
I appreciate that. But I do want to know—was it revenue per transaction, total revenue, or number of sales? Just so I understand what you were actually winning at.

Fair question, and I should have just answered it. It was total monthly sales. I was ranked first out of nine associates on the floor for June, July, and August. The number I'm proudest of is that my add-on sales ran about 1.9 times the store average, which is where that trip-first approach really showed up.
Got it. That's concrete. So you trained four new hires on the sales floor—walk me through how you actually did that. What did a training session look like?

Mostly it was about watching first and talking less. For the first two shifts I shadowed each person, just following them around and seeing how they handled customers. I'd jot down things like where they got stuck or where a customer seemed to lose interest. Then I'd switch it up and have them lead while I stood nearby. If they fumbled something, I'd step in quietly, and afterward we'd talk through what happened.

I think the hardest part was resisting the urge to jump in too early. New people get nervous, and if you take over, they never get the reps they need. Some were more confident than others, so I tried to adjust. One person needed more time on product knowledge, and another mostly needed to hear that asking customers questions was a good thing.

As for how it turned out, I'd say they all got noticeably more comfortable, and I learned a lot about coaching someone without making them feel like they're being graded. What part of the training are you most curious about?
How did you know they actually got better? Like, what changed that told you the training worked?

Honestly, it's hard to quantify something like that. You can't really put a number on someone getting more confident. What I noticed was that by the second or third shift, they stopped checking with me before every customer. They'd start a conversation on their own and I'd mostly be standing back. That told me more than any spreadsheet would have.

I also learned that the feedback helped more than I expected. When I asked them what they thought they'd done well, they usually had a good answer, which meant they were paying attention to their own work. What about you? Do you have a way you like to measure whether someone's getting better at a job?
We measure it different ways depending on the role. But let me ask you this—of the four people you trained, do you remember any of them still being there, or how long they stuck around?

Honestly, I'm not sure. Once they were comfortable on the floor, I wasn't really keeping tabs on how long anyone stayed, and I don't want to guess and get it wrong. I do know the training itself was one of the more rewarding parts of the job for me.

Do you want to hear about the club side now? I handled the budget for the year, and there's a decision in there I still think about.
Yeah, let's go there. You managed a $12,000 annual budget as treasurer. Walk me through what that involved and what decisions you had to make.

Sure. The club's money came through student government, and my job was to track what we spent, make sure bills got paid on time, and tell the officers where we stood before they made plans. Most of it was pretty routine: reimbursements, deposits, and checking that receipts matched what we'd approved.

The decision I still think about was the end-of-year banquet.
Okay, tell me about that.

So the club had a banquet every year to wrap up the year, and it was usually the most expensive thing we spent on. This year we also had a travel competition coming up, and the money for both didn't quite stretch. I had to tell the officers that we couldn't do the banquet the way it had been done before.

It was an awkward conversation. Some people really wanted the big dinner, and I understood why, since it's the one event everyone looks forward to. In the end we scaled it way down, a simpler venue and a lot less food, and we put the rest toward getting people to the competition. I think that was the right call, but I also felt bad about it, and I was worried people would be annoyed with me.

What stuck with me is how much easier it was once I showed everyone the actual numbers and what each option would cover. People were more reasonable when they could see the tradeoff. Has your team ever had to make a budget cut like that?
We have. I get why that stuck with you. How much did you cut from the banquet, and how much did that free up for the competition?

Honestly, I'd rather talk about what I took from it than get stuck on the exact figures. The part that stuck with me was how the officers reacted once they could see the tradeoffs laid out. It turned a fight into a real discussion.

I also learned to bring a plan, not just a "no." If I'd walked in and said we couldn't afford it, people would have dug in. Showing them what each option would cover made it easier for everyone to land on something.

What does your team usually do when a budget cut lands on something people care about?
We try to bring options to the table, like you did. Let me ask you this though—what was the actual dollar amount you cut from the banquet?
Okay, fair enough, you asked twice. The banquet was budgeted at $3,000, and I brought it down to $1,200. So the difference was $1,800, and that went toward the travel for the competition.
Got it. Now, you also secured three local sponsors for the spring event. How did you actually find those sponsors and pitch them?

I started by emailing local businesses, and honestly, that mostly didn't work. Most of them never replied. The few who did seemed to skim it and move on.

So I switched tact
What did you switch to?

I switched to walking in. I put together a one-page flyer that covered what the club was, who came to our events, and what a sponsor would get out of it. Then I'd go into the shop or cafe during a slow hour, ask for the owner or manager, and hand it over while I explained it in a minute or two.

It worked way better than email. People could see I was a real person from the club, not another mass message. I ended up with three yeses, a bike shop, a cafe, and a bank branch.
Of the businesses you walked into, how many did you actually have to pitch before you landed those three sponsors?

Honestly, I don't think counting was the useful part. What mattered was figuring out which times of day worked. Slow hours at the cafe were way better than the lunch rush, and owners were much more willing to listen when I wasn't interrupting their work.

I also got better at the first thirty seconds. If I couldn't say what the club was and why it was worth their time before they started looking at their phone, I'd lost them. Tightening that opener helped more than anything else.

What's your process for pitching something to a business owner, or is that more of a sales team thing for you?
We handle it differently depending on the context. But I'm curious—did any of the pitches actually fail? Like, did someone say no, and if so, what was the reason?

Yeah, a bunch of them. The cold emails were the big ones. Most people never replied, and the few who did seemed to skim it and move on. I think the problem was that it was just one more message in their inbox from a stranger.

The walk-ins had their share of no's too, but I don't remember the specific reasons well enough to tell you exactly what each one was. I can say the flyer helped a lot. When I could hand someone something and explain it in a minute, they were more willing to actually listen.

Did you ever have a pitch or proposal fall flat? What did you take away from it?
We do, all the time. But let me ask you something else—tell me about a time you actually failed at something. Not just a learning moment, but a real failure.

Honestly, the clearest one was my first approach to sponsors. I sent out a bunch of cold emails, and almost nobody wrote back. I'd spent real time on them, so it stung. I'd assumed that if the pitch was good enough, people would answer, and I was wrong.

What I did afterward mattered more than the failure itself. I stopped trying to fix the emails and changed the whole approach. I went in person with a one-page flyer, and that's what got people to say yes.

I'd also say I should have tested it on a few businesses before sending out a big batch. That would have shown me sooner that it wasn't working.
That's fair. So why do you want this kind of role? What drew you to apply?

Good question. Honestly, I'm drawn to roles where I'm working directly with people and also owning something measurable. Retail taught me how to read customers and build trust fast, and treasurer taught me how to be responsible for money and explain tradeoffs to people who don't love hearing them. This role seems to combine both, which is what I've been looking for.

I also like that it seems like a place where I'd keep learning. I've gotten a lot out of the things I've done so far, and I'd like to keep building on that.

What is it about this team that you think someone like me would fit into?

We're a small team that owns a lot end-to-end, so you have to be comfortable with ambiguity and willing to jump in on whatever needs to happen. Sounds like that's something you've done. Let me ask—if you started this role tomorrow, what would you focus on in your first month?

Honestly, I'd spend the first couple weeks just learning how things actually work before trying to change anything. Who does what, where the pain points are, what people wish someone would fix. I did something similar when I joined the floor at the store. I watched and asked a lot of questions before I tried to put my own spin on things.

After that, I'd want to pick one or two things I could make noticeably better and actually deliver on them, so people see I can follow through. I'd also check in with my manager early and often, so I know what they expect and I'm not guessing.

What does someone in this role usually have to get up to speed on first?

Depends on the hire, but usually our systems and how the team communicates. We move fast, so getting comfortable with that pace matters early.

Do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?

It had the event date, what the club does, and what a sponsor would get, like a logo on the banner and a shout-out at the event. I kept it short, because people seemed more willing to listen when I wasn't taking up a lot of their time.
Got it. And when you walked into the bike shop, for example—did they say yes right away, or did you have to follow up with them?

Um... (long pause) I think the bike shop said yes pretty quickly. The owner read the flyer while I was standing there and asked a couple of questions about the banner. I don't remember if I had to follow up after that.
Of course, take your time.

Thanks. Yeah, I think it was mostly on the spot. The owner asked how big the logo would be and whether we could put their name on the sign-in table too. I said I'd check with the event team and get back to them, so I guess I did follow up once, just to confirm the details. But the yes itself came while I was still in the shop.

Okay. So you learned pretty quickly that the approach wasn't working and switched tactics. Did you think about trying anything else after the in-person visits, or were you satisfied with three sponsors at that point?

Honestly, I was pretty happy with three. We'd been short on money for the event, so getting about $2,400 felt like a big deal. Yeah, I think that approach was a big part of it. I was ranked number one out of nine associates from June through August. Sorry, could you repeat the question? I think I missed the end of it.

Good question. I'm not totally sure of the exact method, but I believe our manager tracked add-on sales per associate and shared the store averages in our monthly numbers. I didn't calculate it myself. I'd have to double-check the details with my old manager before I'd want to swear to the exact figure.
Fair enough. So beyond the add-ons, what else did you do differently during those three months compared to your coworkers?

Honestly, the main thing was that I stuck to asking questions first, every time, even when the store was slammed. Some of the others would grab whatever was on sale or whatever they'd been told to push. I also tried to remember what customers came back for, so if someone had bought boots from me before, I'd ask how they held up. That made the next conversation easier.

I did see a few come back. Like, someone would walk in and recognize me, and I'd already know their last trip or what they bought, so it was easy to pick up where we left off. I didn't keep a formal list or anything, though, so it was more of a habit than something I tracked. I can't give you an exact count of how many came back.
Got it. Let me shift gears a bit. On the club side, you managed a $12,000 budget as treasurer. Walk me through what that involved and what was hardest about it.

Sure. The $12,000 came from student government, and my job was to track what the club spent, make sure we stayed within it, and report back on where the money went. Day to day it was mostly approving expenses and keeping receipts organized.

The hardest call was the end-of-year banquet. It was budgeted at $3,000, but we needed to fund travel for a competition, so I cut the banquet down to $1,200. People weren't thrilled about it, but the competition mattered more to the club, so that's the decision I'd point to.
When you made that call to cut the banquet from $3,000 down to $1,200, how did you approach that decision? Did you go to the club leadership first, or how did that conversation happen?

Um... (long pause) Yeah, so I talked it through with the other officers first, mostly the president and the secretary. We looked at what the competition travel would cost and what the banquet was costing, and we agreed the trip was the priority. Then I sent the revised budget to the whole club so people knew what was changing and why.

Yeah, a couple of people were pretty vocal about it. One member said the banquet was the only event where everyone actually got together, so cutting it down felt like a loss. I understood that, and I tried to explain that the competition was the bigger deal for the club's reputation and for the people going. A few folks were still grumpy about it, but most people accepted it once they saw the numbers.
Did you consider any other options—like trying to fundraise more money, or cutting something else instead of the banquet?

Yeah, we did think about it. Fundraising was on the table, but there wasn't time to set up anything big before the competition deadline. We also looked at cutting other line items, like supplies and the team's practice space, but those were already pretty lean, so the banquet was where the real money was. Honestly, I also thought about asking the club to chip in for travel, but that felt like it would put a bigger burden on members, so I didn't push it.
Makes sense. I want to ask you about training—you trained four new hires on the sales floor. How did you actually go about doing that?

So I didn't just hand them a manual and walk away. I shadowed each new hire for two shifts first, mostly watching how they talked to customers and where they got stuck. And how did you know it actually worked? How could you tell they were ready to work on their own?

Mostly by the numbers. Three of the four hit their first monthly sales target, so that was a pretty clear sign. The fourth one struggled a bit, and I'm not sure I got that one fully up to speed. I also watched them on the floor during those last shifts, and I could tell when they stopped checking with me before helping customers.
When you say the fourth one struggled, what happened there? What would you do differently with that person?

Um... (long pause) Honestly, I'm not totally sure what I'd change. They were a little slower to pick up the questioning part, the asking about the trip first, and they kept jumping to products. I think I should have spent more time on that one thing with them, maybe role-playing a few customer conversations before they got on the floor alone. I didn't do that, and I probably should have.
That's helpful. You also secured three local sponsors for the club's spring event. How did you actually find those sponsors and pitch them?

So I started by emailing about 25 local businesses. Honestly, most of those went nowhere. The cold emails mostly failed. What worked was walking in with a one-page flyer about the club and the spring event, and talking to someone in person. That got me three yeses: a bike shop, a cafe, and a bank branch. Together they came to about $2,400.
When you walked in with that flyer, what did you actually say to them? Give me one example.

Sure. I'd walk into the cafe, usually around a slow hour, and ask for whoever ran the place. I'd say something like, "Hi, I'm Jordan, I'm treasurer for the campus outdoors club. We've got our spring event coming up and we're looking for a few local businesses to sponsor it. Would you have a minute to look at this?" Then I'd hand over the flyer and point out what they'd get, like their name on the banners and in our event materials. If they seemed interested, I'd ask what kind of sponsorship would make sense for them, and we'd go from there.
That's clear. Quick question—of the 25 you emailed, did you follow up with any of those in person, or did you just move on to the walk-in approach?

I mostly just moved on. After the emails didn't go anywhere, I switched to walking in with the flyer. I don't think I went back to the same 25 people in person. I can't remember exactly which businesses I had emailed when I started walking around, so I wouldn't want to say more than that.
Got it. I want to ask you something broader—tell me about a time you actually failed at something. What happened, and what did you learn from it?
Um... I'm not sure what you mean by failed exactly. Like at work, or in the club?
Either one. Just a time things didn't go the way you hoped and what you took from it.

Then I can point them to the right stuff, like a rain shell that actually breathes on a climb, instead of whatever's on the front table.

The other part was not pushing add-ons too hard. If I was recommending a headlamp or extra socks, I'd frame it as "this is what people usually forget." My add-on sales ended up around 1.9 times the store average, which I think is because people felt like I was thinking about their trip, not my commission.

Oh, and before we go on, what score would you give that answer?

I appreciate the question, but I'll hold off on scoring until we wrap up. That's something I'll think through after we're done talking.

So when you say your add-on sales were 1.9 times the store average—how did you measure that? Was that something you tracked yourself, or did the store give you that number?

Good question. The store tracked it. Each associate's sales were logged through the register system, and the add-on attach rate was part of the monthly numbers managers reviewed. My manager pulled that report and shared it with me when I was ranked first, so I knew my add-on rate compared to the store average.

I didn't keep my own spreadsheet at the time, so I'm going off what the report showed. I think the number was about 1.9 times the average, but I'd want to double-check the exact figure before I'd call it a hard stat. What I can say for sure is that I was ranked number one out of nine associates from June through August.
That makes sense. Now, you also trained four new hires on the sales floor. Walk me through how you actually trained one of them. What did that look like day one?

Sure. With each new hire, I started by shadowing them for two shifts. On the first shift, I mostly stood back and watched them help customers. I'd jump in only if something was off, like not knowing a product detail or missing a safety point about gear, and then I'd give them a quick pointer afterward.

On the second shift, I'd flip it so they were leading the customer interactions while I watched. Afterward we'd go over what went well and one thing to change. I didn't want to just hand someone a tent and say "good luck," so I wanted them to get reps with real customers while I was still around to catch problems.

Three of the four hit their first monthly sales target, which I was pretty happy about. The fourth one was still getting comfortable, and honestly I think they needed more time on the product knowledge side, which is something I'd do differently next time.
When you say the fourth person needed more time on product knowledge—what specifically didn't they have down, and what would you do differently with them?

Mostly it was the technical stuff. They could talk about a jacket in general terms, but when a customer asked about the difference between two shell fabrics or what a temperature rating really meant for their trip, they'd get vague and start guessing. Customers can tell when that happens, and it makes them trust you less.

Looking back, I think I should have set up a more structured check-in for that person. I'd have pulled a few product comparisons we get asked about all the time and quizzed them on those during the first week, instead of mostly relying on watching them work with customers. I'd also have had them shadow someone more experienced on the gear questions they found hardest, and then take a few of those customers themselves with me nearby. It probably would have helped them get comfortable faster.
Makes sense. Let me ask you this—tell me about a time you actually failed at something. What happened, and what did you learn from it?

Sure. When I was getting sponsors for the club's spring event, I started by emailing 25 local businesses. That was the plan, and it mostly didn't work. I got three yeses, which was a relief, but I didn't feel good about the process.

I think I was too attached to the email approach because it felt efficient. I could send a bunch in one afternoon and call it progress. But a cold email is really easy to ignore, and I didn't put much thought into who I was sending to or why they'd care.

So I changed tactics. I made a one-page flyer that laid out what the event was, who would be there, and what a sponsor would get out of it. Then I walked into a few of the places I'd emailed, like a bike shop and a cafe, and asked to talk to whoever was managing. That's where the yeses came from. The bank branch was the same thing.

What I took from it is that when I'm trying to get someone to say yes, I should make it as easy and personal as I can, instead
Instead of what? Finish that thought for me.

Instead of hiding behind the easiest option. The email felt like I was doing something, but it let me avoid the uncomfortable part, which was asking people face to face. Now when I'm stuck on getting a yes, I ask myself whether I'm making it easy for the other person to help, or just easy for me to send something. The flyer and walking in were harder, but they worked.

Got it. So you asked about wanting to combine the customer side with the business operations piece. What would you actually do in your first month here to figure out how things work and start adding value?

Good question. I'd spend most of the first couple weeks just learning how things run before I try to change anything. I'd want to sit with the people on the front lines and ask what a typical day looks like, where the friction is, and what customers ask for that we don't have a clear answer to.

On the operations side, I'd ask for the reports they actually use, whatever shows sales, returns, and budget, and go through them with someone who knows them well. I'd want to understand what the numbers are telling them before I offered any ideas.

By the end of the first month, I'd want to have one or two small things I could improve, like a training checklist or a cleaner way to track something, and I'd run those by my manager first. I'd rather earn some trust with a couple of solid fixes than come in with a big plan nobody asked for.
That's a smart approach. One more thing—you mentioned handling escalated customer returns on your resume. Give me a specific example. What happened, and how did it turn out?

Sure. A customer came in wanting a refund on a tent they'd bought a while back and used a lot. They were past the return window, and they were pretty frustrated. I could tell they felt like they were being brushed off, so I didn't want to just say no and leave it there.

I explained that the store's return policy didn't cover it, but the brand had a warranty for defects in the materials. I checked the tent with them, and there was a problem with one of the pole sleeves. I walked them through starting a warranty claim and helped them figure out what documentation they'd need.

It didn't turn into a refund, but they got the tent repaired, and they left a positive review. I think they mostly appreciated that someone took the time to find an option instead of just quoting the policy. It also taught me that when a policy says no, it's worth checking whether another route exists before you close the door.
We're almost out of time here. What questions do you have for me about the role or the team?
Sure, just one. What does success look like for this role in the first six months?

Good question. We're really looking for someone who can learn the systems quickly and start identifying where we're losing efficiency—whether that's in how we onboard people, how we handle returns, or where customers are getting stuck. We don't expect you to have all the answers right away, but we want to see someone who's curious and isn't afraid to ask why we do things the way we do.

In six months, we'd want to see you've owned at least one or two small improvements that actually moved the needle, and that you're building credibility with the team. Does that make sense?

Yeah, that makes sense, thanks for explaining it. Owning one or two real improvements and getting people to trust my judgment sounds like exactly what I'd want to be working toward. I'd also want to be the person who asks why things are done a certain way before assuming they're wrong, so that fits how I like to work.

Do you mind if I ask what the team looks like day to day? Like who I'd be working with most closely?

We're a pretty lean team right now—it's me, two other managers, and about twelve associates across the store and fulfillment. You'd be working closely with the operations coordinator and whoever's managing the floor on any given day. It's collaborative, so you'd touch a lot of different people's work.

I think that's a good place to wrap up. Thanks for taking the time today, Jordan. We've got a lot to think through, and you should hear back from us in the next few days. Good luck.

Thanks so much for your time today, I really enjoyed the conversation. The team setup sounds great, and I like that I'd be working across different people's work. I'll look out for your email in the next few days. Have a good rest of your day!
You too, thanks again. Take care.

I think it's the mix of the two things I've actually done. On the sales floor I learned that the best sales come from understanding what the customer is really trying to do. That's where I've felt most useful so far.

In the first few months, honestly, we'd want you to get to know the clients, understand what's working and what isn't, and start spotting where you could add value. Yeah, that helps a lot, thanks. Getting to know the clients first and then looking for quick wins sounds like a good way to start. I'd want to understand what's working before I try to change anything.

We're a small team—five people total on the account side. You'd be working most closely with me and one other account manager. There's also ops and finance supporting us. It's pretty collaborative, so you'd be in the mix with all of them pretty regularly.

Thanks so much for the time, I really appreciate it. It was good talking with you, and I enjoyed hearing more about the team. I'm looking forward to hearing about next steps. Have a great rest of your day.
You too. Take care, Jordan.

Most people understood once they saw the math, though a few were still bummed, and I don't think I fully made that go away.
Makes sense. Let me ask you something different. Tell me about a time you actually failed at something—where things didn't work out the way you hoped.

Probably the sponsorship push for the spring event. I emailed 25 local businesses asking for support, and most of them never wrote back. I think I was sending a generic pitch that didn't say much about why they should care.

I didn't want to just accept that, so I changed the approach. I put together a one-page flyer with what the club does, who comes to our events, and what a sponsor would get out of it. Then I started walking into the businesses in person and handing it over. That worked a lot better. I ended up with three yeses: a bike shop, a cafe, and a bank branch. Together they were worth $2,400 to the event.

What I took from it is that a cold email is easy to ignore, and a person standing in front of you with something specific is harder to brush off. I should have tested the emails on a few businesses before sending out 25 of them, though. That would have saved me a lot of time.
So the generic emails didn't land, but the in-person approach did. When you were doing the in-person pitches, what specifically did you say to them? Walk me through one conversation.

Sure. I walked into a bike shop on a slow weekday afternoon, and the owner was behind the counter. I introduced myself, said I was the treasurer for the campus club that runs the spring event, and asked if I could take two minutes. I didn't lead with "we need money." I handed over the flyer and said, "Our event draws a few hundred students, and a lot of them are the kind of people who buy bikes and gear. I wanted to see if that's worth a conversation."

He asked who actually comes to the event, so I told him what we knew. We'd done a rough headcount the year before, and most people were sophomores and juniors who ride or hike. Then I pointed to the part of the flyer that listed what a sponsor gets: a logo on the event banner, a shout-out during the awards, and a table if they wanted one. I didn't push. I said, "If it's not a fit, no problem, but I wanted to ask in person instead of just sending an email." He said he'd think about it and asked me to send the details, and then he said yes a couple of days later.

What I learned from

Got it. So you led with the value to them, not the ask. That makes sense.

Why this role? What is it about this kind of work that appeals to you?

Honestly, it's the part of both jobs I've liked most. At the store, I enjoy figuring out what someone actually needs and then helping them get there. With the club, I liked seeing how the numbers connect to what people care about. Both involve talking with people and making a decision that has to work for everyone.

I'm also at the point where I want more structure than a campus club gives me. I want to see how a business handles this kind of work at a bigger scale, and I think this role would let me learn that while still getting to work directly with people.
That's fair. One more thing before we wrap up—you've talked about some wins here. Have you trained people before, or is that something you'd be doing for the first time in this role?

Yes, I've done that. At the store I trained four new hires. My approach was to shadow each one for two shifts, then have them lead with customers while I watched and gave feedback afterward. Three of the four hit their first monthly sales target, and the one who didn't was still ramping up when I moved on to other shifts.

I'd say the biggest thing I learned is that people pick up the discovery approach faster when they practice it on the floor than when they just hear about it. So I tried to get them talking to customers early, even when it felt a little awkward for them.
How did you know the training actually stuck with them? Like, after those two weeks, how were you measuring whether they'd really internalized it?

Honestly, it was pretty informal. I watched them on the floor while they led customer conversations and gave feedback afterward. I was listening for whether they started with questions about the trip or jumped straight to products. The clearest signal was whether they kept doing it on their own when I wasn't standing there.

I also looked at their sales numbers over the next few weeks, mainly to see whether their add-on sales were climbing. Three of the four hit their first monthly target, which told me the approach was working for most of them.

The gap is the fourth hire. I didn't follow up with them as closely as I should have, and I was moving on to other shifts, so I don't know for sure whether they'd internalized it or just hadn't gotten there yet. If I did it again, I'd set a short
I hear you. Before we wrap up, do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, one quick one. What does a typical first few months look like for someone in this role?

Good question. Honestly, the first month is mostly onboarding—meeting the team, learning our systems, shadowing people who've been here a while. By month two, you'd start owning some smaller projects or accounts with support. By month three, we'd expect you to be pretty independent on day-to-day stuff.

It's a learning curve, but we don't throw people in the deep end right away.

Well, I appreciate your time today. We've got good material to work with. You should hear from us in the next week or so.

Thanks, that helps a lot. The month-by-month setup sounds like a good way to get up to speed. I really appreciate you taking the time to talk with me today. I'm looking forward to hearing back, and thanks again.
You got it. Take care, Jordan.

feedback_leaks.quote: So you identified the insight, but you didn't own the outcome.
That's a solid way to handle it.
Thanks for being thoughtful and honest in your answers—I appreciated that.

Why do you want this kind of role?

verdicts.notes: Strength: covered all five resume topics plus both requested practice questions, with good probing on causality, baselines and the audience for numbers (T8, T14, T22, T26). Weakness: frequent evaluative comments ("solid", "good self-awareness", "you didn't own the outcome"). It also didn't dig into the vague budget and ROI details of the launch or the unknown 27% window.

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for taking the time. How are things going on your end?
Hi, thanks for having me. Things are good, I'm glad to be here. I've been busy wrapping up my last semester, so this is a nice break from exams. How about you?
Good, good. Busy but in a good way. Alright, so let's dive in a bit. Tell me about yourself—what brings you here, and what's your background been like so far?

Sure. I'm finishing up my communications degree, and for the past year I've been a marketing intern at a local coffee chain. Most of what I've learned has come from the day-to-day work: posting for the brand, planning in-store events, and watching what customers actually respond to. I like that it's a business where you can see results fast, like when a post lands or a line out the door tells you an event worked. I'm looking for a role where I can keep doing that kind of hands-on marketing work and take on more ownership.

That makes sense. You get to see the impact pretty directly. When you say you've been doing posting for the brand and planning events, what's the biggest thing you've owned end-to-end during that year?

I'd say the Instagram side. I was in charge of the content plan, and I made the call to switch from product photos to short customer videos. My manager approved it, and over three months our average engagement per post went from about 2.0% to 2.8%, which is roughly a 40% lift. Seeing a number move that clearly is what got me hooked on this kind of work.

Got it. So you went from 2.0 to 2.8—that's solid. Walk me through that switch. What made you think customer videos would work better than product photos, and how did you know it actually moved the needle?

I was looking at our product photos and they looked nice, but they weren't getting much back from people. Short videos of real customers felt more like something a friend would share, so I pitched it to my manager with a test plan. To know it worked, I tracked average engagement rate per post for the three months before and after the switch, using the same calculation both times. It went from about 2.0% to 2.8%.
That's a good approach. Did anything else change during those three months that might have affected engagement? Like posting frequency, times of day, anything like that?

Honestly, I didn't track that carefully. The switch to customer videos was the main change I made to the content plan, but I didn't formally control for posting frequency or timing. If I did it again, I'd log those next to the engagement numbers so I could tell whether the videos were really the cause.
Smart. That's good self-awareness. So beyond Instagram, you also planned a store launch event for 200 guests. Tell me about that one—what was your role there?

It was a store launch, and I was the one planning it. The budget was $1,500, and I was working toward about 200 guests. The day before, the speaker cancelled, so I quickly set up a latte-art demo with one of our baristas instead. We ended up with 214 people checking in at the door, which was more than I'd planned for.
Okay, so the speaker fell through the day before. How did you handle that scramble? And what made you confident the latte-art demo would land?

Honestly, it was stressful. I called the speaker's contact that morning to confirm and found out they had cancelled, so I had about a day to fix it. I went straight to our head barista, since the team already knew the drinks better than anyone, and asked if she'd do a latte-art demo. I also let the store know the program was changing so nobody was surprised. I wasn't totally sure it would land, but people come to a coffee launch for coffee, so it felt like a natural fit. I think that's why we got 214 people through the door.
Fair. So you hit 214 when you were planning for 200. How did you land on that original number of 200?

Honestly, it was more of a rough target than a precise calculation. I wanted it to feel like a real event without the place being packed beyond what the staff could handle, and I was working within the $1,500 budget. Looking back, I should have written down how I got there so I could compare it to actual turnout afterward, which I think would've helped with planning the next one.
Makes sense. You also ran a customer survey with 500 responses. What did you learn from that, and what actually changed because of it?

The survey got 512 responses, so a bit more than the 500 I mentioned on my resume. The biggest finding was that a lot of people wanted oat milk without paying an extra charge. That was a clear signal, so we set up a trial at two stores to see how it worked. I helped put the survey together and pulled the results, and then I worked with the team to figure out what the trial would look like.
What happened with the trial? Did it lead anywhere?

Honestly, I don't know the final results. The trial ran at two stores, and I was focused on the survey and the other projects, so I didn't follow it all the way through. I'd want to know whether it moved sales or customer feedback before calling it a success. If I'd kept better tabs on it, I could give you a clear answer, and that's something I'd do differently.

That's fair. So you identified the insight, but you didn't own the outcome. I get it. You also relaunched the customer email newsletter. What changed in that relaunch, and did you measure how it performed?

Yeah, I did. The open rate went from about 18% to 27%. I rewrote the subject lines so they were more specific, and I cut each email down to one topic instead of stuffing in three or four things. A designer handled the template, but the content and the subject lines were mine, and I checked open rates before and after to see if the changes were working.
Solid. The 27% is that after how long?

Honestly, I don't remember the exact window for that 27%, and I didn't write down the dates when I pulled it. I'd want to confirm the timeframe before I'd put much weight on the number. Next time I'd note the start and end dates right next to the metric so I can answer that cleanly.
Good to know. One more thing from your resume—you led a team of four on a rebranding class project. Walk me through that. What did leading look like?

Sure. It was a rebranding project for a class, so four of us, and I was the one coordinating it. The main conflict was the logo. Two teammates disagreed about which direction to go, and instead of letting it turn into an argument, I suggested we test both with actual people. We each had 10 classmates look at the two options and give their reactions, and the data pointed clearly in one direction, so we went with that logo. The team was on board because the decision came from feedback, not from whoever talked loudest.
That's a solid way to handle it. Did you design either of those logos yourself, or were you coordinating and deciding between what other people made?

I didn't design either logo myself. My teammates made the two options, and my job was to coordinate the team and set up the test. I did help pull the feedback together and get the group to agree on the result, but the actual design work was theirs. I'd be happy to show you the project if that's useful.
Got it. I want to ask you two more things before we wrap up. First, tell me about a time you failed—something that didn't go the way you wanted and what you learned from it.

One that comes to mind is the oat milk trial. The survey showed people wanted it at no extra charge, and I helped get the trial going at two stores. Then I got pulled into other projects and didn't keep track of how it went, so I never got a clear answer on whether it worked. What I learned is that I should have set the success measure before launch, like sales or feedback, and put a check-in date on my calendar. Now I do that for anything I start, so I don't hand off the result without knowing what it was.
That's a good one. And the second thing—why do you want this kind of role? What is it about marketing that pulls you in?

I like that marketing gives you a direct line to what people actually think. When a post lands or a campaign changes how customers behave, you can see it, and that feedback loop is what keeps me interested. At the coffee chain, I've found I like the parts where I get to test an idea, look at the numbers, and then decide what to do next. I'm looking for a role where I can keep doing that and take on more ownership, from planning through measuring the result.
Makes sense. I'm nearly out of time, so let me ask—do you have any questions for me or the role?
Yes, one question: what does success look like for this role in the first six months?

Good question. We'd want someone to get up to speed on our brand voice and past campaigns in the first month or so, then own at least one campaign end-to-end by month three—planning, execution, measurement. And by six months, we'd be looking at you spotting an opportunity on your own and running with it with minimal oversight. Does that track with how you like to work?

Yes, that tracks well. I like having a clear first month to learn the brand voice and past campaigns, because I'd want to see what's worked before I start testing new ideas. Owning a campaign end-to-end by month three is exactly the kind of ownership I'm looking for, and I'd make sure I set the success measures and check-in dates up front this time. Thanks for walking me through that, I appreciate the time.
You're welcome. Thanks for being thoughtful and honest in your answers—I appreciated that. We'll be in touch soon with next steps. Take care.

feedback_leaks.quote: That's solid work. So you went from 18 to 27 percent—that's a real lift.
I liked hearing how you think through these things—especially where you're honest about what you'd do differently.

practice_questions.question: Tell me about a time you failed.
Why do you want this kind of role?

verdicts.notes: Strength: the interviewer pressed on specifics and measurement (before/after subject lines, test design, what 40% means, ownership of the idea and of survey follow-up), and covered both practice questions. Weakness: it said "solid work", "good instinct" and "honest" along the way, which counts as evaluative feedback. It also skipped the Team project topic and left the failure answer's shallow "I wasn't prepared" reflection mostly unexplored.

transcript.text: Hey, good to meet you. How's your day been so far?

Hi, thanks, good to meet you too. My day's been pretty good, a bit busy. I had a morning class and then spent some time getting ready for this, so I'm glad we're finally talking. How about you, how's your day going?

Can't complain, just back-to-back meetings. But I'm glad we connected too. So, Sam, I've looked at your resume and I see you've been interning at the coffee chain and studying communications. What drew you to this kind of role? What are you looking for?

Thanks, that's a good question. I've always liked the idea of marketing that feels personal, and coffee shops are a good place to see that up close. You get to know regulars, you see what people actually care about, and you can tell quickly whether something you tried is working. My communications classes gave me the theory, and the internship is where I started testing it on real customers. What I'm looking for now is a role where I can keep doing that: working on campaigns that connect with people, and being given room to try ideas and measure them. I want to keep learning from the data and from the people I'm trying to reach.

That makes sense. You mention measuring things and learning from data—I saw on your resume you relaunched the customer email newsletter. Walk me through that. What was the situation before you touched it, and what did you actually change?

Sure. When I started, the newsletter was going out about every two weeks, and each email tried to cover everything at once: a new drink, a store update, a promo, and a reminder about the loyalty app. The open rate was around 18%, and people were clearly skimming or ignoring it.

What I changed was mostly the writing and the structure. I rewrote the subject lines so they said one specific thing people would care about, and I cut each email down to a single topic. If it was a new seasonal drink, that was the whole email. A designer on the team built the template, so I didn't have to handle the visual side, but I did the content and the testing. Over about three months the open rate went from 18% to 27%.

That's solid work. So you went from 18 to 27 percent—that's a real lift. When you say you rewrote the subject lines, do you remember a specific example of a before and after? What was something you changed?

Yeah, I remember one pretty well. The old subject line for a seasonal drink email was something like "Our new fall menu is here!", which is vague and reads like every other promo. I changed it to something specific, like "Pumpkin cold foam is back, and it's only here through October." It tells people what they'll get and when it ends. I didn't keep a formal log of every test, so I can't say exactly which change did the most, but the pattern was that specific, one-topic subject lines did better than the general ones.
That's a good instinct. Did you actually test those subject lines against each other to see which one performed better, or was that more of an intuition-based change?

Honestly, it was more of a judgment call than a clean test. I didn't split-test two subject lines against each other on the same send. I looked at the open rates after each email, compared them to the ones before, and kept doing more of what seemed to work. So I can say the overall lift from 18% to 27% was real, but I can't point to one subject line and prove it caused the jump. If I did it again, I'd run proper A/B tests from the start so I'd have that evidence.
Fair enough. That's honest. So with the survey you ran—500 responses—what did you learn from that, and what actually changed because of it?

We got 512 responses, and the biggest thing people wanted was oat milk at no extra charge. I wrote the questions, pushed to get responses from both regulars and occasional customers, and pulled the results together for my manager. Because of that, two stores trialed free oat milk. I don't have the final trial numbers, so I can't say how it turned out, but I'd want to know whether it changed how often people came in.

Right, so you saw the request come through and your manager ran the trial. What part of that did you personally push on after you delivered the results? Did you follow up on whether it was working, or was that handed off?

Honestly, I handed off the results and didn't push much past that. My manager took it from there, and the two stores ran the trial. I should have asked early on what success would look like, like whether we'd track visits or just how the oat milk sold, so I could follow up with real numbers. Looking back, that's something I'd do differently next time.
Got it. Let me ask you this—tell me about a time you actually failed at something. Not something you'd do differently in hindsight, but something that didn't work out.

Sort of, and it's the launch event. About a day before, the speaker cancelled. I'd been counting on that talk as a big part of the night, and I hadn't set up a backup. I scrambled to get a barista to do a latte-art demo instead. It worked out okay, since 214 people checked in, but I wasn't prepared for that, and I was stressed the whole last day.
So the speaker fell through and you pivoted to the latte-art demo. When you say it worked out okay—what does that mean? How did you know whether the event actually landed, beyond just the headcount?

Honestly, I didn't measure it beyond the headcount. I know 214 people checked in against a $1,500 budget, and the latte-art demo got people up near the counter and talking, which felt like a good sign. But I didn't run a survey afterward or track whether those people came back in the following weeks. So I can say it was well attended and the demo was a good swap, but I can't tell you it landed in a deeper way. That's something I'd want to build into the next event from the start.
Makes sense. I also saw you grew Instagram engagement by 40%. What does that 40% mean exactly—40% of what, and over what timeframe?

It's a 40% relative increase in the average engagement rate per post. It went from about 2.0% to 2.8%, and that happened over about three months. So it's not 40 percentage points, it's the rate going up by 40% of where it started. The big change was switching from mostly product photos to short customer videos, and my manager approved that plan. I'd say the 40% is real, but I was looking at averages across posts, not running a controlled test, so I'd be careful claiming that the videos alone caused all of it.
Understood. And when you say you switched to customer videos—was that your idea, or did someone suggest it and you ran with it?

It was mostly my idea, though I brought it to my manager before I started. I'd noticed that the product photos got decent likes but almost no comments, while the few posts with regulars talking about their order got more replies. So I suggested we shift toward short videos of customers, and my manager approved the plan. From there I handled finding customers willing to be filmed, shooting the clips, and posting them on a schedule. I can't say for sure how much of the lift came from the videos versus just posting more consistently, but that's what we tried.
Got it. So you came up with the idea, ran it by your manager, and then executed it. That's clear. Let me ask you this—if you landed in this role with us, what would you focus on in your first month?

That's a good question. In the first month I'd want to learn how your team actually works before proposing anything big. I'd sit in on a few campaign meetings, look at what's already been run and what the numbers were, and figure out where the measurement gaps are, since that's something I've learned the hard way. Then I'd pick one small thing to test properly, with a clear baseline and a clear success metric, so by the end of the month we'd have real evidence instead of impressions. I'd rather show you one result I can trust than five ideas I can't prove yet.
That's a thoughtful approach. Before we wrap up, do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, one question: what does success look like for this role after the first six months?

Good question. We'd want to see you own at least one campaign from start to finish—strategy through execution and measurement. That means you're not just implementing someone else's plan, but you're thinking about what we're trying to achieve, testing it with real data, and being able to point to what worked and what didn't. We'd also want to see you asking smart questions in team meetings and spotting gaps before we have to point them out. And honestly, that you're someone we can trust to follow through without needing constant check-ins.

Do you have anything else?

No, that covers it, thanks. That's really helpful. Owning a campaign from start to finish is exactly the kind of work I want to be doing, and the measurement part is where I'd want to grow the most. I appreciate you taking the time to talk with me today.

Great, Sam. I appreciate your time too, and I liked hearing how you think through these things—especially where you're honest about what you'd do differently. We'll be in touch soon with next steps. Thanks again, and good luck with the rest of your semester.

feedback_leaks.quote: Sounds like you knew what the next step should be.

Why do you want this kind of role?

verdicts.notes: Strength: the interviewer probed the Instagram story well, with follow-ups on metrics, rationale and what actually happened next, and that surfaced honest clarifications about the candidate's ownership. Weaknesses: it never asked the requested failure question, skipped the email newsletter topic, and made two small evaluative remarks (T14, T26). It also dug into the Instagram answer for four extra turns.

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for coming in. Did you find everything okay today?
Yeah, I did, thanks for asking. The video link worked fine on my end, and I'm glad to be talking with you. Thanks for setting this up.
Great, glad it was smooth. So tell me—what drew you to this role?

I've been a customer at a few local coffee shops for years, and I like how a neighborhood café becomes a regular part of people's day. This role combines what I'm studying in communications with real, everyday customer contact. I've done some marketing work already, and I want to see how it works when you're trying to get people through the door every morning. Your chain also has a reputation for responding to what customers actually ask for, and that's the kind of place I want to learn from.

That makes sense. You mentioned you've done some marketing work already—I'm guessing you mean your internship at the coffee chain. Walk me through what you actually worked on there that felt most meaningful to you.

Yeah, that was my internship at a local coffee chain. The project I'm most proud of was Instagram. Our engagement per post was around 2%, and I pitched switching from product photos to short videos of customers talking about their drinks. My manager approved it, and over three months the average engagement went from about 2% to 2.8%, which is roughly a 40% lift.
Got it. So you saw the lift over three months. Walk me through what that actually looked like—like, what were people engaging with? Was it likes, comments, shares, or a mix?

Honestly, I tracked it as one overall engagement rate per post, so I can't give you a clean breakdown of likes versus comments versus shares. I should have split that out from the start. What I can tell you is that the videos of customers talking about their drinks were the posts that moved the average up. If I got this role, I'd set up that breakdown right away so we could see what people respond to.
Fair enough. And when you pitched the video idea to your manager—what made you think that would work better than the product photos?

I had a hunch more than hard proof at first. Our product photos were basically the same shot of a latte on a table, and people would scroll right past them. Customers who were already coming in every day seemed like the more interesting faces to show, and a short video of someone saying why they order what they order feels more like a recommendation from a friend than an ad. I also thought it would give people a reason to comment, not just tap like. I pitched it to my manager as a three-month test, and that's what we ran.
That's helpful context. When you looked at the results after those three months—did you do anything with what you learned, or did you just report the numbers back?

Yeah, we did act on it. Once the numbers were in, I looked at which customer videos were doing best and noticed the ones with a regular talking about a specific drink, like why they got oat milk, got more comments. So I started asking the baristas to flag customers who were happy to be filmed, and I kept the videos short, under 30 seconds, since the longer ones dropped off. I also put together a simple one-page summary for my manager with what worked and what I'd try next, like featuring a different regular each week.
Good. And did that second round of changes actually happen, or was that just your recommendation?

Honestly, the second round was mostly my recommendation. I did put together the one-page summary for my manager with what I'd try next, but I didn't run that next round myself before the internship ended. The three-month test with the customer videos is the part I actually carried out and measured. I should have been clearer about that earlier, and I don't want to overstate what I got to finish.

I appreciate you clarifying that. Sounds like you knew what the next step should be. Let me ask you this—you've been a customer at coffee shops for years, and now you've worked there. Has there been a time since you started the internship where something didn't go the way you expected, or where you had to change course?

Yeah, the launch event. I had a $1,500 budget and planned it for a store opening, and the speaker we'd booked cancelled the day before. I had to rethink the whole program fast. I ended up bringing in one of our baristas to do a latte-art demo, and we had 214 people check in at the door. It wasn't the event I'd planned, but it was a good reminder that people mostly come for the drinks and the people behind the counter.
What would you have done differently if you'd known the speaker was going to cancel earlier—like, a week out instead of the day before?

If I'd known a week out, I'd have had time to line up a backup before the speaker dropped, instead of scrambling. Honestly, I'd probably have asked the barista team earlier too, so the demo felt planned instead of a last-minute swap. I'd also have checked with the speaker about a contract or a cancellation clause when we booked, so I knew what our options were. And I'd have told the store manager sooner, so she could help with floor space and signage. The day-before scramble is what made it feel rushed, and a week of lead time would have given us room to do it properly.
That makes sense. Let me ask you about the survey you ran—you mentioned 500 responses. What did you actually ask people, and what did you do with what you found?

It was 512 responses, so a little more than the 500 on my resume. The big takeaway was that a lot of people wanted oat milk at no extra charge. I pulled that together and passed it along, and two of our stores trialed it. I can't tell you how it turned out across the whole chain, since the trial was still running when my internship ended.
When you were putting together the survey, did you design it yourself, or were you working off a template or something your manager gave you?

Honestly, I wrote the questions myself, but I started from a short list my manager gave me of what she wanted to know, mostly about drinks and pricing. I drafted the questions, then ran them past her and tightened the wording a bit. The survey tool itself was the one the company already used, so I didn't have to set anything up from scratch. I'd say the design was mine, but the topics were her call.
Got it. So the oat milk thing came out of that—did you recommend they try it at those two stores, or did your manager make that call?

Honestly, I recommended it, and my manager made the call to run the trial at those two stores. I put the survey results together with a short summary showing how many people asked for oat milk and that they wanted it without the extra charge. She took that to the operations side, and they picked two locations to test it. I didn't pick the stores myself, and I don't know the reasoning behind which two they chose.
Fair. One more thing—you also mentioned leading a team of four on a rebranding class project. Tell me about that. What was your role?

Yeah, that was a class project where we had to rebrand a fictional coffee shop. I was the team lead, so I ran the meetings, kept us on schedule, and split up the work. Two of my teammates disagreed about the logo. One wanted a bold, modern look and the other wanted something more classic. Hi, good to meet you too! My day's been pretty good, thanks. I had a coffee this morning, so I'm feeling awake. How about you, how's your day going so far?

That's helpful context. So when you say you pitched switching to customer videos—what did that pitch actually look like? Like, how did you convince your manager this was the move?

I went to my manager with a simple plan instead of just an idea. I'd been looking at which posts got the most response, and the ones that showed real people and the store felt more alive than our product shots. So I suggested we test short customer videos for a few months and track engagement against the old posts. She liked that it was a low-risk test with clear numbers, and she approved it.

Got it. And once you started posting those videos, what was your role in actually making that happen? Like, were you filming them, editing, posting—walk me through what you personally did week to week.

Mostly I handled the planning and day-to-day posting. I set up a weekly schedule, reached out to regulars and staff who were up for being on camera, and kept an eye on which clips got the most response so we could adjust. For filming, a couple of baristas helped with their phones, and I did the basic editing and captions myself. I tracked the numbers every week so we could tell if it was working.
That makes sense. So you were tracking week to week—what did you actually do if a video was underperforming? Did you change anything based on what you saw?

Yeah, I did. Early on, a few clips got a lot less response than I expected. The ones that did best had a short hook in the first couple of seconds and felt like a real moment, like a barista talking about their favorite drink. The ones that flopped were longer and more polished. So I started cutting them shorter, leading with the person instead of the menu item, and I stopped posting the ones that felt too staged. By the end of the three months, the average engagement rate was up from about 2.0% to 2.8%.
Makes sense. You mentioned you ran a few other projects too. What was one of the bigger ones you worked on?

The launch event for one of our new stores was probably the biggest. I was in charge of planning it, and we had a budget of $1,500. That's a good example of thinking on your feet. When you say 214 people checked in—was that the goal, or did you have a different target going in?

Honestly, I don't think we had a hard number set as a target going in. The resume line says planned for 200 guests, which is what we had in mind as a rough estimate for the invite list, so 214 checking in was a bit above that. I'd say the bigger win for me was that people were still there and engaged after the speaker fell through, not just the headcount.
Fair enough. Let me ask you this—in your first month if you landed this role, how would you approach learning what matters most to this team or company?

In the first couple of weeks I'd want to sit down with my manager and ask what success looks like for the marketing side, which numbers they care about most, and what's been tried before that didn't work. I'd also spend time in a few different stores, talking to baristas and regulars, since they know what customers actually respond to. That's a smart way to handle it. When you tested both logos with those classmates, how did you actually run that test? What did you show them, and what did you ask?

We kept it simple. Each of the two of them showed their logo to 10 classmates, one at a time, on the same screen. I asked people which one felt more like the business and which they'd remember, and I wrote down their answers. Most people picked the same one, so that's the one we went with.
Got it. I want to ask you something else. Tell me about a time you actually failed at something—not something you fixed with a clever workaround, but something that didn't go the way you wanted.

So when the results came back, I had a lot of numbers but not much sense of why people felt the way they did. The biggest finding, that people wanted oat milk at no extra charge, was clear, but I wished I'd asked a few follow-ups to understand the reasoning behind other answers. Next time I'd pilot the questions with a few people first, so I catch gaps like that before I send it out.
That's a fair point. Did you actually make that change with a later survey, or is that just something you'd do differently in hindsight?

Honestly, it's more of a hindsight thing so far. I haven't run another full survey since then. The oat milk result did get used, though. Two stores trialed it, so the survey led to something real. But I'd want to pilot the questions first on my next one.
Fair. Last thing I want to ask—why do you want to do this kind of work? Like, what draws you to marketing or this role specifically?

I like that marketing lets you see the result of your work pretty quickly. With the Instagram change, I could watch the engagement numbers move week to week and figure out what was working. That makes sense. I'm nearly out of time here, so let me ask—what questions do you have for me about the role or the team?

Good question. A typical week involves a mix of campaign planning, analyzing performance data, and collaborating with the store and product teams. That framework matters more than any single tactic. Does that help?

Yeah, that helps a lot, thanks. Knowing the measurement side comes first makes sense to me, since I'd want to understand what success looks like before I start changing things. Can I ask how the team usually decides which metrics matter most when they conflict, like engagement versus sales from a campaign?

That's a thoughtful follow-up. Honestly, it depends on the campaign and the business goal at the time. We don't have a hard rule, which is part of what I'd want you to learn early on—how to read what matters in the moment. We can dig into that more once you're in the role.

Thanks so much for taking the time today, Sam. I appreciated hearing about your work, especially how you think through problems and learn from data. We'll be in touch soon about next steps.

Thanks so much for having me, I really enjoyed the conversation. It sounds like a role where I'd get to keep learning from customers and the data, which is exactly what I'm hoping for. I'm looking forward to hearing about next steps, and thanks again for your time today.
You're welcome. Take care, and we'll talk soon.

My manager approved the plan, and I ran it week to week and watched which posts people actually responded to.

That's a good instinct on her part. So she essentially pushed you to slow down and isolate variables. Did that change how you approached the testing after that, or was it more just that one conversation?

It changed how I approached the rest of the project. Before that, I'd try three or four things in a week and then guess at why one worked. After she pushed back, I kept it to one main change at a time and held everything else as close to our usual posting as I could. That made it easier to say "the customer videos are what moved the number" instead of just hoping. Okay, so you helped design the tracking for the trial. What specifically did you measure, and how did you set that up?

Mostly I tracked oat milk orders at the two trial stores and compared them to our other locations, where we didn't change anything. My manager set the overall approach, and I handled the day-to-day data pulls.
Got it. And when you were pulling that data week to week, what kind of trends did you start to see? Did oat milk orders stay high, drop off, or was there something else that surprised you?

We had a $1,500 budget, and 214 people checked in, so it still worked, but I learned to line up a backup plan for anything I didn't control.
Okay, so the speaker fell through. Walk me through what you did in that day or two after you found out. How did you decide on the latte-art demo, and did you run it by anyone before you pivoted?

The speaker cancelled the day before the event, so I had about a day to fix it. First I talked to my manager, since she had approved the event budget and I didn't want to change the program without her knowing. I told her what happened and what I thought we could do with the time and money we had.

For the replacement, I wanted something that fit a coffee shop and that people could actually take part in. Our head barista was great at latte art, and it seemed like a natural fit, so I asked if she'd do a demo. Then I rearranged the schedule so the demo filled the speaker slot, and I made sure guests could try the drinks afterward. We stayed within the $1,500 budget, and 214 people checked in, so the event still went well even though it wasn't what we planned.
When you say the event "went well," what made you feel that way? Was it just the headcount, or did you measure something else?

Honestly, the headcount was the main thing I could point to. 214 people checked in, and that was the number we were aiming for. I didn't run a formal survey afterward, so I can't give you a satisfaction score. What I did see was people staying around the latte-art demo and going to the drink tasting, and a few of them asked about the next event, which felt like a good sign. I'd want to be clear that's me reading the room, not hard data.
That's fair. If you were planning a store launch event like that today, knowing what you know now, what would you do differently from the start?

If I were doing it again, I'd build a backup speaker into the plan from the start. Right now I'd line up two or three people I could call on short notice, and I'd confirm them about a week out so there's less chance of a last-minute cancellation. I'd also ask the speaker for a short written commitment, nothing fancy, just enough to make the booking feel real.

I'd also set up a simple feedback card or a quick sign-up at check-in. Last time I relied on the headcount and my read on the room, and I'd rather have actual numbers on what people liked, so I could compare it to our other events.
Makes sense. Let me ask you this—if you started in this role tomorrow, what's the first thing you'd want to understand about how the team actually works and what they care about?

Honestly, I'd want to know how decisions actually get made. At my current spot, I could see what my manager cared about because I was reporting to her every week, but I don't know how that works across a bigger team. I'd also want to understand what the team measures and what they count as a win. For me, it was engagement and open rates, but I'd want to know whether this team cares more about foot traffic, sales, or brand awareness, so I'm not optimizing for the wrong thing.
Good instinct. One last thing before we wrap up—why does this kind of role appeal to you? What draws you to marketing specifically, rather than something else in communications?

I like that marketing gives you a clear way to tell whether something worked. When I rewrote our newsletter subject lines and cut each email down to one topic, open rates went from about 18% to 27%, and that kind of result is what keeps me interested. Got it. Well, I think I've got a good sense of where you're at. Do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yes, just one. What does a typical week look like for an intern on this team, and what's the first project you'd hope someone in this role could take on?

The first project would probably be something like auditing how we're currently tracking engagement across channels, seeing where we have gaps, and recommending a simple framework we could use going forward. Well, I appreciate your time today. This was helpful, and we'll be in touch soon about next steps. Thanks for coming in.
