Yeah, everything's good, thanks for asking. The video link worked fine on my end. I'm glad to be here, and thanks for making time for me.
Great, glad it worked out. So, before we dive in, I'm curious—what brings you to apply for this role? What's drawing you to marketing right now?

I'm a communications major, and what keeps pulling me back is that marketing is where you can see right away whether something worked. Last year I had a chance to test that at a coffee chain, and I got hooked on the idea that a small change, like a subject line or a different kind of post, can move real numbers. I want a job where I'm learning from actual customer behavior every week, and I think a local coffee brand is a great place to do that because people have strong opinions about what they drink and where they go.
That makes sense. You clearly got a taste of it at the coffee chain. Let me back up a bit—walk me through your background. How'd you end up there, and what was your role?

Sure. I'm a communications major, and I picked up the marketing internship at a local coffee chain last year through a campus job board. My role was basically the marketing team's hands-on person: I handled social media, the customer email newsletter, and some of the in-store event planning. My manager gave me a lot of room to try things, which is how I ended up running a few experiments that I still think about.

Got it. So you were doing social, email, and events all at once—that's a lot. Let's dig into one of those. I saw on your resume you grew Instagram engagement by 40%. Walk me through what you actually changed and how you measured that.

Sure. When I started, our posts were mostly product photos, and the average engagement rate per post was about 2.0%. I pitched switching to short customer videos, like people ordering, a barista's favorite drink, a quick look at the store on a busy morning. My manager approved the plan, so I ran it for three months. I tracked engagement rate per post each week, and by the end it had gone from about 2.0% to 2.8%, which is the 40% on my resume.
Okay, so 2.0 to 2.8 is a 40% relative increase—got it. And those customer videos, were you filming those yourself, or did someone else handle that?

Mostly me, honestly. I had my phone and a small tripod, and I'd film during slower shifts or ask a barista to walk me through a drink. I did the editing too, keeping each clip under 30 seconds. Nobody on the marketing side had a dedicated video budget, so it was just me figuring it out as I went.
That's resourceful. Did you notice any difference in the types of videos that performed better than others, or was the lift pretty consistent across all of them?

Honestly, I didn't break it down as cleanly as I wish I had. I looked at the weekly averages, and the trend was steady, but I didn't tag each video by type and compare them one by one. The ones that seemed to do best were the barista clips where the person was talking to the camera, but that's my impression, not something I measured. If I ran it again, I'd tag every post so I could actually say which format worked.
Fair enough. That's good self-awareness. Let me ask you this—in your first month on the job here, how would you approach figuring out what your Instagram strategy should be?

I'd start by pulling the last few months of data to see which posts did well and which didn't, and I'd tag each one by format this time so I'm not guessing. Then I'd talk to the baristas and a few regulars, since they know what customers actually ask about. From there I'd pick two or three things to test, like the customer videos again with proper tagging, and give each one a clear measure before I start.
Good. Now, you also relaunched the customer email newsletter. What was different about the new version, and did you see a change in open rates?

Yeah, the newsletter was a good one to work on. Open rate went from 18% to 27% after the relaunch. Most of that came from two things: I rewrote the subject lines so they were specific instead of vague, and I cut each email down to one topic. Before, we'd cram a new drink, a store update, and a promo into one email, and nobody knew what to click. A designer did the template, so I focused on the words and the structure.
Nice. And how did you decide what that one topic should be each week? Was there a pattern to what people responded to?

Mostly I went with whatever had a real reason to happen that week, like a new seasonal drink, a store event, or something people had been asking about. I also looked at which topics got the most clicks in the old emails, and that helped me see what people cared about. I wouldn't call it a clean pattern, though. I didn't run a formal test comparing topics side by side. What I can say for sure is that the specific subject lines and the single-topic format are what changed the open rate, and the topic choice was more of a judgment call that I tried to ground in what customers had already responded to.
That makes sense. So you ran that survey with 500 responses—what did you actually want to learn from it, and what did you do with what you found?

I wanted to find out what customers actually wanted from the store, instead of guessing. The survey got 512 responses, which is a bit more than the 500 on my resume, so I'd say over 500 if you want to be precise.

The biggest finding was that a lot of people wanted oat milk, and they wanted it at no extra charge. That was a clear signal. I took it to the team with the numbers, and two stores ended up trialing it. I didn't get to see the full long-term results from that, since the internship wrapped up, but it was the most useful thing the survey turned up.
Did you do anything else with the survey results, or was oat milk the main thing that led to action?

Oat milk was the main thing that led to action. I also pulled out a few smaller points, like what people said about wait times and which drinks they ordered most, and I shared those with the marketing lead in a short summary. But nothing else got a trial the way oat milk did, so I'd be overstating it if I made it sound bigger than that.
Fair. Let me ask you something different—tell me about a time you actually failed at something, or something that didn't work out the way you hoped.

Yeah, the launch event is the one that comes to mind. We had a speaker lined up, and they cancelled the day before. I had about 24 hours to figure something out, so I asked one of our baristas to do a latte-art demo, and we set up a station right in the store. I still wasn't sure it would work, but 214 people checked in at the door on a $1,500 budget, and the demo ended up being what people talked about afterward.
So it sounds like it turned out okay. But what made you feel like it failed, or what would you have done differently?

I guess what made it feel like a miss was that the speaker was the main draw, and losing them the day before meant I was scrambling instead of just running the event. I didn't have a backup plan, so I had to come up with the latte-art demo in about 24 hours. If I did it again, I'd have a second option lined up before the big day and check in with the speaker a week out, not the night before.
That's a good lesson. One more thing—on that rebranding class project, you said you led a team of four. What was your role there, and was there a moment where the team disagreed on something?

Yeah, I was the team lead, so I kept us on schedule and made sure everyone had a clear piece of the work. And yes, there was a real disagreement. Two of my teammates had different ideas about the logo. One liked a bolder design and the other wanted something simpler, and they were both pretty committed to their picks.

Instead of picking one myself, I suggested we test both with people outside the group. We each showed the two options to about 10 classmates and asked which one they'd remember and which felt more like a coffee brand. The simpler one came out ahead, and we went with it. I think it helped that the decision came from the data, so nobody felt like they'd lost an argument.
That's smart. Did the person who wanted the bolder design actually feel good about that outcome, or did they still think you should've gone with theirs?

I can't say for sure how they felt inside. What I saw was that they were fine with it in the moment. They helped with the final version and didn't push back once we'd tested it. Honestly, I think they still liked their design, and I'd be guessing if I said they were fully happy. I did check in with them afterward, and they said the test made sense, but I wouldn't claim more than that.
Makes sense. We're almost out of time, so let me ask—do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, one question: what does a typical week look like for someone in this role, and how much of the work is planned ahead versus reacting to what's happening in the stores?

Good question. It's probably 60-40, planned versus reactive. You'll have campaigns and content calendars you're building out, but stores will have issues, a competitor will do something, or a seasonal opportunity pops up. You need to be ready for both. The person in this role reports to me, and I try to give them space to own the day-to-day while we sync on strategy weekly.

Anything else?

That's helpful, thanks. The 60-40 split sounds like a good balance, and I like that you sync weekly but give space for ownership. I think I'd want to know how the team decides what gets priority when a store issue and a planned campaign collide, but I'm happy with that answer for now. That's all from me.

Great. Well, thanks so much for taking the time to talk through all this today. I appreciated hearing about what you learned at the coffee chain, and how you think through problems. We'll be in touch next week with next steps. Thanks again, Sam.

Thanks so much for having me, I really enjoyed the conversation. I appreciate you walking me through the role and the team. I'm looking forward to hearing about next steps next week. Have a great rest of your day.
You too. Take care!

There was a bit of pushback at first from one of them, who wanted to stick with the design they liked, but once I framed it as "let's see what people actually respond to," they came around.
Got it. We're almost out of time here, so let me ask—do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?

Don't just hand off the data; know what it means. Does that make sense?

Yeah, that makes sense, and it's pretty much how I like to work already. Owning one small project from start to finish, including the numbers, is exactly what I'm hoping for. Thanks for walking me through it, and I'm really interested in this role. Is there anything else you'd like me to follow up on?

No, I think we covered good ground. Thanks for being thoughtful and honest about what you knew and didn't know—that matters to us. We'll be in touch in the next few days with next steps. Good luck, Sam.

Thanks so much, I really appreciate you taking the time. I enjoyed the conversation, and I'm excited about the role. Looking forward to hearing from you in the next few days. Have a great rest of your day!

transcript.text: Hey, good to meet you. How's your day been so far?
Hi, thanks, good to meet you too. My day's been pretty good, a bit of a rush this morning getting here on time, but I'm glad to be talking with you now. How about you, how's your day going?

Good, thanks for asking. Busy as always, but that's the job. So, I've got your resume here. Why don't you walk me through your background a bit—how'd you end up doing marketing work at the coffee chain, and what's that been like so far?

Sure. I'm a communications major, and I wanted real work experience before graduating, so I applied for the marketing internship at the coffee chain. My first few months were mostly learning how they talk to customers, both on social media and through email. Over time I got to own a few projects of my own, which has been the best part. I've been really focused on figuring out what actually gets people to pay attention and act, not just what looks good. If you want, I can go into one of those projects in more detail.
Yeah, absolutely. Which one feels like the best example of that—of figuring out what actually gets people to pay attention?

I'd say the Instagram work. When I took it over, our posts were mostly product photos, and engagement was sitting around 2% per post. I suggested switching to short videos of real customers talking about their drinks, and my manager approved the plan. Over three months the average engagement rate went up to about 2.8%, which is the 40% jump on my resume.
Got it. So you went from 2% to 2.8%—that's the 40% you mentioned. Walk me through what you actually changed week to week. Like, when did you post the first customer video, and what happened?

Honestly, I don't have the exact dates in my head. I started by testing a handful of short customer videos alongside the regular photo posts so I could compare them. I tracked engagement on each one and kept adjusting based on what got people to stop scrolling and actually comment. If you want the specifics on which video did best and when, I'd want to pull up my notes so I don't give you the wrong details.
That's fair. So when you say you kept adjusting—what's one specific change you made based on what you saw?

One thing I noticed early was that the longer videos lost people after the first few seconds. So I cut them down to under 15 seconds and started the video with the customer's face and a line about their drink, not the cup itself. Engagement on those was noticeably higher than the earlier ones, and that's the kind of change that pushed the average up over the three months.
That makes sense. And when you say engagement was noticeably higher—how were you measuring that? Was it likes, comments, shares, or a mix?

Mostly the platform's engagement rate per post, which combines likes, comments, and shares, and I was watching the overall trend rather than one metric alone. I can't break down exactly how much came from each, though, so I wouldn't want to guess at that split. Also, I want to be careful about something I said earlier. I gave you a specific c
No worries. Take your time.

Sorry, I got ahead of myself there. I gave you a specific video length and opening shot earlier, and I can't back those up from my notes. What I can say for sure is that I switched from product photos to short customer videos, my manager approved it, and average engagement went from about 2% to 2.8% over three months.
I appreciate you being honest about that. So your manager approved the switch—what made you confident it was the right direction to try in the first place?

I'd been looking at the comments and DMs, and people kept asking about the drinks themselves, like how a seasonal one tasted or whether it was sweet. The product photos showed the cup but didn't answer any of that. Customers talking about their own orders seemed like a better way to answer those questions, so I put together a short plan with a few test posts and a way to measure them. My manager was open to trying it as a limited experiment, which made it easy to say yes.
Makes sense. So beyond Instagram, you also did work on the email newsletter—you said you relaunched it. What was the state of it before you touched it, and what did you change?

The newsletter was in rough shape. Open rate was around 18%, and the emails were long roundups with five or six topics crammed into each one, so people didn't know what the email was about. I rewrote the subject lines to be more specific and cut each email down to one topic. A designer did the template, so my part was mostly the writing and the structure. After the changes, open rate went up to about 27%.
That's a solid jump. Did you test the subject line changes separately, or did you change the subject lines and the structure at the same time?

Honest answer: I changed them together, so I can't say how much of the lift came from the subject lines versus the one-topic structure. I didn't run a proper A/B test on the subject lines. If I had to guess, the structure probably mattered more, since people could tell right away what each email was about, but that's a guess, not something I measured. Next time I'd split the list and test one change at a time.
That's fair. And when you say the open rate went to 27%—over how many sends did you average that, and how long did you wait before calling it a win?

I don't have the exact number of sends in front of me, so I don't want to give you a made-up count. What I can say is that I was looking at the open rate across the newsletter sends after the relaunch, and I didn't call it a win off one email. It held up across several sends, which is why I felt okay reporting it. If you want the precise send count and timeframe, I'd need to check my notes before I give you a number.
Fair enough. Let me shift gears a bit. You also ran a customer survey with about 500 responses. What was the goal going in, and what did you actually do with what you learned?

The goal was to figure out what customers actually wanted from us beyond the menu we already had. We got 512 responses, which is a good number to work with. The biggest finding was that a lot of people wanted oat milk at no extra charge. I brought that to the team, and two stores trialed it. I didn't run the trial myself, so I can't speak to the final results from those stores, but it was a real signal from the customers that led to a real test.
Did you help design the survey, or did you mostly run it once it was already set up?

I helped design it, though I wouldn't say I owned it. My manager had the basic goal, which was learning what customers wanted beyond the current menu, and I drafted most of the questions. I kept them short and mostly multiple choice so people would actually finish it, and I added a couple of open-ended questions at the end for anything we might have missed. Then I handled distribution and pulled the responses together. I'd want to double-check my notes before I say exactly how many questions it had, though.
Okay. And one more thing on that—did you look at the responses yourself and spot the oat milk pattern, or did your manager flag it?

I went through the responses myself, and the oat milk thing showed up in a lot of the open-ended answers, not just the multiple choice. Once I saw how many people mentioned it, I pulled those comments together and brought them to my manager. So I spotted the pattern, and then we talked about whether it was worth testing.
Got it. I want to ask you something broader before we wrap up. Tell me about a time you failed or something didn't go the way you planned at the coffee chain.

The clearest one was the store launch event. We had a budget of about $1,500 and a speaker lined up, and the speaker cancelled the day before. I had about a day to fix it. I talked to the store manager and we decided to replace the talk with a latte-art demo from one of our baristas, which was something people could watch and actually take part in. We had 214 people check in at the door, so it still drew a good crowd. The lesson for me was to always have a backup plan for anything that depends on one person, and to think about what the audience actually came for.
When you say 214 checked in at the door—how did you count attendance before that, or was that the first time you had a solid number?

I'm not sure how the count was set up beforehand. I know 214 people checked in at the door, but I don't remember whether we had an RSVP list or a headcount target going in, and I'd rather not guess at that. If you want, I can check with the store manager or my notes and get back to you on how we tracked it.
No worries. So the speaker cancelled—was that something you could have seen coming, or was it just bad luck?

Honestly, I think it was mostly bad luck. The speaker had confirmed and we'd been in touch about the details, so nothing in the emails or calls looked like a warning sign. I don't know the reason they dropped out, and I didn't push for it, so I can't say whether there was anything we could have caught. What I did take from it is that we should have had a backup option lined up for anything that depends on one person, even when things look solid.
Makes sense. One last question before we wrap—why do you want to do this kind of work? What's pulling you toward marketing or communications roles?

I like that marketing sits right where people's attention and actual decisions meet. Working on the Instagram posts and the newsletter, I got hooked on the moment when you change something and you can see people respond differently. It's not just making things look nice. You get to test an idea, learn from it, and make the next one better. I also like working with people who aren't marketers, like the baristas who ran the demo, because they know the customers better than any dashboard does. That's helpful. So I've got a couple more things I'd like to circle back to if we have time, but first—do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, I do. What does a typical week look like for someone in this role, and how much of the work is planning versus hands-on execution?

Good question. It's probably 60-40, execution to planning. You'll spend time running campaigns, analyzing results, and working with the creative team, but you're also in meetings scoping out what we're testing next quarter. You'll own projects from start to finish, so you're not just handing things off. It's fast-paced, and you learn quickly what works and what doesn't.

Any other questions?

That's okay. But I'm curious—when you say the feedback was pretty useful, did anything actually change because of it? Like, did the team do anything differently after you got those 500 responses?
Oh, yeah, um, I think so. The big thing people kept asking for was oat milk without the extra charge, and I think two of the stores actually tried it out.

Okay, so that's a concrete ask that came out of the survey. Walk me through your part in that—did you present the results to your manager, or how did that feedback actually get to the people who could make that decision?

Um, yeah, I think I put together a summary and shared it with my manager. Honestly, I don't remember the exact meeting. I know the oat milk thing was the one that stood out, and that's kind of what got people talking.
Sure. And do you know if the oat milk pricing change actually moved the needle for the business, or did you check back on that after they rolled it out?

Um, I'm not totally sure, honestly. The two stores trialed it, and I think they were watching sales, but I didn't really get to see the results myself. I moved on to some other projects after that, so I don't know if they ended up rolling it out everywhere or what the numbers looked like.

That's a solid approach. And when you presented the results to your team, how did the two people who disagreed react to that?

Um, I think they were both kind of okay with it? Nobody really fought it once they saw the feedback. One of them was a little annoyed at first, I think, because it was her version that lost, but she came around. It wasn't a big blowup or anything.

Makes sense. So we're almost at the end here. Before we wrap, I want to ask you something more open-ended. Tell me about a time you actually failed at something—at work, in school, wherever. What happened?

Um, yeah, I think I just like the part where you figure out what actually makes people pay attention to something. Like, with the Instagram stuff, seeing a real customer talking about their order got way more response than the product shots did, and that was kind of satisfying. I like that it's a mix of creative stuff and actually looking at what's working. Honestly I'm still figuring out exactly what kind of marketing I want to focus on, but I know I want to keep doing work where I can see the results.
That's fair. Well, I appreciate you walking through all of that. Do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?

There are meetings, but we try to keep them focused. You'd probably have a couple standing meetings with your team each week, and then project-specific stuff as needed.

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for coming in. Did you find everything okay today?
Yeah, everything's good, thanks for asking. The video call worked fine on my end. I'm glad to be here, and I appreciate you making time for me.
Great, glad it's working smoothly. So, what drew you to this role? What made you think it'd be a good fit for you?

I've been drawn to marketing for a while, mostly because I like seeing how small changes in how a brand talks to people actually move the needle. Coffee is a good example. People are loyal to a place they feel like they know, and I think a local chain has a lot of room to build that. When I saw this internship, it seemed like a place where I could learn by doing, across social, events, and email, instead of just reading about it in class. I also like that it's a local brand, so you can see the results pretty quickly.

That makes sense. You mentioned seeing results quickly with a local brand—I'm curious, in your time at the coffee chain, what's one result that actually stuck with you? Like, something where you could point to it and say, yeah, that worked?

The one that really stuck was Instagram. We noticed our product photos weren't getting much response, so we switched to short videos of actual customers. Over about three months, our average engagement rate per post went from roughly 2% to 2.8%. What I liked was that it was a clear before and after, and the team could see it in the numbers, not just feel good about it.

Okay, so you went from 2% to 2.8%—that's the 40% you mentioned on your resume. What specifically did you do to make that switch happen? Like, was that your idea, or how did you get the team to try it?

Honestly, the idea came out of looking at our post numbers. Product shots were getting the same few likes every time, so I put together a plan to switch to short videos of real customers and took it to my manager. She approved it, and we tested it over about three months. I tracked engagement each week so we could see whether it was working.
Got it. So you proposed it and tracked it—did you actually shoot and edit those customer videos yourself, or did someone else do that part?

Good question. I wouldn't want to overstate it. The team handled the filming and editing together, and my part was putting the plan together, pitching it to my manager, and tracking the engagement each week. So I can speak

No problem. So you were really driving the strategy and measurement side of it. That's clear.

Let me ask you about something else on your resume—you ran a customer survey with 500 responses. What did you actually learn from that, and did anything change because of what you found?

Sure. The survey got 512 responses, so we went a bit over the 500 on the resume. The team pulled out a few themes, and the big one was that a lot of people wanted oat milk, and they wanted it without paying extra for it. That was a clear signal, so we decided to trial it, and two of our stores ran that trial. I'd say the survey was the team's work overall, and that finding is what really stuck with us.
When you say the team pulled out the themes—what was your part in analyzing the survey results?

Fair question. I ran the survey, so I set it up, got it out to customers, and kept track of the responses. For the analysis, I went through the written comments and grouped them, and that's where the oat milk pattern jumped out. Then I brought it to the team, and we talked through whether it was worth a trial. So I was closer to the center of it than I made it sound a minute ago.
Okay. So you did the legwork on finding that pattern. Did you follow up on whether the trial actually moved the needle for the stores that ran it?

Honestly, I don't have a clean answer on that. Two stores ran the trial, and I know that's what the team decided, but I didn't pull together the results for those stores myself. I'd be guessing if I gave you a number, and I'd rather not do that. If I'd been in charge of that follow-up, I'd have wanted to compare sales and oat milk orders at the trial stores against the stores that didn't try it.

Fair enough. I appreciate that you didn't guess. 

Let me ask you this—tell me about a time you actually failed at something. Could be at the coffee chain or anywhere else.

Sure. The one that comes to mind is our store launch event. We'd planned it for a while, with about a $1,500 budget, and the speaker we'd lined up cancelled the day before. We had to figure out something fast. Our team decided to swap in a latte-art demo by one of our baristas. I handled reaching out to her and getting the setup sorted that day. It wasn't the event we'd planned, and I'd have liked more lead time. But we still had 214 people check in at the door.

What I took from it is that a backup plan matters as much as the main one, especially with events. Now I always ask, early on, what happens if a key piece falls through.
That's helpful context. When you say 214 people checked in—was that close to what you were expecting, or did that number surprise you?

Honestly, I don't have a target number I can point to. We didn't go in with a hard attendance goal that I can remember, so I can't say whether 214 beat it or fell short. What I can say is that it was a solid turnout for a store event, and it was good enough that the day still felt like a win after the speaker fell through. If I'd been the one setting the goal, I'd have wanted a number to measure against.
Makes sense. So when you were planning the event originally, how'd you come up with that $1,500 budget? Did someone give you a number to work with, or did you build it from scratch?

I don't remember exactly how that number got set, to be honest. I know $1,500 was the budget we worked with for the event, but I'd be making up the back story if I said who came up with it or how we built it. I'd rather tell you that than guess. If it helps, I can talk about how I'd approach a budget now: start with what the event needs to do, then price out the big items first.
That's fair. Shifting gears a bit—on your resume you mention you led a team of four on a rebranding class project. Walk me through what that actually looked like.

So it was a class project where we had to rebrand a small business, and there were four of us. The team split up the work, like research, the messaging, and the visuals. The big moment was when two of my teammates disagreed about the logo. One liked a bolder design and the other wanted something simpler. Instead of arguing about it, the team decided to test both. We each had 10 classmates look at the two versions, and we went with the one that people responded to more. It kept us from spending the whole week debating taste.
Got it. So when the two teammates disagreed, what did you actually do in that moment? Like, did you suggest testing both, or did something else happen?

Honestly, I was the one who suggested it. Both of them were pretty set on their designs, and the debate was going in circles. I said we should stop arguing and get some real feedback. I had each of them run their logo past 10 classmates, and we went with the one people responded to more. I should have said that up front instead of talking about the team's decision.

Right. That makes sense. So you stepped in and reframed it around data instead of opinion. That worked.

One more thing—why do you actually want this kind of role? I know you talked about the coffee chain earlier, but what is it about marketing work that pulls you in?

I like that marketing forces you to pay attention to what people actually respond to. You can have a strong opinion about a post or a subject line, but the audience tells you whether it lands. I found that really satisfying at the coffee chain, especially with the Instagram switch and the newsletter, where you could see the numbers move.

I also like the mix. Social, events, email, and design all touch the same customer, so you get to see how the pieces fit together. I'd like to keep learning that across a team, and I think this role would give me that.
That's clear. Before we wrap up, do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, I do. What does a typical week look like for an intern here, and is there a project you'd want the new person to own by the end of the summer?

Good questions. A typical week is pretty mixed—you'd be helping with social content, supporting event planning, and touching the email calendar. There's usually one bigger project running in the background. This summer, we're planning a redesign of our website, so there'd be a chance to own some of the messaging side of that, working with the design team.

Thanks for taking the time to talk through all this. We've got a lot to discuss internally, and we'll be in touch in the next week or so. Good luck with the rest of your semester.

verdicts.notes: Strength: the interviewer caught "we" language early (T6, T16) and got the candidate to state their own role, then probed details like the budget and the logo preference. Weakness: it skipped the email newsletter topic entirely, and it gave small bits of evaluative feedback ("That's solid", "That's smart"). It also never followed up on the survey trial result or the vague "why this role" answer.

Hi, thanks for having me. Things are good, thanks for asking. I've been wrapping up a few things with school and getting ready for this, so it's nice to finally talk. How's your day going?

I'm a communications major, so I like the idea of taking something people already enjoy and figuring out how to make them want to come back.

That makes sense. You mentioned seeing what works with real customers quickly—I'm guessing that's something you've experienced in your current internship. Can you walk me through one project where you actually saw that feedback loop in action?

Sure. The one that really showed me the feedback loop was Instagram. Our team noticed our posts were mostly polished product photos, and they weren't getting much back. So we decided to try short videos of actual customers, like people talking about their drinks or what they order. We ran it for about three months and kept an eye on the numbers as we went. Average engagement per post went from about 2 percent to about 2.8 percent. That's where the 40 percent comes from. What I liked most was how fast the data told us something. We could see within a few weeks which kinds of videos people responded to, and we adjusted from there.
Got it. So when you say "we decided" to try the videos and "we kept an eye on the numbers"—what was your specific piece of that? What did you actually do versus what did the rest of the team handle?

Sure, I can be more specific. I was the one who made the switch. I was running the posting, so I changed the content from product photos to short videos of customers talking about their drinks. I pitched it to my manager, and she approved the plan. Then I tracked the engagement numbers each week and adjusted which kinds of videos we posted. So "we" was a bit of a habit on my part, but the change itself was mine to make, with my manager's sign-off.
That's helpful. So you were deciding what to post and tracking how it performed. When you adjusted which kinds of videos you posted, what's one change you made based on what you saw?

One thing I noticed was that the videos where the customer was just talking naturally did better than the ones that felt staged. So I leaned toward those, shorter and more casual, and cut back on the ones that felt like ads. I don't want to make it sound more scientific than it was, though. It was mostly watching which posts got more reactions and comments and doing more of that.
Fair enough. So you made that shift and stuck with it for the rest of the three months, or did something else surprise you as you kept going?

Yeah, something did surprise me. I figured the customer videos would work best with regulars, but some of the most engaged posts were from people who didn't come in very often. Their videos seemed to get more attention because they were a little different from what people usually see from the shop. So I started looking more at who was in the videos, not just how they looked. I kept the switch for the full three months, but that's the part that changed how I picked which customers to feature.
That's interesting. Did that insight lead to anything? Like, did you change how you approached finding or asking customers to be in the videos after that?

Not in a big way, honestly. I was mostly asking people who were already friendly with the staff and happy to be on camera. Looking back, I also got a bit ahead of myself with that point about less frequent customers. It was more of a hunch from a few posts than a clear pattern, so I wouldn't want to make it sound stronger than it was. What I'm more confident about is that the casual, unposed videos did better, and that's what we
No worries. Sounds like you learned something useful either way. Let me ask you this—tell me about a time you failed. What's something that didn't go the way you hoped?

Sure. The one that comes to mind is the store launch event. We planned it for about 200 guests with a $1,500 budget, and the main speaker cancelled the day before. We were scrambling. The team talked it through, and we decided to swap in a latte-art demo with one of our baristas. It wasn't the plan we'd built, and I wasn't sure it would land.

It ended up going fine. About 214 people checked in at the door. What I took from it is that we should have had a backup for the program, not just the venue and the food. We don't really have a backup plan for anything that depends on one person showing up. So now we always line up a second option before we confirm a speaker.

I hear you. So the event didn't fall apart, which is good. But I'm curious—when the speaker cancelled, what did you personally do in that scramble? Walk me through your role in deciding to swap in the barista demo.
My part was smaller than it might sound. The team was figuring out what to do,
Take your time.

Honestly, I was the one who planned the event, so when the speaker dropped out, it fell to me to find a replacement fast. I talked to my manager, suggested the latte-art demo, and then I lined up one of our baristas to do it. The team helped with the logistics, but the swap was my call. I was also a bit vague before, so I should say that plainly.
I appreciate that. So you made the call and it worked out. What would you do differently if you were planning that event from scratch now?

I'd line up a backup program before the event, not just a backup for the venue and food. Right now we confirm one speaker and hope they show up. If I did it again, I'd have a second option ready, like a barista demo or a local roaster, and I'd check in with the speaker a week out and again the day before. I'd also set aside some of the $1,500 as a cushion so a last-minute swap doesn't mean scrambling for money on top of everything else.
That's solid. You mentioned the budget was $1,500 for 200 guests. How did you break that down? What were the big line items?

I don't have the exact line-item breakdown in front of me, and I'd rather not guess at specific dollar amounts. The big buckets were food and drinks for the guests, the space and setup, and some printed materials and signage. Food and drinks took the largest share, as I recall. If you want the exact split, I can dig up the budget sheet and send it to you. I'm sure we tracked it, I just don't have the numbers memorized.
Fair enough. I appreciate the honesty. Let me ask you this—you also ran a customer survey with 500 responses. What did you learn from that, and what actually changed because of it?

The survey was 512 responses, so a bit more than 500. The biggest thing people kept coming back to was oat milk. A lot of customers wanted it, and they wanted it at no extra charge. That was the clearest signal in the whole thing.

What changed is that the team took that finding and ran a trial. Two stores tested offering oat milk without the upcharge. I helped put the survey together and analyzed the results, so I was close to the data, but the decision to trial it came from the team and leadership. I don't know yet how the trial turned out in terms of sales, so I'd want to check that before I say it was a success.

Good—so you saw the signal and passed it up, and they moved on it. Before the survey, did you have a sense of what you were looking for, or did you just ask a bunch of questions and see what came back?

Mostly we had a rough idea. We wanted to know what made people come back, what they'd pay more for, and what annoyed them. But we kept the questions pretty open, so we weren't steering people too hard toward an answer. That's partly why the oat milk thing stood out. It came up in a lot of the open-ended comments, not just the multiple choice questions. I'd say the goal was to learn what customers cared about, and I was glad we didn't go in with a specific answer already in mind.
Makes sense. One more thing before we wrap up—you led a team of four on a rebranding class project. What was your role there, and did anything come up where you and the team didn't see eye to eye?

I was the team lead, so I kept us on schedule and made sure everyone had a clear piece to own. The one real disagreement was over the logo. Two of my teammates had different favorites, and both felt strongly about theirs. Instead of picking one based on who argued harder, we had both designs tested with about 10 classmates each. We asked them which one they remembered, which one fit the brand, and which one they'd want on a cup. The results pointed pretty clearly one way, so we went with that one. Both teammates were fine with it because they'd seen how people reacted, not just heard our opinions.
That's smart. But I'm curious—what was your gut on the logo? Did you have a preference going in, or did you stay neutral the whole time?

Honestly, I had a slight lean going in, but I tried not to let it drive anything. I figured if I pushed my favorite, the other two would dig in harder, and then we'd just be arguing about who was more stubborn. So I kept my opinion to myself and let the testing make the call. I was a little surprised when the results didn't match my lean, but that was kind of the point of testing it.
Fair. Okay, I think that covers the main ground. Do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, one question: what does a typical week look like for someone in this role, and who would I be working with most day to day?

Good question. You'd be working pretty closely with our store operations team and the regional manager. A lot of your time early on would be supporting store events, social media, and maybe some customer feedback loops like you've been doing. You'd also sit in on some broader marketing planning with our small central team. It's not a huge operation, so you'd wear a few hats, but you'd have pretty direct visibility into what's working and what's not. Does that sound like the kind of thing you're looking for?

That sounds like a good fit. I like that it's small enough that I'd see the results of what I'm working on, not just hand off a deck and hear nothing back. Working with store ops would be useful too, since that's where the customer stuff actually happens. Thanks for walking me through it. I really appreciate you taking the time today.
Great. Thanks for being thoughtful in your answers, and for the specifics. We'll be in touch soon with next steps. Good luck with wrapping up school, and thanks again.

verdicts.notes: Strength: the interviewer covered all five topics and both practice questions. It pressed on personal ownership in the survey (T16–T21) and the newsletter (T26). Weakness: it asked about the store launch event only as a failure question, and it never asked for a concrete result on the team project. It also leaked mild praise at T24 and T30, and its hypothetical "what if" questions in T8 and T24 were less useful than asking for specifics.

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for taking the time. How are things going on your end?

Hi, thanks for having me. Things are going well, thanks for asking. I've been finishing up my last semester and getting ready for the summer, so it's a busy but good stretch. I'm excited to talk about the marketing role, since it's the kind of work I've been trying to get into.
That's great. Sounds like good timing then. So walk me through your background a bit—how'd you end up where you are now, and what's your experience been like so far?

Sure. I'm a communications major, and I've been doing marketing work through a local coffee chain as an intern. That's where most of my hands-on experience comes from. I got into it because I like figuring out what makes people actually care about a brand, not just what sounds good on paper.

Over the past year, the team I've been on has done a few things I'm proud of. We worked on the Instagram account and shifted away from mostly product photos toward short customer videos. Over about three months, the average engagement rate per post went from around 2% to about 2.8%, which is roughly a 40% lift. We also planned a store launch event, and when our speaker cancelled the day before, we switched to a latte-art demo from one of our baristas. About 214 people checked in that day, on a budget of $1,500.

We also relaunched the customer email newsletter. Open rates went from about 18% to 27%, mostly because we tightened up the subject lines and went to one topic per email. And we ran a customer survey that got 512 responses. The biggest thing people wanted was oat milk at no extra charge, and two of our stores ended up trialing that.

Those are the highlights. What would you most like to hear more about?

That's helpful context. Let me dig into the Instagram work a bit, since that's something you led. When you shifted to those customer videos, what was the thinking there? Like, why did you believe that would move the needle?

Sure. I was the one who made the switch. Our posts were mostly product photos, and they weren't getting much response. I figured short videos of real customers would feel more like a person talking than an ad, and people tend to engage more with that. I pitched the change to my manager, and she approved it. Then I tried it over a few months and tracked how the engagement rate moved.

Got it. So you noticed the product photos weren't working, pitched the idea, and then ran it. When you say you tracked how it moved—what did that process actually look like? Like, how were you measuring week to week?

Honestly, it was pretty simple. I looked at the engagement rate on each post, which is the likes, comments, and shares divided by reach, and then tracked the average across the posts each month. I didn't build a detailed weekly dashboard or anything fancy. I'd check the numbers from the Instagram insights, see how the latest posts compared to the ones before, and keep an eye on whether the videos were actually getting more response than the product photos had.

I'll be upfront that three months isn't a huge sample, so I wouldn't call it a perfect experiment. But the trend was consistent enough that we kept going with it. If I did it again, I'd want to set up a clearer baseline before making the change, so the comparison would be cleaner.
That makes sense. You mentioned your manager approved it—what would you have done differently if she'd said no to the video idea?

Honestly, I'd have taken her feedback seriously and tried to figure out what was behind it. Maybe she had concerns about brand consistency, or about the time it would take to film and edit. I'd want to understand that before pushing back.

If it still made sense to me, I might have proposed a smaller test first, like a few customer videos alongside the regular product posts, so we could compare the two without committing the whole account to it. And if she still said no, I'd have kept posting the product photos and looked for other ways to make them land better, like tighter captions or posting at different times. I'd still want to know why it wasn't working, even if we didn't make the video change.
Fair enough. Now, let me ask you this—tell me about a time you actually failed at something, or something that didn't go the way you hoped.

Sure. The one that comes to mind is the store launch event. Our speaker cancelled the day before, so we had a pretty stressful evening trying to figure out what to do. We didn't have a backup plan for that, which in hindsight was a gap.

The team pulled together and we switched to a latte-art demo from one of our baristas. It went okay. About 214 people checked in on a $1,500 budget. But I wouldn't call it a win, because the event was built around a speaker and we had to scramble. Now when we plan events, we line up a backup activity ahead of time, so one cancellation doesn't throw the whole thing off.
What would you have done differently in the planning phase, before the cancellation happened?

Honestly, the biggest thing would have been confirming the speaker earlier and more firmly. We had a verbal yes and assumed that was locked in, and we didn't check in with them close to the date. A reminder a week out and a written confirmation would have given us warning if something was shifting.

We also should have planned a backup from the start. Once we knew the speaker was a risk, we could have lined up a second activity, like a barista demo or a tasting, and kept it on standby. That would have made the cancellation a small change instead of a scramble.
Makes sense. So stepping back—why are you interested in this kind of marketing role? What draws you to it?

I like work where you can see whether something actually landed. On the coffee chain side, we'd try something, look at the numbers, and figure out what people responded to. The Instagram switch to customer videos and the newsletter changes were both like that. Seeing the engagement and open rates move made me want to keep doing this kind of work.

I also like that marketing sits right where people and business meet. The survey taught me that. Customers wanted oat milk at no extra charge, and that's a real product decision, not just a campaign. This role looks like it has that same mix of creative work and data, and that's the part I'm most excited about.

That's clear. Let me ask you about the survey real quick. You ran it with 500 responses and found out about the oat milk request. Walk me through what you personally did—like, how did you design it, who ran it, and what happened after you got the results?
Sure. The team ran the survey, and we got 512 responses. The main thing that stood out was that people wanted oat milk
Sorry, I want to make sure I'm clear on your specific role. Did you design the survey questions, or did someone else do that?

Honestly, the questions were a team effort. I was part of the group that put them together and helped get the survey out, but I don't want to take credit for designing it on my own. I was more involved in going through the responses afterward and pulling out what stood out, and that's where the oat milk finding came from.
Got it. So you analyzed the results and surfaced the oat milk insight. What did you do with that finding once you had it?

Honestly, I'm not sure I can say I did the most with it personally. I flagged the oat milk request when I was going through the responses, and I shared it with my manager and the team. From there, the team decided to try it out, and two of our stores ran a trial with oat milk at no extra charge. I helped put the findings together for that conversation, but the decision and the trial were the team's call.
Fair enough. Let me ask you about the rebranding class project you led. Walk me through what that project was and what your role actually was.

Sure. It was a rebranding project for a class, and I was the one coordinating the group of four. We had to pitch a refreshed brand identity by the end of the semester, so I kept us on schedule and made sure everyone had a piece they owned.

The logo was the tricky part. Two of my teammates strongly disagreed about which direction to go. Rather than just picking one, I suggested we test both with people outside the group. We showed each version to 10 classmates, asked which one felt more trustworthy and which one they'd remember, and went with the one that did better. The group was on board because it wasn't just one person's opinion. That's probably the part I'm most glad I handled that way.
That's a smart approach. What if the testing had come out split, or what if people had no clear preference between the two?

Honestly, we would've had to make a call anyway, but we'd have made it differently. If the feedback was split, we'd look at the reasons people gave, not just the votes. Maybe one version got picked for trustworthiness and the other for memorability, and that would tell us which quality mattered more for a coffee brand.

If people had no clear preference, that's useful too. It probably means both options were fine, so we'd pick based on what fit the brand's overall direction, or we'd test a third option with a slightly different angle. We'd also talk to a few people one-on-one, since a short survey doesn't always catch why someone likes something.

With only 10 people, a split result would be a signal to dig deeper, not a final answer. We'd be upfront with the group about that, so nobody felt like the decision was just a coin flip.
Got it. Last thing before we wrap up—you relaunched the email newsletter and saw open rates go from 18 to 27 percent. What was your specific role in making that happen?

I rewrote a lot of the subject lines myself, and I also pushed for going to one topic per email instead of cramming in several. The designer handled the template, so the look of the emails was their work. The open rate went from about 18% to 27%, and the subject lines and the one-topic change were the parts I owned most directly.
Makes sense. Do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yes, one question: what does a typical week look like for someone in this role, and how much of the work is hands-on versus planning?

Good question. It's pretty mixed. You're running campaigns and tracking results, so there's definitely hands-on work—writing copy, analyzing data, that kind of thing. But you're also planning ahead, working cross-team, and making sure things align with the bigger strategy. I'd say it's probably 60 percent execution, 40 percent planning and collaboration, though it shifts depending on what's live.

Well, I think we've covered a lot of ground. Thanks for taking the time to talk through all this, Sam. We'll be in touch soon about next steps.

Thanks so much for the time, I really enjoyed the conversation. That 60/40 split sounds like a good balance, and it fits what I've been looking for. I'm happy to send anything else over if it would help, and I look forward to hearing about next steps.
Perfect. We'll be in touch. Take care!

That's a solid way to break a tie.

verdicts.notes: Strength: good ownership probing on the "we" answers (T6, T18, T22), and it covered all topics plus both practice questions and invited the candidate's questions. Weakness: it cut the candidate's truncated answers short (T7, T9) without getting the number or the baseline, and it gave evaluative praise several times (T8, T16, T22, T26).

Okay, that's solid. Let me zoom in on the Instagram piece since you mentioned it first. You said you noticed the posts weren't getting much response and switched to customer videos. Who actually made that call to try videos—was that your idea, or did someone else suggest it?

I appreciate that honesty. So you learned the lesson about what resonates, which is useful. Did you measure anything else beyond the engagement rate? Like, did you look at whether those videos actually drove people to the stores, or was it just the engagement metric?

Mostly just the engagement rate. That was the number we tracked week to week, so that's what we could speak to. If I were running it again, I'd want to add something like a promo code or a check-in question to see that. It's a gap I'd want to close in this role.
That makes sense. Let me ask you about the survey—you got 512 responses about oat milk. How did you actually collect those 512 responses? Where did people take it?

I want to be careful here, because I don't remember the exact details of how we distributed it, and I'd rather not guess. I know the survey got 512 responses and that the oat milk question stood out. The team handled the rollout, and I can get you the specifics if you'd like. What I can say is that the response count was big enough that we felt confident acting on the oat milk finding, which is why two stores went ahead and trialed it.
Fair. And when those two stores trialed oat milk, did you track what happened after that? Like, did it move the needle on sales or traffic, or was it just a pilot that sat there?

I don't know, honestly. The trial ran, and that's what I can speak to. I don't have the sales or traffic numbers from those two stores, so I can't tell you whether it moved the needle. I'd want to see that data before saying it worked. If I were on the team now, I'd want to set up a clear comparison, like the trial stores versus similar stores without oat milk, so we'd know what it did.

We had to move fast on the schedule and the signage, and it was a bit messy. But 214 people checked in, and the demo ended up being the part people talked about most.

What I took from it is to always have a backup plan for anything that depends on one person, especially a speaker. I'd want to lock in a second option early next time, even if it's just a rough one. Happy to get into a different example if you'd like one that's less about logistics.

No, that works. I'm curious though—when you say the demo "ended up being the part people talked about most," how did you know that? Did you ask people, or is that more of a feeling you got from being there?

That was more of a feeling from being there than something we measured. We didn't run a survey or ask people afterward. I saw a lot of folks gathered around the barista, and I heard people talking about it on the way out, but I wouldn't call that real data. If I'd been planning it properly, I'd have set up a quick feedback card or a follow-up question so we'd actually know what people remembered.
Makes sense. So let me ask you this—in your first month on this job, if you were hired, what would you actually want to dig into first? What would you prioritize?

I'd start by just learning the current numbers. Before I suggest anything, I'd want to know what's being tracked now for social, email, and the stores, and what the baseline looks like. From my experience, I've seen how easy it is to celebrate an engagement number without knowing whether it's leading to store visits.

Speaking of which, I'd want to figure out whether we can connect the online stuff to what happens in the stores. Things like promo codes or a quick check-in question could help with that. I'd also love to look at that oat milk trial and see whether it's worth expanding.

I'm still figuring out exactly where I want to land, but I know I want work where I'm close to the customer and the data, and this role looks like a good place to learn that.

Got it. That makes sense. So I've got one more thing I want to circle back on. You mentioned leading a team of four on a rebranding class project. Can you tell me a bit about that—what was the project, and what did leading it actually look like?

Sure. It was a rebranding project for a class, and the team was four of us. The main job was figuring out a new logo direction for a fictional local brand. I was the one coordinating, so I kept us on schedule and made sure everyone had a piece.

That's helpful. Before we wrap up, do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?

Good question. You'd be working pretty closely with our social media manager and the email coordinator—they'd be your day-to-day people. A typical week is a mix of planning content, pulling together analytics, and supporting campaign launches. You'd also spend time in the stores occasionally just to stay connected to what's actually happening on the ground. It's not a sit-at-a-desk-all-day kind of role.

Any other questions?
Sounds good, that's a nice mix. I like that it's not all desk work. Thanks for walking me through it, and I appreciate you taking the time today.

So tell me a bit about yourself and what you've been up to at the coffee chain.

(long pause)
Take your time.

Last thing before we wrap up—why are you interested in this kind of role? What's drawing you to it?

Any other questions?

That sounds like a good mix. I'd be curious how the analytics side feeds into planning, like whether the team reviews results weekly or after each campaign. But that's the only other thing I was wondering about. Thanks for your time today, I've enjoyed talking with you.

That's a great follow-up question—we can dive into that if you move forward in the process. Thanks for taking the time, Sam. We've got a lot of candidates to talk to, but we'll be in touch either way in the next week or so. Good luck wrapping up the semester.
