That's a solid improvement. When you say you rewrote the subject lines, what was the difference between the old approach and the new one? Do you have an example?

The old ones were pretty vague, something like "Store news this month," so people had no idea what was inside. We changed them to name the one thing in the email, like the new seasonal drink or a specific date for an event. So instead of a general hook, you'd see exactly why it was worth opening. We didn't have a fancy process for it. We just wrote a few versions and kept the ones that were clearest.
Got it. And after the open rate went up to 27%, did you measure anything else, or did the team actually see whether that change drove any behavior—like visits or purchases?

Honestly, we mostly tracked opens, since that's the number the email platform showed us clearly. We didn't set up a good way to link the emails to visits or purchases, so I can't tell you how much it moved sales. That's a gap I'd want to close next time, maybe by tying promo codes or specific offers to each email so we could see what people actually did after opening.
That's a thoughtful observation. Let me shift gears a bit. On your resume you also mention growing Instagram engagement by 40%. What does that 40% mean exactly, and what changed to make that happen?

So the 40% is about engagement rate per post. On average, it went from about 2.0% to about 2.8% over three months. That's the percentage of people who saw a post and liked, commented, or shared it, so it's a better measure than just follower count.

The team decided to change what we were posting. Before, it was mostly product photos, like a latte on a counter. We shifted to short videos of customers, like someone picking up their order or telling us their favorite drink. My manager approved the plan, and we ran it for a few months and tracked the numbers as we went.
When you say the team decided to shift to videos, what was your specific role in that decision? Did you come up with the idea, test it, or something else?

Honestly, I was the one who pushed for it. I looked at which posts were getting the most engagement and noticed the customer-focused ones did better than the product shots. So I proposed switching to short customer videos, and I ran those posts myself. My manager approved the plan, and then we tracked the numbers over the three months. The team helped with ideas for who to feature, but the switch was my call.
Fair enough. I'm curious—when you were looking at which posts performed better, was that just a gut check or did you actually compare the numbers side by side?

Yeah, I actually pulled up the numbers. I went through the post insights and sorted them by engagement rate, so I could see the product shots and the customer posts next to each other. The customer ones were clearly ahead, and that's what made me want to test it properly instead of just going with a hunch. I'd say it was more data than gut, though I'll admit I didn't have a fancy analysis setup. It was mostly a spreadsheet and a lot of scrolling.
Makes sense. So you've had some wins with testing and measurement. I'm curious about the flip side—tell me about a time something didn't work out the way you planned.

Sure. We planned a store launch event with a speaker lined up as the main draw. Then, the day before, the speaker cancelled. The team had to decide fast, so we went with a latte-art demo from one of our baristas instead. It wasn't the event we'd planned, but we kept the rest of the night on track. We had about 214 people check in at the door, and the budget stayed at $1,500. The big takeaway for me was to have a backup plan for anything that depends on one person showing up.
That's a reasonable lesson. But I'm asking more about something where you personally made a call that didn't pan out, or where you learned something the hard way. Does that land differently?

Yeah, that lands differently. The clearest one is the newsletter. I focused on getting opens up and never set up a way to tie those emails to visits or purchases. So when someone asks what the redesign actually did for sales, I don't have a good answer. I learned to figure out what success looks like before we launch, not after. Now I'd want a tracking link or promo code in each email from day one.
That's fair. So you knew it was a gap while it was happening, or did you realize it only after the fact?

Honestly, I realized it after the fact. Once the open rate jumped to 27%, we were happy and kind of stopped there. It was only later, when someone asked what the change did for sales, that I realized we had no way to answer. That's when it clicked that we should have figured out what to measure before we launched.
Got it. Let me ask you this—if you started in a role like this tomorrow, and you were working on a similar project in your first month, what would you do differently from day one?

That's a good question. Honestly, the first thing I'd do is sit down with whoever owns the goal and agree on what success looks like before touching anything. For the newsletter, that would have meant deciding up front how we'd connect an email to a visit or a purchase, like a promo code or a tracking link in each one.

Second, I'd try to get a small test running early, before committing to a full rollout. With the Instagram switch, we ran it for a few months, which was fine, but I'd want faster feedback in the first few weeks so we could adjust sooner.

And third, I'd ask the team what they already know. Half the useful answers were sitting with the baristas and the store managers, and I didn't always go to them first.
That's solid. I saw you also ran a customer survey with 500 responses. What did you learn from that, and what actually changed because of it?

We ran the survey with about 512 responses, so a little more than the 500 on my resume. The biggest thing that came out of it was that people really wanted oat milk, and they wanted it without an extra charge. That was the clearest signal in the whole set of answers.

The team decided to test it. We trialed free oat milk at two stores to see whether it made a difference, and we tracked what happened there. I'd want to look at those results more closely before saying how much it changed, but it gave us real data to work with instead of just guessing what customers wanted.
When you say you'd want to look at the results more closely, what would you actually want to see? Like, what would tell you whether the oat milk trial was worth rolling out everywhere?

The first thing I'd want is a comparison against stores that didn't run the trial, so we could tell whether the change came from the oat milk or from something else, like a busy season. Then I'd look at how often people actually ordered oat milk drinks and whether that was a real shift or just people swapping their usual drink.

Cost mattered too. Free oat milk has a real price tag, so we'd need to see whether the extra orders, or the bigger baskets, covered it. If the trial brought in new visits, that would count for a lot more than if it only changed what existing customers ordered.

The team would also want to hear from the baristas and the store managers. They'd know if the line got slower or if people were asking for it a lot more than the sales numbers showed. If the numbers looked good across those things, I'd say it's worth rolling out, maybe in a few more stores first before going chain-wide.
Good thinking. Before we wrap up, do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yes, one question. What does success look like for this role in the first few months?

Great question. Honestly, in the first month or two, we're just looking for you to get your feet under you—learn how we work, meet the team, understand our current projects and what's already in motion.

After that, we'd want to see you owning a small project or two end to end. Nothing huge, but something where you can show good judgment about what to measure and what to actually do with the results. We care a lot about that here—testing, learning, adjusting. So if you can demonstrate that mindset early, that's a win for us.

Any other questions?

That helps a lot, thanks. I think I'm all set. I'd really like to work on something where the team cares about testing and learning from the results, so this sounds like a good fit. Thanks for your time today.
Thanks, Sam. I appreciate that, and I enjoyed talking with you. We'll be in touch soon with next steps. Take care.

feedback_leaks.quote: Yeah, that's exactly the kind of detail that matters.
That's a solid plan. I appreciate that you're thinking about the details.
That's a good example of using data to cut through opinion.

practice_questions.question: Tell me about a time you failed.
Why do you want this kind of role?

verdicts.notes: Strength: the interviewer pressed on metrics (the 40% baseline, newsletter before and after, which change caused the lift, survey follow-through) and covered all five resume topics plus both practice questions. Weakness: it often cut the candidate off or let them ramble without redirecting, and it gave evaluative praise ("solid", "smart", "good example") in five turns. It also never probed the store launch event beyond the backup-plan question, such as the result or the budget.

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for taking the time. How are things going on your end?

Oh, hi, thanks for having me. Things are good, honestly, pretty busy. I just got back from campus and the bus was late, which is so typical, and there was this guy with a huge dog that kept sniffing my backpack, and I was like, okay, that's a new experience. I had a coffee on the way over, which is kind of funny given the whole interview thing, but it's a local place so I figured that's on brand. My professor, Dr. Alvarez, keeps telling us to stop overthinking interviews, and I'm trying, I really am. So yeah, good. How about you? Is it as hot where you are as it is here? It's been brutal.

Ha, yeah, the heat's been rough everywhere. Glad you made it here okay, dog and all.

So tell me a bit about yourself—what's brought you to this point, and what are you looking to do next?

Sure, so, I'm finishing up my communications degree, and I'm going into my last year, which is kind of wild to say out loud. I've been doing marketing stuff mostly through a part-time thing at a local coffee chain, which is how I ended up here, honestly, because I kept seeing their posts and thinking, I could make these better. My professor, Dr. Alvarez, says every good marketer is basically a nosy person who likes watching what people do, and I think that's me. I like the stuff where you can see whether something worked. Like, last spring I was on the Instagram account, and I wanted to see if the posts were doing anything, so I switched from just product photos to these short videos of actual customers talking about their drinks. Engagement went up, and my manager was cool about letting me keep going with it. Anyway, what I'm looking for next is a place where I can do more of that, where I get to test stuff and see real results, not just post and hope. Does that sound like what you guys are doing?
That makes sense. So when you say engagement went up—you mentioned 40% on your resume—what was that 40% measuring exactly, and what were you comparing it to?

Okay, so, the 40% is engagement rate per post, meaning likes, comments, and saves divided by how many people saw the post. Before I started, we were averaging about 2%, and over the three months I was testing videos, it got up to about 2.8%. Which is 40% more, but I'll admit that sounds bigger than it is in real terms, and my roommate made fun of me for putting it on my resume like it was a huge deal. Honestly the thing I'm proudest of is that I was pretty nervous about pitching the video idea, since it meant changing something that already had a look, and my manager was like, sure, try it, just tell me what happens. I did tell her, and I had a little spreadsheet, which I think is what made it feel real to her. I was also reading this blog about social media metrics the whole time, which I found way more entertaining than I expected. So yeah, 2% to 2.8%, over about three months. Does that match how you guys measure it, or do you use something different?

Got it—thanks for clarifying that. So you ran the experiment, tracked it, and showed her the numbers. That's solid.

You mentioned you were nervous pitching the video idea. Walk me through what happened—what made you nervous, and how did you actually bring it up to your manager?

Okay, so the nervous part was mostly that the Instagram account had this really clean look, all these flat-lay photos of drinks on marble tables, and I was basically saying, hey, what if we get rid of that for a while? I kept thinking about how my roommate always says I overthink everything, which, fair, and I also had this whole moment where I imagined my manager saying no and me having to go back to making the same posts forever. Anyway, I didn't want to just walk in with a big idea, so I waited until a slow afternoon, which was a Tuesday I think, and I brought up a couple of the competitor accounts that were doing more of the customer stuff. I said I wanted to try it for three months and track it, and if it didn't work, we'd go back. She was like, sure, just tell me what happens, which
Okay, so you came prepared with examples and had a plan. That's smart. Did she give you any pushback, or did she just say yes right away?

Honestly, not really, which kind of surprised me. She asked how I'd measure it, and I think I said something about the spreadsheet, and she was like, okay, that's fair. I had been bracing for this big debate, so I kind of didn't know what to do with a yes. I ended up sitting there for a second like, wait, that's it? Which is so on brand for me, I spend forever preparing for a fight that doesn't happen. My roommate says I should just walk into things more, and I think she's right, even though I still like having my notes ready. Anyway, the pushback I did get was from my own head, mostly. So yeah, she said yes, asked a couple of practical questions, and then it was just me and a spreadsheet for three months. Is that kind of how you handle new ideas on your team, or does somebody usually push back

We can talk about that in a bit. Let me ask you this though—over those three months running the videos, what actually went wrong? Like, did everything go smoothly, or were there things that didn't work the way you expected?

Oh, yeah, plenty went wrong, and honestly that's the part I like talking about more than the win. The first few videos were kind of a mess. We filmed one in the back room because it had better light, and you could hear the espresso machine screaming the whole time, so I spent like an hour trying to edit out the noise. Some customers were totally fine being on camera, and some just wouldn't look at the lens, which, relatable. I also had to remember to get permission every time, which I forgot once, and I had to pull that post down, so I learned that the hard way. There's this stretch of the blog I read about how averages can hide stuff, and that's kind of what happened, because some videos did great and a few flopped, and
What do you mean by flopped? Like, what was the difference between the ones that did well and the ones that didn't?

Okay, so, the flops were mostly the ones where the customer felt stiff. The good ones were usually a regular who was just talking about their own order, like why they always get oat milk or something their barista remembers about them, and those felt real. The bad ones were longer, and the person would kind of read off a script or stare at the lens like they were waiting for a dentist. I didn't track that as carefully as I should have, honestly. I was so focused on the overall average that I didn't really sit down and compare individual videos until later, and by then I was kind of tired of spreadsheets. My roommate says I'd be happier doing actual field work, like watching people in the shop, which is probably true, because the best part was when a customer forgot the camera was there. Anyway, the short, casual ones were the clear winners in my head, but I'd want to check that properly before I said it with a straight face. Is that the kind of detail you'd want to see when you review a campaign?
Yeah, that's exactly the kind of detail that matters. So if you were doing this again—or if you're in a similar situation in a new role—what would you actually do differently from the start?

Okay, so, honestly, the first thing I'd do differently is track the individual videos from day one instead of just watching the average. I know I said that already, but I think it's the big one. My roommate keeps saying I should write things down more, and she's right, although she also thinks I should stop color-coding my notes, which is non-negotiable for me. I'd also get the permission forms sorted before anyone picks up a camera, because forgetting that once was embarrassing and I had to pull the post down. And I'd probably film somewhere quieter, since the espresso machine in the background made me want to throw my laptop out a window. I also think I'd ask a couple of the baristas what customers were actually saying about their drinks, because they know more than the spreadsheet does. Anyway, I'd keep the same basic approach, test it, track it, show the numbers, but just be more organized about the boring parts. Does that sound like something your team would want from someone starting out?

That's a solid plan. I appreciate that you're thinking about the details.

Let me shift gears for a second. Tell me about a time when you actually failed at something—not just something that was messy or didn't go perfectly, but something that didn't work out.

Okay, so, the closest thing to a real failure was the store launch event I planned. We had a speaker lined up, and the day before, they cancelled. I was panicking in the back of the store, and my roommate, who was there to help, kept saying, just breathe, Sam, which did not help at all. The budget was $1,500, so I couldn't exactly throw a whole new speaker on the calendar. One of the baristas, Jordan, I think, offered to do a latte-art demo, and I was like, sure, that's better than an empty room. I'd been so focused on the speaker part that I hadn't planned anything else, and I still kind of feel bad about that. Honestly, 214 people checked in, which I was happy about, but I spent the whole night feeling like it was a backup plan and not the real event. I think the
Hold on—so you went from expecting a speaker to pivoting to a latte-art demo. What would you do differently if that happened again?

Okay, so, honestly, I'd have a backup plan before the event even existed. I was so locked into the speaker that I didn't have a Plan B, which is kind of embarrassing for someone who's supposed to be organized. My roommate said something like, you should've had a list of three things, and she's annoyingly right about that. I also think I'd have talked to the speaker a week earlier, not the week of, just to check in, because maybe I would've noticed they were getting cold feet. The latte-art thing actually worked out better than I expected, and a few people told me it was the highlight, which was nice to hear. But I'd still want a plan that doesn't depend on one person showing up, and I'd probably ask the team earlier what they'd be comfortable doing. There's a whole blog post I read about contingency planning, and I'm pretty sure I skimmed it, which is the same mistake I made with the event. So yeah, backup plans, earlier check-ins, and actually reading the boring stuff. Does your team usually have a backup for things like that, or is it more of a wing-it kind of place?

We try to plan ahead, yeah. So let me ask you this—you've got this internship experience, you're finishing your degree, and you're looking for what comes next. Why do you want this kind of role specifically? Like, what's pulling you toward marketing or communications work?

Okay, so, why marketing? Honestly, it started as a bit of a joke. My roommate and I were in a coffee shop last year, and I was looking at the menu board thinking it was kind of a mess, and she said, well, why don't you fix it? I didn't, obviously, but I kept noticing things like that. Dr. Alvarez says marketing is basically people-watching with a spreadsheet, and I think that's a big part of why I like it. I also like that you get to see if something worked. Like, with the newsletter, I rewrote the subject lines and cut each email down to one topic, and more people opened them, which felt really good, even though a designer did the template and I took all the credit in my head. Then there was the team project in my rebranding class, where two of my teammates disagreed about the logo, and instead of arguing about it, we had both versions tested with about ten classmates each. Watching people pick one without knowing who made it was kind of the moment I thought, okay, this is what I want to do. I'm still figuring out whether I want to be on the creative side or the data side, which
You mentioned the newsletter—you said open rates went up after you made changes. What were they before and after?

Okay, so, the open rate went from about 18% to 27%. That's a real jump, and I was pretty happy about it, though I'll admit my roommate says I celebrate numbers like they're sports scores. Before I touched it, the newsletter was kind of a grab bag, like a sale notice, a new drink, and a story about the owner's dog all in one email, which, honestly, I think confused people. So I rewrote the subject lines to be more specific and cut each email down to one topic. The designer did the template, so I can't take all the credit, even though I definitely did in my head. I was also reading about subject line testing that week, and I got a little obsessed with it. Anyway, 18 to 27 percent, and I'd want to check whether the timing of the sends changed too, because I think I moved them to Tuesdays around then. Do you guys usually track open rate, or do you look at clicks more?
We track both. So you changed the subject lines, you cut down to one topic per email, and you might've changed the send time too. Which of those do you think actually made the difference?

Honestly, I can't say for sure, and that's kind of embarrassing because I should be able to. I changed a bunch of things at once, so I don't have a clean answer. My gut says the one-topic-per-email thing mattered most, because the old newsletter was like three emails stuffed into one, with a sale, a new drink, and a story about the owner's dog. But I also rewrote the subject lines, and I was reading about subject line testing that week, so I might be giving them too much credit because I like them. The send time thing, I'm not even sure I changed it on purpose. I think I moved things to Tuesdays, but I'd have to check my notes, which, you know, are color-coded, so that's a whole process. My roommate would say I should've split the changes up and tested them one at a time, and she'd be right. Anyway, if I were doing it again, I'd change one thing per send and see what moves. Is that how your team usually sorts out which change did what, or do you just accept that a bunch of things happen at once?

That's a fair question. We try to isolate variables when we can, but yeah, sometimes you've got to move fast and figure it out later.

You mentioned leading a team project on rebranding in your class—you said two teammates disagreed about the logo and you tested both versions. Walk me through what that disagreement actually looked like and how it got resolved.

Okay, so, the disagreement was pretty low-key at first, which is kind of funny in hindsight. We were a team of four, and two of my teammates, Marcus and Priya, had completely different logos they were attached to. Marcus had this clean, minimal one with just a bean shape, and Priya had something more hand-drawn with a script font, and they both kept saying, no, mine is obviously better, in that polite way where you can tell someone's annoyed. I was the one who had to keep the group together, which was stressful, because I'm not great at refereeing. My professor, Dr. Alvarez, always says the best way to end a debate is to stop arguing and get some data, which I thought was a little cheesy at the time. So we decided to show both versions to about ten classmates each, without telling them who made what. We asked which one they'd trust on a coffee cup and which one they'd remember. Priya's version got more votes on trust, and Marcus's won on memorability, so it was honestly kind of a split, but the bigger surprise was that the hand-drawn one felt more local to people, which was the thing we were going for. We went with that one, and Marcus was gracious about it, mostly. I'd say it's one of the few times I felt like a group project actually worked, and I still think about how weird it was to watch people pick a logo without knowing who made it. Anyway, that's the story. Does your team usually handle design disagreements like that, or does it go to whoever's the boss?

That's a good example of using data to cut through opinion. So in that moment—when Marcus and Priya were both stuck on their own ideas—what did you actually do to move things forward? Like, did you pitch the testing idea, or did someone else?

Okay, so, I pitched it, I think. Nobody else was going to, because we'd been going in circles for like forty minutes and everyone was just staring at their laptops. There was this awkward silence in the library study room, and the radiator was making this clanking noise every few seconds, which did not help me think. I remember Marcus saying something like, we could just vote, and Priya said, we'd just be voting for our own friends, and that's when I jumped in. I said maybe we could show both versions to some classmates and see which one people actually responded to, and I had this whole list of questions I'd written on my phone in case anyone pushed back. Nobody did, which, again, I kept expecting a fight and kept not getting one. Honestly, I think the reason it worked is that it didn't make either of them wrong, it just made the decision about the coffee cup and not about who was right. My roommate says I should've pitched it earlier, before the arguing got so long, and she's probably right, but I was still getting the notes organized. Anyway, yeah,
Got it. You've got a couple more things I want to circle back on before we wrap up. You ran a customer survey with 500 responses—what did you actually learn from that, and what changed because of it?

Okay, so the survey, yeah, that one was a lot of spreadsheets. The number on my resume is 500, but it was actually 512 responses, which I should probably fix, because I rounded it down in my head and then forgot I'd done that. The big finding was that people really wanted oat milk, and they didn't want to pay extra for it. Like, a lot of people said they'd switch to oat if it didn't cost more, which, honestly, is kind of a fair thing to want. My roommate says every customer wants everything for free, and she's not wrong. So we took that to the team, and two of the stores ended up trialing oat milk at no extra charge. I don't know the full results from that trial, because I was already moving on to the next project, and that's kind of the story of my whole internship, I start things and then I'm on to the next thing. Anyway, that's the survey. Did you guys do anything like that with customer feedback, or is it more of a comment box kind of thing?
We do surveys when we need them. So you found out people wanted oat milk—did you actually push to see how that trial went, or did you just hand it off?

Honestly, I handed it off, and I'm a little embarrassed about that. I sent the survey write-up to my manager and the store leads, and then the trial was kind of out of my hands. I think I assumed someone would circle back, which is a bad assumption, because nobody circles back unless you ask. I did mention it in a team meeting once, and somebody said the two stores were "doing okay with it," but I never got actual numbers, like how many people ordered oat or whether anyone complained about the cost to the store. My roommate would say that's the exact thing I keep doing, starting something and then running off to the next shiny project. And the next project was the newsletter, which, yeah, I didn't really follow up on the oat trial either. I should have asked for the sales numbers and the cost per drink, because that's the part that actually tells you whether it was worth it. Anyway, if I were doing it again, I'd put a check-in date on the calendar before I left the project. Does your team usually track that kind of follow-through, or does it depend on who owns the project?
We do track it. Last question before we wrap—do you have anything you'd like to ask me about the role or the team?
Yeah, just one, if that's okay. What does a typical week look like for someone in this role, like how much of it is hands-on campaign work versus meetings?

Good question. It depends on the project, but I'd say it's probably 60-40, with the 60 being actual work—writing, testing, analyzing—and the 40 being meetings, stakeholder updates, that kind of thing. Your first month or two will probably be heavier on the learning side, so more shadowing and meetings than you might expect. But yeah, you'll get your hands dirty pretty quickly.

Thanks so much for taking the time today, Sam. We've got a lot to think about, and we'll be in touch soon.

Oh, that's really helpful, thanks. The 60-40 split sounds about right for what I'm hoping for, and I like that you said I'd be doing real stuff pretty quickly. I'm a big note-taker, so I'll probably write that down, color-coded, obviously. Thanks so much for your time today, and for being patient with my rambling. I really appreciate the chance to talk with you, and I hope the heat lets up on your end soon. Have a good rest of your day.
You too, Sam. Take care, and safe trip back.

feedback_leaks.quote: So you brought in data to settle it. That's smart.
You clearly think about your work, and that matters.

practice_questions.question: Tell me about a time you failed.
Why do you want this kind of role?

verdicts.notes: Strength: the interviewer pressed on personal ownership in the Instagram, survey and team-project answers, and covered both practice questions and the candidate's questions at the end. Weakness: it regularly evaluated the candidate ("good self-awareness", "that's smart", "you clearly think about your work"), it skipped the email newsletter topic entirely, and it asked a first-month question that went unprobed.

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for coming in. Did you find everything okay today?

Yeah, yeah, everything's good, thanks for asking. Honestly the video link worked on the first try, which I was really nervous about, because last week my friend's Zoom froze during her final and she had to restart the whole thing, and she was so stressed she, like, called her mom from the hallway. I had a coffee before this too, from that place near my apartment, which is kind of funny given the whole interview, but it was good, they do this cold brew that's way too sweet for me. Anyway, I'm happy to be here, thanks for setting this up.
Ha, glad the tech cooperated. And yeah, cold brew can be hit or miss. So tell me a bit about yourself—what brings you to this role, and what's your background been like so far?

Sure, so I'm finishing up my communications degree this spring, and I've kind of been all over the place with it, which I think is actually a good thing? I started out thinking I'd do journalism, then I took a social media class and got way more into the marketing side, mostly because it's the part where you can see whether what you did worked. My roommate says I'm too into spreadsheets for a communications person, but I like knowing the numbers. I've been doing a marketing internship-type role on the side for a local business, and before that I did a bunch of group projects that were honestly more stressful than any job I've had. What drew me to this role is that you guys are a local chain, so it's not some huge corporation where you're a tiny cog, and I've always liked coffee shops, I spent most of my second year basically living in one near campus with a laptop. Anyway, the Instagram stuff is probably what I'm most proud of, because I changed how we posted and the engagement went up, but I can get into that whenever you want.
Nice. So you mentioned the Instagram work—that's something I want to dig into. But first, when you say you changed how you posted, what specifically did you change?

Oh, right, yeah. So before, our feed was basically all product photos, like a latte on a white table, the pastry shot from above, the same kind of thing every coffee shop posts. My manager and I were kind of looking at the numbers and nobody was really engaging with it. My cousin is obsessed with those little cooking videos where people are just talking to the camera, and I kept thinking about that. So I pitched switching to short videos of actual customers, like someone saying what their order is, or a barista doing a quick thing. My manager was pretty open to it, which I was surprised by, because the place has been around for like fifteen years. We tested it over about three months. The average engagement rate per post went from around 2.0% to about 2.8%, which is the forty percent I put on the resume. I should be honest that it's an average, so a couple of posts did way better than others, and I'm still not sure which part helped most. Do you want me to walk through how we picked which customers to film?
Actually, before we go there—when you say your manager was open to it, what was your role in actually making those videos happen? Like, did you film them yourself, edit them, post them?

Yeah, so mostly I did the planning and the posting, and I filmed a lot of them, but I didn't really edit most of them, which, I know, is kind of a gap. My manager had a rule that anything with a customer's face in it needed them to sign off, so I'd basically be the one who stood by the counter asking people, "Hey, would you mind saying your order to my phone real quick?" Honestly that was the hardest part, because some people were super into it and some people would just put their hand up and walk away. There's this one guy who did like four takes of ordering a flat white and he kept saying "flat white" in this really dramatic voice, and that one ended up being one of the top performers, so I still don't totally know why. For editing, we used a basic app on my phone for trims and captions, and I think the one thing I did do is write all the captions and pick which clips to post. I posted most of them myself on a schedule, usually around the morning rush, because that's when the most people are scrolling near the shop, or at least that's my theory. I should probably tell you that I'm not a video person, so if you want someone who's great at editing, that's not really me yet.

Got it. So you were doing the outreach, some filming, captions, and the posting strategy. That makes sense. When you picked which clips to post and when—how did you decide what to post next? Like, were you looking at which ones performed best and then doing more of that, or did you have a plan going in?

Honestly, it was a little of both, and I'm not sure I'd call it a real system. I went in with a plan to alternate between customer clips and behind-the-scenes stuff with the baristas, mostly because I didn't want the feed to feel like one long ad. Then I'd check the insights on the app every so often, which is kind of like my roommate checking her step counter, she's really into it. When something did well, like the flat white guy or a clip of someone's weird order, I'd try to film more of that kind of thing for the next few posts. But I'll be straight with you, some of it was just gut feeling, and I didn't keep a formal log of what I tested, which I wish I had now that you're asking. If I were doing it again, I'd write down the variable I changed each time, like the length of the clip or whether there was a caption on the first line,

That's fair. So you were learning as you went. I'm curious—in that three-month window, did you actually sit down with your manager and look at the data together to decide what to do next, or was this more something you were just tweaking on your own?

Mostly I was tweaking on my own, though my manager was around for the big stuff. At the start, we sat down together and looked at the numbers from the old posts, which honestly was kind of depressing, because the engagement was so flat that you could almost hear it. Then she signed off on the video idea, and after that it was more like she'd check in now and then and say "how's it going," and I'd tell her what I'd seen in the app. I don't think we ever had a formal review of the data every week, which, looking back, is probably a thing I should have pushed for. My cousin always says if you don't schedule the check-in it just doesn't happen, and she's kind of right about everything, which is annoying. I did send her a screenshot once when the flat white video blew up, and she sent back like six fire emojis, so that was a pretty big meeting for me. Anyway, if I did it again, I'd book a short sit-down every two weeks with my manager to look at the same three numbers and decide one thing to test next.
That's good self-awareness. Let me shift gears a bit. You also ran a customer survey with 500 responses. What did you learn from that, and what actually changed because of it?

Okay, so the survey was kind of a fun one. We got 512 responses, which is a little more than the 500 on my resume, so I guess I rounded up, sorry. The biggest thing that came out of it was that a lot of people wanted oat milk, and they wanted it without paying extra for it. I was honestly surprised, because I expected people to complain about the prices in general, but it was really specific. I actually did the survey on a paper form at the counter for a week, and my hand was cramping by the end, which is not something they tell you about in marketing class. My professor for my research methods class, Dr. Alvarez, always says never trust a survey you wrote in one sitting, so I rewrote the questions twice, which I think helped. What changed afterward is that two of the stores trialed oat milk at no extra charge, and I think they were testing whether it changed how often people came back. I don't know the final results yet, because I got moved onto the newsletter stuff, which is kind of a bummer because I wanted to see how it turned out. I'd say that's the part I'm most curious about, whether the trial actually moved anything. Do you know if they ended up keeping it?

I don't have those details, but that's a good question to follow up on if you get the chance. So you got the feedback, the stores ran a trial—what was your role in actually setting up that trial, or was that all your manager?

Honestly, I wasn't really the one setting up the trial, so I don't want to take credit for it. I put together the survey summary, with the oat milk thing at the top, and I sent it to my manager, and I think she brought it to the managers at the two stores who decided to try it. I remember feeling kind of weird about it, because I'd spent a whole week at the counter with that paper form, and then it just kind of disappeared into the operations side. My roommate says that's basically what every intern job feels like, but she also works at a bank, so I don't know how much to trust her. I did ask my manager if I could help with the follow-up once they had numbers, and she said maybe, so I'm still hoping. Mostly my part was making the survey and the summary clear enough that somebody would act on it, and that's the part I'm happi
Makes sense. So shifting gears again—tell me about a time you actually failed at something. What happened, and what did you take from it?

Oh, a failure, okay. So the one that comes to mind is the launch event, which, I'll be honest, technically went fine, but there was a moment where I thought it was going to be a total disaster. We had a budget of about fifteen hundred dollars, and we had a speaker lined up, like a local food writer, and she cancelled the day before. I was panicking so hard, and I remember sitting in my car in the parking lot of the grocery store, because I couldn't concentrate at home, and I was trying to call everyone I knew. Anyway, I ended up asking one of the baristas, Marcus, if he'd do a latte-art demo, and he said yes, which saved the whole thing. We ended up with 214 people checking in at the door, which was more than I expected. What I took from it is that I should have had a backup plan for the speaker before the event, not the day before, and I've since started asking for a second option for anything that depends on one person. My friend says that's just basic event planning, and she's right, I just didn't know it yet. Honestly, the thing I'm still a little annoyed at myself about is that I didn't send a follow-up survey to the attendees, so I have no idea how many of those 214 people actually came back.

Got it. So you improvised and it worked out, but you're saying the real failure was not planning ahead. When you say you didn't send a follow-up survey—was that something you thought about doing at the time, or is that something you wish you'd thought of?

Honestly, it's more the second one. I didn't even think about it at the time, because I was so focused on getting through the night, and once the event was over I was just exhausted and kind of glad it was done. Looking back, that's a pretty obvious miss, since I had 214 email addresses from the check-in sheet, or at least the ones people were willing to give. My manager actually mentioned later that the other stores do a follow-up thing, and I thought, oh, I could have done that. I did send one thank-you email to the people who signed up for the newsletter, but I didn't ask them anything, so I didn't learn anything from it, which is kind of the whole point of a survey. My cousin would say I should've put it on the checklist before the event, and she'd be right, because I've now got a checklist on my phone with about twelve items, including "follow-up survey" with a little star next to it. If I'm being honest, that checklist is probably the most useful thing I got out of the whole event.
That's practical. Let me ask you this—if you started in this role tomorrow, what would you do in your first month to get up to speed on how the business actually works?

Okay, first month, I'd want to actually be useful fast, so I'd start by just hanging out in the stores for a few shifts, like standing near the bar during the morning rush and watching how people order and where they get stuck. I think you learn more about a coffee shop in twenty minutes at the counter than from any deck. I'd also ask to sit in on whatever the store managers meet about, because I'm pretty sure the oat milk thing got decided somewhere in a meeting I wasn't in, and I'd love to know how that stuff gets decided. Then I'd want to look at the numbers they already track, like sales by day and which drinks move, and try to figure out what questions they're actually asking. I'd also make sure I'm on the schedule for the Instagram posting, because I left that a little messy when I moved on, and I'd feel bad if nobody picked it up. Honestly, I'd probably also make a checklist on my phone, because that's apparently my thing now. My roommate says I should just relax and let people show me things, and she's probably right, but I'd rather come in with a plan and then be flexible about it.

That sounds thoughtful. I want to circle back to something you mentioned earlier—you led a team of four on a rebranding class project. Tell me about that, and specifically, was there a moment where you and the team disagreed on something?

Yeah, the rebranding project, that was a whole thing. It was for a capstone-type class, Professor Okafor's branding course, and we had four people, and I was kind of the one who ended up coordinating everybody, which I didn't totally sign up for, but nobody else wanted to make the group chat. We were working with a fake coffee brand, which honestly is harder than it sounds, because you can't just say "we think it looks cool" and get anywhere. Anyway, yes, there was a disagreement. Two of my teammates, Priya and Devon, were really split on the logo. Priya wanted this clean, minimal thing with a single line drawing of a bean, and Devon wanted something more hand-drawn and kind of vintage, with a script font. They both got pretty heated about it in the group chat, and at one point Devon sent a message that was just a bunch of exclamation points, which, we all know what that means.

So I did something I'm kind of proud of, which is I suggested we stop arguing and just test it. We had both of them put together a version, and then I had each of them show their logo to ten classmates, not in our group, and ask a few questions, like which one they'd remember and which one they'd walk into. I wrote down the answers on a spreadsheet, because of course I did. The minimal one got more "I'd remember it" votes, but the vintage one got way more "I'd try this place" votes, which was kind of the whole point of the brand. We ended up combining them, the clean bean drawing with a more personal script for the name. Priya was a little annoyed at first, but she admitted the

So you brought in data to settle it. That's smart. But I'm curious—when Devon sent those exclamation points and things got heated, what did you actually do in that moment? Like, did you jump in right then, or did you wait?

Honestly, I waited, which I think was the right call, though I was kind of freaking out at the time. I read Devon's message in the library and almost replied right away with something super diplomatic that would've come out sounding passive-aggressive. So I closed my laptop, went and got a bagel from the place across from the library, and came back to it about an hour later. My roommate says I'm too much of a planner, but in this case waiting helped, because by the time I wrote in the group chat, nobody was typing in all caps anymore. I kept it short and said something like, "Can we each show our version to some people outside the group and see what sticks?" Priya replied with a thumbs up, and Devon sent a GIF of a dog, so I took that as a yes. Then I had to actually find twenty people to show the logos to, which was its own nightmare, and I ended up standing outside the student center with a tablet like a weird survey guy. Do you usually jump in right away
No, I think you're asking me a question now. Let me ask you this instead—when you look back at that whole thing, what would you have done differently if you could do it over?

Oh, sure, I can do that. Honestly, the thing I'd change is that I'd have set up the rules for the logo test before anyone started arguing, not after. Right now I was just making it up as I went, like which questions to ask and how many people to show each version to. I ended up with ten people per logo, which is fine, but it's not a huge sample, and I didn't write down the exact question wording, so I can't fully tell you how much the "I'd try this place" answers were about the logo versus whoever I happened to catch outside the student center. My professor for the branding course, Okafor, actually said something about that during feedback, and I nodded like I understood, but I didn't really. I'd also have made it clear from the start that the group would decide together on the criteria, so Priya and Devon weren't just watching me pick a winner, even if it was a fair process. And I think I'd have checked in with Devon one-on-one before the group chat blew up, because I'm pretty sure the real issue was that he felt like his idea was getting dismissed, and nobody asked him about it. Priya ended up being fine, but I think Devon was still a little quiet for the rest of the project, which I didn't handle well.
That's thoughtful. One last thing before we wrap up—why do you actually want this kind of role? Like, marketing at a coffee chain specifically, or is it more about the type of work?

Good question, and I'll try to give you a real answer, not just the thing I think sounds good. Honestly it's a bit of both. I like the work itself, which is figuring out what people respond to and then testing it, and the Instagram thing hooked me on that, even though I was kind of winging a lot of it. But the coffee part is real too. I spent a ton of my second year in a shop near campus with my laptop, and I noticed how much of what people do there is just small decisions, like what to order, whether to come back, whether they feel like they belong somewhere. That's basically marketing, I think. And you guys being a local chain matters to me, because I'd rather see the results of what I do than get lost on some giant brand team. My roommate says that's a very neat answer, and she's kind of right, but I mean it. Also the oat milk thing kind of made me want to be in the room when those decisions get made, so, yeah.

Do you have any questions for me? I'm not sure what the normal ones are, but I'd like to know what a typical first month looks like for someone in this role.

Good question. Honestly, it varies a bit depending on what we need most that month, but typically you'd spend the first couple weeks getting to know the stores, the team, and what's actually tracking in our systems. Then we'd probably have you own one small campaign or project to get your hands dirty—nothing huge, just something to learn how we work. After that, it's about finding where you can have the most impact. We're not huge, so you'll definitely see the results.

Do you have anything else for me?

(long pause) Hmm, yeah, I think that makes sense. Um, one thing I'm curious about is whether the oat milk trial ended up getting extended or made permanent, because that's kind of the thing I'm most curious about from the survey, and if it's something I could follow up on in the first month, I'd love to know that. Also, I should probably ask what the Instagram account looks like right now, since I kind of left it in the middle, so I'd want to make sure someone's keeping up with the video posts. Sorry, that's a lot, but those are the two I'd really want to know. Thanks so much for your time, this was really great.

Those are both smart questions. The oat milk thing—I don't have the final numbers in front of me, but it's definitely something worth asking about on day one. And yeah, the Instagram has been a little quiet since you moved on, so that's actually something we'd want to get back to. Thanks for being straightforward about that.

I really appreciate you coming in and being so honest about what you did and didn't do. You clearly think about your work, and that matters. We'll be in touch either way, and good luck with finishing up your degree.

practice_questions.question: Tell me about a time you failed.
Why do you want this kind of role?

verdicts.notes: Strength: the interviewer covered all five topics and both practice questions, and pressed on metrics (T6, T22, T26), which exposed weak measurement on the survey and newsletter. Weakness: it let rambling answers go without redirecting, never followed up on the newsletter's vague window or the vague motivation answer at T17, and gave several small evaluative comments ("good instinct", "good lesson").

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for taking the time. How are things going on your end?

Oh, hi, yeah, thanks for having me. Things are good, honestly, it's been kind of a hectic week. I was up pretty early today because my roommate's alarm goes off at like six every morning, and I swear it's not even for him, it's just a whole thing with his phone. Anyway, I had a really good cup of coffee on the way over, which, given that I'm applying to a coffee company, felt like a sign. My commute's about twenty-five minutes on the bus, and I spent most of it rereading my notes, which I probably should've done last night instead of rewatching that baking show. How about you, how's your week been?

Ha, yeah, those early mornings are rough. My week's been solid, thanks for asking. Alright, so tell me a bit about yourself—your background, what you've been doing, and what's got you interested in this role.

Sure, so I'm finishing up my communications degree, and I'm a marketing intern right now at a local coffee chain, which is actually how I got into this whole thing. I've always liked the idea of working somewhere people come in every day, and I'm the kind of person who notices things like whether a line is moving too slow or whether the music is too loud, so when I started looking at marketing I kind of gravitated toward the customer side. My first real project was on the Instagram account, and I kept seeing the same product photos get almost no response, so I pushed to switch to short customer videos. My manager let me test it for a few months, and the average engagement per post went from about 2% to 2.8%, which is about a 40% bump. I also helped plan a store launch event, which had a budget of fifteen hundred dollars, and 214 people checked in, though that's a whole story because our speaker cancelled the day before and I ended up getting one of the baristas to do a latte art demo, which honestly ended up being the best part. Anyway, that's the short version. What's got me interested here is that your brand seems to take the customer experience seriously, and that's the stuff I care about most, so I'd really like to bring that kind of thinking to a team like yours.

That's helpful context. I want to dig into that Instagram work a bit more. You mentioned switching to customer videos and seeing that engagement bump. What exactly did you change about how you were posting, and how did you decide that was the right move?

Okay, so, the big change was basically stopping the product shots. Our feed was full of these really polished photos of the drinks on a marble counter, and they just weren't getting much response. It reminded me of when my mom sends me those perfect vacation pictures and I scroll right past them. Anyway, I pitched short videos of actual customers, like someone telling us their usual order, or a regular talking about why they come in on Tuesdays. My manager was open to it, so we tried it for about three months. The average engagement per post went from around 2% to 2.8%. I'd say the way I decided was mostly from watching what people actually reacted to, plus a lot of scrolling through other coffee shop accounts late at night, which I probably should've been doing less of. Honestly, the people part felt more real to me than the product part, so that's what I leaned into.

Got it. So you were looking at what was working for other accounts and what your own audience was responding to. When you say engagement went from 2% to 2.8%, what were you actually measuring there—likes, comments, shares, or something else?

Okay, so, honestly, I'd have to double-check the exact formula, but it was the engagement rate from the Instagram insights tab, which as far as I remember is basically likes, comments, and shares, and I think saves too, divided by how many accounts saw the post. I know that sounds like a lot of nerd talk, and my roommate would tell you I get way too excited about dashboards. I was kind of obsessed with that tab for a while, honestly more than I was with my actual classes that semester. I checked it every morning on the bus, which is how I ended up with those weird little charts saved on my phone. The part I'd be careful about is that I mostly tracked it per post and didn't do a super rigorous comparison against a control, so I'd say the trend was pretty clear, but I wouldn't claim it was a perfect scientific result. What I can say for sure is that the videos got more comments, and people were tagging their friends, which felt like a better sign than just a heart.

That makes sense. So you noticed the qualitative shift too—more comments, people tagging friends. That's good instinct. When you were running those videos, how much of the actual day-to-day work of creating and posting them fell on you versus your manager or other folks on the team?

Honestly, most of the day-to-day was mine, which I kind of liked, though it also meant some weeks I was doing it at eleven at night. I'd usually get a barista or a regular to agree to be filmed, which took more talking than you'd think, because people get weird about being on camera, and one guy was so nervous he kept asking if he could just do the shot again. My manager signed off on the plan and looked at the captions before anything went live, so she was the approver, but the planning, the asking people, the filming on my phone, and the editing in a basic app were all me. I did get a little help from a friend who's into video, who showed me how to cut a thirty-second clip without it looking like a hostage video, which I appreciated. The one thing that wasn't mine was the posting schedule, since that went through the social tool the company already uses. So yeah, I'd say about ninety percent of the hands-on work was on me, and I think that's part of why I'm comfortable taking on a role where I'm expected to just get things done.
Fair enough. Let me shift gears a bit. Tell me about a time when something didn't go the way you planned—a project or something you were working on that didn't land.

Yeah, so the launch event is the one that comes to mind, though it went okay in the end, which is kind of the funny part. We had a budget of fifteen hundred dollars and I'd spent weeks on it, and the plan was to bring in a local speaker who does coffee sourcing stuff. Then the day before, she emailed to say she had to cancel because of a family thing, and I remember staring at my screen thinking, great, what now. I was already running on about four hours of sleep, which, as you can probably tell, is kind of my default state. I ended up calling one of our baristas, Marcus, who's honestly really good with people, and asked if he'd do a latte art demo instead, and he said yes almost too quickly. The next day I was basically running around taping signs to doors, and I'm pretty sure I had cold brew on my shirt the
Sorry, you cut off there—you had cold brew on your shirt, and then what?

Ha, yeah, sorry, I was about to get to that. So I'm standing there with this big brown stain on my shirt, and I'm thinking, okay, nobody's going to notice, which was not true, because Marcus pointed it out about five minutes before doors opened. I ran to the back and grabbed a store polo, which was a little too big, and honestly I looked like I was working a summer job at a golf course. Anyway, the demo ended up being the best part of the night. Marcus was doing these really detailed tulips and hearts, and people were lined up asking him questions, and a bunch of folks said it was more fun than a speaker would've been. We had 214 people check in at the door, which was more than I'd hoped for, and I think a lot of that was just people wanting something to do on a weeknight. The thing I'd say I learned is that having a backup plan matters more than the original plan, which sounds obvious, but I didn't really get it until I was standing there with a stained shirt and a cancelled speaker. I'd also say I should've had a backup lined up earlier, so I'm not scrambling the day before again.
That's a good lesson. So when you think back on it, what would you actually do differently if you were planning an event like that from scratch right now?

Honestly, the first thing I'd change is that I'd lock in a backup before anything else. I was so focused on getting the speaker that I never asked what happens if she bails, and it's kind of funny because I'd been reading this planning book my roommate left on the couch, and it literally has a whole chapter on that. I'd also get a confirmation call a week out, not just an email, because I think a call would've caught her hesitating earlier. And I'd probably ask a barista to be part of the planning from the start instead of after everything fell apart, since Marcus was the reason the night worked. Oh, and I'd keep a spare shirt in my bag, which sounds silly, but that golf course polo was not a good look. So yeah, mostly it's build the backup first, then do the fun stuff. Are you going to ask me about the newsletter next, or is that a different section?
We'll get to that. But first, why do you want this kind of role—what is it about this position that appeals to you?

Okay, so, honestly, I think it started on the bus. I was riding in one morning and watched this guy get his coffee order wrong, and the barista just fixed it with a joke and everyone in line was laughing. That's kind of the stuff I like, the little moments that make a place feel like somewhere you want to be. My sister keeps telling me I overthink everything, and she's probably right, but I was also thinking about how my friend who works at a bookstore talks about her regulars like they're family. Anyway, what appeals to me about this role is that it sounds like you're trying to build that same feeling at scale, and marketing is where I get to work on that, figuring out how people hear about you and what makes them come back. I'd love to be part of a team that cares about the customer experience as much as the product, because that's what I've been chasing in every project I've done so far
Makes sense. Let me ask you about the survey you ran—you mentioned 500 responses. Walk me through that. What were you trying to learn, and what did you actually do with what you found?

Sure, so the survey was actually the thing I'm probably proudest of, mostly because nobody asked me to do it. We wanted to know what customers actually thought about the menu and the store, and I put together a short questionnaire, mostly multiple choice with a couple of open boxes at the end, and we shared it through the app and the newsletter and a little QR code on the counter. My manager was into it, and I think the goal was to get a broad sense before we changed anything. I'll be honest, I'm a little fuzzy on the exact response count, but it came in around five hundred, and the big thing that came out of it was that people really wanted oat milk without an extra charge. Like, that was the loudest message in the open answers. We ended up testing it at two of the stores, and I think people were pretty happy with it, though I'd want to check the sales numbers before I said for sure that it was a win. What I took from it is that customers will tell you exactly what they want if you actually ask them in a way that's easy to answer, and I'd love to do more of that kind of listening in a role like this.
Good. So you got the feedback about oat milk, and then what happened? Did you personally push to test it at those two stores, or did someone else drive that?

Honestly, it was a mix. I put together a quick summary of the open answers, and oat milk kept coming up over and over, so I brought it to my manager with the notes. Whether I was the one who pushed the hardest or whether she was already leaning that way, I'm not totally sure, because there were a couple of meetings that week and I was running on coffee and about five hours of sleep. My roommate says I remember everything about a spreadsheet and nothing about who said what in a meeting, which is probably fair. The two stores that tested it were the ones with the most regulars, I think, but I'd have to look that up. I did end up going in on a Saturday to watch the counter for a bit, and a bunch of people asked about the oat milk before they even ordered, which was kind of fun to see. Is there anything specific you want to know about how the test was set up?
Yeah, actually. When you say people were "pretty happy with it," how did you measure that? Did you check sales, ask customers, look at anything concrete?

Honestly, the answer is not much, and I should've been clearer about that earlier. I didn't set up a proper comparison, like tracking oat milk orders against the stores that didn't test it, which is the thing I'd do now. What I had was my Saturday at the counter, where I stood by the register for a while, and a lot of people asked about oat milk before they even got to the front. Some of them said stuff like "oh, finally," which I took as a good sign, but that's a pretty small sample and I was mostly people-watching. My roommate, who is way more into this stuff than I am, keeps asking if I looked at the point-of-sale data, and I keep saying I'll pull it, and then I forget because I'm busy rewatching that baking show. So the honest version is that I think people liked it, but I can't back that up with numbers yet. If I were in this role, I'd want to set up a simple before and after on orders and repeat visits, and ask a few regulars directly. Does that kind of measurement setup come up a lot in the work here?
It does, yeah. Alright, let me ask you about the newsletter relaunch. What was the state of it before you touched it, and what did you actually change?

Okay, so the newsletter was kind of a mess when I got to it. It went out whenever someone remembered, and the emails were these long things that tried to cover the new drinks, a store hours change, and a reminder about the loyalty card, all in one go. I think I was the one who noticed people were probably skimming and bailing halfway down, which is a weird thing to notice about your own inbox, but I'm on a lot of email lists and I know how I feel about them. The first thing I changed was the subject lines. I rewrote them to be more specific, so instead of "News from Our Team!" it was something like "Oat milk is coming to two stores," which, yeah, I'm pretty sure I was obsessed with that for a week. Then I cut each email down to one topic, so if there was a new drink, that was the whole email. A designer on the team did the actual template, which I was really glad about, because my version looked like a flyer from a high school bake sale. Open rate went from 18% to 27%, which is a pretty good jump, though I'
Hold on—open rate from 18% to 27%. How long was that measured over? Like, was that comparing one email to another, or an average before and after?

Yeah, so, I'd have to dig into the dashboard to give you the exact window, and I don't want to make something up. I think it was an average across a few sends before I changed things compared with a few after, not one email against another, but honestly I'm not sure how many emails were in each group. The email platform we use has this little analytics page that I looked at constantly, mostly because watching a number go up is weirdly satisfying, and I think I kept screenshots of it on my phone like I did with the Instagram stuff. My roommate would definitely call me out for not writing down the date range, and he'd be right. What I can say is that the drop from one topic per email was the change I felt best about, and the open rate went up after that. If you want, I can pull the actual dates and send you the exact comparison, because I'd rather give you the right answer than guess in an interview. Is that the kind of thing you'd want to see?

That's fair. I appreciate the honesty. One last thing before we wrap up—you mentioned leading a team on a rebranding class project. Tell me about that. What was your role, and how did the team actually work together?

Yeah, so that was a group project for a branding class last year, and I was the one who got put in charge of the team of four, mostly because I'd volunteered to make the schedule and nobody else wanted to. We were rebranding a fictional coffee shop, which sounds fun, and it kind of was, though one of my teammates had a very strong opinion about the color palette that I still think about. The team itself worked pretty well overall. We split things up, one person on research, one on the copy, one on the visuals, and I kind of floated between everything and made sure we were all hitting our deadlines. The big moment was when two of my teammates totally disagreed on the logo. One wanted something clean and minimal, and the other wanted something more hand-drawn and a little quirky, and they were both pretty dug in. So instead of arguing about it for another hour, I suggested we test both with actual people. We each grabbed ten classmates, showed them both versions, and asked which one they'd walk into. The minimal one won pretty clearly, which, honestly, surprised the quirky-logo person, but she was cool about it once she saw the numbers. I'd say the main thing I took from it is that when people disagree, getting real feedback usually ends the argument faster than trying to win it in the room. I think we got a decent grade on it, though I'd have to check, because I'm pretty sure I still haven't looked at that email.
That's a good instinct. So when you saw that the minimal logo won in the testing, did you actually learn anything from that result, or was it mostly just a way to settle the disagreement?

Honestly, I think it was both, though I'd say I learned more than I expected. Going in, I was mostly thinking about how to get my teammates to stop arguing, because we had a deadline and I was getting that tight feeling in my chest. But when I looked at the answers, people weren't just picking the minimal one because it looked nicer. A few of them said it looked more like a place they could trust with their coffee, and the quirky one felt like a fun place to hang out but maybe not one to grab a quick drink at. That stuck with me, because it's basically the same thing I noticed with the Instagram videos, where the real stuff seemed to land better than the polished stuff. My roommate would say I'm reading too much into ten classmates, and he's probably right, it was a pretty small group. But it did make me realize that the question you ask matters a lot. We asked which one they'd walk into, not which one they liked best, and I think that's why we got an answer that was actually useful.
Got it. Alright, we're running short on time here. Do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, just one, if that's okay. What does a typical week look like for someone in this role, especially how much time goes to planning versus actually getting things out the door?

Good question. It's probably seventy-thirty, maybe eighty-twenty some weeks. A lot of it is planning campaigns, working with other teams, analyzing what's working. But we also have to move fast—we're constantly testing new things, so you're never just planning forever. You get to see your work live pretty quickly, which I think you'd like given what you've told me. Alright, I think we're good. Thanks so much for taking the time today, Sam. We'll be in touch within the next week or so.

Thanks, that sounds great, and I really appreciate the time. The seventy-thirty split actually sounds about right for how I like to work, and getting to see things go live fast is honestly the part I'd be most excited about. I'll keep an eye out for your email, and if you need anything else from me before then, just let me know. Thanks again, and have a good rest of your day.
You too, thanks. Take care.

Hey, good to meet you too! Honestly, it's been kind of a day. I got up later than I wanted, so I had to rush across campus, and the bus was packed, which, I don't know, is pretty typical for a Tuesday, right? My roommate also left a sticky note about the dishes, which is a whole thing we have going on. Anyway, I'm happy to be here, and I'm excited to talk about the marketing role.

That's really helpful context, and I appreciate the specifics on the Instagram work. So when you say the engagement rate went from 2.0% to 2.8%—was that the only change you made, or were there other things happening at the same time that might have moved the needle?

Honestly, that's a fair question, and I should be upfront that I can't fully isolate it. The main thing I changed was switching from product photos to short customer videos, and that's the one I'd point to. I didn't set up a clean test where some posts were videos and some were photos, so I can't say for sure how much of that jump was the videos themselves. Three months is also a stretch where other stuff could have been going on, like seasonal traffic or what people were already talking about in the area. I think the honest answer is that it was the biggest change I made, and the numbers moved in the right direction, but I'd want to do a proper comparison before I told anyone it was all me. Yeah, I'd want to set it up so I'm not guessing. Then I'd try to split things up, like running some posts as videos and some as photos at the same time, so it's not just before and after. Anyway, for a first month, I'd keep it simple, maybe two or three post types, check in every week, and be ready to drop whatever isn't moving. Does that match how your team usually approaches it, or do you already have a setup you use?

We can get into our process in a bit. Let me ask you about something else on your resume—you mentioned leading a team of four on a rebranding class project. Tell me about that and what your role actually was.

Yeah, that one was a group project for a branding class, and I was the one they put in charge, which I think was partly because I'd already been doing the Instagram stuff and the professor figured I'd be organized. It was a team of four, and honestly the first two weeks were mostly me trying to get people to show up to meetings on time, which, if you've ever been in a group chat with college kids, you know is its own kind of project. Our client was a made-up bakery, which our professor insisted was real enough, and we had to redo the whole visual identity. Two of my teammates really disagreed on the logo, one wanted something script-y and kind of fancy, and the other wanted something bold and simple. They were both pretty stubborn, and I remember thinking the group chat was going to be the thing that broke us up. The part I'm proudest of is that nobody felt like they lost an argument to me. Is that the kind of thing you were asking about, or did you want more on how we split up the actual design work?

It reminded me of when my roommate made us all rate pizza places blind, and the winner was the one nobody had heard of, which was a whole thing. As for how I knew the simple one won, I'd be lying if I said it was a clean result. I didn't set up a formal tally or track exact numbers, and it was only ten people per logo, so it's a small sample. But the simple logo got more "I'd remember that" and "I'd go in there" answers, and that was consistent enough that both of my teammates looked at
Got it. So you ran it informally, which makes sense for a class project. Did you actually write down the responses, or were you just kind of keeping track in your head?

Honestly, mostly in my head, which I'm not proud of. I had a rough sense of which logo people picked as they went, but I didn't write down each answer, so I can't pull up exact counts now. It's kind of like when my roommate and I argue about whose turn it is to take out the recycling, and we both swear we're right, and neither of us has a single written record. The good news is the result was lopsided enough that nobody really disputed it, but I'd definitely keep a simple tally next time, even if it's just tick marks on a sheet of paper. The big thing that happened was the speaker cancelled the day before. I was kind of panicking, and then I remembered one of the baristas did latte art that people always stop to watch, so I asked her if she'd do a demo instead. She said yes, and honestly it ended up being the thing people talked about. In the end, 214 people checked in at the door, which is more than the 200 I'd planned for, so I guess that's a good problem. I'd say my actual role was planning the logistics, finding the replacement, and making sure the budget didn't go sideways. What kind of event planning have you done?
That's a good save on the speaker. Quick question though—when you say 214 people checked in, how did you count that? Was there a sign-in sheet, or did someone scan badges, or what?

Yeah, so there was a sign-in table right by the door, and people gave their name and email as they came in. I think it was a sheet on a clipboard, but I'm honestly not 100% sure, because the manager had the tablet thing set up for something else that night and I was running between the door and the coffee bar. I did a count at the end by going through the list, which is the number I gave you. Now that I think about it, some people probably walked in without signing, especially the ones who came with friends, so 214 is what we captured, not necessarily everyone who showed up. My friend who keeps talking about Thursdays was actually there, and she didn't sign in, so I guess she's proof of the undercount. Anyway, that's a good point to bring up, because if we'd used badge scans or something, I'd have a cleaner number. What did you usually use for headcounts at events you've worked on

Okay, so I found out the afternoon before, which, yeah, not ideal. My first instinct was honestly to just stare at the screen for a second. Then I started thinking about how I'd have to tell the manager, and whether we should just cancel the whole night, which I didn't want to do because we'd already printed the flyers. It reminded me of that time my roommate's flight got cancelled before Thanksgiving and he spent four hours on hold, and I kept thinking, please don't let me be on hold with anyone. Anyway, I made a list of three quick options, and the latte art idea was the one that stuck. I walked over to the coffee bar and asked the barista, and she was pretty excited about it. Looking back, the thing I'd do differently is I should've had a backup speaker or a backup plan written down before the event, not just in my head at 4 p.m. the day before. How do you usually handle it when a spe
That makes sense. So you came up with three options—what were the other two besides the latte art demo?

Okay, so one was moving the whole event to the following week, which the manager wasn't thrilled about because the flyers already had the date on them. The other was turning it into a more casual tasting night with no speaker at all, just a few drinks and people milling around. Honestly, I think the tasting idea was closer to the one we'd have used if the latte art hadn't worked out. Now that I'm saying it out loud, I'm not sure I wrote those down as clearly as I should have, so I'm
Fair enough. Let me shift gears a bit. You also ran a customer survey with 500 responses. What did you learn from that, and what actually changed because of it?

Okay, the survey. We got 512 responses, which is a little more than the 500 on my resume, so I'll take that as a win.
