A lot of people wanted it, and a bunch of them said they'd switch their order if it didn't cost extra, which honestly made me think about my roommate, who has a whole speech about oat milk being the only correct choice. Anyway, the manager took that to the regional team, and two stores trialed it at no extra charge. I don't know yet how it's going overall, and I'd want to see the numbers before I said it was a huge deal. What I can say is that people actually told us something specific and we did something with it, which doesn't always happen. Did your team run surveys like that, or do you mostly rely on what comes in through social?
We do a bit of both. Before we move on, I want to circle back to the email newsletter you relaunched. What changed, and how did you measure whether it actually worked better?

Okay, the newsletter. It was kind of a mess when I got it. It was going out pretty much every week with a little bit of everything in it, like a coupon, a store update, a random recipe, and a survey link all in one email. Our open rate was around 18%, and I was pretty sure people were just scrolling past it. So I rewrote the subject lines to be more specific, like saying what's actually in the email instead of something vague like "Sip with us!" I also cut it down to one topic per email, which my professor would say is basic, but apparently it's not what we were doing. A designer on the regional team did the template, so I can't take credit for how it looks, though I did tell her what I wanted it to feel like, which was less corporate. The open rate went from 18% to 27%, and that
That's solid. So the open rate went up to 27%—did you check whether people were actually doing anything with it, or was it just the open that moved?

Honestly, I mostly looked at opens, because that's the number that showed up at the top of the dashboard, and that's what I was trying to fix. I'd have to go back and check whether clicks moved too, and I don't want to guess at that in an interview. The coupon was in some of the emails, so in theory we could have tracked redemptions at the register, but I don't think I ever asked the manager to pull that. It's kind of like my roommate and his fitness app. He's thrilled that he opened it every day, but he's not sure he's actually going to the gym. An open is just someone looking at the email, so I'd want to look at clicks and, if we could, whether people came in afterward. That's the piece I'd want to add to the next one. Does your team usually track email past the open, or do you mostly watch the open rate?
We'll get into that. I want to ask you about something else though—tell me about a time you actually failed at something, or something that didn't go the way you planned.

Yeah, honestly, the launch event is the one that comes to mind. The speaker cancelling wasn't really my fault, but I had no backup plan written down, so I was scrambling the afternoon before. I ended up with the latte art demo, which worked out, but only because one barista was up for it. If she'd said no, I'd have been stuck choosing between moving the whole thing and doing a tasting night with no real plan for it. It's kind of like when my roommate tried to cook a new recipe for a dinner party with no backup, and we ended up eating cereal at ten. So I'd say the failure was less about the event itself and more that I was relying on luck and my memory instead of writing things down. Now I always try to have a second option ready before the day of, even if it's

Honestly, I think it's the same thing that got me into it in the first place. In that media writing class, my professor kept asking why some posts make people stop scrolling and others get ignored, and I got kind of obsessed with figuring it out. Then when I started doing the Instagram work, I liked that I could try something, watch what people actually did, and change it. That's the part that pulls me in. I also like that this company treats regulars like people and not just a sales number, and I think that's something I'd want to be part of. Do you have a sense of what the first few months in this role would look like?

Not rocket science, but it takes someone who can measure things and isn't afraid to change course. We'll figure out the specifics together.

Thanks so much for taking the time to talk with me today. I appreciate you being straight with me about what you know and don't know—that matters more than perfect answers. We'll be in touch soon.

Thanks so much, that's really nice to hear. And honestly, the "I'm not sure" stuff is the part I'd want to get better at, so it's good to know it didn't sink me. Appreciate you taking the time today, and I'm excited about the role. I'll keep an eye out for your email. Have a good rest of your afternoon!
You too, Sam. Take care!

Mostly me, honestly. Dana signed off on the overall plan, since she's the one who had to say yes to changing how we send things out, and she read a couple of the drafts before they went live. That's fair. So you did the research and the pitch, and then it moved out of your hands. Let me ask you this—looking back at your internship overall, is there something that didn't go the way you expected? Like, a time when something didn't work out?

Oh, yeah, the launch event. That one was a bit of a mess, and I learned a lot from it. We had a speaker lined up, a local person who runs a sustainability thing, and we'd built the whole night around her talk. Then she cancelled the day before, which, I get it, stuff happens, but I was up until like midnight trying to figure out what to do. My roommate was asleep on the couch and I kept waking her up to ask if a latte-art demo sounded dumb, and she was like, "Sam, go to bed." Anyway, I ended up asking one of our baristas, Marcus, if he'd do a demo, and he was super into it, which was lucky. We had a $1,500 budget, and 214 people checked in at the door, which felt good, though honestly a bunch of people came for the free drinks, not the talk. The part
So the speaker cancelled the day before. When you pivoted to the barista demo, how did you decide that was the move? Like, did you consider other options, or was that your first instinct?

Honestly, it was mostly my first instinct, and I didn't really weigh a bunch of options the way I probably should have. I was lying there at midnight going through everything, like, could we just do a longer Q&A, or cancel and refund people, or just let it be a drinks night. A cancellation refund felt like giving up, and a Q&A with no speaker felt awkward. Then I thought about the one thing people actually came in for, which is the coffee, and our baristas are genuinely good at latte art, so I figured people might enjoy watching that. My professor, Dr. Okafor, always says that when plans fall apart you should go back to what the audience already cares about, which I think I got from her, though I'm not sure I'd have remembered it at midnight if my roommate hadn't been awake. I asked Marcus the next morning, and he said yes right away, and then he came in on his day off to practice, which was really nice of him. I'd say it worked okay, but I'll be honest, a lot of people came for the free drinks more than anything, so I'm not totally sure we got the message across the way we'd planned.
Right. So people came for the drinks more than the event itself. What would you do differently if you were planning another launch event in your first month on the job somewhere new?

Oh, that's a good question, and I've actually thought about it a bunch since then, probably more than I should have. The first thing I'd do is lock in a backup plan before the event, not at midnight the night before. I'd confirm the speaker a week out and have a second option ready, like a shorter talk or a demo, so it's not a total scramble. My roommate was not thrilled with my midnight texting, so that's a lesson for both of us. I'd also ask the team earlier what people actually want from the night, because we assumed the talk was the draw and it turned out the free drinks were. Honestly, that's kind of funny, since I'd been watching this show about a bakery where everybody's there for the cake and nobody cares about the speech, and I didn't connect it to our event at all. So I'd build the whole thing around the thing people already come in for, and then maybe add the talk as a bonus. And I'd make sure we had a clear way to follow up with the people who came, like a sign-up for the newsletter, so the night actually turns into more visits instead of just one good Thursday

That makes sense. So you'd bake in the backup plan and actually measure whether people come back. Let me ask you this—why do you want a role like this one? Like, what's pulling you toward marketing or this kind of work?

Yeah, so, honestly, the thing that got me into marketing was that I like the moment when something you made actually changes what somebody does. Like with the Instagram stuff, I'd post a video and then see a comment from someone saying they'd been meaning to try the place down the street, and that little jolt of "oh, that worked" is kind of addictive. I was telling my roommate about it last week and she said I sounded like a golden retriever with a brand deal, which, fair. I also think I'm drawn to the stuff that's a little messy, like the launch night falling apart and having to figure it out in real time, because I'd rather be figuring things out than just executing a plan someone handed me. And I've been reading about your company's recent store openings, and I think there's a lot of room to do the kind of customer-first stuff I've been trying, like the videos and the survey, but on a bigger scale and with better tracking so we can actually see what's working. That's the part I'm most excited about, honestly, getting to build something that's measurable and not just vibes. I'll stop there, because I could keep going, but I think that's the core of it.
That's helpful. One more thing—you mentioned leading a team on a rebranding class project. Tell me a bit about that. What was your role, and did anything tricky come up?

Yeah, the rebranding project. So it was a class thing, a team of four, and I ended up as the one who kind of kept us moving, which wasn't really an official title, it just sort of happened. We had a group chat that was basically chaos, and I started making a shared doc with a timeline, and then people just started looking to me to say what was next. My professor, Dr. Okafor, once told us that group projects are really just logistics with feelings, which I wrote down and now quote way too often.

The tricky part was the logo. Two of my teammates really disagreed about it. One loved this bold, almost aggressive redesign, and the other wanted something softer that looked more like the original. Both of them were pretty attached, and the vibe in the group got kind of tense for a few days. I didn't want to just pick the one I liked, because that felt like I'd be deciding it on taste, and my roommate, who thinks I'm too much of a people-pleaser, said I was overthinking it. So I suggested we each test both logos with ten classmates, just a quick poll and a couple of questions about what the brand felt like. Everyone agreed, sort of grudgingly at first, and the results actually pointed pretty clearly toward one of them, and the person who'd pushed for it was happy, and the other one was surprisingly gracious about it. We went with the data, and I think that's probably the thing I'm proudest of from that project, that we could disagree without it turning into a fight. Sorry, I think I went on a bit there.

No, that's useful. So you brought data into a disagreement instead of just making a call. Quick follow-up—when you tested the logos with classmates, what exactly did you ask them? Like, how did you phrase it so you'd actually get useful feedback and not just opinions?

Oh, good question, and honestly I wish I could say I had some perfect survey design, but it was pretty scrappy. I made a little one-page form with both logos side by side, and I labeled them A and B so nobody would know which one was whose. I tried really hard not to ask "which do you like better," because that just gets you a gut reaction, and my professor, Dr. Okafor, keeps saying people are terrible at explaining why they like something. So I asked a couple of questions: which one felt more trustworthy, which one they'd expect to see on a place they'd walk into for coffee, and what three words they'd use to describe each one. I also made sure I didn't tell anyone which logo had which teammate's name attached. It was funny, because one of the classmates I asked wrote "A feels like a sports team" and then later said that was a compliment, so I'm still not totally sure what I was measuring, but it was more useful than arguing in the group chat for three
Got it. Well, I think we've covered a lot of ground. Do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, just one, if that's okay. What does a typical first few months look like for someone in this role, like what would you want me to have figured out by the end of it?

That's a fair question. Honestly, the first month or so is about getting your bearings—meeting the team, understanding what's working and what isn't, and listening more than you're pitching. By the end of the first few months, I'd want you to have a sense of what success looks like here, what our constraints actually are, and ideally to have run at least one small thing end-to-end so we can see how you work. Not something huge, just something real. Does that help?

Yeah, that helps a lot, thanks. Running one small thing end to end sounds right to me, honestly. I'd rather prove it on something real than just talk about it, and I think that's the part I'd be most nervous and most excited about. Plus, I'd want to figure out early what you all already measure, because that's the kind of stuff I wish I'd had on the Instagram project. Okay, I'm going to stop there before I start telling you about the bakery again. Thanks so much for your time today, I really appreciate it.
Ha, no problem at all. Thanks for being thorough and honest about everything—I appreciated that. We'll be in touch soon about next steps. Good luck with the rest of your semester.

verdicts.notes: Strength: covered all five resume topics plus both practice questions, with sharp probing on metrics, methodology, and follow-through. Weakness: nearly every turn opens with praise or evaluation, which leaks feedback; the interviewer also did not redirect the rambling and accepted vague T3/T7 answers without asking for specifics.

transcript.text: Hey, good to meet you. How's your day been so far?

Hey, good to meet you too! Yeah, my day's been pretty good, thanks for asking. I actually almost didn't make it on time, because the bus was late again, which is kind of a running joke at this point. I ended up walking part of the way, and honestly that was nice, I passed this little bakery that smells incredible every single morning, and I'm pretty sure it's the reason I've been thinking about pastries all day. I had a coffee before this, which, given that I'm interviewing at a coffee place, feels a little on-brand. So yeah, pretty good. A bit caffeinated, a bit nervous, but good.

Ha, that's great. Coffee definitely feels on-brand. I appreciate you making the time to get here.

So I'm curious—what drew you to this kind of role? What made you interested in applying?

Thanks, I'm really glad to be here. So what drew me to it... I think it started back in my second year, when I was doing a project on how small businesses talk to their customers, and I kept coming back to coffee shops because they're kind of the perfect case study. Everyone has a favorite place, people really care about it, and the relationship is pretty personal even though it's a quick transaction. My roommate also works at a cafe downtown and she's always complaining about the chaos, and I used to think that sounded miserable, but then I started hanging out there and seeing how much the regulars look forward to things, like seasonal drinks or whatever the barista is experimenting with that week. That's when I realized I wanted to be the person figuring out how to get people excited about the stuff behind the counter, not just the one pulling shots. I've done some social media work and a launch event for a store, and I've got a bit of experience with email and surveys too, so this felt like a natural next step. I think it's the mix of creative stuff and actually watching whether it works that appeals to me.

That makes sense. You've got a real perspective on why people connect with coffee shops, and you've done some hands-on work already. 

Let me dig into one of those projects. You mentioned growing Instagram engagement by 40%—what exactly was that 40% measuring, and what was the baseline you're comparing it to?

Oh, good question, and I'll be honest, I had to go back and check my notes on that one. So the Instagram thing was back when I was helping out with the social accounts for my part-time job at the store, and my manager was the one who let me try something different, which I was really grateful for. Honestly the account had been posting mostly product photos, like a latte on a white table, and they just weren't getting much response, so I was kind of over it. It reminded me of those stock photos on a dentist's website. Anyway, I started doing short videos of actual customers and the staff, like a regular ordering their usual or a barista explaining a drink, and I'd post those a few times a week. It was the kind of thing I'd scroll past myself, but people actually stopped for it. So the number is engagement rate per post, which is likes, comments, and shares divided by followers, and it went from about 2.0% to about 2.8% over three months. That's where the 40% comes from, since 2.8 is 40% higher than 2.0. I know that's not a huge follower count story, but I liked that it was something we could actually see working.

That's a solid explanation, and I appreciate you walking me through the math. So you went from product photos to featuring actual people and stories, and that's what moved the needle.

When you first started posting those customer and staff videos, did you run into any pushback from your manager or anyone else on the team about doing things differently?

Honestly, not really, which I was a little surprised by. I think my manager was just tired of the account looking like a catalog, and when I pitched the idea she said to go for it, as long as we kept an eye on the numbers. I'd actually been watching a bunch of those small business accounts on my own time, the ones run by a single person with a phone, and they all had this kind of messy, real feel that the big chains don't. My roommate said I sounded like a character from some cooking show who's always "trusting the process," which is pretty accurate. There was one barista who was a little nervous about being on camera, so we only filmed her from behind the bar at first, which turned out to work fine. Anyway, the short answer is no real pushback, just a manager who was willing to test something. Is there anything specific you were wondering about with that?

No, that's helpful. It sounds like you had good instincts and your manager trusted you to run with it.

Let me ask you about the customer survey you ran—the one with 500 responses. What did you actually learn from that survey, and did anything change at the store because of what you found?

Oh, the survey. I should say it was actually 512 responses, not exactly 500, because I rounded when I put it on my resume and I don't want to be sloppy about that. We put it together over a couple of weeks, mostly a short form that customers could fill out at the register or on their phones by scanning a code on the cups. It had a mix of questions, like how often people come in, what they order, and what would make them stop coming. I was honestly expecting people to ask for more seasonal drinks or cheaper pastries, and those came up, but the one that kept jumping out was oat milk. A lot of people wanted it, and they wanted it at no extra charge, which was a little bit of a headache because the upcharge is how the store makes money on it. My manager was pretty interested, though, and she went to the regional team with it. I think two stores ended up trialing free oat milk for a few weeks, and I'm not totally sure how it turned out past that, since I'd moved on to the Instagram stuff by then. I remember thinking that the survey was a good example of how a small question can end up changing what a store does. Does that answer what you were asking, or did you want more on how I analyzed the responses?

No, that's good context. So you got this clear signal about oat milk, passed it along to your manager, and she escalated it. But you didn't stick around to see whether the trial actually moved the needle for the store—was that just timing, or did you not follow up on it?

Yeah, it was mostly timing, though I'll admit I didn't push to follow up either. I was wrapping up the survey work right around when I took on the Instagram project, and the store got busy with the holiday rush, so the oat milk trial kind of drifted off my radar. I did ask my manager once, in passing, and she said the early numbers looked okay but it was too soon to call. I never got the final read, and honestly that's something I'd do differently now. I think I was so focused on getting the data in that I didn't plan for what happens after, which is kind of the whole point of a survey. Looking back, I should have asked for a check-in date when we handed it off, and I didn't. I'm trying to be better about closing that loop on my projects now, since a result you never measure is kind of just a guess with better formatting.

That's a really honest take, and it sounds like you've thought about it since then. I respect that.

Let me shift gears. Tell me about a time when something didn't go the way you planned—when you failed at something.

Oh, that's a good one to ask about, because the launch event was basically a disaster in the making. So I was planning the store launch for about 200 people, with a $1,500 budget, and we had this speaker lined up, a local guy who does sustainable sourcing talks. Then he cancelled the day before. I was at my kitchen table at like eleven at night, and my roommate was asking if I wanted to watch the new episode of some baking show, and I was just staring at my laptop thinking, what do I even do now? My manager was really calm about it, which helped, though I think she was more worried about me than the event. So I went to the store the next morning and asked one of the baristas, Jess, if she'd do a latte-art demo, and she said yes, and honestly it ended up being the thing people talked about. We had 214 people check in at the door, which was more than I'd hoped for. The part I still think about is that I almost wanted to cancel the whole thing, and I didn't, and I'm not totally sure whether that was the right call or just stubbornness. Anyway, what I learned is to always have a backup plan, and maybe a backup for the backup.

That's a good story, and you handled the pressure well. But I'm curious about something—you said you're not sure whether cancelling would have been the right call. What would have made that decision clearer for you at the time? Like, what would you have checked or asked before deciding to push forward?

Good question, and honestly I've thought about it a lot. I think what would have helped is knowing what the event was actually for, because I'd kind of been treating it like it had to happen, and that's different from it being the goal. Like, was the point to get people through the door, or to get them talking about the new stuff we were putting on the menu? If it was the second one, a speaker was just one way to get there, and maybe a smaller thing would've been fine. I also should have asked my manager directly what she'd be okay with if it fell apart, because I was guessing at that, and she was calm but I don't really know what calm meant. I probably would have checked the budget too, since we had some room left, and whether Jess and the other baristas could handle a demo on short notice without it wrecking their shift. I didn't do any of that, I just panicked a little and started calling people. So yeah, I think a couple of quick questions before deciding would have made it a lot clearer than staring at my laptop at eleven at night.

That's thoughtful. You're right that knowing the actual goal changes what success looks like.

You mentioned leading a team of four on a rebranding class project. Walk me through that—what was the project, and what did you actually do as the lead?

Yeah, that one was from my branding class last year, and honestly it was kind of chaotic but I learned a lot. The assignment was to rebrand a local business, and our group picked a used bookstore downtown that had a really loyal following but a logo that looked like it was from 1995. There were four of us, and I was the one who got named lead, mostly because I'd been the most vocal about wanting to get started early, which is probably why I got stuck with it. My job was basically keeping us on schedule, splitting up the work, and making sure we had something to present on time. We had a little drama when two of my teammates couldn't agree on the logo. One of them loved a bold, almost hand-drawn look, and the other wanted something cleaner and more minimal. They were both pretty stubborn, and I remember sitting in the library thinking, how do I not make this a fight? So I had both of them test their versions with about ten classmates each, just a quick show-and-ask, and we went with whichever one people actually remembered and liked. I think it was the hand-drawn one, but I'm honestly not 100 percent sure now. What I took from it is that when people disagree, getting a little bit of real data usually calms things down faster than arguing about taste. Also, I should say the professor gave us a B-plus, and I was a little annoyed, but I've mostly gotten over it.

So you brought in real feedback to settle the disagreement, which is smart. But I'm curious—when you tested both versions with classmates, what exactly did you ask them? Like, were you asking which one they liked better, or something else?

Good question, and I'll admit I didn't plan it as carefully as I should have. I basically showed each version to about ten classmates and asked two things: what the business was, and what they thought it said about it. Then I asked which logo they remembered after I took it away, which felt like a better test than just asking which one they liked, since anyone can like a pretty picture. My roommate actually suggested that, after she'd been ignoring my project for a week and then suddenly had opinions about fonts. I wrote the answers on a sticky note, and I think it was pretty clear the hand-drawn one stuck with people, but the notes are a mess and I had to squint at my own handwriting. Looking back, I probably should have asked them why they picked what they picked, because that might have told us more than the vote did. Anyway, that's what I did, and I'd tighten it up next time.

Makes sense. So you got a signal, it was enough to move forward, but you recognize the method could've been sharper.

I want to ask about the email newsletter you relaunched. What was wrong with it before you took it on, and what did you actually change?

Okay, the newsletter. So before I got to it, the store had been sending one of these long emails once a month that felt like it was written by a committee, which I guess it was. It had a news section, a menu update, a random recipe, a note from the owner, and a bunch of links, and honestly I'd never open it either. My roommate got it too, and she said she only ever read the headline and then deleted it. The open rate was around 18%, which isn't terrible for a small store, but it wasn't great either, and I kept thinking nobody actually knew what the email was supposed to do.

So what I changed was mostly the subject lines and the structure. I rewrote the subject lines so they sounded like something a friend would send, like "the oat milk question" or "new drink, tried it so you don't have to," and I cut it down to one topic per email instead of six. That way, if someone only cared about the seasonal drink, they'd open it and get exactly that. A designer on our team did the template, which I'm grateful for, because I would have made something that looked like a flyer from a dentist's office. Open rate went from 18% to 27%, which I was pretty happy about. I'll be honest, I don't know exactly how much of that was the subject lines versus the single-topic thing, since I changed a couple things at once. If I did it again I'd test those separately.

That's solid work, and you're right that you changed two variables at once. Did you check whether people were actually clicking through to anything in those emails, or was it just about the open rate?

Honestly, mostly just open rate. The store's email tool showed clicks too, and I glanced at them now and then, but I never pulled them into a proper comparison, so I can't give you a real number on click-throughs before and after. Which is kind of a problem, because an open only tells you the subject line worked. My roommate, who I keep quoting, says the subject line is basically a promise, and if the email doesn't deliver on it, people just stop opening. I think I was so happy about going from 18 to 27 that I stopped there. I did notice that the seasonal drink email got more clicks than the others, at least from what I remember seeing, but I didn't write it down, so I'd be guessing. If I'm being straight about it, I'd want to track clicks and maybe even whether anyone came in asking for the drink, since that's what the store actually cares about. Anyway, short answer: no, I didn't check clicks in any real way.

Fair enough. You're being honest about what you didn't measure, which is useful.

So if you landed in this role and your first month was to pick one thing and really nail it, what would you tackle first, and how would you approach it?

Okay, if I'm honest, I'd probably pick the newsletter, because it's the one I left most unfinished. I'd start by pulling the click data for the last six months, so I could see which emails people actually acted on instead of just opening. My roommate would say that's the boring part, and she's right, but I think it's where the real answer is. Then I'd talk to the store staff, especially whoever's on the register, and ask whether anyone has mentioned an email or a drink they heard about. That feels a little old-school, but it's the thing the store actually cares about. I'd also want to test one change at a time this time, like keeping the same single-topic format and only changing the subject line, so I'd know what actually worked. And I'd set a check-in date at the start, which is something I should have done with the oat milk survey. I'd probably also ask my manager what a good result would look like for her, since I've learned the hard way that I'm guessing otherwise. Sorry, that got long. Short version: p

No, that's good. You're thinking about how to actually measure impact and close the loop, which is what matters.

We're nearly out of time, so I want to ask—do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, just one, if that's okay. What does a typical week look like for someone in this role, especially how much time goes to the stores versus the corporate side?

Good question. It's pretty split, honestly. You'd spend maybe two to three days a week in stores talking to staff and customers, seeing what's actually happening, and the rest of the time working on campaigns, analysis, that kind of thing. A lot of it depends on what's live at the moment, but you're never totally desk-bound, which I think you'd appreciate given your background.

Any other questions, or are we good?
Nope, that's a great answer, thanks. I think I'm good. Honestly, the store time sounds like the part I'd enjoy most, so that's encouraging. Thanks so much for your time today, I really appreciate it.

Thanks for coming in, Sam. I enjoyed talking with you—you've got good instincts, and I like that you think about what you'd do differently. We'll be in touch soon.

Take care, and thanks again.

feedback_leaks.quote: I appreciate you being straight about what you actually remember.
That makes sense for an intern role.

verdicts.notes: Strength: the interviewer covered most resume topics with natural, relevant follow-ups, including the Instagram specifics, the survey trial ownership, and both practice questions. Weakness: it never returned to the newsletter, let the rambling go unchecked, and gave small evaluative remarks at T8, T20 and T24. At T7 it did not press for a measured baseline after the candidate admitted not having the breakdown.

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for coming in. Did you find everything okay today?

Yeah, totally, thanks for having me. Honestly the video link worked on the first try, which is a small miracle because last week my laptop decided it hated me and I had to borrow my roommate's, and he's got this giant poster of a cat in a tuxedo right behind his desk, so if you see that in the background, that's him, not me. Anyway, I got here early, I was going to say I left my place around, I don't know, twenty minutes before, and I took the bus, which is its own story because the driver was singing along to the radio the whole way. Super nice guy. So yeah, everything's good, I'm just a little caffeinated, which, given that I work at a coffee place, is probably not a surprise to you.

Ha, fair enough. Coffee hazard of the job, right? Well, I'm glad you're here and the tech cooperated. So let's dive in—walk me through your background a bit. How'd you end up in marketing, and what have you been doing at the coffee chain?

Yeah, coffee hazard for sure. So, how I got into marketing... honestly it's kind of a funny story. I started out thinking I'd do journalism, I was on the school paper freshman year and I loved writing, but then I realized I cared more about why people choose one thing over another than about the story itself. My advisor, Dr. Alvarez, who is this incredibly intense person who wears a different colored blazer every single day, basically told me to take her consumer behavior class, and that was it, I was hooked. And then I needed a job, and the coffee chain was hiring, and I figured it'd be a good way to see the other side of things. So I've been there about a year and a half, and I've been doing marketing stuff on the side, which is how I ended up doing a few things that I'm actually pretty proud of. The big one is the Instagram work. We were getting a lot of product photos on there, and they just weren't landing, so I pitched switching to short customer videos. My manager approved it, and over about three months our average engagement per post went from around 2.0 percent to 2.8 percent, which is the forty percent number on my resume. I also relaunched the email newsletter, where our open rate went from 18 percent to 27 percent, mostly because I rewrote the subject lines and made each email about one topic. A designer did the template, so I can't take credit for how it looks. Those are probably the two things I'd point to first.

Got it, that's helpful. So on the Instagram piece—you said engagement went from 2.0 to 2.8 percent. When you switched to the customer videos, what specifically changed about how people were interacting with those posts compared to the product photos?

Oh, good question, and I wish I had a slide ready for that. So, I was kind of obsessed with the analytics for those three months, mostly because I'd check them on the bus, which is where I do all my real thinking. I think the biggest shift was that the videos were the kind of thing people wanted to talk about, like one of our baristas, Marcus, who has this totally unhinged way of frothing milk that we filmed for like fifteen seconds. Customers would tag their friends under those, which the product shots never really got. The product photos were basically a menu on a wall, and people would scroll right past. I'd have to pull the exact breakdown of likes, comments, and saves to tell you which one moved the most, and honestly I didn't split it out as carefully as I should have. But the general idea was people went from looking at the drink to watching the person making it, and that seemed to make them stop scrolling. Does
That makes sense. So it sounds like comments and tags went up. Did you see an increase in saves or shares, or was it mostly the comments?

Honestly, I can't give you a clean answer on saves versus shares, and that's on me. I was pulling the analytics up on my phone during my bus ride, and the bus has this bumpy stretch right before the library, so half the time I was squinting at the screen while the driver hit the brakes. What I remember is that comments and tags were the thing I kept noticing, because people were actually replying to each other, which is kind of the dream for a social account. I think saves went up too, but I'd be guessing if I gave you a number, and I don't want to make one up in an interview. The number I can stand behind is the overall engagement rate, going from about 2.0 to 2.8 percent. If I had to pick one thing I'd want to check next, it would be whether the videos drove saves, because that usually means people want to come back to something, and for a coffee shop that could mean they're thinking about ordering it. Does that help, or should I dig up the breakdown and send it to you?

No, that's fine—I appreciate you being straight about what you actually remember. So when you pitched switching to videos in the first place, what made you think that was the right move? Like, how did you know that would work better?

Yeah, good question, and I'll be honest, it wasn't some big data moment. I was scrolling through our own account one night, and the product photos were all these pretty overhead shots of cups on a wooden table, and they just looked like every other coffee account on the internet. Then I noticed that the few times we'd posted something with a person in it, like a barista pouring or someone laughing with a friend at the counter, those were the ones people actually responded to. So I kind of put two and two together. I also remember sitting on the bus thinking about how I never stop to look at a picture of a drink, but I will stop to watch a thirty-second clip of someone doing something a little weird with milk. That's basically the logic I pitched. I didn't have a formal test or anything before I brought it to my manager, so I framed it as a trial for about three months, which I think is part of why she said yes. She liked that it was low risk and we could look at the numbers at the end. Which, now that I think about it, is probably the thing I should have been more rigorous about tracking from the start.
Makes sense. Okay, so you've got the Instagram work and the newsletter. You also mention planning a store launch event for 200 guests on your resume. Walk me through what that involved.

Yeah, the launch event. So this one was a bit of a rollercoaster, and I'll admit I'm still a little scarred. We had a budget of fifteen hundred dollars, which sounds like a lot until you start pricing out pastries and a sound system. My job was basically to get people through the door and make it feel like an actual event, not just a Tuesday with free samples. I did the social posts, I worked with the store manager on the layout, and I made a check-in list so we could see who showed up. The resume says 200 guests, but the honest number is 214 people checked in at the door, which I like because it's a little more specific and I think the check-in list was one of the few things I did right the whole time. The big problem was that the speaker we'd booked cancelled the day before. I was at the store late that night, and I remember staring at the ceiling thinking about it, which is also when I remembered my roommate's cat poster, and I'm not sure why. Anyway, we ended up doing a latte-art demo with one of our baristas instead, and honestly it was a better fit for a coffee shop. People loved it. Someone even asked if they could get a lesson, which I think is a good sign. So the event worked out, but mostly because we scrambled and the barista was great, not because the plan was perfect.
So the speaker cancelling the day before—that's a pretty big curveball. How did you handle that moment when you found out? Like, what was your first move?

Okay, so I found out through a text from the speaker's assistant, which was a fun way to start the day before a big event. My first instinct was to panic a little, and then I think I just started typing a list on my phone, which is what I do when I'm stressed, like my brain needs something to organize. The store manager, Dana, is really calm, and she basically said, "Okay, what do we have?" So we went through the budget, the space, and the time slot, and the latte-art idea came up because one of our baristas, Jordan, does these crazy detailed leaves and hearts that people film on their phones all the time. I'm a bit of a worrier, so I wanted to make sure we didn't just throw something together, so I texted Jordan that night and asked if they'd be up for it. They said yes, which was a huge relief. Honestly, I'd like to say I had a grand plan, but mostly I just tried to keep things moving and not let the guests
That's helpful. So you texted Jordan that night and they said yes. Did you prep with them at all before the event, or did they just kind of wing it the day of?

Yeah, we did a little prep, though it was pretty scrappy. Jordan and I met for about forty-five minutes the morning of the event, before the doors opened, which was not a lot of time, but Jordan is super comfortable on that bar, so it wasn't like starting from zero. We figured out which two drinks they'd make, I think a cortado and a flat white, because they're visual enough that people can see the difference, and we planned about fifteen minutes of demo with a little Q and A at the end. I also asked Jordan to talk through what they were doing as they went, like explaining why the milk needs to be at a certain temperature, because I figured people would be more into it if they got a bit of the why. Jordan was great about it. They were a little nervous about talking in front of a crowd, which, same, so we kind of practiced the handoff, like I'd introduce them and then get out of the way. There was one moment where the milk got too hot and Jordan just laughed and said "well, that's a learning experience," and honestly that's the part people seemed to like most.
Nice. So you've got the Instagram, the newsletter, the launch event. You also mention running a customer survey with 500 responses. What prompted that, and what did you actually do with the results?

Oh, the survey. Okay, so this is one I actually enjoyed, which is weird because surveys are usually the thing nobody wants to do. We'd been getting a lot of comments at the counter about oat milk, like people would ask Dana if we had it, and then they'd kind of sigh when we said it was an extra fifty cents. I was on the bus again, because the bus is basically my office, and I thought, we're just guessing what people want, so why don't we ask them? I wrote a short survey, maybe eight questions, and we put it on the receipts, the newsletter, and a little QR code by the register. The resume says 500, but the real number is 512 responses, and I'm kind of proud of that because it's more specific. Most of the answers were about the usual stuff, like which drinks people order most and how often they come in, but the big finding was that a lot of people wanted oat milk at no extra charge. Some people even said they'd come in more often if that happened. So we took that to the team, and two of the stores trialed it. I don't know the final numbers from that trial, and honestly I should go back and check, because I'd hate to tell you a result

Got it. So the survey showed people wanted oat milk at no extra charge, and a couple stores trialed it. Did you have any role in setting up or running that trial, or was that handed off to someone else after you gave them the results?

Honestly, mostly handed off, and I'm a little bummed about that. I put together a one-page summary of the survey results, with the oat milk finding up top and a couple of charts, and I sent it to Dana and our regional marketing person, Priya. From there the decision was above my pay grade, so Priya and the ops team set up the trial at two stores. I was asked to help with the signage, so I made the little table tent cards that said something like "Oat milk, no extra charge, for a limited time," and I walked over to the closer store one afternoon to drop them off. That's about as hands-on as I got, and I wasn't in the room when they decided which stores or how long it would run. I think I was the one who kept asking about the results, which is probably why I'm the one who should go back and check the final numbers. Also, I may have spent the whole walk over there thinking about whether oat milk is actually the same as regular milk for latte art, because Jordan has opinions about that, and I still don't fully understand them.

Fair enough. So you identified the insight, but you weren't really involved in whether it actually moved the needle. That makes sense for an intern role. Let me shift gears a bit. You mention on your resume that you led a team of four on a rebranding class project. Tell me about that.

Yeah, that one was a class project for my brand strategy course, and it was a good example of why group work is so hard. There were four of us, and I got put in charge mostly because I'd been the one who kept the group chat from dying, which I think says more about my texting habits than my leadership. The client was a made-up local bakery, but we treated it like a real assignment, and our professor, who I swear is the only person on campus who wears a different sweater every day, was really strict about the reasoning behind every choice. The tricky part was the logo. Two of my teammates were pretty convinced of two different directions, and they were both kind of digging in, and the whole thing was getting tense. I remember sitting in the library thinking about how I didn't want to just pick my favorite because that wouldn't be fair to either of them. So I suggested we each test both logos with ten classmates, just a quick show-and-tell with a couple of questions about what the bakery felt like and whether they'd walk in. It wasn't a huge sample, and I'd be the first to say that, but it gave us something other than our own opinions to point to. We went with the one that people connected with more, and honestly the teammate who lost the argument was great about it. I think the bigger lesson
So you ran a quick test with classmates to break the tie. Did that actually settle the disagreement, or did you have to do more work to get buy-in from the person whose logo didn't win?

Yeah, it mostly settled it, which surprised me a little. The test was pretty informal, so I wasn't sure people would take it seriously, but once we showed everyone the numbers, like which logo more people said they'd walk into the bakery for, the argument kind of died on its own. Nobody likes arguing with a bar chart, I think. My teammate, Priya, no, wait, that's my regional manager, sorry, the teammate's name was Eli, was the one who'd pushed hardest for the other logo. He was disappointed, I could tell, but he said something like, "Fair, the classmates liked this one more," and then he actually helped refine the winning design, which I didn't expect. I did have to check in with him one-on-one after class, mostly just to say I hadn't picked a side to make a point. I think that conversation mattered more than the test did. Honestly, I'm not sure I'd have handled it as smoothly if the sample had been bigger or if the results had been closer. That's the part I'd want to do better next time, like setting up a clearer decision rule before the test instead of after.
That's thoughtful. So you've done a bunch of stuff at the coffee chain and the class project. Can you think of a time when something didn't go the way you wanted, and what you learned from it?

Oh, yeah, there's a pretty obvious one, and it's kind of the Instagram thing again, sorry. I didn't set up a clean way to track the breakdown from the start. I was so focused on the overall engagement number going from 2.0 to 2.8 percent that I didn't really split out likes, comments, and saves by post type, so now when someone asks which change did the most work, I'm stuck guessing. I noticed it around month two, when I was going through the numbers on the bus, and the bumpy stretch by the library did not help my focus. My roommate, who has the cat-in-a-tuxedo poster, always says I'm better at vibes than spreadsheets, and he's kind of right. What I learned is that I should have decided what I was going to
So you realized partway through that you weren't tracking the right things. Did you go back and fix it, or did you just kind of accept that gap and move on?

Honestly, I mostly just accepted it and moved on, which I'm not proud of. Once I saw I hadn't split things out, I thought about going back and pulling the old data, but the posts from those first months weren't tagged by type, so I'd have had to go through each one by hand. I told myself I'd do it when things calmed down, and then the newsletter got busy and the launch event was coming up, and it just sort of slid. I did start tagging new posts by format after that, so at least going forward I can see which type is doing what. But the earlier stretch is kind of a black box now. And yeah, my roommate's cat poster is still watching me from the background, so maybe he's right that I should lean on the spreadsheet a little more.
Got it. Last thing before we wrap up—why marketing? Like, what draws you to this kind of work, and what would you want to do in a role like this one?

Yeah, good question, and I'll admit I've thought about it more on the bus than anywhere else. What got me is that marketing is basically trying to figure out why people do the things they do, and I've always been that person who notices why someone picked the oat milk latte over the regular one, or why a post made them stop scrolling. Journalism was the first thing I wanted, and I still love writing, but I kept caring more about the reasons behind a choice than the story itself. Dr. Alvarez, the one with the different blazer every day, pushed me toward consumer behavior, and that's when it clicked. Since then I've been pretty drawn to the testing side of things, like the survey and the logo thing, where you get to ask people what they actually want instead of guessing. In a role like this, I'd want to be someone who can come up with an idea, test it, and then actually follow through on the numbers, which, as you've probably noticed, is the part I'm still working on. I'd love to get better at the tracking side and be the person who can say with confidence which change did what. Honestly, I'd also just like to work on something where I can see the results of what I'm doing, like a campaign that people actually talk about.
That's fair. Well, I appreciate you walking through all of that. Before we wrap up, do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, I do, just one. What does a typical week look like for someone in this role, and how much of it is hands-on versus meetings?

Good question. Honestly, it depends on the project, but I'd say it's probably 60-40, maybe 70-30 hands-on to meetings on a normal week. You're doing a lot of campaign work, some analysis, writing briefs, that kind of thing. But you're also coordinating across teams, so there are check-ins. If you landed here, you'd probably spend your first month just getting to know how we work and what the current priorities are, so expect a few more meetings upfront. After that it settles out a bit.

Oh, that's really helpful, thanks. Sixty-forty or seventy-thirty hands-on sounds about right to me, because I'd much rather be making things than sitting in meetings, though I know a few check-ins are part of the deal. And the first-month thing makes sense, I'd want to learn the priorities before jumping in and maybe breaking something. I'm also kind of relieved to hear there's a settling-in period, since I'm definitely going to need to get better at the tracking stuff, so having time to set up better habits from the start would be good. Thanks for walking me through that, I really appreciate it.
You're welcome. Well, thanks for taking the time today, Sam. We'll be in touch soon with next steps. Good luck with everything.

practice_questions.question: Tell me about a time you failed.
Why do you want this kind of role?

verdicts.notes: Strength: the interviewer stayed in role and covered every resume topic and both requested questions. Follow-ups were grounded in specifics, such as probing the relative 40% jump, the unverified 214 count, and who owned the newsletter lift. Weakness: it spent four turns on the Instagram story and let the rambling candidate drift. It also leaked mild praise ("useful self-awareness", "Good question") and never pressed for numbers on the customer-consent answer at T9.

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for coming in. Did you find everything okay today?

Yeah, yeah, everything's fine, thanks for asking. Honestly the video link was a little rough at first, my laptop kept freezing and I had to close about fifteen tabs, one of which was a recipe for banana bread I'd been meaning to try, which is a whole other thing. My roommate keeps leaving her dishes in the sink, so I basically got out of the apartment early just to avoid that, and the bus was actually on time for once, which felt like a small miracle. Anyway, I'm glad to be here, and I'm excited to talk about the role.

Ha, glad the bus cooperated. And hey, banana bread is worth saving for later.

So what drew you to this role? What's got you interested in this kind of work?

Oh, totally, the banana bread is staying on my list. So, what drew me here... I've always liked coffee shops, honestly more than I probably should. I spend a lot of time in them studying, and I started noticing how people talk about their local spot, like it's the place they go when they need a little normal in their day. That got me thinking about how a brand can feel that personal, and that's kind of what communications is about, right? My advisor actually told me to look at local chains instead of the big national ones, because you get to see your work land with actual neighbors, and I think she was right. The Instagram stuff I did for my last internship was the first time I really got to see that happen. I switched from product photos to short videos of customers, and over three months our engagement per post went from about 2 percent to 2.8, which I know sounds small, but it was a 40 percent jump, and my manager signed off on the whole plan. That's the kind of work I want to keep doing, where you can actually see whether the thing you made is working.

That makes sense. You mentioned the Instagram engagement went from 2 percent to 2.8 percent—so that 40 percent bump was the relative increase. What made you decide to switch from product photos to customer videos specifically? Was that your idea, or did something point you in that direction?

Yeah, you caught that, it's a relative jump, so it sounds bigger than it is in real numbers, which my roommate pointed out when I was bragging about it, and then she went back to complaining about the dishes. Anyway, the switch was mostly my idea. I was scrolling through our feed one night, which is apparently what I do instead of sleeping, and the product photos all looked the same: a latte on a marble counter, the same angle, the same lighting. It felt like an ad, and I'd probably have scrolled past it too. Then a regular had posted a short clip of herself ordering her usual while the barista laughed at something, and it got more comments than anything we'd done in weeks. My advisor has this line about how people trust other people more than they trust brands, and I'd heard it so many times I kind of rolled my eyes, but that clip made me think she was right. So I pitched a plan to my manager, mostly customer clips plus a few behind-the-scenes shots, and she signed

Got it. So you spotted the pattern, made the connection to what your advisor had said, and brought it to your manager. When you pitched it to her, what was her reaction? Did she have any concerns, or was it pretty straightforward?

Oh, she was great about it, mostly. She didn't push back much, which was a relief, though she did ask me how we'd get customers to agree to be filmed, and honestly I hadn't thought about that at all. I had this whole picture of the videos and zero plan for the permission part, so I just said I'd make a simple release form and ask people at the counter, and she seemed fine with that. The one thing she really cared about was that we keep the posts on brand, so no random stuff, which, fair enough. She signed off on the plan that week, and I spent the next few days running around with my phone trying to catch people mid-order. Some of the clips were terrible, shaky and too dark, but the ones that worked were the ones where the customer forgot the camera was there, and I think that's the whole trick. Anyway, I learned a lot about patience, and also that baristas are way more photogenic than I expected, which is not really a professional observation, but there you go.

That's helpful context. So you came up with the release form on the spot when she asked. How did that actually go in practice? Did you get pushback from customers when you asked them, or did most people say yes?

Honestly, most people said yes, which surprised me a little. I thought I'd get a lot of "no thanks" or people giving me the side-eye, but the ones who said no were pretty chill about it. The trick I figured out was asking before I pulled the phone out, because if you start filming and then ask, people get weird. My roommate says I'd make a great salesperson because I can talk my way into anything, but really I just felt awkward the whole time and tried to keep it short. The form was basically one page with a checkbox and a line for a name, and I printed it at the library, which took three tries because the printer on the second floor hates me. A couple of the regulars were happy to do it on the spot, and one guy wanted to see the video before he'd sign, which was fair. So yeah, mostly yes, and the people who said no just got their coffee and left, which is exactly how it should be.
Makes sense. So you got the videos shot and started posting them. When you look back at that whole project now—from the idea through execution—is there anything you'd do differently?

Yeah, I'd have done the permission part first. Like I said, I had this whole picture of the videos and no plan for getting people to agree, so I was kind of winging it at the counter. If I'd written the release form before I pulled out the phone, I'd have saved a few awkward days and the library printer wouldn't have gotten to me three times. I also wish I'd tracked engagement by post type from the start. I mostly looked at the overall average, which went from about 2 to 2.8 percent, but I can't tell you for sure which clips did the work, and I'd really like to know that. My advisor would probably say something smart about measuring before you make the change, and I'd roll my eyes, and then she'd be right, like she usually is. Oh, and I'd have brought a better tripod. I was holding my phone at weird angles for a week, and my arm still hasn
That's useful self-awareness. You mentioned you ran a customer survey with 500 responses at some point—tell me about that. What were you trying to learn?

Oh, the survey, that was a whole thing. We put it out at the register and on the email list, and I think we ended up with 512 responses, which is more than the 500 I put on my resume, so I'm not going to complain. I was supposed to be doing it for a class project, but my manager wanted something useful too, so it kind of became both. Honestly, I almost gave up on it halfway through because the QR code on the cups kept getting smudged and I had to reprint the table tents. My roommate also found it hilarious that I was reading survey answers on the bus like it was a novel. Anyway, the main thing we wanted to learn was what would make people come back more often, and what was annoying them without them saying so. The biggest answer was
What was the biggest answer? What did people say was keeping them from coming back more often?

Oh, right, the biggest one was oat milk. People kept saying they'd come in more if oat milk didn't cost extra, and the upcharge was the thing that annoyed them, even though nobody really complained about it out loud. I didn't expect that to be the top answer. I thought we'd get stuff about the seating or the line at 8 a.m., and we did get some of that, but the oat milk comments just kept piling up. My roommate, who is weirdly passionate about oat milk, was thrilled and then immediately asked for a free latte, which is not how surveys work. Anyway, the company ended up trialing it at two stores, which felt like a big deal for a survey I almost gave up on because of the table tents. I'm still not totally sure how much the trial moved the needle, since I didn't get to see the numbers all the way through, but it was cool to watch the data turn into something the store actually tried.
So the oat milk thing went to a trial at two stores. Did you have any hand in that decision, or did your manager just take it and run with it?

Honestly, my manager took it and ran with it, and I was kind of thrilled just to be in the room. I put the survey summary together, with the oat milk comments pulled out and a little chart, and I presented it at a team meeting. I think I talked for like five minutes too long, and at one point I was explaining how the QR code got smudged, which nobody asked about. But the decision to trial it was above my pay grade. I'm not even sure who signed off on the two stores, whether it was the regional person or someone from corporate. I just know it wasn't me. My roommate would say I should have pushed harder for it, and she's probably right, but I also didn't want to be the intern who tells people what to do with the milk. So I did my part, handed over the numbers, and let the people who actually own the menu make the call.
That makes sense. Let me ask you this—you've talked about the Instagram stuff, the survey, and some other projects. Tell me about a time you actually failed at something. What happened?

Oh, failure, that's a fun one to think about, because I have a few, and most of them involve a printer. Okay, so the one that actually stings is the launch event. We had a budget of $1,500 and I was supposed to bring in a speaker, which I'd sort of been building the whole thing around. Then the speaker cancelled the day before, and I was standing in the back room at like 9 p.m. trying not to panic while the barista on shift kept asking if I wanted a fresh cup of anything. I ended up pivoting to a latte-art demo with one of the baristas, which honestly went fine, and we still had 214 people check in at the door. But I didn't have a backup plan, and I should have. My advisor says every event needs a plan B, and I'd heard that a hundred times, so yeah, I was kind of an idiot about it. The demo worked out, but I got lucky, and I know that. I'd want to have a backup speaker lined up next time, or at least a second option, so I'm not sprinting on fumes the night before.
When you say 214 people checked in—was that close to what you were expecting, or did that surprise you?

Honestly, it was a little higher than I'd planned for, which was nice, but also kind of stressful. We'd been hoping for maybe 150 or so, and then a bunch of people showed up, and I was scrambling to make sure the coffee didn't run out. Anyway, the line at the door got long, and my roommate, who came to support me, said it looked like a fire drill. Part of me thinks the latte-art demo was a better draw than a speaker would've been, because people could watch it happen right in front of them. I'm not totally sure whether that's a real insight or just me being relieved it worked. My advisor would probably tell me to check the actual attendance numbers against the sign-in sheet, and she'd be right, because I never did a proper count after the fact.
So you didn't actually verify the 214 number afterward?

Honestly, no, I didn't do a proper count afterward. The 214 came from the check-in sheet at the door, and I tallied the names that night while I was half asleep on the couch, so it's probably close, but I never went back and cross-checked it against anything. Somebody could have signed in twice, or a few people might have walked out before the demo ended, and I wouldn't know. I put it on my resume and in the interview because it was the number I had, and I should've double-checked it before I said it out loud. My advisor would definitely call that out, and she'd be right. If I can get the sign-in sheet back from the store, I'll recount it, because I'd rather fix that than have someone ask me about it later and get caught.
Fair enough. You mentioned you led a team of four on a rebranding class project. Walk me through that one—what was the project, and what did you actually do?

Oh, the rebranding project, yeah, that one was a lot of group chat drama. It was for a branding class, and the assignment was to take a local business and figure out what its identity should be, so our group picked a bakery across the street from campus, mostly because the owner gave us free muffins. There were four of us, and I got put in charge, which I think happened because I'd been the one who made the spreadsheet for the group project before that. Two of my teammates really disagreed about the logo. One wanted something clean and minimal, and the other wanted something hand-drawn and a little messy, and they were both getting pretty heated about it in the chat at like midnight. So I did something I'd been reading about, which was to have both of them test their versions with about 10 classmates each and see which one people actually remembered and liked. I know, very professional, my roommate said it sounded like a middle school science fair. But the hand-drawn one won, and the person who lost was surprisingly gracious about it, and we put the winner into the final deck. We got a decent grade, though I'm honestly not sure the professor loved our final presentation, because I rambled through the slide about typography for way too long. I think the main thing I learned was that people argue less when there's a way to just check.
When you set up those tests with your classmates, did you come up with that approach on your own, or did someone suggest it?

Honestly, I came up with the idea, but I stole the bones of it from a reading for my design class. The professor had assigned this article about how teams usually fight over aesthetics when they should be testing what people actually respond to, and I remember thinking that sounded obvious and also kind of annoying, because it meant I'd have to do more work. But when my two teammates were going back and forth at midnight, the article popped into my head, and I thought, fine, let's just test it. I had to talk my teammates into it, which was its own thing. One of them, the minimal-logo person, said it was a waste of time, and the other one said yes immediately, so I ended up doing a bit of a sales pitch in the group chat. My roommate, who was on the couch next to me while this was all happening, said I sounded like a very tired mediator on a reality show. Anyway, the testing itself was pretty simple. I asked classmates to look at each logo for a few seconds, then tell us what they remembered and whether they liked it, and we wrote down the answers on index cards, which I still think is the best part of the whole project. The hand-drawn one came out ahead, but I'll
You said one of them pushed back and called it a waste of time. How did you handle that? What did you say to get them on board?

Honestly, I didn't say anything that clever. The minimal-logo teammate, Jordan, I think, was pretty annoyed, and I could tell it wasn't really about the test, it was that they'd spent a lot of time on that design and didn't want to see it lose to something they thought looked messy. So I kind of just said, look, we're not deciding whose work is better, we're deciding what the bakery's customers actually remember, and if yours wins, it goes in the deck with your name on it. I also said we'd do the same test on both of our favorites and not just the two they hated. My roommate says that was basically a bribe, but I think it was more like being fair. I'm not sure it was the right move, honestly, because they stayed kind of quiet in the chat for the rest of the night. But they did show up for the index cards, so I'll count that as a win, even if it was a grumpy win. Also, did I mention the muffins were really good? Because they were, and I may have eaten two while we were counting.
Got it. One more thing—you relaunched the customer email newsletter at some point. What changed, and how did that go?

Oh, the newsletter, yeah, that one's kind of my favorite because the numbers actually moved. The old one was a mess, honestly. It was this long email with five or six topics stacked on top of each other, a new drink, a coupon, a staff pick, store hours, and nobody could tell what to click. So I rewrote the subject lines first, which took forever because I kept reading them out loud to my roommate until she got annoyed and said just pick one. Then I cut it down to one topic per email, which felt scary at first, like I was throwing stuff away, but it made the whole thing easier to read. A designer on our side did the template, which I'm very glad about, because I was not going to be the one making it look good. Our open rate went from about 18 percent to 27 percent, and I was pretty proud of that, though I should say I didn't track clicks as carefully as I should have, so I can't tell you how much of that turned into people actually coming in. My advisor would definitely ask me about that, and she'd be right, so I'm going to start pulling those numbers now.
So the open rate went from 18 to 27 percent. Was that your part of the project, or did other people have a hand in that improvement?

Mostly me, on the writing side. I rewrote the subject lines and cut each email down to one topic, and that's what I'd point to if someone asked what changed. The designer did the template, so the look of it wasn't mine, but the content and the subject lines were. My manager signed off on the direction, and I think she was glad someone was willing to actually test something instead of just sending the same thing every week. I'll admit I didn't run a formal A/B test, so I can't say for sure how much of the lift came from the subject lines versus the one-topic change. Probably both, but I'd want to see that split before I claimed too much.
That makes sense. Before we wrap up, do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, just one, if that's okay. What does a typical week look like for the person in this role, and how much of it is hands-on work versus meetings?

Good question. It's pretty hands-on, honestly. You'd be running social, helping with email campaigns, maybe some event planning—stuff where you're actually making things and seeing the results. There are meetings, sure, but probably not more than a few a week. A lot of it depends on what's going on with the brand at any given time, but the goal is to keep you moving and not stuck in back-to-backs.

Thanks for taking the time to talk through all this, Sam. We'll be in touch soon about next steps.

Oh, that sounds great, honestly. I'd much rather be making things and checking results than sitting in meetings all day, so that's a good fit for me. Thanks so much for taking the time, and I really appreciate you walking me through it. I'm looking forward to hearing about next steps. Oh, and I hope you have a good rest of your day, and I'll probably be thinking about that banana bread now.
Ha, go for it. Take care, Sam.
