It also curtly deflected the candidate's question at T12 and stayed on the Instagram and launch details for a long time.

transcript.text: Hey, good to meet you. How's your day been so far?

Hey, good to meet you too, thanks for making the time. My day's been pretty good, honestly, kind of a slow start. I had a coffee on the way over, which, given the job I'm applying for, feels a little on theme. Then my bus got stuck behind a delivery truck for like fifteen minutes, so I was sitting there thinking I'd be late, and I was refreshing my email every two seconds. But it turned out fine, I got to the coffee shop near my place a few minutes early and just sat in my car for a bit. Anyway, yeah, it's been good. How about you?

Ha, I appreciate that. Yeah, it's been busy but good. Glad you made it here with time to spare.

So let's dive in. Walk me through your background a bit—how'd you end up where you are now?

Sure, yeah. So I'm a communications major, and I kind of fell into marketing by accident. My first real exposure was a professor, Dr. Hal, who made us redo every assignment about four times, and I'm still a little annoyed about it but I'm also grateful. Anyway, I ended up interning at the coffee chain, and the first thing I got to work on was their Instagram. The posts were all these really polished product shots, and I pushed for short videos of customers instead. My manager said yes, which I didn't expect, and over three months the average engagement per post went from about 2% to about 2.8%. Before that I'd also helped with a store launch and a newsletter, and I ran a customer survey too, which was kind of my favorite part because people had opinions about oat milk that I did not expect. So that's basically how I got here, I think. Is there a specific part you want me to go into more?
Nice. Yeah, let me dig into the Instagram piece a bit more. So you said engagement went from about 2% to 2.8%—was that the engagement rate, or the total number of engagements?

Yeah, it was the engagement rate, so the average engagement per post as a percentage of followers, not the raw count. I should've been clearer about that earlier. I actually had to look it up again this morning because I couldn't remember which one we tracked. The analytics dashboard is kind of a mess, and I spent a while on the wrong tab, which is basically my whole week in a nutshell. The 40% on my resume is the relative jump, from about 2% to 2.8%, so it sounds bigger than the raw change. I just didn't want to round up in a way that would look sketchy if someone checked. My manager was great about it, though. She let me run the test for three months, and I think that's the part I'm proudest of, not the number itself.

Got it. So you were pretty deliberate about how you communicated that number. That makes sense. When you say your manager let you run the test for three months—what did you actually do during those three months? Like, week to week, what was your part?

Yeah, so, week to week. Honestly, I don't have a neat log of it, and I wish I did, because my notes app is a graveyard of half-finished to-do lists. The basic plan was that I'd stop posting the polished product shots and start putting up short videos of actual customers, like someone ordering, or a regular talking about their usual drink. I'd write up the idea, my manager would look at it, and she approved it. Then it was a lot of asking people if we could film them, which is harder than it sounds, because some people are great on camera and some freeze the second you point a phone at them. My roommate says I'm too optimistic about that kind of thing, and she's probably right. I'd check how the posts were doing, adjust the captions or the timing, and try again. Dr. Hal would've made me redo that whole process four times, so I guess I did get some practice. Was there a particular part of the process you wanted me to walk through?
No, that's helpful. So when you were adjusting captions or timing—did you notice any patterns in what actually worked? Like, was there a type of video or a time of day that performed better?

Yeah, I think there were some patterns, but I'd be guessing if I gave you a specific time of day, and I don't want to make something up in an interview. The analytics had a bunch of tabs, and I was mostly checking whether the overall number was moving, not slicing it up by hour. What stood out to me was that the videos where the customer seemed relaxed and was just talking about their order did better than the ones where someone was clearly reading a script. People can tell. I also remember the captions got shorter over time, because my manager pointed out that nobody reads a paragraph under a video at 8 a.m. while they're waiting for their latte. If you wanted the real answer, I'd pull up the dashboard and look at the breakdown instead of relying on my memory, which, as you can tell, is not my strongest skill. Did you want me to talk about how I'd set up a test like that differently next time?
Yeah, actually—if you were starting that project over tomorrow, what would you do differently?

Oh, that's a good question. Honestly, the first thing I'd do is track things properly from day one. I was mostly watching the overall number go up or down, which is fine, but I never really split it out by video type, and now I'm kind of guessing about what worked. It's like my roommate with her meal prep: she swears she'll log everything, and then three weeks in she's just eating cereal over the sink. I'd also set up a simple spreadsheet before posting anything, with a column for who was in the video, what the order was, and what time it went up. The consent stuff would be different too. I'd get a little release form ready before I ever pulled out my phone, because asking people on the spot was awkward and I lost a couple of good takes that way. And I'd probably check in with my manager every two weeks instead of just when something looked off. Does that kind of structure work for the way your team tracks things?
That's fair. We'll talk about our process later if you make it through. Let me ask you this—you mentioned the store launch event on your resume. Walk me through that one. What was your role there?

Yeah, the launch event was a fun one, and also a little stressful. My role was mostly planning and coordinating, so I helped set the schedule, handled a lot of the day-of logistics, and talked to the vendors. We had a $1,500 budget, which sounds like a lot until you start buying cups and napkins and somebody wants a banner. The big thing that happened was that the speaker we'd booked cancelled the day before. I was at my kitchen table at 11 p.m. with my roommate, who was trying to watch a show, and I was basically panicking into my laptop. We ended up asking one of the baristas, who does latte art, to do a demo instead, and honestly it went better than I expected. About 214 people checked in at the door, which felt like a lot for a Tuesday. I'd say the lesson I took from it is that you always need a backup plan, and maybe a backup for the backup. Did you want me to get into how we handled the day-of stuff, or was there something about the planning you wanted to know?
How did you count the 214? Was that everyone who showed up, or just the ones who checked in?

Good question, and honestly, that's the number I'm most sure of, because it's the check-in count from the door. We had someone at a table with a sign-in list, and that's where the 214 came from. I don't think I'd call it a headcount of everyone who showed up, though. Some people came in with a group and only one person checked in, and I definitely saw a few folks walk in, grab a drink, and leave without signing anything. There was also a bunch of traffic from the people who were just there for the latte art demo and didn't want to wait in the line. So if someone asked me for an exact attendance number, I'd say 214 checked in, and the real number was probably somewhat higher. That's the kind of thing I wish I'd tracked better, the same way I wish I'd split up the Instagram numbers. My roommate, of course, thinks I'm overthinking it, but I'd rather be precise than get caught saying something that doesn't hold up. Did you want to know how we counted the drinks or the sales that day instead?

No, that's clear. So you planned the event, handled logistics, and then had to scramble when the speaker dropped out. When you and your roommate were sitting there at 11 p.m., what made you think of asking the barista to do the latte art demo?

Honestly, it was a mix of luck and my roommate being distracted. She was half watching her show, and at one point she said something like, "Why doesn't the coffee place just do the thing where they make the leaves in the foam?" I think I snapped at her for not helping, and then I realized she'd said something useful. The barista, Jordan, had been one of the people I filmed for the Instagram videos, and he's great on camera because he doesn't seem nervous at all. He'd already told me he did latte art at the weekend shifts, so I knew he could do it. I texted him the next morning, and he said yes before I'd even finished the message. I still feel a little bad for the speaker, who was really nice and just got sick. Did you want me to talk about how we set up the demo space, or was it more the decision to switch that you're

No, I think that covers it. Let me ask you something different. Tell me about a time when something didn't go the way you wanted it to—not just the speaker cancelling, but something where you felt like you actually failed at something.

Yeah, I think the one that stings most is from the group project in my rebranding class. I was leading a team of four, and I'd kind of assumed everyone was on the same page about the logo, so I didn't check in for like a week. By the time I did, two of my teammates were basically arguing about it in our group chat, and one of them had already shown the professor a draft I hadn't even seen. It was one of those moments where you realize you were the leader and you weren't really leading. I felt pretty embarrassed, and I spent that whole night reorganizing my notes like it would fix things
What did you actually do to fix it? Like, after you realized you'd dropped the ball?

Okay, so the first thing I did was actually talk to both of them, which sounds obvious now but I was too busy feeling bad to do it right away. I messaged them both and said something like, "I dropped the ball, can we figure this out together?" and one of them was really gracious about it, and the other was still pretty annoyed, which, fair. Dr. Hal had told us the week before that groups fall apart when nobody's sure who decides things, so I think I was half-remembering that while I was typing. Anyway, the fix was that we both thought our logo was obviously better, so instead of arguing more, I suggested we each have ten classmates look at both versions and tell us which one they'd remember. We went with the one that more people picked, and honestly it wasn't the one I'd been pushing. My teammate who'd shown the professor the draft ended up being the one who ran most of the testing, which
How did that feel, going with the one that wasn't yours?

Honestly, it stung a little at first, mostly because I'd been so sure mine was better. But when I saw the results, it was hard to argue with, since more people remembered the other one, and that's kind of the whole point of a logo. I think I was also relieved, because I'd been stressed for a week and it felt good to just have an answer. My roommate asked me that night how it went, and I basically complained about it for twenty minutes while she was eating cereal over the sink, which, yes, is also her thing now. The teammate who'd gone to the professor was kind of quiet about it, so I made a point of saying in the group chat that his idea for the testing was what made it work. I still think my version had some nice touches, so I'm not totally over it, but I'd rather have a decision that holds up than be right in my own head. Is that the kind of thing you'd want from someone on your team, or do you handle that differently?
Fair answer. So you mentioned running a customer survey with 500 responses on your resume. What did you actually learn from that, and did anything change because of it?

Yeah, so the survey got 512 responses, and the resume says 500, which is me rounding down because "500" looked cleaner. I should probably fix that on the resume. The big finding was oat milk. People kept bringing it up in the comment boxes, and a lot of them said they'd order more often if it didn't cost extra. I was honestly surprised, because I'd assumed price was the main thing people cared about. Some of the comments were pretty funny, like one person who wrote three paragraphs about their barista's oat milk situation in 2019. Anyway, the survey went to my manager, and she brought it to the district team, and two of the stores ended up trialing oat milk at no extra charge. I don't know how those trials turned out, since I'd already moved on to the Instagram stuff by then, so I'd have to check on that before I said anything definitive. My roommate thinks I'm way too excited about survey data, and she's probably right. Did you want to know how I wrote the questions, or what I'd change about the survey itself?
What would you change about it?

Honestly, the first thing I'd change is that I'd ask a better follow-up on the oat milk stuff. We had a comment box, and people wrote a lot, but I never asked a straight question like "would you order more if it was free?" so I had to read between the lines. I'd also make the survey shorter, because I think some people quit halfway through, and I'd want to know how many did before I'd trust the whole thing. My roommate read over one of the drafts and said the questions were "a little like a college application essay," which, rude, but she has a point. I'd also want a question about how often people come in, since that tells you a lot more about whether something like oat milk would actually matter. I'd probably run it past my manager before sending it out, too, just so somebody else catches the dumb wording. Is that the kind of feedback loop your team uses for surveys, or do you usually just send and see what comes back?

We tend to test with a small group first, so yeah, similar idea. One last thing before we wrap up—why do you want this kind of role? Like, marketing specifically, or is there something else pulling you toward it?

Yeah, good question, and I've thought about it more than I usually admit. Marketing kind of found me. I was a communications major and I figured I'd do PR or something with writing, but then I got into the Instagram work and realized I liked the part where you test something, look at what happens, and change it. That's the part that gets me. It's not just making things look nice, it's figuring out what people actually respond to, which is basically what the survey and the video stuff were about. I also like that it's a little messy and you're always learning. I'm not going to pretend I have it all figured out, since I still can't remember which analytics tab I was looking at last week, but I like that kind of problem. Plus, honestly, I'd like to work somewhere where I'm around people who care about the product. I'm a big believer in good coffee, which, yeah, is maybe a weird thing to say in a job interview, but it's true. Is there anything else you'd like to know about what I'd bring to the team?
No, I think that covers it. Do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, just one. What does a typical week look like for someone in this role?

Good question. So it varies, but you're usually split between running campaigns and analyzing what's working. Some weeks you're deep in planning, other weeks you're pulling data and figuring out what to double down on. There's also a fair amount of collaboration with the product and sales teams, so you're not siloed. It's a mix of strategy and execution, which it sounds like you'd be into based on what you've told me.

Alright, well thanks for taking the time to talk today. We've got a lot to think about, and we'll be in touch within the next week or so. Good luck with the rest of your day.

That's helpful. I appreciate you being real about where you want to grow.

verdicts.notes: Strength: the interviewer probed the metric definition, the follow-through on the survey and the Instagram insight, and the pattern across stories, and it covered both practice questions. Weakness: it kept dropping small evaluative remarks ("solid reflection", "that's smart"), skipped the email newsletter topic, and did not redirect the rambling or cut-off answer at T19.

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for coming in. Did you find everything okay today?

Yeah, yeah, everything's good, thanks for asking. Honestly the video call link took me a minute, I was in the wrong app first, because my roommate had been using my laptop for his econ thing and he'd signed me into some weird account, so I had to log out and then the password reset email went to spam, which, classic. I finally got in about two minutes ago, and I'd just made a coffee, which I probably shouldn't have because now I'm kind of jittery, so if I talk fast that's why. Anyway, yes, all good, thanks for having me, I'm excited to be here.

Ha, I get it. No worries at all. Take a breath—we're good on time.

So tell me a bit about yourself. How'd you get into marketing, and what have you been doing most recently?

Okay, yeah, thanks, I'll try to slow down. So I'm a communications major, and I kind of fell into marketing by accident. My intro class professor, Dr. Ferreira, had this way of talking about brands like they were characters in a show, which, honestly, I'm pretty sure I got that from the show I've been binge-watching, the one about the ad agency in the nineties. Anyway, I started looking for something local because I like being somewhere I can actually walk into, and I've been working as a marketing intern at a coffee chain for a few months now. The most recent thing I've really dug into is Instagram. We were getting a lot of product photos that just sat there, so I pitched switching to short customer videos, and my manager approved it. Over about three months the average engagement per post went from around 2.0 percent to 2.8 percent, which I know sounds small, but on a feed that size it's a real difference. I'm also still kind of proud that it came from actual people in the store, not from me sitting at a desk guessing.
That's helpful context. So when you say engagement went from 2.0 to 2.8 percent, what exactly are you measuring there? Is that likes, comments, all of it?

Good question, and honestly I should be more precise about that. I think our dashboard counts likes, comments, and saves, and I'm pretty sure shares too, all divided by the number of followers, but I'd have to double-check the exact formula before I swear to it. Our social media person, Priya, set up the reports, and I kind of just read them, which is a little embarrassing to admit. The 40 percent on my resume is the relative jump, so going from 2.0 to 2.8 is a 40 percent increase, even though the actual gap is less than one percentage point. I should've been clearer about that on paper. Like, I got really into the videos, and I was looking at the comments a lot, because people were tagging their friends and asking which drink was in the clip. That's the part I'd want to dig into more, if that makes sense.

That makes total sense. So you saw people actually engaging with the content in a different way once you switched to videos. Did you do anything with that insight? Like, did you pitch changing what you were filming, or how often, or anything else based on what you were seeing in the comments?

Honestly, not as much as I should have. I mentioned in our team chat that people kept asking what drink was in the clips, and someone said maybe we could name the drink in the caption, which sounded like a good idea. I don't think I pitched a formal change to how often we post, or anything like that. I was kind of focused on the video format itself, and I didn't want to overload the feed. Oh, and the store I'm at has this one barista, Marcus, who's amazing with latte art, and people always stop to watch him, so I keep thinking he'd be a great person to feature. I did pitch that to my manager, and I think she said maybe for next month, so I'm kind of waiting on that. I know that's a bit of a loose answer, but that's where things are right now.
Got it. So you had the data and the idea, but you didn't push it forward much beyond the initial suggestion. What would you do differently if you were starting that project over?

Yeah, that's fair, and honestly I've thought about it a bit since. Looking back, I'd set up a simple test from the start instead of just switching formats and hoping. Like, I'd pick two or three things, maybe captions that name the drink, a barista feature, or posting a little more often, and try one at a time so I could tell what actually moved the numbers. My roommate's always saying I need a spreadsheet for everything, which is annoying, but he's kind of right. I'd also loop in Priya earlier, because she knows how the dashboard calculates things, and I was just reading her reports without really understanding them. And I'd write the follow-up pitch down with a date attached, instead of letting it sit in a chat thread. So I guess the short version is I'd treat it more like an experiment and less like a one-time win, and I'd push the next idea a lot harder than I did.

That's a solid reflection. Let me shift gears a bit. On your resume you mention running a customer survey with 500 responses. What did you actually learn from that, and did anything change because of what you found out?

Okay, so the survey, yeah. It was about 512 responses, which is why I put 500 on the resume, and I know that's a little rounded, so I should probably fix that. We ran it in-store and through the app, and I spent way too long on the question wording, because my professor always says one bad question ruins the whole thing. There was also this one afternoon when the espresso machine kept beeping and a customer literally filled it out with the manager yelling in the background, which was chaos, but anyway. The big takeaway was that a lot of people wanted oat milk at no extra charge. Like, the upcharge was a real complaint, more than I expected. So the company trialed it at two stores, and I think the plan was to see whether it changed how much people bought and whether the upcharge was actually what was putting them off. I was mostly on the survey side, so I don't know the final call on whether it went chain-wide. I'd have to check with my manager on that, which, sorry, I know that's not the crisp answer you wanted.

No, that's fair. So you ran the survey and found something actionable, but you weren't really part of what happened after. Did you follow up with your manager to see what the trial showed, or did you just move on to the next thing?

Honestly, I moved on. I sent the summary deck to my manager, and then the next week was all Instagram and the launch stuff, so I never circled back to ask how the oat milk trial turned out. I did hear from a coworker that the two stores were kind of split, one had a bump and the other didn't really, but I don't know if that's real or just the break room talking. That's probably the thing I'd change. Like, I'd put a date on the calendar to check the results, because the survey was the part I cared about, and then I just kind of let it go. Which, looking at it now, is the exact same pattern as the Instagram thing, where I found the good stuff and then didn't push it all the way through. I'm starting to see a theme in my own work, and it's not a flattering one.

I appreciate you noticing that pattern yourself. Let me ask you this—tell me about a time you actually did fail at something. Not just something you'd do differently, but something that didn't work out.

Yeah, okay, a real failure. The launch event is the one I'd pick, though honestly it wasn't all failure. We had a budget of $1,500 and a speaker lined up, a local roaster who does a whole talk on sourcing, and I'd spent weeks on the promo. Then the speaker cancelled the day before. I was panicking, and I was also kind of running on two hours of sleep because I'd been up late on the Instagram stuff, which I think is part of why I didn't handle it great. My manager was out, so I had to make the call myself. I ended up getting one of our baristas, a guy named Devon, to do a latte-art demo, which was fun, and people seemed to like it. About 214 people came through the door, which felt like a good number. But the honest part is I didn't check with anyone before I swapped it, and I didn't tell the roaster's team until the morning of, so they found out kind of abruptly, and I think that burned a bit of goodwill. Like, I got the event to happen, but I didn't handle the people side well. I'd say that one's a fail on communication, even if the room looked fine.

That's a concrete example. So you made a quick call to keep the event running, but you didn't loop in the roaster until the last minute. What would you have done differently, knowing what you know now?

Oh, that's a good question, and honestly I've replayed that morning a bunch of times. The first thing I'd do is call the roaster the minute I heard they were out, not wait until I'd already made a plan. Like, I was so stuck on fixing the room that I forgot the roaster was a real partner who'd also put time into this, and they probably would've wanted a say. Maybe they could've moved to a different date, or done a shorter talk, or even sent a recorded piece for the event. I also should've called my manager, even though she was out. I kept thinking she was unreachable, but a two-minute text would've been better than making the call alone. I think I was running on about two hours of sleep and a lot of adrenaline, which is basically the same mistake I keep making, where I'm so focused on the output that I skip the people part. So if it happened again, I'd take a breath, tell the roaster first, and maybe send a short note saying the latte-art demo was a backup and I'd love to bring them back for a future event.
Makes sense. So you've got a pattern where you focus on the output and skip the communication piece. Why do you want to move into a role like this one? What's pulling you toward marketing?

Okay, the why. Honestly, a lot of it is that I like seeing people react to something real. At the coffee shop I can watch someone stop at the window to look at Marcus doing latte art, and that's the kind of thing I find way more interesting than a spreadsheet, even though I obviously end up in spreadsheets anyway. Dr. Ferreira's class is part of it too, the way she talked about brands having personalities. I was kind of skeptical at first, and then I was walking around noticing logos and packaging for weeks. I also took the bus across town for my interview today, and I spent the whole ride thinking about how your brand shows up on a phone screen versus a sign on a building, which is maybe a weird thing to be thinking about on a bus. Where I want to grow is exactly the stuff we've been talking about: taking an idea from the first good result all the way through, and keeping the people side in view while I do it. I think a role like this one would make me do that more, which is kind of the point. So that's what's pulling me in, and honestly,

That's helpful. I appreciate you being real about where you want to grow.

Let me ask you one more thing before we wrap up. You led a team of four on a rebranding class project. Walk me through that—what was your role, and did anything go sideways with the group?

Yeah, sure. So that was for my branding class last spring, and I was the one who got put in charge, mostly because I'd volunteered to make the group chat and nobody else wanted to. There were four of us, and our job was to rebrand a fake campus bakery, which, the bakery was kind of the best part because we had to pick a name, a color palette, all of it. My role was basically keeping everyone on the same timeline and pulling the final deck together. Honestly, the thing that went sideways was the logo. Two of my teammates, Aisha and Tomas, totally disagreed. Aisha wanted a hand-drawn look, kind of cozy, and Tomas wanted something clean and modern. They were both pretty firm, and the group got stuck for like a week, which, looking back, was mostly me avoiding picking a side because I didn't want anyone mad at me.

Then I finally did something I'm kind of proud of. I had both of them test their versions with ten classmates each, just a quick survey asking which one people remembered and which one they'd walk into. The hand-drawn one actually won on recall, but Tomas's version scored higher on "would you buy from this place," so we ended up blending them. We kept the warm lettering but used a cleaner layout. Our professor said it was the strongest project in the section, which was nice, but honestly the bigger lesson for me was that I should've set up the test in week one instead of letting the argument drag on for a week. Which, yeah, you can probably see the pattern again. I wait too long to make the call, and then I'm the one who finally makes

So you used data to break the tie instead of just picking a side yourself. That's smart. But you said you were avoiding picking a side because you didn't want anyone mad at you. Do you think you'd handle that differently now, or is that still something you're working on?

Yeah, honestly, I'm still working on it. I'd like to say I've changed, but the Instagram thing and the roaster thing and the logo thing are all kind of the same move, where I'd rather wait for the problem to sort itself out than be the person who makes a call and gets some pushback. And I know that's not great for a team.

What I'd do differently now is name the disagreement early and say out loud, something like, "Okay, we've got two strong directions, let's pick a way to test them by Friday." That way I'm not picking a winner, I'm just running the process, which feels less personal. I think the hard part for me isn't the data, it's being okay with someone being annoyed at me for a day. Aisha probably would've been fine, honestly, she was just as stuck as I was. So I'm working on it, and I'd say I'm a lot better at it when I've already got a plan in front of me, which is kind of a funny thing to admit in a job interview.

I think that's fair self-awareness. 

Last thing—do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, just one, if that's okay. What does a typical first few months look like for someone in this role, like what would you want me to have figured out by the end of it?

Good question. Honestly, the first month is mostly about understanding how we work—who owns what, how we talk to each other, what actually matters to the business versus what just looks busy. By the end of month two or three, I'd want you to have picked one small thing you can actually move, run it start to finish, and tell me what you learned. Not a big campaign, just something real where you can see the whole cycle. And I'd want to know you're talking to the people involved, not just the metrics.

Does that make sense?

Yeah, that makes a lot of sense, and honestly it's pretty much the thing I'm trying to get better at. Picking one small thing and seeing it all the way through, with the people side included, sounds like exactly the kind of goal I'd want. I'd probably start by sitting down with whoever owns the work and asking what's been sitting unfinished, because I'm pretty sure I've got a few loose threads from my last role, like the oat milk follow-up I never chased. So yeah, that's a good target. Thanks for walking me through it, and for being patient with my rambling today.
You're welcome. Thanks for being thoughtful and honest throughout this. We'll be in touch either way within the next week or so. Good luck with everything, and thanks again for coming in.

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for taking the time. How are things going on your end?

Hi, thanks for having me. Things are good, busy week with finals coming up, but I'm glad to be here. The coffee shop job has been keeping me on my toes too, so this is a nice break. How about you, how's your week going?
Can't complain. Busy on this end too, but that's the job. Good luck with finals—what are you studying?

Thanks, I appreciate that. I'm taking a mix of classes for my communications major, mostly a media writing course and a research methods class, which is a lot of reading and a lot of coffee. Honestly the research methods one has been useful for the job, since I ran a customer survey this year and it helped me figure out what I was doing. Anyway, should we jump in? I'm ready whenever you are.
Yeah, let's get going. So tell me a bit about yourself—walk me through what you've been doing, starting from where you are now.

Sure. I'm a communications major, finishing up my junior year, and for the past year I've been a marketing intern at a local coffee chain. Most of my work has been on social media, the customer email newsletter, and a couple of store events.

The thing I'm proudest of is the Instagram work. I was looking at our posts and they were mostly product photos that nobody was really engaging with, so I pitched switching to short videos of actual customers and the staff. My manager approved it, and I ran it for about three months. Engagement went up a lot, and that's been the biggest thing I'm proud of.

I also relaunched our email newsletter, and I did a store launch event, which had a few hiccups but ended up working out. Before all that, I was in a team project for class where I led four people on a rebrand, which was my first real experience managing people who didn't all agree with each other.

What about you? What does the team you'd be on look like?

I'll tell you more about that in a bit. But first, let me dig into the Instagram work a little. You said engagement went up a lot—what numbers are we talking about? Like, 40% more than what, and compared to when?

Honestly, it's hard to pin down one number for that. Engagement moves around a lot from week to week, so I'd rather not throw out a figure that's not the whole picture. What I'd say is that the biggest thing I learned was that people engage more with real people than with polished product shots. I'm happy to walk through how we tested the change, if that's more useful?
That's fair. So walk me through it—how did you actually test the change and measure it?

So my manager signed off on it, and I basically ran it as a trial for about three months. I kept posting, but I switched the format from product photos to short videos of customers and staff. I was watching how people reacted to each post compared to the older ones, like likes, comments, and saves, and I kept a simple spreadsheet so I could see the trend over time.

Honestly, I don't love how rigorous it was. I didn't set up a clean control group or anything like that. It was more like, here's what we did, here's what seemed to happen, and it kept looking better. The biggest thing I took from it is that customer-focused content just outperforms the polished stuff for a coffee brand. What about on your end? How do you usually decide whether a social campaign is working?
We'll get to that. But I'm curious—after those three months, what did you actually do with what you learned? Did the account keep posting that way, or did something change?

Yeah, we kept going with it. The video format became the default for most posts, and I'd still pull in product shots now and then when there was a new drink or a seasonal menu. My manager was on board, so it wasn't a big decision after the trial. I also started checking the numbers every couple of weeks instead of just when I remembered to, which helped me catch when a post wasn't landing.

Got it. So you stuck with the videos and kept an eye on things. Did you ever look back at the actual engagement numbers to see if they stayed up, or was it more just a gut feeling that it was working?
Fair question, and I should have just given you the number
No worries. Do you remember what it ended up being?

Yeah, I do. The average engagement rate per post went from about 2% to about 2.8% over those three months. That's where the 40% comes from, since it's a 40% jump relative to where we started, not 40 percentage points. I should have said that up front instead of dodging. It's a small account, so I'd treat it as a directional result, not a hard finding.
That makes sense. So 2% to 2.8%—that's real movement, even if the account is small. Did you share those numbers with your manager, or was it more just you tracking it?

Yeah, I shared it with my manager. I sent her a quick summary after the three months, with the before and after numbers, and she was happy to keep the video format going. Mostly it was a short update, though, not a big presentation. Honestly I'd have liked to do more with it, like put together a proper report for the company, but I didn't get to that.
Why didn't you get to that? What got in the way?

Honestly, it was mostly timing. Right after the Instagram trial ended, I got pulled into the email newsletter relaunch and then planning the store launch event, and those had hard deadlines. The Instagram results were already working, so the report got pushed down the list. Looking back, I should have made time for it, because a clear write-up would've helped the company see why the change was worth keeping. It's something I'd do first next time.
Makes sense. Let's talk about the email newsletter relaunch. What was wrong with the old one, and what did you change?

The old one was kind of a catch-all. Each email had like four or five different things in it, a new drink, a store update, a promo, and a reminder about the rewards app, so nothing really stood out. The subject lines were pretty generic too, like "Newsletter from [Store]," which I don't think anyone felt like opening.

So I rewrote the subject lines to be specific and actually say what's inside, and I cut each email down to one topic. If we had a new seasonal drink, that's the whole email. A designer on the team did the template, which made it look a lot cleaner, but the content side was mostly me.
Okay, so you cleaned it up. Did you measure whether people actually opened it more after the relaunch?

Honestly, it's hard to say for sure. Open rates bounce around a lot depending on the day and the subject line, so I didn't want to read too much into a few sends. What I did notice was that people replied to the one-topic emails more often, and the store managers started asking me what was coming up next. That's what made me think it was working.

What I learned from it is that less is more. Trying to cram everything into one email made it so nothing got attention. Do you send newsletters at your company? I'm curious how you decide what goes in each one.

We do, yeah. I'll circle back to that. But I want to understand the measurement piece a little better. You said open rates bounce around—did you actually look at the open rate before and after the relaunch, even if it was noisy?

Yeah, I did look at it. I should've just said so the first time. The open rate went from about 18% to about 27% after the relaunch.

I'll be upfront that I didn't run a clean comparison. The lists were different sizes, and I sent at different times of day, so it's not a controlled test. But the jump was big enough that I felt good about the change, and the replies and the managers asking about the next email backed it up.
That's a solid jump. So you saw the 27%, the managers were engaged, people were replying—did anything go wrong with the relaunch, or did it just work out?

Mostly it just worked, but there were a few things I'd do differently. The biggest was timing. I didn't send everything at the same time of day, so it's hard to say how much of the jump came from the new format and how much came from when people happened to see the email. Next time I'd keep the send schedule consistent so I could tell what was actually making the difference.

The other thing was the designer. We were trying to get the template done while I was also on the event, so the first version took longer than I wanted, and I had to rush a couple of the early sends. It turned out fine, but I'd plan the design work earlier.

Got it. So you'd plan ahead and control the variables. That makes sense. Let me shift gears—you mentioned the team project where you led four people on a rebranding class project. Tell me about that. What was the disagreement, and how did you handle it?

Sure. We were doing a rebrand for a fake local bakery, and the team was split on the logo. Two of my teammates each had a design they were really attached to, and the arguing was getting nowhere. Everyone was just defending their own favorite.

I didn't want to pick one because I liked it more, so I suggested we test both. Each of them showed their logo to about ten classmates who weren't on the project, and we asked which one they'd walk into a bakery for and which one felt more trustworthy. We went with the one that did better, and the designer who lost was fine with it because it wasn't my opinion versus theirs anymore.

What I learned is that getting people to agree is easier when you give them something to look at besides each other. Has your team ever had a disagreement like that? How did you settle it?

We have, yeah. I'll tell you how we handle it in a bit. But I'm curious—after you went with the winning logo, how did the rest of the project go? Did the losing designer stay engaged, or did you have to manage that?

Honestly, it went pretty well. The designer who lost was a little quiet for a day or two, which I get, since it's annoying when your favorite doesn't win. I checked in with them directly and told them the feedback was useful, and I asked if they'd take the lead on the color palette and the menu layout. That gave them something real to own, and they got into it again.

The hardest part was making sure nobody felt like they'd been overruled. We all had to agree on the test beforehand, so when the results came in, it was easier to accept. I'd say the team got stronger after that, because everyone trusted the process more than they trusted any one person's opinion, including mine.
That's solid. So you gave them ownership over something else. Did that actually work, or did they stay a bit checked out?

Yeah, I think it worked. They got really into the color palette, and they came back with a few options that were honestly better than what I'd have picked. By the time we put the final deck together, they were presenting the palette themselves, so it didn't feel like they were sitting on the sidelines anymore.

There was a little bit of hesitation at first, and I'm not sure I got it all the way right. I probably should have checked in more often during that stretch. But by the end, they seemed happy with how it turned out. Did your team ever have someone who felt sidelined like that? How did you bring them back in?

We have. I'll get to that. But before we move on—you've talked about the Instagram work, the newsletter, and the class project. You also mentioned planning a store launch event. What happened there, and what went wrong?

So the big thing that went wrong was the speaker. We had a local roaster lined up to talk about sourcing, and they cancelled the day before. We had a lot of the event already promoted, so I had to figure out something fast.

I ended up asking one of our baristas if she'd do a latte-art demo instead. She was great, and people actually gathered around and asked questions. Honestly, it was a better fit for a coffee shop than a talk would've been. But I was scrambling the whole day before, and I didn't have a backup plan built in, which I should have.

I'd say the lesson for me was always having a plan B for anyone outside the company you're relying on. It's hard to qu
How many people showed up to the event?

Honestly, it was a good crowd for a Tuesday, and that's what I remember most. The barista's demo drew people in, and the line at the counter was out the door for a while. I don't want to give you a number off the top of my head, though. Counting people at a busy event is always a bit of a guess. What I'd focus on is that the event got people into the store who don't usually come in. Did your company ever have to pivot an event at the last minute?
We have. But I'm curious—you said the event was for 200 guests. So did you hit that number, or was it less?

feedback_leaks.quote: So you owned that decision and ran with it. That's good.
That's smart thinking on the cost side.
You clearly spend time thinking about the customer side of it, which is good.

verdicts.notes: Strength: the interviewer repeatedly pushed on evasive answers (newsletter open rates, the 40% Instagram metric, survey counts) until real numbers came out, and probed ownership of the oat milk test. Weakness: frequent evaluative comments ("solid lift", "That's good"), and the interviewer didn't press the dodged oat milk count or the 200-guest headcount. It also didn't follow up on the vague answer about why the candidate wanted the role.

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for coming in. Did you find everything okay today?

Hi, yes, thanks for having me. Everything's good. The video link worked fine on my end, so I'm glad we didn't have to troubleshoot anything. I'm excited to talk about the marketing internship. Coffee chains are a fun space to work in, especially on the social side.

Great, glad it all came through smoothly. Yeah, coffee is a fun category. So I'm curious—what drew you to this kind of role in the first place? Like, marketing in general, or was it something specific about working at a coffee chain?

Honestly, a bit of both. I'm a communications major, and I kept gravitating toward the projects where you're trying to get people to actually care about something, like a brand, a product, a place. Marketing felt like the most direct version of that.

With coffee specifically, I think it's because it's such a daily habit. People come in every morning, they have a regular order, they have opinions about it. That's a really interesting thing to build a brand around. I like that you get real feedback fast, from real customers, in person.

Plus I've been a regular at a few local shops for a while, so I already know the vibe. I've noticed what makes people come back, and it's usually not just the drink. It's the whole experience, and I'd love to help shape that.

That makes sense. You clearly spend time thinking about the customer side of it, which is good. So let me dig into some of the work you've actually done. I see on your resume you relaunched the customer email newsletter. Walk me through that—what was wrong with it before, and what did you change?

Sure. Before, the newsletter was kind of a catch-all. Each email had a promo, a new drink, store news, and a bunch of links, so nothing really stood out. People would skim it and move on.

I rewrote the subject lines so they said what was actually inside, and I cut each email down to one topic. If it was a new seasonal drink, that was the whole email. A designer on the team did the template, so I could focus on the content and the timing. Honestly, the part I learned the most from was just being ruthless about cutting things. It's hard to quantify how much that helped, but it felt like the right direction.
Fair enough. Did you actually measure whether it worked? Like, did you look at open rates before and after, or anything like that?

Yeah, we kept an eye on how people responded. I think the bigger thing I took from it was how much the subject line changes whether anyone opens the email at all. I went in thinking the content mattered most, and it turned out the first few words did a lot of the work. Honestly, that surprised me, and it's changed how I write everything since.
I hear you on the subject line insight. But I'm asking more literally—did you pull the numbers? Like, what was the open rate before you changed it, and what was it after?
Yeah, we did. The open rate went from about 18% to about 27%. Most of that came from the subject lines and cutting each email down to one topic.
Okay, good. So 18 to 27—that's a solid lift. What made you decide to focus on subject lines specifically? Did someone suggest that, or was that your own thinking?

Mostly my own thinking. I was going through the old emails and noticed that the subject lines were pretty vague, like "News from the team" or "Something new this week." I figured if people couldn't tell what was inside, they weren't going to open it. My manager was fine with me testing that, so I rewrote them and kept the content focused on one thing.

Got it. So you owned that decision and ran with it. That's good. Let me ask you about another project—you ran a customer survey with 500 responses. What were you trying to learn, and what actually happened with what you found out?

Sure. We wanted to know what was making people happy or annoyed about their visits, and whether there were things we were missing. We kept it pretty simple, mostly a few questions about what people ordered, what would bring them back more often, and what they'd change.

The thing that stood out most was oat milk. A lot of people asked for it, and they didn't want to pay extra for it. Two of the stores tried offering it at no added charge for a while. I found that really useful because it showed me that a survey can point you to something concrete, not just general feedback. It also made me realize how much you have to be careful about how you read the results. People say what they want, but you have to think about what it would actually cost the business.
That's smart thinking on the cost side. So when you say the oat milk thing stood out—how many people mentioned it? Was it like half the responses, or a smaller slice?

Honestly, it's hard to put an exact count on that. I didn't go in with a tally sheet, so I'd be guessing if I gave you a percentage. What I can tell you is that it came up enough that the managers took it seriously enough to test it.

What I really got out of it was how easy it is to read survey results the wrong way. Something can sound like a big deal in the comments, but then you have to ask whether people would actually keep coming back if the price stayed the same. Are you running any surveys at your place right now? I'm curious how you'd set up the questions.

We do run them from time to time, yeah. I'll get into more of how we think about that if we move forward. But I'm curious about something else first—you mentioned the oat milk test. Did you have anything to do with setting that up, or was that just the managers taking your survey and running with it?

Mostly the managers ran with it. I pulled the results together and put the oat milk finding in front of them with a summary of what people were asking for. They decided to try it at two stores, and I stayed involved enough to see how it went, but the call was theirs. I was a little nervous about how much to push a recommendation when I was new, so I kept it to "here's what the data says" and let them decide.

Looking back, I'd probably push harder on the follow-up next time. Figuring out what to measure during the trial would have been a good thing for me to own.
That's honest. So if you were doing a project like that now, in your first month here, what would you actually do differently?

Honestly, I'd spend more time before the trial started. I'd sit down with the managers and agree on what success looks like, like whether oat milk sales go up, whether people come back more often, and what it costs us if it's free. Right now I think I'd just hand over the findings and hope someone followed up.

I'd also talk to the baristas early. They're the ones pulling the shots and hearing the complaints, so they'd probably know if oat milk was going to be a headache during rush, or if people were already asking for it at the counter. Survey comments are one thing, but they'd have the day-to-day picture.

And I'd set a check-in date at the start, so the test doesn't just fade out after a few weeks.
Good. That's concrete. Let me shift gears a bit. You also led a team of four on a rebranding class project. Tell me about that—what was the goal, and how did you actually lead it?

Sure. It was a class project where we had to come up with a rebrand for a local business. Our goal was to make the brand feel more current without losing what made it loved by its regulars. I was the one coordinating, so I set up the weekly check-ins and kept us moving toward the final pitch.

The hardest moment was when two of my teammates really disagreed about the logo. One wanted something bold and modern, the other wanted to keep it simpler and closer to the original. Both were pretty convinced they were right, and it was getting tense.

Instead of picking a side myself, I suggested we test both with people outside the group. We showed each version to about ten classmates and asked which one they'd trust more and which one they'd remember. The simpler one won on trust, and the bold one got more on memorability. We ended up combining the two, keeping the cleaner layout with one stronger color.

I think what I learned is that leading a team isn't about having the right answer. It's about setting up a way to figure out the answer so people can let go of being right. Honestly, the team dynamic was a bigger challenge than the design itself.
That's a solid approach. So when you say you combined them—what did that actually look like in the final logo?

Sure. We kept the simpler layout, so the name and icon stayed clean and easy to read, and we pulled in the bolder color from the modern version. It was one strong accent color on the icon and the key lines, and everything else stayed neutral. That gave it some energy without making it look busy.

Honestly, it was a bit of a compromise, and my teammates had to give up a little on both sides. But when we showed the final version back to the group, it was the first time everyone seemed happy with it.
Got it. So you've got one more thing I want to ask about before we wrap up. You grew Instagram engagement by 40%. What does that 40% actually measure, and what changed to make that happen?

Honestly, the way that number got calculated is a little fuzzy for me to walk through right now. What I can tell you is what changed. We moved away from mostly product photos and started posting short videos of customers, like people ordering, a barista talking about a drink, or someone's reaction to their first sip.

My manager was open to trying it, so I put together a plan and we ran it for a while. Video just felt more like the store, you know? People could see the energy of the place instead of a latte sitting on a table. What I took from it is that people respond more to other people than to the product by itself. It's hard to quantify exactly how much of the lift came from that versus the posting schedule, but the direction was clear.
I hear you. But I want to push a little on the 40%—40% of what, exactly? Like, were we measuring likes, comments, total impressions, reach? And compared to when?

Fair question, and I should've been clearer the first time. It's average engagement rate per post, so likes, comments, and the other interactions divided by how many people saw each post. It went from about 2.0% to about 2.8% over three months. That's the 40%.

It's a modest number in absolute terms, but it was a real shift, and it was the first time I saw the video posts clearly outperform the product shots.
Okay, that's clearer. Thanks. So one more thing before we wrap—tell me about a time you actually failed at something, or something that didn't go the way you planned.

Sure. The one that comes to mind is the store launch event I planned. Our speaker cancelled the day before, which was a stressful call to get. I had to figure out what to do fast.

I ended up swapping in a latte-art demo with one of our baristas. It was a good call in the end, and people seemed to enjoy it more than a talk, but I'll be honest, I was panicking for a few hours beforehand. I didn't have a backup plan built in, and I think that's the part I'd change. Now I always ask, "What's our plan B if the main thing falls through?" before the event, not the night before.
That's fair. So you had 200 guests there that night—did the demo actually work out, or did people seem disappointed about the speaker change?

Mostly it worked out. The barista was great, and people hung around the counter watching. A few folks asked me afterward if there'd been a talk, but nobody seemed upset about it. I think they were just happy to have something to do.

Honestly, I don't want to get hung up on the headcount. The crowd was solid, and that's what I remember. What I'd tell you is that the demo worked because the barista knew her stuff and wasn't reading from a script, so people could ask questions as she went. Next time I'd still want a backup I can confirm earlier in the week, though.
Makes sense. Alright, I think I've got a good picture of your work. Do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, just one. What does a typical week look like for an intern here, and how much of it is hands-on work versus shadowing?

Good question. It really depends on the project, but typically you'd spend maybe half your time on your own work—running campaigns, analyzing data, that kind of thing—and the other half shadowing or collaborating with the team. We try to give interns real ownership pretty early, so you're not just watching. You'd probably start with smaller projects and build up to bigger ones like you did with the newsletter.

Thanks for taking the time today, Sam. We'll be in touch soon about next steps.

Thanks, that's really helpful. Half on my own projects and half shadowing sounds like a good balance, especially early on. I'd love to start with something small and work up.

Thanks for taking the time to talk with me today. I really enjoyed it, and I'm excited about the possibility of joining the team. I look forward to hearing from you about next steps.
Great. Thanks again, and have a good rest of your day.

feedback_leaks.quote: No, that's a fair answer. I appreciate you being straight about the tracking piece—that's actually more useful than a polished number.

verdicts.notes: Strength: the interviewer probed measurement well (T6, T12, T14, T22), asked for concrete examples, and covered both practice questions. Weakness: it let evasive answers go without follow-up (T7 never got a real metric or the 40% baseline, T11's budget and T23's logo result were dropped, and T17 got no numbers), it skipped the newsletter topic, and T8 praised the candidate's answer.

transcript.text: Hey, good to meet you. How's your day been so far?

Hi, good to meet you too! My day's been pretty good, a little hectic. I had a long class this morning, so I'm glad to finally sit down and talk about something I actually enjoy. How about you, how's your day going?
Yeah, it's been busy but good. Thanks for asking. So, I'd love to get a sense of your background. Can you walk me through your experience so far, starting from where you are now?

I'm a communications major, finishing up my junior year. Right now I'm a marketing intern at a local coffee chain, which has been my main hands-on experience. I mostly handle social media, the customer newsletter, and some event planning for store openings.

Before that, I did a lot of group projects in class, which is where I got comfortable leading people who don't always agree with each other. The internship is where things got real, though. You learn fast when a post flops and you have to figure out why.

What I like most is that I get to see how a marketing idea actually lands with customers, not just in a case study. Is there a particular part of my background you'd like me to go into?

That's helpful context. Let's dig into the internship a bit. You mentioned handling social media—I saw on your resume you grew Instagram engagement by 40%. Walk me through what you actually changed to make that happen.

Sure. The big change was moving away from our standard product photos. We were posting a lot of pictures of drinks on a plain background, and they just weren't getting much response. So I pitched switching to short videos of real customers, like someone talking about their usual order or a regular who's been coming in for years. My manager liked the idea and let me test it.

I learned a lot from that. Customers respond to people more than products, and comments started turning into actual conversations. I also got better at writing captions that invite people to reply instead of just liking the post.

What was the thing you were most curious about with that?
Got it. So when you say engagement went up 40%, what was that measuring exactly? Like, was it comments, likes, shares—what metric moved the most?

Honestly, the way we tracked it was a bit messy, and I'm still figuring out how to talk about it well. What I can say is that the videos made a clear difference in how people interacted with the posts. Comments went up the most, mostly because the captions asked questions that people wanted to answer.

Looking back, the bigger thing I learned was how hard it is to tell whether a change actually worked. Reach can jump for reasons that have nothing to do with you, so I've gotten a lot more careful about separating what looks good from what's really working. Is that the kind of measurement question you're getting at, or were you thinking more about how we set up the test?

No, that's a fair answer. I appreciate you being straight about the tracking piece—that's actually more useful than a polished number. So when you switched to those customer videos, did you keep doing the product photos at all, or did you completely stop?

We didn't stop completely. We still posted product shots now and then, mostly for new menu items or seasonal drinks, since people sometimes want to see exactly what they're ordering. But the videos became the main thing, and the product photos became more of a supporting piece. I'd say that mix was a big part of why the change worked.
Makes sense. Let me shift gears a bit. You also planned a store launch event for 200 guests. What was your role in actually pulling that together, and what was the budget you were working with?

My role was mostly the day-to-day planning and coordination. I worked with our store manager on the timeline, handled the invitations and promotion on social and in the newsletter, and coordinated with vendors for the setup. The part I learned the most from was the week before the event, when things kept changing.

On the budget side, honestly, I was more involved in deciding where the money went than in tracking every dollar, so it's hard for me to give you a clean figure. What I took away was how much trade-offs matter. Every choice, like whether to spend on food or on a speaker, means you're not spending on something else, and I got better at asking what would make the biggest difference for guests.

What would you like to know more about from that event?
What actually happened that week before the event when things kept changing? Give me one concrete example.

One big one was the speaker. We had someone lined up to talk about sourcing and the coffee farms we work with. The day before the event, they cancelled. How did you know that guests actually enjoyed the latte-art demo more? Like, how did you measure that?

Honestly, I didn't measure it in any formal way. There wasn't a survey or a sign-in question about the demo. I was going off what I saw in the room. People gathered around the demo, stayed longer than I expected, and a bunch of them were taking photos and videos. That's not as rigorous as I'd like, and I'd probably set up a quick feedback question next time so I'd have something better than my own impression.
That's fair. Shifting to another project—you ran a customer survey with 500 responses. What did you actually learn from that, and what changed because of it?

The main takeaway was that people really wanted oat milk, and they wanted it without paying extra for it. That came through pretty clearly across the responses, and it wasn't something our team had been assuming.

What changed is that two of our stores trialed offering oat milk at no added charge. I helped put together the write-up for the managers, mostly summarizing what customers said and where the feedback was strongest. I'll be honest, I don't know yet how the trial turned out for sales, so I'd want to see that data before saying it was a clear win.

What I got out of it was how useful it is to ask customers open questions. Some of the best comments were things we wouldn't have thought to include as multiple choice.
Did you design the survey yourself, or did someone else put it together?

I had a big hand in it. I drafted most of the questions, including the open-ended ones, and my manager went through them and made some changes before we sent it out. I was still pretty new to survey design, so I learned a lot from her notes about wording questions so they don't steer people toward an answer.

What's your experience with survey design? Have you built one yourself?

I've done a few over the years. It's trickier than people think. Let me ask you something different—in your class projects, you mentioned leading a team of four on a rebranding project. What was that about, and what made it your job to lead?

The project was a rebrand for a fictional local business, and our professor split us into teams. I ended up leading mostly because I had the most experience in the marketing side of things, and nobody else really wanted to take on the coordinating. So I volunteered, and the group seemed fine with it.

The hardest moment was when two of my teammates disagreed about the logo. Both had strong opinions, and it was getting tense. Instead of picking one myself, I suggested we have both versions tested with about ten classmates each, and we went with whichever one people responded to better. It took a bit of extra work, but it got everyone off the "my idea versus yours" track.

What I'd say I learned is that when people disagree, it helps to get the group focused on what evidence would settle it. Does that kind of situation come up in the work you do?
It definitely does. So you tested both logos with classmates—what did that test actually show? Which one won?

Honestly, that one's a bit fuzzy for me now. It's been a while, and I was more focused on keeping the team together than on the details of the results. What I remember is that the feedback was pretty clear in the end, and the group accepted it without much fuss.

The bigger takeaway for me was that once we agreed on how to decide, the argument stopped being personal. Both of my teammates were willing to let the test make the call, and that's something I've tried to bring into the internship since then.

Yeah, a few. The one that comes to mind first is on the Instagram side. Early on, I was so excited about the customer videos that I didn't set up a clear way to measure them before we started. So when people asked whether it was working, I had to piece together an answer after the fact, which is not a good position to be in. I learned to decide what success looks like before I change anything, not after.

It also made me more careful about how I talk about results. I'd rather say "this looks promising, and here's what I'm not sure about" than oversell it.

Have you had a project where the measurement side got messy like that?

Sure, happens to everyone. So here's something I'm curious about—if you were starting in a marketing role here in your first month, what would be the first thing you'd want to understand about how we actually measure whether something's working?

That's a good question, and I think it's the right one to start with. I'd want to know which numbers the team actually looks at week to week, and which ones people just mention in meetings. There's usually a gap between the metrics on a dashboard and the ones that really guide decisions, and I'd want to understand that gap early.

I'd also ask how you separate a real change from normal ups and downs. With social, for example, a post can do well for reasons that have nothing to do with the content. So I'd want to know what the team considers a meaningful lift, and whether there's a habit of comparing against a baseline before trying something new.

Honestly, after my own experience with the Instagram test, I'd want to set that up before I started anything. How does the team usually decide what counts as a win?
We'll definitely talk about that if things move forward. I do want to ask—why are you interested in this kind of role? What's pulling you toward marketing work, versus something else?

I've always liked the point where creativity meets people's actual choices. Marketing is the place where you get to figure out why someone walks in, orders something, and comes back. That mix of curiosity and real-world feedback is what keeps me interested.

Working at the coffee chain really sealed it for me. Seeing a customer video get people talking, or watching a crowd gather around a latte-art demo, made it clear that I like building things people respond to. I also like that I'm still learning how to measure whether something works, so there's a lot of room to grow.

Before this, I was pretty torn between marketing and something more on the research side. But I like being close to the customer and to the decisions that come out of the work, so marketing felt like the better fit.

What about your own path into this kind of work?
I started in communications, actually, so there's some common ground. Well, we're getting close on time, so let me ask—do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?

Good question. It varies a lot depending on what's live, but there's usually a mix of planning work, reviewing performance data, and collaborating with other teams. You'd probably spend time on strategy and campaign setup early in the week, then shift to analyzing how things are performing and adjusting. A lot of cross-functional meetings too—we work pretty closely with product and sales.

Anything else?
Thanks, that helps. No, I think that covers it for me. I really appreciate you taking the time to talk today, and I'm looking forward to hearing what's next.
Great. Well, thanks for taking the time, Sam. We've got what we need, and we'll be in touch soon. Good luck with the rest of your semester.

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for taking the time. How are things going on your end?
Hi, thanks for having me. Things are good, a little busy with finals coming up, but I'm glad to be here. The coffee shop is a place I really like, so I was excited when this came up.

That's great to hear. Yeah, finals are always a lot. Well, we're glad you're interested.

So let's start with the basics — can you walk me through your background a bit? Where are you from, what's your major, and how did you end up at the coffee shop?

Sure. I'm originally from a suburb outside Columbus, Ohio, and I'm a communications major with a minor in marketing. I've always liked how brands talk to people, which is why I gravitated toward marketing classes.

I got into the coffee side of things through a part-time job at a local shop during my second year. I started on the register, but I got curious about the social media and the email newsletter, and I asked if I could help with those. That's kind of how I ended up focusing on marketing work instead of just serving drinks. I like that a small team lets you see the whole process, from the idea to how customers react to it.

That makes sense. You kind of worked your way in, which is cool.

So you mentioned the email newsletter — I see on your resume you relaunched it. What was wrong with the old one, and what did you actually change?

Honestly, the old one was kind of a mess. It tried to do everything in one email: a new drink, a store update, a coupon, and a link to a blog post, all at once. People didn't really know what to click on, so I think a lot of them just skimmed it and left.

When I took it over, I focused on two things. First, I rewrote the subject lines so they were short and said exactly what was inside. Second, I cut each email down to one topic. If it was about the seasonal drink, that's all it was about. A designer on the team did the template, which made it look a lot cleaner, but most of the actual change was in the writing.

It's hard to say exactly how much that all mattered, but it was the most fun part of the internship for me. Seeing the results come in and figuring out what people actually responded to taught me a lot about how to think about an audience.
Got it. So you rewrote the copy and simplified the format. Did you measure the results at all — like open rates, click rates, anything like that?

Yeah, we tracked things like that. It's hard to boil it down to one number, though, because open rates can shift with the season and what else was going on that week. What I took away was more about learning how people read emails. Once we had one topic per email, it was much easier to see which subjects people cared about. I still think about that when I write anything now.
That's fair. Do you remember what the open rates actually looked like before and after, even roughly?

Yeah, okay, I can give you rough numbers. The open rate was around 18% before I took it over, and it got up to about 27% after I'd made the changes. I'd say that's the part I'm most proud of, though I should be honest that I didn't run a formal test, so I can't say for sure how much of that came from the subject lines and how much from the one-topic format.

That's a solid jump. And I appreciate you being clear about what you can and can't claim from it.

You also ran a customer survey with 500 responses. What was that about, and what did you actually do with what you learned?
