The biggest thing that stood out was oat milk. A lot of people wanted it, and they didn't want to pay extra for it. Two of the stores tried offering it at no added cost for a while. I didn't own that decision, but I got to help pull the feedback together and present it, and that was a good experience for me. It taught me that the people who answer a survey are often the ones who care most, so you have to read the comments
That makes sense. So you pulled together the feedback and presented it to the team. When you say you presented it — what did that look like? Did you make a recommendation, or just hand over the data?

Mostly I pulled the data together into a short deck with a few charts, and then I made a recommendation, which was the oat milk idea. I didn't want to just say "here's a lot of data, good luck." My manager wanted to know what to do with it, so I suggested we try it in a couple of stores and see what happened.

Presenting to people who've been running the shop for a long time was a bit nerve-racking. Some of them had doubts about the cost, which was fair. I tried to answer those by saying we were testing it, not committing to it. I think that's a skill I'm still working on, making a recommendation sound like a suggestion and not a sales pitch.
Fair point. You framed it as a test, which probably helped. Did they end up trying it, and if so, did you track whether it actually moved the needle?

Yeah, two of the stores tried it. It's hard to say whether it really moved the needle, though. The trial ran on its own schedule, and a lot of things change in a coffee shop in a few weeks, like the weather and what's on the seasonal menu. What I took from it was more about how to frame a suggestion so people are willing to test it. Honestly, that was probably the bigger lesson for me.
Got it. Let me shift gears a bit. On your resume you mention growing Instagram engagement by 40%. Can you walk me through what that means and what you actually did to make that happen?

Sure. The main thing I did was switch up what we were posting. We'd been mostly doing product photos, just pictures of drinks on the counter. I pitched more short videos of actual customers, like people reacting to a drink or talking about why they come in. My manager liked the idea and let me try it.

As for what "40%" means exactly, it's hard to quantify engagement that cleanly, because it moves around with the algorithm and with whatever else is happening that month. What I can say is that the customer videos got people commenting and tagging their friends in a way the product shots never did. That taught me a lot about what makes people actually stop scrolling.
I hear you on the algorithm. But when you say engagement went up 40%, what were you actually measuring? Like, was it likes, comments, the number of people who saw the post?

Okay, fair question. I was looking at engagement rate per post, meaning likes, comments, and shares divided by reach. It went from about 2.0% to about 2.8% over three months. That's the 40% on my resume. Honestly, I should've just said that the first time. Three months is a short window, and I didn't have a control, so I can't say the videos were the only thing that changed.

Appreciate the clarity. That's a more honest picture. So you pitched the idea and your manager let you run with it. How much of the actual day-to-day work — like filming, editing, posting — did you do yourself?

Honestly, I did a lot of it myself. I'd film on my phone during slow hours, usually when a barista agreed to be in the clip, then cut it down in a basic editing app. I wrote the captions and scheduled the posts too. I didn't have a videographer or anything like that.

It was more hands-on than I expected. Some weeks I'd film three or four clips and only one would be usable. I had to get better at asking people to talk on camera without it feeling staged, which was harder than editing.

That's good to know. You were doing the full cycle yourself, not just the strategy piece.

I want to ask you about a time you failed or something didn't go the way you planned. What comes to mind?

Sure. The one that comes to mind is the store launch event I planned. The speaker I'd booked cancelled the day before. I was pretty stressed, because the whole thing was built around her talk.

I spent that evening figuring out what I could actually do. I ended up asking one of our baristas, who's great with latte art, if she'd do a live demo instead. She said yes, and it turned into the part people kept talking about afterward. People were filming her and asking questions, which I hadn't expected.

What I took from it is that a plan almost never goes exactly how you wrote it down, so you need a backup. I also learned to ask people for help earlier instead of trying to fix everything alone. I'd been so focused on making the original plan work that I didn't start looking at alternatives until pretty late.
That's a good recovery. How many people actually showed up to the event, and did you have a target in mind going in?

Honestly, the turnout was more of a question for the store manager and the people who ran the door. I was mostly focused on making the event work on the day. What I remember is how much the demo changed the feel of the room, with people crowding around and asking the barista questions. That's probably the part I'd want to talk about more, because it showed me that a backup plan can end up being better than the original.
Fair enough. But I'm curious — your resume says you planned a launch event for 200 guests. Was that the target, or did 200 people actually show up?

Okay, I'll give you the real number. 214 people checked in at the door. The 200 on my resume was the number we planned around, so we were a bit over that. The budget was $1,500, which I should've mentioned earlier.

Got it. So you came in on budget and hit your target. That's solid.

Let me ask you this — if you landed here and started in the first month, what would you want to focus on to prove yourself and learn the role?

Good question. I'd want to spend the first few weeks really listening before I changed anything. I'd sit in on the store meetings, talk to the baristas and the people at the register, and ask what customers keep asking for. I learned on the survey that the feedback you get from people who answer is useful, but the conversations you have face to face fill in a lot.

After that, I'd pick one thing I could own and do well. Maybe it's the Instagram content, since I already know that process, or maybe it's looking at the newsletter again and seeing what's working now. I'd rather show I can finish one thing properly than start five things and not follow through.

I'd also want to check in with my manager early and often, so I know what they care about most. I'm still figuring out how much to run with on my own versus when to ask first, and I think that would be the best way to learn that.

That's a thoughtful answer.

I've got one more thing I want to circle back to. You mentioned leading a team of four on a rebranding class project. Can you tell me a bit about that — what the project was and what your role actually looked like?

Sure. It was a rebranding project for our marketing class. We had to pick a brand and redo its identity, including the logo, colors, and how it talked to customers. I was the team lead, so I kept us on schedule, split up the work, and was the one who pulled everything together for the final presentation.

The hardest part was the logo. Two of my teammates strongly disagreed about it. Each had a clear favorite, and the conversation was getting stuck. Instead of picking one myself, I suggested we test both with people who weren't on the team. We showed both versions to ten classmates and asked which they'd trust more and why. The results pointed pretty clearly in one direction, so we went with that one. I think both
That's a good approach — bringing in outside feedback to break the tie. Did the person whose logo didn't win feel okay with how it went down, or was there some lingering frustration?

Honestly, there was a little frustration at first. Priya had put a lot into her version, and I could tell she felt like it got overlooked. I talked to her one-on-one before we presented and told her the test results, and I showed her what people said about her design. She didn't love it right away, but she said it made sense once she saw the feedback. By the end she was helping with the presentation, and I think she was glad we'd settled it based on something other than who argued the loudest.

Good. You noticed the frustration and handled it directly.

We're nearly out of time, so let me ask — do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, one question. What does a typical week look like for someone in this role, and what would you most want the new person to get up to speed on first?

Good question. A typical week is a mix of day-to-day stuff — managing social, email, in-store promotions — and then longer projects like campaign planning or customer research. The person in this role owns a lot of the customer-facing voice, so getting that tone right early matters a lot.

What I'd want them focused on first is just listening. Understanding who our customers are, what they actually respond to, and how the team works. You seem to already think that way, which is good.

Any other questions?

Thanks, that helps a lot. I think the tone part is what I'd want to get right first, so that's useful to know. I don't have any other questions right now. I really appreciate you taking the time, and I'm excited about the chance to talk more.

Great. Well, we really appreciate you coming in and being so thoughtful about your answers. It was good to talk through your work at the shop and hear how you think about problems.

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for taking the time. How are things going on your end?
Hi, thanks for having me! Things are good, busy week with finals coming up, but I'm glad to be here. The coffee chain's been on my mind a lot lately, so I'm excited to talk about it.
That's great. Finals and work at the same time—that's a lot. How much longer until you're done with those?

Just about three weeks left, so I'm in the thick of it. Honestly, the nice thing is that the marketing work has kind of been a break from the textbooks. It keeps me grounded in actual people instead of just theory. Juggling both has taught me a lot about prioritizing, which I think helps when you're on a team with deadlines.

Makes sense. So you're getting a taste of the real thing while you're still in school. What is it about marketing work specifically that's drawing you in? Like, why this kind of role rather than something else?

Good question. I think what gets me is that marketing sits right where the numbers and the people meet. In class you can build a beautiful campaign on paper, but at the coffee shop you see right away whether a post makes someone walk in or scroll past. That feedback loop is addictive to me.

I also like that it's a mix of creative and analytical work. I'll spend part of a day writing copy and then the next part looking at what actually worked and why. It's hard to quantify how much I've learned from that back-and-forth, but it's definitely changed how I think about a problem. I'd rather be doing something where I can see the result of my work than something where it disappears into a big department.

That makes sense—you get to see cause and effect pretty quickly. So when you look at the work you've done at the coffee chain, what's one project where you really felt that connection between what you did and the outcome?

I'd say the Instagram work. When I took it over, we were posting mostly product photos, and they just weren't getting much response. I switched to short videos of actual customers, like someone ordering their usual or a barista explaining why they love their job. My manager was on board with the plan, so I got to test it for a few months.

What stuck with me was how fast people reacted. A post with a regular customer in it would get comments from other regulars, and you could see the store's community show up online. It made me realize the content that worked was the stuff that felt real, not the polished stuff I'd been trained to make in class.

The part I still think about is that I almost didn't push for it. I was worried it would look too casual. Seeing it work made me a lot more willing to test ideas instead of just playing it safe.
That's helpful. So you mentioned the Instagram work got a 40% engagement boost—what was the baseline there, and how are you measuring that 40%?

Honestly, the exact math is a bit fuzzy for me, and I'd rather not throw out a number I can't back up. What I can tell you is that the engagement picked up pretty clearly once we started posting the customer videos. It's hard to quantify the full effect, since the store was also doing other things that month.

What I took from it was more about how to measure things. I started looking at which posts people actually saved or shared, not just likes, and that changed how I thought about what "working" means. Is that the kind of thing you'd want to see in a marketing role, how someone thinks about measurement, or are you more interested in a specific campaign?

I appreciate the honesty there. Yeah, how you think about measurement matters a lot. So when you say the store was doing other things that month—what were those, and how did you figure out what was actually driving the engagement change?

Okay, I'll give you the actual numbers, since you asked again. The average engagement rate per post went from about 2 percent to about 2.8 percent over three months. That's where the 40 percent comes from.

And I should correct what I said before. I brought up other things the store was doing that month, and I can't point to anything major. I was kind of hedging. The honest answer on what drove it is that I switched to customer videos, and the engagement moved after that. I didn't run a clean test, so I can't prove it was only the videos. What I did was watch which posts got saved and shared, and the video posts consistently did better than the product shots. That's the reason I'm fairly confident in it, but I'd call it a strong signal, not proof
That's a much clearer picture. So you're at 2.8 percent engagement—was that considered good for the coffee chain, or did you have a target you were aiming for?

I'm not totally sure, to be honest. I don't think anyone gave me a formal target, so I was mostly just trying to beat where we started. What I did learn is that the number matters less than whether it's moving in the right direction and whether people are actually saving and sharing the posts. I'd want to know what a benchmark looks like for a local shop before I'd call 2.8 good or bad.
Fair enough. Let me shift gears a bit. On your resume you also ran a customer survey with 500 responses. What did you learn from that, and what actually changed because of it?

Yeah, that one was a lot of fun. The biggest thing that jumped out was oat milk. A bunch of people said they'd come in more often if it didn't cost extra, and it came up again and again in the comments. I didn't expect it to be the headline.

What changed is that two stores trialed oat milk at no extra charge. I don't know yet how that's going to turn out, so I can't really tell you whether it paid off. But I think the bigger lesson for me was about who you ask. The survey got way more useful once I broke the answers down by store and by how often people came in, instead of just looking at the overall average. Honestly, it's hard to say exactly how much that changed the decision, but it made me a lot more careful about not treating every customer like they're the same
That's good thinking. What was your part in running that survey? Like, did you design it, collect the responses, analyze it—walk me through what you actually did.

Sure. I did most of the hands-on work. I wrote the questions with my manager, mostly keeping them short so people would actually finish it. Then I set up the survey link and put it up at the registers, on the store's email list, and on Instagram. I also made a couple of in-store QR code signs, which helped get people on their phones while they waited in line.

For the analysis, I pulled everything into a spreadsheet and started sorting. The first pass was just the overall averages, and that's where the oat milk thing jumped out. Then I split the answers by store and by how often people came in, which is when the picture got a lot more useful. Regulars and occasional customers wanted pretty different things.

I'll be honest that I didn't do anything fancy statistically. It was mostly careful sorting and reading the open-ended comments. If I'm being real, I'd say the design of the questions was probably the part I'd do differently next time, because a few of them were a bit leading.
That's helpful. So when you say a few of the questions were leading, what's an example of one you'd change?

Yeah, one I'd change was something like "How much would you like us to offer oat milk at no extra charge?" That's a leading question because it already assumes you want oat milk and that free is the right answer. A more neutral version would be something like "What would make you order more drinks from us?" and then let people fill in their own answers, or give a list of options that includes things like faster service, more seating, or a different menu.

I didn't realize how much the wording was steering people until I was reading the comments. A lot of the answers just echoed the question back to me. That's why I'd be careful about how much weight to put on the oat milk result. It's real that people brought it up, but the way I asked probably pushed some of them toward it.
Good self-awareness on that. Let me ask you about the rebranding project you led in class. You had a team of four—what was your role, and what was the biggest challenge you ran into with the group?

The team project was a fun one. I was the team lead, so I ran the meetings, kept us on schedule, and made sure everyone had a piece they cared about. We were rebranding a fictional coffee shop, which meant a lot of talking through the logo, colors, and tone.

The biggest challenge was the logo. Two of my teammates strongly disagreed about which direction to go. One loved a bold, modern look, and the other wanted something more classic and warm. Both had good reasons, and it got a little tense.

What I ended up doing was having both of them test their versions with about ten classmates each. Whichever one people responded to more clearly was what we went with. I think that helped because it took the argument out of "whose idea is better" and made it about what people actually responded to. Honestly, the team was a little annoyed at first, but I think they came around once they saw the feedback.
So you settled it with feedback from outside the team. How did you actually collect that feedback? Like, what exactly did you ask those classmates?

I kept it pretty simple. I made two versions of the logo mockup, one bold and modern, one classic and warm, and showed each classmate one of them. Then I asked a few things: what the first thing they noticed was, what the shop felt like to them, and whether they'd walk in based on the logo alone.

I also asked them to explain their reaction in their own words, because a yes or no doesn't tell you much. Some of the best feedback was things like "this one feels like a place I'd sit down in" or "this one looks like it's trying too hard." That helped us see what the logo was actually communicating.

It wasn't a formal study, and I'd be the first to say that. But it gave us something better than two people arguing from their gut.
Makes sense. I want to ask you about something—tell me about a time you actually failed at something, either at the coffee chain or in school. What happened?

Probably the launch event. We had a speaker lined up, someone from the coffee industry, and they cancelled the day before. I was the one running the event, so I spent that evening scrambling. It felt like a failure in the moment because the whole thing was built around that talk.

What I did was call a barista on the team who does latte art really well and ask if she'd do a live demo instead. We rearranged the space so people could gather around the counter, and I rewrote the event description to match. It ended up being one of the more fun parts of the night, and people kept asking about it afterward.

The part I'm still a bit annoyed at is that I didn't have a backup plan. I'd treated the speaker as a sure thing. Now I always ask myself what I'd do if the main piece falls through, and I usually have a second option ready before the event.
That's a good lesson. When you say it ended up being one of the more fun parts of the night—how did you know that? Like, how were you measuring whether the event actually went well?

Honestly, mostly from watching people. There was a crowd around the counter during the demo, and a few people came up to me afterward asking about it, which is how I knew it landed. I didn't have a proper way to track it, though, so I'd call it a gut read more than anything measured.

I think the real lesson was about having a plan B and not treating the main piece as a sure thing. Is there a particular kind of event you'd want to run, or are you more curious about how I'd plan one from scratch?
We're almost out of time, so I want to make sure I ask you what you've got for me. What questions do you have about the role or the team?
Sure, I've got one. What does a typical week look like for an intern on the marketing team, and how much of it is hands-on work versus shadowing?

Good question. A lot of it depends on the project, but you're usually running something—a campaign, content, an analysis—while also sitting in on strategy meetings so you see how it all fits together. It's maybe 60 percent hands-on, 40 percent learning. You're not just watching.

Anything else?

No, I think that answers it. Thanks for explaining that. It sounds like a good balance, and I'd like to be doing real work while I'm still learning. I really appreciate you taking the time to talk with me today.
Thanks for coming in, Sam. I enjoyed talking through your work—I think you've got good instincts about measurement and testing ideas. We'll be in touch soon about next steps.

Thanks so much, I really appreciate it. I enjoyed the conversation too, and it made me think harder about the stuff I did this year. I'm looking forward to hearing about next steps. Have a great rest of your day!
You too. Take care, and good luck with those finals.

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for coming in. Did you find everything okay today?
Hi, yeah, thanks for having me. Everything's good. The video link worked fine on my end, so no complaints. Thanks for asking. It's nice to meet you.
Nice to meet you too. So, tell me a bit about yourself—what brings you here, and what's been on your plate lately?

Sure. I'm finishing up my communications degree, and I've been doing a marketing internship-type role for a local coffee chain, mostly on social media and customer stuff. I like it a lot because you can see right away whether something works. Lately I've been trying to figure out what actually gets people to show up and stick around, which is a bit of a rabbit hole honestly. I also just wrapped a store launch event, which was a lot of moving parts. What about you guys, what does the team look like day to day?

We're a small team, so you'd wear a lot of hats—that's the fun part. We'll get into what the role actually looks like in a bit.

But I'm curious about that rabbit hole you mentioned—figuring out what gets people to show up and stick around. What have you actually found out so far?

Honestly, the biggest thing I've learned is that people respond more to other customers than to our own stuff. We used to post mostly product photos, and then we switched to short videos of regular customers talking about their drinks. Engagement picked up pretty noticeably, which was a relief because my manager had signed off on the change and I didn't want it to flop.

The survey was interesting too. People kept asking for oat milk without the extra charge, and that turned into a trial at two of the stores. I'm still not sure if that's the answer to getting people to come back, or just the thing people were loudest about.

What about your team? What's the stuff that's been working for you guys?

Good question—we can dive into that. But first, let me ask about the engagement you mentioned picking up. When you say it picked up noticeably, what numbers are we talking about? Like, how much did it actually move?

Honestly, it's hard to quantify exactly. It moved in the right direction, and I was happy with it, but I'd rather not throw out a figure I can't fully back up on the spot. What I took away from it was how much the customer videos did better than the product shots, and that changed how I think about the whole account.

Can I ask what you guys have been seeing on your side? I'm curious whether you've tried anything like that.

I appreciate that honesty. We can talk shop more in a second. But I want to stay with this for just a moment—when you switched to customer videos, did your manager or anyone else measure the change, or was it more just a gut feeling that it was working better?

Oh, no, we did track it. My manager looked at the numbers pretty closely, since she had to approve the change in the first place. I'd say it was more than a gut feeling. I was pulling the stats every week to see if it was holding up.

But I'll be honest, I spent so much time on the logistics that I didn't really step back and think about what the numbers meant. What I've taken from it is that the customer voice matters more than polished photos, and I'm still figuring out how far that goes. Did you guys ever try something similar?
That makes sense. So when you were pulling those stats every week, what metric were you actually looking at? Like, was it likes, comments, reach—what told you it was working?

Mostly engagement rate, so how many people interacted with each post compared to how many saw it. Likes and comments by themselves can be misleading, so that's the one I paid attention to.

Honestly, though, I'm better at talking about what I'd do differently. Next time I'd set up the tracking before we change anything, so I'm not reconstructing it afterward. What does your team usually use to measure social stuff?

Smart thinking on that. We'll talk about measurement in a bit.

Let me shift gears—you mentioned the store launch event. Walk me through what that looked like from your end.

Sure. It was a lot of moving parts. We had a speaker lined up, and the day before, they cancelled on us. That was a bit of a scramble. I ended up swapping in a barista doing a latte-art demo, which turned out to be the part people kept talking about.

Honestly, most of what I learned was about planning for things to go sideways. I was running the logistics and the promotion at the same time, so I was juggling a lot. Looking back, I'd build in a backup plan for the main draw from the start. What was the biggest surprise on your last event?
That's a solid lesson. Quick question—how many people actually showed up to the event?

Honestly, I'd have to dig through the check-in notes to give you a solid count, and I don't want to guess in front of you. What stuck with me more was how fast the latte-art demo came together. The barista was amazing, and I think it taught me that a good backup can end up being better than the original plan. Is your team usually good at pivoting like that when something falls through?
Fair enough. So you don't have the exact number, but do you remember roughly—was it close to the 200 people you were aiming for, or did it fall short, or what?

Okay, I'll be straight with you. It was 214 people who checked in at the door, so a bit over the 200 we were aiming for. We had a $1,500 budget, and that's the part I'd want to talk through more, because I was figuring out how to stretch it while the speaker situation was falling apart.
Okay, so you landed the headcount. When the speaker bailed and you switched to the barista demo, how did that affect the budget? Did you have to spend more, less, or about the same?

Honestly, that's hard to pin down. The money side got tangled up with everything else that week, so I'd rather not guess at a number. What I'd really focus on is how I had to rethink the whole program in one day. Do you guys usually set aside some budget for stuff like that, or does it come out of the main pot?

We do, actually. But I want to circle back on something—you mentioned you were running logistics and promotion at the same time. What exactly did you do, versus what did someone else on the team handle?

Mostly I was the one coordinating everything. I did the planning, kept track of the timeline, and handled the promotion, like getting the word out and making sure people knew about it. When the speaker fell through, I was the one who had to figure out a replacement. The barista did the latte-art demo itself, and she was great, but I was the one who brought her in and made the schedule work around it.

I'm not sure I can split it more cleanly than that without making it sound more organized than it was. It was a lot of me running between things at once. What does a typical event look like on your team? Is it one person owning it, or is it split up?

We usually have one owner, so that tracks. Let me ask you something different—you've talked about the survey you ran, the store launch, the social media work. Of all that, tell me about a time something didn't go the way you wanted. What happened, and what did you learn from it?

Honestly, the speaker cancelling was the one that stung most. We'd promoted the event for weeks around that speaker, and then they pulled out the day before. I had to scramble to find a replacement, and I was juggling the promotion at the same time, so some of the messaging was still pointing people toward the original plan.

What I learned is that I was treating the plan as fixed, when I should have had a backup for the main draw from the start. Now, anytime something is built around one person or one vendor, I ask what happens if they drop out and who I'd call next. I also try to keep the promotion general enough that it doesn't fall apart if one piece changes.

Has your team ever had something like that happen? How did you handle it?

Yeah, we've been there. But I want to dig a little deeper on your piece of it—when the speaker cancelled and you had to scramble, did you tell your manager right away, or how did that conversation go?

Yeah, I let her know pretty quickly. I didn't want her finding out from someone else. I think I texted her the same day, then we talked through the options: whether to cancel, reschedule, or swap in something else. She was supportive about the barista idea, and we agreed I'd run with it.

I'll admit the details of that conversation are a bit blurry now, since so much was happening that week. But the main thing I took away was that she wanted to hear about problems early, even if I didn't have the fix yet. How do you guys like to get updates when something goes sideways?
That's the right instinct. Okay, let me ask you something else—why are you interested in this kind of role? What's pulling you toward it?

Honestly, I like that you can see the results fast. With social media or an event, you post something or run something and within a few days you know if it landed. That's different from a lot of school projects, where you turn something in and never find out how it did.

I also like working on the customer side of things. The survey was probably my favorite part. People will tell you exactly what they want if you ask them the right way, and then you get to try to actually do something about it. Like the oat milk thing, where people wanted it at no extra charge and we got to test it at two stores. That kind of thing is what I want to keep doing.

And a small team sounds right up my alley, since I've mostly been wearing a bunch of hats already. What does the role look like in the first few months?

Good question. We'll walk through that more once we know if this is a fit. But before we run out of time here, I want to ask—you've talked about a lot of wins. Tell me about a time you actually failed at something. What happened?

Honestly, the clearest one I can think of is the newsletter. I'd been sending it out, and it wasn't really getting opened. I figured the content was the problem, so I kept adding more to each email. Lots of topics, lots of links, and I didn't stop to check whether anyone was actually reading past the subject line.

It took me a while to see it. I was trying to say everything at once, so nothing stood out. Once I cut each email down to one topic and rewrote the subject lines, things started to shift. I'd say the lesson was that I was guessing about what people wanted instead of testing it. Now I try to change one thing at a time so I can tell what actually made the difference.

Has anything like that come up on your team, where the first fix you tried was the wrong one?
Yeah, all the time. So when you say things started to shift after you cut it down—what did that actually look like? Open rates before and after?

Honestly, I don't have the exact figures in front of me, and I'd rather not guess. It was more of a feel thing at the time, though I did notice people were actually clicking through more. What I'm more curious about is how you guys decide what to test first. When you've got a list of possible fixes, how do you pick which one to try?

We can talk about that. But I'm going to push back a little here—you said you didn't stop to check whether anyone was reading past the subject line. So at some point you must have looked at the data to realize the newsletter wasn't working. What made you finally dig into the numbers?

Fair catch. I did look at the numbers eventually. I was checking the email dashboard pretty regularly, and the open rate just wasn't where I wanted it. That's when I stopped assuming the content was the issue and started looking at what people were actually doing.

I'll be honest, I should have looked a lot sooner. I was so focused on adding stuff that I wasn't really watching the results. What made the difference was seeing the pattern once I went back through it.
Okay, that makes sense. We're almost out of time here, so let me ask—what questions do you have for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, I've got one. What does success look like for this role after the first six months?

Good question. Honestly, it depends on what we land on for your first projects, but we're looking for someone who can own something start to finish—plan it, run it, measure it, and tell us what actually worked. Not just execute, but think about what the data is telling you.

And we want to see you ask for help when you need it, not spin your wheels. Sound reasonable?

Yeah, that sounds right to me. Owning something start to finish is what I'm after. Honestly, the part I'd want to get better at is the measuring piece, like setting up the tracking before we change anything instead of piecing it together afterward. I'm a lot better at doing than at stopping to check what the numbers mean, so I'd want that to be a habit.

And asking for help, yeah, I'm good with that. I usually flag things to my manager early, even when I don't have the answer yet.

Thanks for your time today. It was good talking with you.

Thanks for coming in, Sam. I appreciated your honesty throughout—especially when you said you didn't have exact numbers instead of guessing. That matters to us. We'll be in touch early next week with next steps.

Take care.

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for taking the time. How are things going on your end?
Hi, thanks for having me. Things are good, a little busy with finals coming up, but I'm glad to be here. The coffee chain's been on my mind a lot lately, so I'm excited to talk about it.
Nice, finals are rough. Which school are you at, if you don't mind me asking?

Oh, it's a state school, nothing fancy. Communications is my major, so a lot of my classes are about writing and social media, which is part of why this role caught my eye. Honestly, the marketing side is what I'm most excited about. Are you on the team that works with the store managers, or more on the corporate side?

I'm on the corporate side, so I work with folks across all the locations. But we do partner pretty closely with the stores on campaigns and local stuff.

So let me start by just walking through your background a bit. You've been at the coffee chain as an intern—how long have you been there, and what's drawn you to that company specifically?

It's been a few months now, and I've been working on social media and some store promotions. What drew me in was how much the stores feel like part of their neighborhoods. People come in for the coffee, but they also stay to talk, and I liked the idea of helping that community side show up online and in person. Plus, I'm a big believer that a good brand should feel like it's built on real people, not just a logo.
That makes sense. So when you say you've been working on social media and store promotions, walk me through what a typical week or month looks like for you. What are you actually doing day to day?

Sure. It's a mix, honestly. A big chunk of my week is Instagram. I look at what posts did well, figure out why, and plan the next batch. Lately I've been moving away from the straight product shots and making short videos with customers, which my manager signed off on. I also help with the email newsletter, mostly writing and tweaking the emails.

Then there's the store side. I've helped plan a launch event and a couple of smaller in-store things, so some weeks it's a lot of coordinating with the store teams, making sure they have what they need.

Mostly it's juggling. One week I'm writing captions, the next I'm running around for a event setup. Keeps things interesting. What kind of day-to-day are you guys mostly doing on the corporate side?

We're pretty spread across strategy, analytics, campaign planning, some content creation. Varies a lot depending on the quarter.

I want to dig into a couple of the things you mentioned. Let's start with the Instagram work. Your resume says you grew engagement by 40%. Help me understand what that means—40% of what, and compared to when?

Yeah, that's a fair question. Honestly, it's hard to quantify something like that cleanly, because engagement moves around a lot from week to week depending on what's going on. What I'd rather talk about is what I learned from the switch to customer videos. Product photos get a quick like and people keep scrolling. The videos got people actually commenting and tagging their friends, which told me a lot about what this audience wants from us. Is there a specific part of the Instagram strategy you're most curious about?

I appreciate that perspective. But I do want to understand the 40% number—it's on your resume, so I'm curious what you were measuring. Was it likes, comments, reach, followers? And what time period are we talking about?

Okay, fair enough, you asked twice, so I'll be straight with you. The 40% is engagement rate, meaning the average engagement per post as a share of our followers. It went from about 2% to about 2.8% over three months. So it's a relative jump, 2.0 to 2.8 is 40%, which is a bit of a mouthful, and I should've explained that on the resume. The main thing that changed was switching from product photos to short customer videos. My manager signed off on that plan. I'm still learning how much of the bump was the videos versus just timing, so I wouldn't want to overclaim it.
That's helpful, thanks. So you ran that experiment—the switch to videos—and saw the lift. What would you do differently if you were starting that project over today?

Honestly, I'd set up the test better from the start. I didn't pin down a clean baseline before switching, so I'm not fully sure how much of the bump was the videos and how much was just timing. I'd want to run the videos alongside some product posts for a couple of weeks so I could compare them directly.

I'd also track more than engagement. Comments and tags are nice, but I'd want to know whether people who engage actually come into the store, maybe with a promo code or a "show this post" offer. Right now I can't say that, and it's the question the business would care about.

Do you guys usually test things like that on the corporate side, or is it more of a gut-check kind of thing?

We do test, though the rigor varies. Good instinct on tracking it back to store traffic though—that's the kind of thinking we need.

Let me ask you about the customer survey you mentioned. You ran one with 500 responses. What did you learn from it, and what actually changed because of what you found?

The big thing was oat milk. A lot of people said they'd come in more often if oat milk didn't cost extra, and that came up more than anything else in the free-text answers. It wasn't the sort of thing I expected going in, so it stuck with me.

What changed is that two stores trialed no-upcharge oat milk. I didn't get to see the full results of that, so I can't tell you whether it moved sales. I helped pull the survey findings together for the store managers, and I think that was the most useful part, since they could see what customers were actually asking for.

Honestly, I'd want to dig into whether the people who asked for oat milk were already regulars or new customers. That would change how I'd recommend the chain act on it.
That's smart thinking. So you pulled the survey together for the managers—walk me through what you actually did there. Did you analyze the data, write it up, present it to them?

Mostly the first two, and a bit of the third. I got the raw responses from the survey tool, then went through the free-text answers and grouped them into themes. Oat milk came up way more than anything else, so that became the headline. I put together a short write-up with a few charts for the store managers, and my manager looked it over before it went out.

I didn't present it live. I sent it over and then answered a few follow-up questions from the managers, which was a little nerve-wracking since I was still getting my head around the data. Honestly, I learned a lot from that. I'd want to be more careful next time about separating what people said from what I was reading into it.
What do you mean by that—separating what they said from what you were reading into it? Give me an example.

Sure. A couple of people wrote something like "oat milk should be free," and I grouped that under "price complaints" with the others. But when I went back, some of those comments were really about wanting oat milk at all, and a few were from people who seemed to be asking for a dairy-free option, not complaining about cost. So I was putting my own label on what they meant.

The other thing was "they'd come in more." The survey asked what would make people visit more, and oat milk showed up a lot, but nobody said "I'd come in more often." I wrote it that way in the summary because it sounded like a takeaway, and the managers read it as a sure thing. It's a reasonable guess, but it's a guess.

Next time I'd quote a few actual comments next to each theme, and I'd flag anything I'm inferring as an inference.
That's good self-awareness. Okay, let me shift gears. You also led a team of four on a rebranding class project. Tell me about that—what was the project, and what was your role in leading it?

The project was for a marketing class. We were given a local business and asked to rebrand it, so new logo, colors, a messaging refresh, and a short presentation at the end. There were four of us.

My role was mostly keeping things moving. I set up the schedule, split up the work, and made sure we all knew who was doing what before each check-in. When the group got stuck, I was usually the one who pushed us to make a decision instead of going in circles.

The hardest moment was a disagreement about the logo. Two of my teammates had really different ideas, and both were pretty attached to theirs. Rather than picking one myself, I suggested we test both with people outside the group. We each showed the options to about ten classmates and asked which one they connected with and why. We went with the one that did better, and I think that kept things from turning into a personal fight.
That's a smart move. But I'm curious—what if the vote had been split, or what if the person whose logo lost felt pretty frustrated about it? How would you have handled that?

Honestly, I think a split vote would have been more useful than a clear winner. It would've meant the two logos were both working for different people, so I'd go back and ask what the test responses said about why. Maybe one had the stronger look but the other communicated the business better. Then I'd see if we could combine the strongest parts, or at least agree on what we were optimizing for before picking again.

If the person whose logo lost was frustrated, I'd talk to them one-on-one before the group meeting. I'd want them to know their work wasn't dismissed, and I'd walk them through what the classmates actually said. I'd also ask if there was anything from their design we should keep. People usually take a loss better when they can see the reasoning and still have a say.

I'll be honest, I don't remember exactly how that conversation went. I think it helped that we'd agreed on the test ahead of time, so it felt like the process decided rather than me. But I can see how it could have gone sideways if someone felt blindsided.
Makes sense. Let me ask you something different. Tell me about a time you failed at something—either at the coffee chain or in school, wherever. What happened, and what did you take from it?

Probably the launch event. The speaker we'd booked cancelled the day before, and I didn't have a backup lined up. I spent that evening scrambling, and honestly I was more stressed than I needed to be.

We ended up doing a latte-art demo with one of the baristas instead. It went fine, and people seemed to like it. But looking back, the failure wasn't the cancellation, since those happen. It was that I'd treated the speaker as a fixed part of the plan without asking what the event was really for. Once I asked that, the demo made more sense.

Now I always ask the store team and the speaker for a rough backup idea early on, even if it's just a list of two or three options. And I try to say what the event is for in one sentence, so if something falls through I'm not starting from zero.
That's a good lesson. Quick question—how many people showed up to that event? And how did you count attendance?

Honestly, the attendance thing is hard to pin down. It was a busy night, and I was more focused on keeping the demo running than on the numbers. I think the bigger takeaway for me was how the event came together after the speaker fell through. The barista was great, and the store team really stepped up.

If I did it again, I'd set up a simple sign-in plan ahead of time so the count isn't an afterthought. Is attendance something your team usually tracks for store events, or is it more about sales after the fact?

We track it, yeah. It matters for ROI. But I hear you—you were focused on execution that night, which is fair.

Let me ask you this. You've been at the coffee chain for a few months now. Why do you want this kind of role—marketing, working with a brand? What's pulling you toward it?

Honestly, I like that marketing sits right where people's everyday choices meet a brand's story. I'm drawn to figuring out why someone picks one coffee shop over another, and then helping a place say something that's true about itself.

The store work has made that feel more real to me. Watching people come in, talk to the baristas, and stick around made me care about the community side of a brand, not just the logo. I want to keep working on that kind of thing, where you're trying to get people to actually show up, not just notice you.

What's the part of the job you'd say is the most fun for the people on your team?

I'd say it's when you see a campaign actually land with people and move the needle on something that matters—sales, loyalty, traffic. There's a real feedback loop.

We're almost out of time, so let me ask—what questions do you have for me or the team?

Thanks, that's a great answer. I'm curious, when a campaign does land, how does your team usually figure out what actually made the difference? Is it mostly store traffic and sales, or do you dig into the customer side too?

Good question. It depends on the campaign, but we usually start with sales and foot traffic, then layer in survey data or social listening if it's a bigger initiative. We're getting better at connecting online engagement back to in-store behavior, which is where I think we need to go. It's tricky though.

That's probably a good place to wrap up. Thanks for taking the time today, Sam. We've got a lot to think about, and we'll be in touch soon about next steps. Good luck with finals.

You've got some solid thinking around testing and learning from what doesn't work

transcript.text: Hey, good to meet you. How's your day been so far?
Hey, good to meet you too! My day's been good, pretty busy getting ready for this. I had a coffee before the call, so I'm awake now. How about you, how's your day going?
Good, good. Busy but moving. Thanks for taking the time to chat with us. So, I'd love to hear a bit about your background. Walk me through your experience so far—how'd you get to where you are now?

Sure, happy to. I'm finishing up a communications degree, and for the past year or so I've been a marketing intern at a local coffee chain. Most of my work has been on social media, the customer newsletter, and some in-store events. I've also done a fair amount of group work in school, which taught me a lot about getting people to agree on a direction. Honestly, the internship is where I figured out I really like the mix of creative work and looking at what customers actually respond to.

That makes sense. So you've got a mix of creative and data-driven stuff going on. Let me dig into one of those a bit. You mentioned the in-store events—I see on your resume you planned a store launch event for about 200 guests. Tell me about that. What was your role in that, and how'd it actually go?

Sure. I was the main person running point on it, so I handled the planning, coordinating with the store manager, and making sure the schedule and the space worked. The day before, our planned speaker cancelled, which was stressful. I ended up getting one of our baristas to do a latte-art demo instead, and people really seemed to enjoy it. Honestly, the biggest thing I took from it was how much last-minute flexibility matters. Turnout was really good, though it's hard to say how much of that was the event versus the timing.
Okay, so you had to pivot pretty quick when the speaker dropped. That's useful to know. How did you actually track that 200 guests number? Was that a firm count, or more of an estimate?
Oh, good question. It was a count at the door. We had check-in, so 214 people checked in. I should've been more precise earlier. The resume says about 200 because that's the rounded version I used.
Fair enough. So with the pivot you made—the barista demo instead of the speaker—what would you have done differently if you could run that event again?

Honestly, I'd build in a backup plan from the start. I had one speaker locked in and no real Plan B, so when they dropped out, I was scrambling the day before. Now I'd have a second option lined up, or at least check in with the speaker a few days out instead of assuming everything's still on.

I'd also want to be clearer about what we were trying to get out of the event, because that would've shaped the replacement. The demo worked, but I was mostly thinking about keeping people busy, not about what they'd take home. Next time I'd think that through earlier.

That's smart. You're thinking about it differently now. Let me shift gears a bit. You also mentioned the email newsletter on your resume—you relaunched it. What actually changed when you relaunched it, and how'd you measure whether it was better?

Sure. The big shift was that we stopped trying to cram everything into one email. We used to send a mix of promos, store news, and random stuff, and I cut it down to one topic per email so people knew what they were opening. I also spent a lot more time on subject lines, which honestly taught me more than anything else in the project.

As for whether it was better, that's a tricky one. Newsletter performance depends on a lot of things, like what's happening with the store that week and the season, so it's hard to quantify how much of any change was the redesign versus everything else. What I really took from it was how much the subject line does before anyone even reads the email. I'm still learning how to test that properly.

That's a thoughtful answer. But let me push a little—did you actually look at open rates or click rates before and after the redesign? Even if there were other things going on, you'd have some baseline to compare to, right?

Yeah, we did. Open rate went from about 18% to 27%. I should've led with that instead of talking around it. I rewrote the subject lines and cut each email to one topic, and a designer did the template, so I can't say exactly how much each change contributed. But the numbers did move, and that's what got me looking at subject lines more closely.
Got it. So you saw the lift. What part of that did you personally own versus the designer, and what would you do differently about how you tested it?

I owned the writing side: the subject lines and the decision to cut each email down to one topic. The designer built the template, so I'd give them credit for how it looked.

On testing, honestly, I'd do it differently. I changed the subject lines and the structure at the same time, so I can't tell you which one moved the open rate. Next time I'd split the list and send two subject lines to small groups before picking a winner, and I'd change one thing at a time so I actually know what worked.
Smart. That's the right instinct. Okay, one more thing on the internship side. You grew Instagram engagement by 40%. What does that 40% actually mean—40% of what, and compared to when?

Good question, and I'd want to be careful with that one. Engagement is tricky to pin down, because it depends on what you count, likes, comments, saves, and whether you're comparing to a normal week or a slow one. I'd say the bigger thing I took from it was the shift in content. We moved away from mostly product photos to short videos of actual customers, and that changed how people responded to the posts. Honestly, that's what I'm most proud of, more than the percentage itself.
I hear you on the content shift being the real story. But I still need to understand the baseline. When you say 40%, what metric did you measure, and over what time period?

Okay, I'll give you the actual numbers. It's average engagement rate per post, meaning interactions divided by followers. It went from about 2.0% to 2.8% over three months. That's the 40%. I should've just said that the first time instead of hedging. The change was from product photos to short customer videos, and my manager signed off on the plan.
Thanks for the clarity. So you pitched the idea, your manager signed off, and you ran it. What was your manager's role beyond that, and what would you say was yours?

My manager approved the plan and gave the go-ahead to switch from product photos to customer videos. Beyond that, she was pretty hands-off, which I appreciated. I think she trusted me to run it, but I'm not totally sure what she was watching for behind the scenes.

My part was writing up the plan, figuring out which customers we could film, getting their okay, and then keeping the posts going every week. I also looked at which videos did best and used that to decide what to make next. I'd say I did the day-to-day work, and she set the direction and signed off.
Got it. So in your first month here, if you landed this role, how would you approach figuring out what to work on first? What would you want to understand before you started making changes?

Good question. I'd spend the first couple weeks mostly listening and looking at what's already there before changing anything. I'd want to know what the goals are for the marketing team right now, whether it's foot traffic, online orders, or just brand awareness, because that changes what I'd prioritize. I'd also sit down with the store managers and a few baristas to hear what customers are actually asking for in the shop. Honestly, some of the best ideas I've had came from just hearing people talk about the product. And I'd want to see the current numbers on social and email so I know where things stand before I touch anything. Then I'd pick one or two things to start with, instead of trying to fix everything at once.
That's solid. Okay, I want to make sure I hit a couple more things with you. Tell me about a time you failed—something that didn't go the way you wanted.

Sure. The one that comes to mind is the rebranding class project. Two of my teammates really disagreed about the logo, and the team got stuck. I didn't want to just pick one of them, so I had both of them test their options with about ten classmates each. Honestly, I think I should've set that up earlier. We lost a good chunk of time arguing before anyone tested anything, and I let it drag on longer than it needed to. The test did settle it, and we went with the data, but I could've gotten there faster if I'd pushed for a decision process at the start instead of waiting until people were frustrated.
So you brought in data to break the tie, which worked. But what would you actually do differently if you were leading that again?

I'd agree on how we'd decide before anyone started arguing for their favorite. Something like, "We'll test both logos with a small group and pick by Friday." That way the testing isn't something I have to pull out of the team after people already dig in.

I'd also check in with each teammate separately early on. I think part of the disagreement was that they each felt their idea wasn't being heard, and I didn't notice that until it was already a fight. If I'd talked to them one on one first, I might have caught that sooner.
That's good insight. Last one before we wrap—why do you want this kind of role? What's drawing you to it?

I like that this role sits right where I've been spending my time. At the coffee chain I've gotten to do both the creative side, like the videos and the newsletter, and the side where you look at what's actually working and adjust. I've found I like that combination more than either one alone.

I'm also drawn to working somewhere that's close to the customer. Some of my best ideas, like the oat milk thing from our survey, came from people just telling us what they wanted. I'd like a job where that kind of feedback actually shapes what the team does, and where I can keep learning how to test and measure things better, which is something I'm still working on.
Makes sense. We're nearly out of time, so let me ask—what questions do you have for me or the team?
Yeah, I've got one. What does a typical week look like for someone in this role, and what does the team usually spend most of its time on?

Good question. It varies week to week, but you're usually split between running campaigns—social, email, that kind of thing—and working on bigger projects like store events or product launches. Right now the team's focused a lot on the relaunch we're doing in the spring, so there's a lot of planning and testing happening. You'd be hands-on with both the day-to-day stuff and the bigger picture work.

Any other questions before we wrap?

No, I think that covers it for me. Thanks, this was really helpful. The spring relaunch sounds like a good time to jump in, so I'm glad to hear there's so much testing going on. Thanks again for the time, and I look forward to hearing from you.

Great. Thanks so much for taking the time today, Sam. We really enjoyed talking with you. You've got some solid thinking around testing and learning from what doesn't work, and that comes through in what you've done. We'll be in touch soon. Take care.

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for taking the time. How are things going on your end?
Hi, thanks for having me. Things are good, a little busy with finals coming up, but I'm glad to be here. The coffee chain's been on my radar for a while, so I'm excited to talk.
Nice, that's great. Finals are rough—what are you studying, by the way?

Communications, with a focus on marketing. Most of my classes are about how brands talk to people, which is pretty much what got me into this field. Right now I've got a media writing class and a consumer behavior course, so my weeks are a lot of drafting and reading case studies.
That makes sense. So walk me through your background a bit—how did you end up at the coffee chain, and what have you been working on there?

So I'm a communications major, and I started at the coffee chain as a marketing intern a little over a year ago. I'd been a regular there for ages, so when they posted the internship I jumped at it.

Most of my time has gone into social media and the customer newsletter. On Instagram, I noticed our product photos weren't getting much back from people, so I pitched switching to short videos of actual customers and staff. My manager approved it, and it's been fun to see what clicks. I also helped relaunch the email newsletter, mostly rewriting subject lines and keeping each email to one topic.

I also helped with a store launch event and ran a customer survey, which was probably my favorite project. Honestly, what I learned from it is how much people care about small stuff, like their milk options.
Cool. Let's dig into the Instagram work a bit. You mentioned growing engagement by 40%—what was the baseline there, and over what timeframe did that happen?

Honestly, it's hard to pin down one clean number on that. Engagement moves around a lot depending on the post and the week. What I'd rather talk about is what I learned from switching to the customer videos. The staff ones did way better than I expected, mostly because people recognized their baristas. Do you want me to walk through how we picked which videos to post?
I appreciate that. So when you say the staff videos did way better—better than what, and how were you measuring that?

Okay, fair question, and I was dodging a bit. The engagement rate per post went from about 2 percent to about 2.8 percent over three months. That's the 40 percent you saw on my resume. I measured it using Instagram's built-in insights, so it's the share of people who liked, commented, or shared out of everyone who saw the post.
That makes sense. So over those three months, did anything else change on the account—like posting frequency, or the time of day you posted?

Honestly, the big change was the switch to customer and staff videos. I didn't set out to change much else on purpose. I don't remember the exact posting schedule or timing shifts from those three months, though, so I'd want to check my notes before giving you specifics. Is it posting frequency you're curious about, or whether the timing changed?

I was just wondering if there were other factors in play. Sounds like the video content was the main lever you pulled, which is fair. Let me ask you this—what would you do differently if you were running that same project again?

That's a good question, and I think I'd do a few things differently. First, I'd set up a clearer baseline before making the switch, so I could track changes more cleanly. I was kind of learning as I went, and I didn't isolate the video change as well as I could have.

I'd also get more input from the team before launching. My manager approved the plan, but I could've looped in the baristas earlier, since they're the ones on camera and they had good ideas about which moments were worth filming.

And honestly, I'd try a small test first, maybe a few videos over a couple of weeks, before committing to the full switch. That way I'd have better evidence on what was actually driving the results.
That's thoughtful. Let me shift gears—tell me about a time when things didn't go the way you planned.

Sure. The one that comes to mind is the store launch event. We had a speaker lined up, a local roaster, and then they cancelled the day before. I was pretty stressed. I'd already told people about the talk, and the whole plan was built around it.

I had to think fast. I talked to the store manager, and we decided to swap in a latte-art demo with one of our baristas. She's really good, and honestly, the crowd seemed more into it than they would have been into a talk. Most people stuck around to watch and ask questions.

What I took from it is that a backup plan matters as much as the main one. Now I always ask a second person to think through what we'd do if a key piece falls through.
Good example. When you were planning that event originally, how many people were you expecting, and how did you end up counting actual attendance?

Honestly, I don't want to throw out a number I'm not sure about. Attendance at an event like that is always a bit fuzzy, since people drift in and out. What I remember more clearly is how the store manager and I split up the work on the day, and how the latte-art demo changed the vibe in the room. Do you want me to walk through that?
I get it—events are messy. But your resume says you planned it for 200 guests. Did you end up getting close to that number, or was it pretty different?

Okay, fair enough, I should just give you the actual number. The event was planned for about 200 guests, and 214 people checked in at the door. So we were a bit over. I counted with the check-in sheet at the entrance, which is why I can be specific about it.
Got it. So the check-in sheet gave you a solid count. What about the budget for the event—did you manage that, or was that someone else's job?

Yeah, I was involved in the budget side, mostly keeping track of what we were spending on food, drinks, and the space setup. The store manager had the final say on approvals, so I'd check with her before anything big got ordered. It was a good lesson in how much small purchases add up. Keeping a running list on a shared doc helped a lot. What would you want to know about how we handled it?
That's useful context. Did you come in under budget, over, or right on target?

The budget was $1,500. I don't remember the exact final total off the top of my head, though, and I don't want to guess whether we came in under or over. I'd have to pull the receipts from the shared doc to say
Fair enough. Let me ask you this—why are you interested in this kind of role? What draws you to marketing, especially at a place like this?

Honestly, it's the stuff I actually like doing. I like figuring out why people pick one place over another, and a coffee shop is a good test of that because people are there every day and they have opinions. The survey was my favorite project because I got to see that firsthand. People cared a lot about things like oat milk, and that taught me that good marketing starts with listening.

As for this company, I've been a customer for a long time, so I know the brand from the inside. I like that it's local and that the stores feel like part of the neighborhood. I'd like to help keep that feeling while also making the marketing sharper.
That's a solid answer. Let me ask about the survey—you ran it with 500 responses, which is a good sample. What did you learn from it, and what actually changed because of what you found out?

The biggest thing was that people really wanted oat milk, and they didn't want to pay extra for it. That came up over and over in the open-ended answers, more than I expected. Some people said they'd switch coffee shops over it.

What changed is that two stores trialed offering oat milk at no extra charge. I didn't get to see the full results from that, so I can't say how it turned out. But it was cool to see a survey actually lead to something a store could test.
That makes sense. Did you have a hand in designing the survey itself, or was that mostly set up by someone else?

I had a big hand in it. I drafted most of the questions, and then my manager went through them with me and cut a few that were leading. We also argued a bit about whether to keep the open-ended questions, and I'm really glad we did, since that's where the oat milk comment came from. Was there a part of the survey process you wanted to hear more about?
Just curious—what would you do differently if you were running that survey again?

Good question. I think I'd make the open-ended questions the first thing people see, not something tacked on at the end. A lot of the best stuff came from those, and I'd want more people to answer them.

I'd also pilot the survey with a handful of customers before sending it out. A couple of my questions were confusing, and I only caught that after responses started coming in. A quick test run would have saved us some cleanup.

And honestly, I'd try to tie each question to a specific decision up front. Some of what we asked was interesting but didn't really lead anywhere, so next time I'd know what we were trying to change before writing the first question.

Makes sense. One more thing before we wrap up—you mentioned leading a team of four on a rebranding class project. Walk me through that a bit. What was your role, and did anything come up that you had to navigate?

Sure. I was the team lead, so I kept us on schedule, split up the work, and made sure we had something ready for each check-in with our professor. We had four people with different strengths. One teammate was great at research, another handled the slides, and so on.

The tricky part was the logo. Two of my teammates strongly disagreed about which direction to go. Both had good reasons, and the debate was getting heated, and honestly, I didn't want to just pick a side and make one of them feel shut down. So I suggested we test both designs with a group of classmates, about ten people, and see which one they responded to. We showed them both and asked a few questions about what they thought the brand stood for. The results pointed pretty clearly in one direction, and we went with that one. It took the decision out of personal opinions, and both teammates were fine with it because they'd seen the data.

What I took from it is that when people disagree, getting real feedback usually settles it faster than arguing does.
That's a smart move. Alright, we're running short on time here. Do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, one question: what does a typical week look like for someone in this role, and what would you most want the intern to get better at by the end of the internship?

Good question. A typical week is a mix—some social media planning and posting, helping with email campaigns, maybe sitting in on customer research or event planning. You'd get exposure to a lot of different pieces of marketing, not just one channel.

As for what we'd want you to improve on, honestly, it's tightening the connection between what you measure and what you actually change because of it. A lot of interns come in with enthusiasm but don't always track whether their work actually moved the needle. If you can get better at that—setting a baseline, testing, then knowing what to do next—you'd be really valuable to the team.

Thanks for taking the time today. We'll be in touch soon about next steps.

Thanks so much for taking the time, and for the detailed answer. That's really helpful. Honestly, the measurement piece is something I've been thinking about a lot since the Instagram project, so I'd like to get better at it. I appreciate you walking me through the role, and I look forward to hearing about next steps. Have a great rest of your day.
You too, and good luck with finals. Take care.

That's solid. So you were pretty hands-on with it.
That's a smart approach. I appreciate that you're thinking about isolating variables.
That's a good way to handle it.

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for coming in. Did you find everything okay today?
Yeah, I found it fine, thanks. The video call link worked on the first try, which is always a relief. Thanks for setting this up.
Of course, happy to have you here. So, tell me—what drew you to this role? What kind of work are you looking to do?

I'm really into marketing that feels personal, you know? I've been working on social stuff for the coffee chain this past year, and I like seeing how a small change, like posting a short video of a real customer instead of a product shot, can actually get people to engage. I'd like to keep doing that kind of hands-on work, figuring out what connects with people and then testing it. Honestly, I'm still figuring out exactly what I want long term, but I know I like being close to the customer side of things.
That makes sense. So when you say a small change like that video post got people to engage—do you remember what the actual difference was? Like, how much more engagement are we talking about?

Yeah, so the average engagement rate per post went from about 2% to about 2.8% over three months. That's the 40% on my resume. I switched from product photos to short customer videos, and my manager approved the plan. I'd say it wasn't just the videos, though. I was also watching the numbers every week to see what worked.

Got it. So you were testing and adjusting as you went. When you say your manager approved the plan—what was your role in actually executing it? Like, were you the one filming the videos, posting them, deciding when to post?

Mostly me, yeah. I came up with the video idea and pitched it to my manager, and once she approved it I handled the rest. I'd ask customers at the counter if they were up for a quick clip, usually with their permission to post, and then I'd edit them on my phone. For the newsletter, that's open rate, and I'd also look at clicks, since an open doesn't always mean someone did something. For social, I'd track engagement rate per post, like I did with the videos, and check which posts got comments versus just likes. I'd want to see the trend over a few weeks, not just one good post.

So you scrambled and made it work. What would you do differently if you were planning something like that again?

Honestly, I'd have a backup speaker lined up before the event, not the day before. Like, having a second person on standby who could step in, or at least a plan B that doesn't depend on one person. I'd also confirm the speaker a week out and again a couple days out, so I'd catch a cancellation sooner. I think I was lucky the barista was willing to jump in. Next time I wouldn't want to rely on luck like that.

Yeah, that was mine. I didn't want to just pick one because I was the lead, and neither of them was going to back down, so I figured testing it would settle it without anyone losing face. I'd seen the same kind of thing with the Instagram stuff, where you just try both and see what people actually respond to.
Makes sense. So you ran a customer survey with 500 responses at the coffee chain. What were you actually trying to figure out with that survey?

The biggest thing that came out of it was oat milk. A lot of people wanted it, and they wanted it at no extra charge, which is kind of a big ask for a coffee chain. Um... (long pause) Sorry, I'm not totally sure what the final decision was. The two stores ran the trial, and I know it was something they were watching, but I wasn't involved in the rollout call. Changing one thing and watching people actually respond feels more real to me than just making something look nice.

Some of my classmates are going into straight design or straight business, and I could see myself doing either. But I keep coming back to the customer side, like figuring out what people want and then building something around it. That's probably why I like this kind of role.
Got it. We're almost out of time here, so let me ask—do you have any questions for me about the role or the team?
Yeah, just one. What does a typical week look like for someone in this role, and who would I be working with most?

Good question. You'd be working pretty closely with the social and email side of things, so you'd be hands-on with posting, testing, that kind of work. You'd also collaborate with our product team on launches. A typical week is probably half execution—creating and posting content—and half analysis, looking at what's working and planning what to test next. You'd report to me, and we'd check in weekly on metrics and priorities.

verdicts.notes: Strength: the interviewer probed the Instagram, newsletter, launch and logo stories with relevant follow-ups on measurement, causality and ownership, and covered both practice questions and all five topics. Weakness: it didn't press on the vague survey answers (T15, T17) or the unclear engagement-rate formula (T7), and it left the survey outcome unexamined.

transcript.text: Hi, thanks for taking the time. How are things going on your end?

That's a fair point. I can't say for sure. The 18% was my first look at it, not a history I pulled, so I don't know if it was already trending up or down before I touched it. Got it. One more thing I want to circle back to—you mentioned growing Instagram engagement by 40%. What does that 40% actually mean? Engagement compared to when, and what specifically did you change?

Sure. I'm a communications major, and I've been doing marketing stuff for about a year and a half, mostly through school and a part-time internship at a local coffee chain. Most of my work there has been social media and email. I started by helping with the Instagram account, and my manager gave me room to try something different. We switched from mostly product photos to short customer videos, and over three months our average engagement per post went from about 2% to about 2.8%. That's roughly a 40% jump, which was a good feeling.

I also helped plan a store launch event. We had a budget of $1,500 and about 214 people came through the door. The speaker cancelled the day before, so we brought in one of our baristas to do a latte-art demo instead. It worked out better than I expected.

That's helpful. So on the Instagram piece—when you switched to customer videos, what made you think that was the right move? Was that your idea, or did something point you in that direction?

Yeah, that was mostly my idea. Our posts were almost all product shots, like close-ups of drinks, and they weren't getting much response. I figured people would relate more to real customers, so I pitched short videos to my manager. They approved it, and we tested it for about three months. That's when the engagement went up.
Got it. And how did you decide what kind of customer videos to post? Like, did you film them yourself, or how did that work logistically?

Mostly I filmed them myself on my phone. I'd ask regulars if they wanted to be in one, and most people said yes.
